Some exercises are meant to be seen. A "show of force" is an exercise whose audience is as much political as military. Announcing it publicly, holding it far from home and making it large are ways of telling other governments: we can operate here, at this scale. The drills announced this week were described as taking place far from the Gulf and involving both naval forces and special-operations units.

Special operations change the signal. Naval drills demonstrate reach. Adding special-operations forces, small units trained for raids, ship boardings and quiet work in contested places, suggests a government wants to show it can do more than sail ships in formation. That combination is one reason analysts are paying close attention.

What analysts watch next: the size of the forces actually involved compared with what was announced, whether the drills run longer than planned, how close they come to other countries' forces and what officials say while they are under way. An exercise that ends on schedule usually tells you one thing. One that keeps growing tells you another.

A note on language: officials and analysts often use "exercise," "drill" and "maneuvers" interchangeably. What matters more is scale, location and timing, which is why careful analysts wait for drills to begin before drawing conclusions.

Closer to home, the routine continues. Training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule, and the air station said late last month that base services were operating normally after a routine inspection.
As any veteran will tell you, early reports from far away are often incomplete. Coastline Public Radio will follow the exercises as more becomes public, and will stick to what can be confirmed.

stories.headline: Port Aransas rides a strong summer: charters booked, bait shops busy
stories.summary: Businesses on Mustang Island say this has been a good season. Here is what to know if you are headed to Port Aransas this weekend.
body: Port Aransas is having a good summer. Charter boats are booked, the bait shops are busy and restaurants on the island have lines out the door on weekend nights.

Businesses on Mustang Island report a strong season, helped by steady crowds since early summer. At Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, owner Bill Hargrove says the shop has hardly had a quiet morning.
"I've had people waiting in the parking lot before I unlock the door," Hargrove says. "I asked one fella if he'd been there all night. He said, 'Not all night.'"
Anglers have been working the jetties, the surf and the bays, and kids are catching their first fish off the piers. Charter captains are running full trips on most weekends.

Headed over this weekend? Expect waits for the ferry at midday. Arriving early, or coming in from the south on the JFK Causeway and Highway 361, can help. Park only where it is allowed and check local beach rules before you drive on the sand.
Bring some cash for the smaller shops and bait stands, and be patient at the fuel docks and boat ramps, which are busiest early in the morning and again in the late afternoon.
Around the jetties, keep a close eye on kids. The rocks are slick and sharp, and big ships passing through the channel can push wakes onto the rocks without much warning.
Heat safety still applies. Take breaks in the shade, drink water and watch for signs of heat illness, including dizziness, headache and confusion.
Harborline 6 will be on the island this weekend. Send us your best catch photo.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Explainer: one channel, two businesses — how Corpus Christi's refiners share the water with crude exporters
stories.summary: The same ship channel that carries record export cargoes also serves the refineries along the Inner Harbor. Why that matters when the schedule is this full.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The export boom gets the headlines. The refineries were here first.

Corpus Christi's ship channel serves two energy businesses at once. Crude export terminals load tankers bound overseas, at a pace that is now near record. Refineries along the Inner Harbor take in feedstock and ship out gasoline, diesel and other products. Both depend on the same water.

"People talk about the export story and forget there is a refining town at the end of that channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows.

How the two fit together. Much of the crude that feeds both the export docks and the refineries arrives by pipeline from inland fields. The channel's main job for exporters is getting loaded tankers out. For refiners, the channel brings in some crude and feedstock by water and carries products out by tanker and barge, alongside pipelines and trucks.

Where they meet. Every deep-draft ship uses one entrance at Port Aransas and one route across the bay. A crude tanker outbound and a products tanker inbound are in the same lineup, handled by the same pilots and tugs.
Why it matters now. With crude loadings near record and tankers routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage, the lineup has little slack. A delay for one kind of ship becomes a delay for the other.

What a disruption would mean. Holloway said the two businesses would feel a channel interruption differently. "An exporter with no ships has no sales that week. A refiner has more options, because pipelines keep running both ways, but storage fills and product has to go somewhere," she said. "Neither likes it. They just dislike it on different timetables."
The port says the channel is open and customers' schedules are being met.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Bait, ice and a few tall tales: Bill Hargrove's long view from the jetties
stories.summary: Bill Hargrove has sold bait near the Port Aransas jetties for decades. He has ridden out two hurricanes there, and he has opinions about almost everything else.
body: Bill Hargrove opens the shop before the gulls are fully awake. By 6 a.m. the aerators are bubbling in the live-bait tanks, the ice machine is groaning, and the first truck of the morning is idling in the shell lot outside Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties.
"Shrimp, ice, a weather report and a lie about where the reds are biting," said Hargrove, 64, ticking off his inventory. "Only one of those is free, and I won't tell you which."

Businesses in Port Aransas report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy, and Hargrove's register agrees. He has watched the island through good seasons and bad ones, and he can tell you which year the tarpon came back and which year the beach washed out, though the details shift a little depending on who is asking.

The jetties are his landmark and his living. Twin rock walls guard the pass where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf, and every big ship headed to or from the port slides between them. Hargrove's customers fish the rocks while tankers pass close enough to feel through your feet. "Tourists take pictures of the ships," he said. "Locals take pictures of the fish. The ships don't care either way."
He knows the island's lore, too. He will tell you that a president once came to Port Aransas to fish for tarpon, and that the town was once called Tarpon, both of which happen to be true.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes at the shop, including Harvey, which tore through Port Aransas and left much of the island in pieces. He does not romanticize it. "People think riding one out makes you tough. It makes you lucky," he said. "Everybody tells me I'm too old to do it again. Everybody's probably right."

For now, the worry is simpler: keeping enough bait in the tanks for a summer that won't slow down. "Good year," Hargrove said, sliding a bag of ice across the counter. "Knock on wood. Actually, knock on something sturdier than wood. This is Port A."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Summer scorecard: tankers, tourists and a depot that's hiring
stories.summary: From the export docks to the bait shops, the Coastal Bend economy has had a busy summer. A few soft spots are worth watching.
body: With August under way, the Coastal Bend's summer economy looks busy almost everywhere you check.

The port: Crude export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel have been loading tankers at a near-record pace all summer, and vessels waiting for berths have been a routine sight at the anchorage off Port Aransas. "The export machine is running about as hard as it can," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That's good news for the region. Every tanker that loads is work for pilots, tug crews and line handlers."

The bases: Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, a steady source of skilled jobs, and training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule. The air station completed a routine readiness inspection late last month with base services operating normally. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer, bringing short-term work for longshore crews and truck drivers.
The islands: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters booked and bait shops busy. Mustang and Padre islands have drawn heavy crowds since early summer.

Soft spots: Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, but fuel costs have squeezed margins. "Fuel is the first bill and the biggest one," Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen told the Ledger last month. And in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, transit gaps make it harder for households without cars to reach jobs across town, a cost that rarely shows up in economic statistics.

What to watch: Late summer is also the peak of hurricane season on the Gulf Coast. For a regional economy this tied to the water, a busy August can turn quickly on things no one controls, from weather to fuel prices to a single disruption in a crowded channel.
For now, the cash registers on the island, the paychecks at the depot and the tankers in the channel are all telling the same story: it has been a good summer.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Inside the depot's hiring push: why the Army's helicopter repair shop wants local mechanics
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot is recruiting helicopter mechanics this summer. The work is exacting, the hangars are hot and the jobs tend to last.
body: The short description of the work at Corpus Christi Army Depot is that it fixes helicopters. The long description takes a while.

The depot, on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, is the Defense Department's primary depot for rotary-wing aircraft maintenance. Army helicopters arrive worn from years of flying, and the depot's civilian workforce takes them apart, inspects and repairs airframes, rebuilds engines and components and sends the aircraft back to units. This summer, the depot is hiring helicopter mechanics to keep that work moving.

"These are careers, not gigs," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "People come in as mechanics and retire as mechanics, and in between they've touched aircraft that flew all over the world. There's a lot of pride in these hangars."

Kowalczyk said the depot looks for people with aviation maintenance training, military experience or industrial trade backgrounds, and it trains new hires on Army procedures and standards. The work is precise, documented and inspected at every step. "Everything gets checked, and then it gets checked again," she said. "That's the culture."
The hangars are also hot in August, and Kowalczyk did not pretend otherwise. "It's South Texas. Our folks hydrate, and they look out for each other," she said.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot's hiring matters beyond the base fence. Its civilian payroll ripples through Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the skills it builds, from sheet metal and hydraulics to wiring and avionics, are the kind that stay in a community.

The work also connects to readiness far from Texas. Helicopters rebuilt here go back into service with years of flying left in them, and the pace of that work affects how many aircraft Army units have available. That link is why depot hiring is about more than local jobs. For job seekers, it also means steady hours and federal benefits in a region where many skilled trades rise and fall with oil and construction.

The depot shares the air station with Navy flight training squadrons, which have flown a normal summer schedule, and with a Coast Guard air station. Openings are posted on USAJOBS, Kowalczyk said, and the depot encourages applicants who are new to aviation to apply if they have strong mechanical skills.

stories.headline: Before the heart of hurricane season, relief warehouses fill and freight firms sign on standby
stories.summary: Relief agencies are stocking shelves and freight forwarders are signing standby contracts so supplies can move quickly if a storm hits the Coastal Bend.
body: In warehouses around Corpus Christi this month, the shelves are filling: pallets of bottled water, tarps, cots, hygiene kits and nonperishable food, stacked, shrink-wrapped and waiting for a storm everyone hopes will not come.

Relief agencies are stocking their warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders that move supplies into disaster areas are signing standby relief contracts, agreements that let agencies call on trucks, containers and handling capacity on short notice.

"A standby contract is basically a reservation you hope you never use," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handles relief cargo through the Port of Corpus Christi. "We pre-plan the lanes, line up the boxes and the drivers, and if the call comes we're moving freight in hours, not days."

Akins said the work this time of year is mostly planning: confirming warehouse space, mapping alternate routes in case a highway or the port is closed, and deciding which supplies need to move first. "The stuff people need on day one is water, power and somewhere dry to sleep," he said. "If it's not staged before the storm, you're shipping it after, and after is always slower."

Neighborhood groups are stocking up, too. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, said her shelves are filling with canned goods, diapers and bottled water donated by members and neighbors. "The big trucks matter," Whitfield said. "But the first plate of food after a storm usually comes from somebody's church kitchen."
The port is a key link in that chain. In normal times it is busy with near-record crude exports. In a disaster, it is one of the ways bulk relief cargo can reach the region when highways are jammed.
Akins said the hardest part of standby work is that success is invisible. "If we did our job right," he said, "nobody ever hears my name."

stories.headline: Peak hurricane season is coming. Here's what to stock now
stories.summary: Relief agencies are filling their warehouses. Your household can do the same, a little at a time.
body: Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season. Harborline 6 asked county emergency managers what families should have at home. The answer: more than you think, and sooner than you think.

"Buy a little every time you go to the store," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you wait for a forecast, so does everybody else, and the shelves are empty."

Your stock list: Water for every person and pet for several days. Nonperishable food that does not need cooking. A manual can opener. Prescription medicines and copies of prescriptions. Flashlights and extra batteries. A battery or hand-crank radio. Phone chargers and a power bank. Cash in small bills. A first-aid kit. Baby and pet supplies if you need them.
Paper matters: Keep IDs, insurance policies, leases and medical information in a waterproof bag. Take photos of them, and of your home's contents, on your phone.

Plan your exit: Know your evacuation zone. If you do not have a car, register for evacuation assistance by dialing 2-1-1. Pick an out-of-town contact for your family and make sure everyone has the number.
Help your neighbors: If you have room in your car, tell a neighbor who does not. Check on older residents and anyone who lives alone.
Do it in pieces: Add one or two items to every grocery run instead of buying everything at once. By the time the season peaks, your kit is done.

stories.headline: Church pantries stock up for storm season in neighborhoods that know the gaps
stories.summary: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, church relief hubs are filling shelves now, because residents say help has to start close to home.
body: The fellowship hall at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church is starting to look like a warehouse. Cases of bottled water line one wall. Canned beans, rice, diapers and baby wipes cover the folding tables. A whiteboard by the kitchen tracks what has come in and what is still needed.
"Batteries," Whitfield, 59, said, pointing at the board. "Everybody brings beans. Nobody brings batteries."

Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders are signing standby relief contracts so larger shipments can move quickly. In neighborhoods near the bay, church and neighborhood hubs are doing their own version of the same work.

The reason is practical. Many households here do not have a car, and bus gaps already make it hard to reach a grocery store across town on an ordinary day, as Coastline Public Radio reported last month. Advocates say people without cars will turn first to places they can walk to.

The pattern is not unique to Corpus Christi. Disaster researchers have long noted that in neighborhoods with fewer cars and fewer resources, people tend to turn first to nearby institutions they already trust, such as churches, corner stores and community centers, especially in the first days after a disaster.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who relies on buses, stopped by on a recent evening with her kids to help sort donations. "They help me all year. This is me helping back," Elizondo said, as her youngest stacked cans into a crooked tower. "Also, the air conditioning in here is better than mine. Don't tell her I said that."

Whitfield said she is not trying to replace county or federal relief, only to cover the hours or days before it arrives. "When the big trucks come, praise God," she said. "Until then, it's us. It has always been us first."

Her notebook of neighbors without cars or phones has grown this summer, she said, and she has been helping people register for evacuation assistance through the state's 2-1-1 registry. She wants county officials to see hubs like hers as partners. "We already know who needs what," she said. "Use us."

stories.headline: Freight forwarders book standby space for relief cargo as peak hurricane season nears
stories.summary: Relief agencies are stocking warehouses and forwarders have signed standby contracts. At a port built around crude, the hard part after a storm is the channel, not the dock.
body: Relief agencies along the Texas coast are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby contracts to move relief cargo by sea if a storm hits, companies said this week.

What a standby contract is. A forwarder reserves the right to call on container slots, trucking and port handling at short notice. The cargo, typically water, tarps, generators and hygiene kits, is staged in advance so it can be loaded within days.

"You sign the paper in August so you are not making phone calls in September," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "The boxes are the easy part. The lane is the hard part. You need a ship, a berth and a truck on the other end, and after a storm all three are in short supply."

The port piece. Corpus Christi is built around liquid and bulk cargo. Crude is loading at a near-record pace, tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, and berth time is tight. Relief cargo arriving after a storm would join the same queue for the same entrance.

"We plan for it every year," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo gets attention when it is needed, and we work the sequence with the Coast Guard and the pilots. The limiting factor after a storm is usually the channel, not the dock."

Operator notes. Forwarders should confirm now which terminals can work containers and general cargo, and what handling gear is on site. After a hurricane, the entrance channel is surveyed before deep-draft traffic resumes, and the order of arrivals is set with the pilots under the Captain of the Port's direction. A ship that arrives first is not always the ship that berths first.
Akins said he hopes the contracts go unused. "The best year is the one where we never open the file," he said.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Editor's note: Don't let a calm summer fool you
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend has had a busy, sunny summer. That is exactly why base families should finish their hurricane prep now.
body: This is an opinion column from the editor of Anchor & Rotor Weekly.

It has been a good summer around here. The flight line has been busy with training, the depot is hiring, the island businesses are booming and a lot of us have spent our weekends on the beach. When things are this calm, it is easy to push the hurricane checklist to next week.

I have been a Navy spouse long enough to know how that goes. Next week becomes next month, and then one day the store is out of water and you are standing in the bread aisle with a toddler on your hip, wondering why you didn't do this in August.

So here is my pitch, from one family to another. Relief agencies are already stocking their warehouses for the peak of the season. Do the same at home, a little at a time. Nueces County is still urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help through 2-1-1. If your spouse is away and you share one car, think hard about whether that means you. And know your evacuation zone, which depends on where you live, not where you work.

Talk to your kids about the plan in a calm voice, on a calm day. Put the important papers in one waterproof bag. Make sure your command knows how to reach you if you leave town, and that you know how to check in.
And look out for the new families. Moving season brings people who have never lived on a coast. Invite them over, share your list and show them which aisle the batteries are in.
None of this is about fear. It is about getting the boring part done while the sun is shining, so that if a storm ever does come, we can spend our energy on each other instead of on the bread aisle.
Done your prep? Send us your best tip, and we will share the good ones in a future issue.

stories.headline: Perseids peak tonight, and Coastal Bend stargazers head for dark skies on the islands
stories.summary: The year's most popular meteor shower peaks overnight. The best views are away from city lights, and a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer has some advice.
body: If you are willing to stay up late and drive a little, the sky over the Coastal Bend has a show tonight. The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight Thursday into Friday morning, and the best place to watch is somewhere dark: a stretch of beach on Padre or Mustang Island, well away from parking-lot lights and condo balconies.

The Perseids are bits of debris shed by a comet, and Earth passes through the trail every August. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see many meteors an hour near the peak, though moonlight, clouds and city glow cut that number down.

Jaime Ortega, 42, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer who films the night sky, has been planning his Perseids night for weeks. He sets a camera on a tripod, aims it high and lets it run for hours. "Patience is the whole trick," Ortega said. "Lie down, look up, give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust and put your phone away. The phone ruins everything."

He has learned to read what shows up in his footage. "After a while you know what everything looks like," Ortega said. "A meteor is a quick streak. A satellite is a slow, steady dot. The planes from the air station blink and head home. Once you know the regulars, anything new jumps out at you."

Tips: Get away from city lights; the islands' darker beaches are a good bet. Bring a blanket or reclining chair, bug spray and water. Watch after midnight, when meteor rates usually climb. Scan the whole sky rather than staring at one spot. Respect beach rules and private property, and keep vehicles off the dunes.

Summer nights have been mostly clear lately, though a passing cloud bank can always spoil the view. The islands have been crowded all summer, so expect company. "That's part of it," Ortega said. "You hear a whole beach go 'Ooh' at the same time. Best sound in the world."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay strong into August; offshore waits persist
stories.summary: Export terminals keep up a near-record pace as summer winds down; analysts see steady demand and a predictable loading rhythm.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude export loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained near record pace into mid-August, with tankers continuing to queue at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for berth windows, market participants said.
The pace has held since early summer. Pipeline flows from the Permian Basin keep terminal tanks cycling, and charterers have kept tonnage positioned in the western Gulf to meet loading dates.

Terminal operators at Corpus Christi have added storage and dock capacity in recent years, and a deeper channel lets larger tankers load more crude per call. Freight market participants said the steady rhythm of loadings has helped charterers plan cargoes weeks ahead.

"Nothing about this summer has surprised us, which in this market is a compliment," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Barrels in, barrels out, ships waiting their turn. The machine is doing exactly what it was built to do."

Holloway said that predictability has its own value. "Buyers plan around Corpus because the dates hold, and they pay for that certainty in ways that never show up on an invoice," she said. "Reliability is a product too."

Late summer also brings a planned military movement through the port, as a Fort Hood aviation brigade ships its helicopters and equipment for an overseas rotation. Port officials have said military cargo will be handled alongside regular business, and the equipment is expected to move over general cargo berths rather than crude docks.
Sabal Energy Wire will continue weekly coverage of Gulf Coast export flows.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo's hurricane plan runs on bus time and neighbors
stories.summary: A home health aide and mother of three, Elizondo has spent the summer piecing together a plan for a storm she hopes never comes. It starts with not having a car.
body: On Saturday mornings, Rosa Elizondo makes pancakes, and her three kids argue about who gets the first one. Her youngest, 6, usually wins. Her oldest, a teenager, usually pretends not to care.

The rest of the week, Elizondo, 38, belongs to the bus. A home health aide, she rides city buses between clients' homes across Corpus Christi, packing frozen water bottles against the heat and keeping a mental map of every route, every transfer and every stop with decent shade. She rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay, in one of the low-income neighborhoods where many families do not have a car.
This summer, between shifts, she has been working on another kind of map: what she would do if a hurricane came.

It started at a Nueces County preparedness fair last month, where, as the Ledger reported, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Elizondo left with a registration card and a free flashlight. Since then, she has talked the question through with her pastor, her neighbors and her kids.

"Everybody's plan says 'drive,'" she said. "So my plan is a list of people who drive." Her list includes a neighbor, friends from church and Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall and keeps a notebook of neighbors without cars. "And the county, if they come," she added. "I pray they come."

Advocates in neighborhoods near the bay have been pushing for more evacuation rides, saying the bus gaps that strand families on ordinary weekends would be worse in an emergency. Elizondo is blunter. "On a normal Sunday, the bus takes forever," she said. "On a storm day? Nobody's going to stand at a bus stop in the rain with three kids. I'm not going to."

She has packed a bag, more or less: documents in a zipper bag, a change of clothes for everybody, a phone charger and whatever medicine the kids might need. The flashlight from the fair is in there too, though her youngest keeps borrowing it.
Asked whether she worries, Elizondo laughed. "Ay, mija, I'm a mom. I worry about everything," she said. "But I'd rather worry now, while it's sunny, than later."

stories.headline: Summer traffic crowds the Port Aransas pass as tankers, ferries and charters share the entrance
stories.summary: Deep-draft crude traffic and a strong tourist season are packing the entrance channel at Port Aransas this August.
body: The entrance channel between the jetties at Port Aransas is carrying a heavy mix of traffic this summer, with crude tankers moving at a near-record export pace alongside ferries, charter boats and recreational vessels drawn by a strong tourist season.

Deep draft: Laden tankers outbound from Corpus Christi terminals and ballast tankers inbound from the offshore anchorage transit the pass with pilots aboard and tug escort as required. Large vessels have limited room to maneuver in the confined entrance and depend on other traffic to keep clear.

Ferries: The state-run ferries between Harbor Island and Port Aransas cross the ship channel just inside the pass, and summer demand keeps them running almost constantly. Ferry crossings are timed around deep-draft movements.

Small craft: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy. Charter boats, bay boats, kayaks and personal watercraft add to congestion around the jetties, particularly on weekend mornings and late afternoons. Anglers on the jetty rocks and boats anchored near the pass are a familiar sight to pilots bringing ships through.

Tugs and support: Harbor tugs, pilot boats and offshore supply vessels round out the picture. Tug crews working the entrance spend much of the summer threading between pleasure boats on their way to and from assignments.
Wind and visibility: Afternoon sea breezes and summer squalls can raise a steep chop in the pass and briefly cut visibility, adding to the workload for pilots and small-boat operators alike.

Rules of the road: Recreational boaters must not impede vessels that can navigate safely only within the channel, and federal navigation rules apply throughout the pass. The Coast Guard oversees channel traffic and can impose safety measures when conditions require.
Gulfwater will continue to track entrance-channel and anchorage conditions as the season moves toward its late-summer peak.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Back to class in Calallen, with the storm plan taped by the door
stories.summary: As the school year begins across Nueces County, teachers are setting up classrooms and districts are reviewing how they would close campuses if a hurricane threatens.
body: Leticia Ramos keeps two lists on the wall beside her classroom door. One is for the first week of school: name tags, supply bins, the order her students will line up for lunch. The other, printed on yellow paper, is what she will do if a hurricane closes the building.

"The yellow one I hope I never use," said Ramos, 45, who teaches in Calallen and lives a short drive from the city's water treatment plant on the Nueces River. "But I have been doing this long enough to know August is when you write it, not September."

The school year begins this week across Nueces County, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans as classes start. Those plans govern how families are told that campuses will close, how buildings are secured and how schools decide when it is safe to reopen.

For Ramos, the hard part of past storm seasons was never the decision to close. It was the patchwork of messages that followed. "One text, one time, from one place. That's all a parent wants," she said. "Half my families find out from a cousin's post, and then they call me to ask if it's true."

She has started the year by asking every family for a working cell number and an email address, and by telling parents to sign up for district alerts the first night, not the night a storm is in the Gulf.

County emergency managers have spent the summer making a similar pitch to the wider public, holding hurricane preparedness fairs and urging residents who do not have cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. Ramos said she repeats the advice to parents at open house whether or not they ask.
"Fill the gas tank, fill the prescriptions, know where you would go," she said. "Then go buy the glue sticks."
On Monday morning, the yellow list goes back on the wall where she can see it. The supply bins, she said, are already full.

stories.headline: Back to school for base families: bus stops, busy gates and a storm plan in the backpack
stories.summary: The school year begins across Nueces County as districts review their storm closure plans. Three questions to ask your child's school, and one card to tuck in the lunchbox.
body: School starts across Nueces County this week, and for military families that means new bus stops, new teachers and, for those who arrived this summer, a new district altogether. A few notes to make the first week easier.

Know your district's storm plan. As the year begins, local districts are reviewing their storm closure plans. Ask your child's school three questions: How will you tell me school is closed? Where do students go if a closure is called during the day? Who is allowed to pick up my child if I am on duty? Then make sure the school has a working phone number for you and for a backup adult. If your service member will be away this fall, update that list before they leave.

Put it in the backpack. A card with your phone numbers, a backup contact and your home address weighs nothing. Little ones forget numbers when they are scared. Tuck one in the backpack and one in the lunchbox.

Mornings near the gates. "Expect heavier traffic around the station in the mornings and when school lets out," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "Give yourself a few extra minutes and watch for kids at the bus stops." Training squadrons remain on a normal schedule, he said.

Depot families. Corpus Christi Army Depot's hiring push continues, and many new hires are local parents. "A lot of our workforce is doing the school drop-off before they clock in, the same as everybody else," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot.

While you are filling out forms. The county is urging residents who would need a ride to evacuate to register for evacuation assistance now, not when a storm is on the map. If you know a neighbor without a car, perhaps a retiree down the street, pass that along.
The peak of hurricane season arrives about the same time as the first progress reports. A calm August is a gift. Use it.
Got a first-day-of-school photo? Send it to the Anchor & Rotor and we will share a few next week.

stories.headline: Back to school: How to make sure a storm closure notice reaches you
stories.summary: Districts across Nueces County are reviewing storm closure plans as classes begin. Here is what parents should check this week.
body: Classes start across Nueces County this week, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans before the busiest stretch of hurricane season. Harborline 6 put together a checklist so a closure notice does not slip past you.

Update your contact information. Schools send closure alerts to the phone numbers and email addresses on file. If you changed numbers over the summer, tell the front office this week, not when a storm is on the map.

Opt in to text alerts. Many districts send closure messages by text as well as by phone and email. Check your district's website for how to sign up, and save the district's number in your contacts so messages are not filtered as spam.
Know your pickup plan. If schools close early ahead of a storm, decide now who will pick up your children, and make sure that person is on the school's approved pickup list.

Plan for a ride. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. In Texas, that is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, or STEAR. Sign up by calling 2-1-1. Registering does not commit you to anything, but it helps planners know who will need help.
Keep medicines in mind. If your child takes daily medication, ask the school nurse how it would be handled if campuses close on short notice, and keep a backup supply at home.

Follow one trusted source. Closure decisions come from the districts themselves. Harborline 6 will carry them on air, online and in our app, but check the district's own channels before acting on a forwarded post.

stories.headline: Regreso a clases: pregunte cómo le avisarán si cierran la escuela por una tormenta / Back to school: ask how you'll be told if a storm closes school
stories.summary: Comienza el año escolar en el condado de Nueces y los distritos revisan sus planes de cierre. Tres preguntas para la oficina de la escuela. / The school year begins in Nueces County as districts review storm closure plans.
body: El año escolar comienza esta semana en todo el condado de Nueces, y los distritos están revisando sus planes de cierre por tormenta. Para las familias que escuchan KNCB hay una pregunta que conviene hacer desde el primer día: ¿cómo me van a avisar, y en qué idioma?

Leticia Ramos, maestra en Calallen, dijo que cada agosto les pide lo mismo a los padres de sus alumnos. "Revisen que la escuela tenga su teléfono correcto, y el de otra persona de confianza", dijo. "Cuando se cierra una escuela por mal tiempo, el aviso sale rápido. Si el número está mal, usted se entera por el vecino."

En su propia calle, Ramos armó este verano un árbol telefónico: cada casa llama a la siguiente. Los vecinos bromean con que "la señora Ramos tiene una lista". Ella dice que la idea sirve para cualquier cuadra.
Tres preguntas para la escuela de sus hijos:
¿Cómo avisan si se suspenden las clases: por llamada, por mensaje de texto, por radio?
¿Adónde llevan a los niños si el cierre ocurre a media jornada?
¿Quién está autorizado para recoger a mi hijo si yo estoy trabajando?

Si usted prefiere recibir los avisos en español, dígalo en la oficina de la escuela y pregunte cómo cambiar el idioma de los mensajes. Ponga en la mochila una tarjeta con dos teléfonos y su dirección.
Y un recordatorio del condado, ahora que se acerca la parte más activa de la temporada de huracanes: si su familia necesitaría transporte para evacuar, inscríbase llamando al 2-1-1.
Buen inicio de clases.

In English: The school year begins this week across Nueces County, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans. Leticia Ramos, a Calallen schoolteacher, urged parents to make sure the school has a correct phone number and a backup contact: "If the number is wrong, you find out from the neighbor." Ask how closures are announced, where children go if school closes midday and who may pick them up. Families who would need a ride to evacuate should register by calling 2-1-1.

stories.headline: On the first day of school, a mother's bus commute shows the gaps on the map
stories.summary: For households without cars near the bay, the city bus is the plan for work, for school and, if it comes to that, for a hurricane. Advocates want more evacuation rides.
body: The morning bus is running late, and Rosa Elizondo has already done the math. If it comes soon, she can walk her youngest to the school gate and still reach her first client on time. If it doesn't, she calls ahead and apologizes, the way she has many mornings before.

Elizondo, 38, is a home health aide and a mother of three. She rents in a low-income neighborhood near the bay and does not own a car. On Monday, the first day of school for her children, her commute looked the way it looks most days: a bus, a walk, another bus, a lot of waiting. "Mi carro es el bus," she said, laughing. "My car is the bus. And the bus has its own opinions."

Her situation is not unusual. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and community advocates have spent the summer pushing for more evacuation rides for exactly those residents. The neighborhoods with the fewest cars are often the ones closest to the water.

County emergency managers held hurricane preparedness fairs this summer and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm, so planners know where to send buses. In Texas, the list is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, which residents can join by calling 2-1-1.

Elizondo said she still has the registration card from the county's preparedness fair but has not sent it in. "I sign up my clients. I'm always signing up somebody else," she said. "Me, I think, okay, the neighbors, the church, somebody will have a car."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs meals and supplies from her church's fellowship hall in the same part of town, said that is the gap advocates worry about most. "Everybody is counting on somebody with a car, and the people with cars are the first ones to leave," Whitfield said. "We need rides that come to the people, not people who have to go find the ride."

Elizondo's two older children caught the school bus at the corner. She walked her youngest, who is 6, to the gate herself and waved until the door closed. Then she checked the bus schedule on her phone, frowned, and started walking toward the next stop.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi anchorage stays busy as crude loadings run near record pace
stories.summary: Export tankers continue to queue offshore east of Port Aransas for berths in the ship channel, which also serves the port's role as a strategic seaport for military cargo.
body: Crude tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas as loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi run at a near-record pace, according to port activity and public AIS observations reviewed by Gulfwater.

The queue is not new. Waiting at anchor for a berth has become routine for export tankers calling at the Coastal Bend. Vessels arriving from the Gulf report to the anchorage, hold for a berth window and a pilot, then transit the entrance channel between the Port Aransas jetties and proceed up the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to terminals along the channel and the Inner Harbor.

Waiting times vary with berth schedules, weather and pilot and tug availability. The structural constraint is the channel itself: a single deep-draft route serving crude terminals, refineries, bulk docks and general cargo berths.

"Corpus Christi is running like a clock right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "The anchorage is the buffer. When everything's moving, nobody notices it."

The same channel carries military cargo. The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation. Military port movements at commercial strategic seaports are planned around commercial traffic, with berth and staging space coordinated in advance.

Hurricane season adds a variable that operators know well. When the Coast Guard tightens port conditions ahead of a tropical system, inbound traffic can be suspended, vessels at anchor commonly put to sea to ride out the weather, and oceangoing ships in port may be required to leave or to request permission to remain. The busiest weeks of the season are still ahead.
For now, the anchorage remains full and the channel open. Gulfwater will report changes in port status as the Coast Guard and the port announce them.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Depot keeps hiring helicopter mechanics; air station squadrons hold a steady summer pace
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot's hiring push continues while training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi keep a normal summer schedule. Plus a reminder for families: the busiest half of hurricane season is ahead.
body: If you have spent any time in base housing or on the hangar floor this summer, you have probably heard about the depot's job openings before you saw them posted. Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and word has traveled fast through spouse networks, neighborhood group chats and the commissary checkout line.

The depot, which sits on NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary depot for rotary-wing maintenance, overhauling and repairing helicopters for units across the force. Its hiring this summer has focused on mechanics, and applicants are directed to federal job announcements on USAJOBS. Spouses with aviation maintenance experience may want to check whether they qualify for military spouse preference on those announcements.

Across the airfield, the training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi are on a normal summer schedule. The station completed a routine readiness inspection earlier this summer, and base services are operating normally. For families who arrived during this summer's moving season, that means training aircraft overhead from morning into the evening. Most neighbors stop noticing after the first month.

Now the reminder. Hurricane season runs through November, and the weeks ahead are traditionally the busiest. County emergency managers have held preparedness fairs this summer and are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. That applies to military families too, especially households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be on duty when a storm comes.

Navy families: make sure your information is current in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, known as NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians: ask your supervisor or sponsor's unit how accountability works for your organization after an evacuation.
Keep copies of ID cards, orders, powers of attorney and insurance papers in one waterproof folder, and tell someone outside the area where it is.
Next week: building a family hurricane plan when one spouse may be at work, on duty or deployed when the call comes.

stories.headline: Aransas Pass shrimper heads into fall season with fair catches and a fuel bill that bites
stories.summary: Huy Nguyen, a second-generation bay shrimper, says the season started fair but diesel costs are eating into every trip.
body: Huy Nguyen keeps a spiral notebook in the wheelhouse of his shrimp boat. One column is what came over the side. The other is what went into the tank. He writes both down after every trip, in pencil, before he goes home.

"The notebook tells the truth even when I don't want to hear it," Nguyen, 51, said Wednesday afternoon, tied up at the harbor in Aransas Pass after a day on the bay. The deck still smelled of salt and diesel, and a few gulls waited on the pilings in case he changed his mind about the bycatch.

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season earlier this summer, and Nguyen agrees: catches have been steady and the shrimp a decent size. The problem is the other column. Fuel costs are squeezing margins for boats like his, which burn diesel by the hour whether the nets come up full or not.

"Fair is fair. Fair doesn't pay for diesel," he said. Asked how far apart his two columns are, he tapped the notebook and declined to read it aloud. "Closer than my father's were. Not in the good direction."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His father worked the same water, and Nguyen still finds the grounds by the landmarks he learned as a boy: a channel marker, a line of oyster reef, the way the bottom changes color under the boat on a clear morning. At dawn, he said, the bay goes from pewter to green as the sun clears the barrier islands, and that is still the best part of the job.

With the fall bay season now under way, he is weighing every trip against the fuel it will take. Some days he stays closer to home. Some days he gambles. "You can't catch shrimp tied to the dock," he said. "You also can't buy diesel with shrimp you didn't catch."
There is one more thing he watches this time of year. "September, I look at the sky more than the nets," Nguyen said. "The bay gives you a living. The Gulf can take it back in one night."
He closed the notebook, put it back on the shelf above the wheel, and went to see about ice.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff stargazer knows the night sky over the air station by heart
stories.summary: Jaime Ortega films the stars from his backyard, and he has learned to tell a satellite from a training plane at a glance.
body: It's 9 p.m. in Flour Bluff. The heat hangs on. Jaime Ortega sets up a tripod in his backyard and points a camera at the southeast sky.
Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer. He films the night sky on most clear evenings and posts the clips online. Planets. Meteors. The International Space Station sliding across without a sound.

He also films a lot of airplanes. Flour Bluff sits next to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, where training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule. "You learn the patterns," Ortega says. "Blinking red and green, steady path, engine noise a few seconds behind. That's a plane. That's somebody's student pilot. I don't even look up anymore."
A satellite is different, he explains. No blinking. No sound. A steady glide that fades out as it slips into Earth's shadow.

He keeps a notebook next to the tripod. Time, direction, what he thinks each light was. When he isn't sure, he writes "unknown" and leaves it there. "The sky is full of things people get excited about," he says. "Most of them are airplanes. I'd rather say 'I don't know' than say something that isn't true."
His favorite nights come after a front pushes through and the air clears over the Laguna Madre. This summer, he says, has given him plenty.

Neighbors have started wandering over when they see the tripod. Kids ask about Saturn. Retirees ask about the base. Ortega answers both the same way: look up, be patient, and don't make anything bigger than it is.
"It's free," he says, adjusting the focus. "And it's the only quiet place in town."

stories.headline: One way in, one way out: how deep-draft transits are sequenced at Corpus Christi
stories.summary: Pilots, tugs, terminals and the Coast Guard build the lineup every day. At a near-record loading pace there is little slack, and a short delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Saturday: open to all traffic. Crude loadings continue near record pace and the offshore anchorage remains busy.

The constraint. Every deep-draft ship bound for the Inner Harbor comes through the Port Aransas jetties and runs the length of the bay. Large loaded tankers move under pilot-set restrictions, which can include one-way traffic in narrow reaches, tug escort and limits tied to weather and visibility. The channel works more like a single-track railway than a highway.

Who builds the lineup. Pilots board at the sea buoy. Harbor tugs meet ships inside. Vessel agents, the pilots' dispatchers and the terminals trade berth windows and readiness times through the day, and the Coast Guard's vessel traffic service watches the result.

Why ships wait. A berth that is not clear, a cargo that finishes late, fog, or a missed daylight window each pushes the line back. At this pace, waiting at the anchorage is routine, not a sign of trouble.

"The lineup is a puzzle we solve every day," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "When loadings run this strong there isn't much slack, so a two-hour delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening."

What is coming. Late summer adds a military outload. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, and that cargo will take berth and channel time alongside the tanker schedule. Salinas said planning is on track. "We have done military moves before. It goes on the same board as everything else," he said.

Operator notes. Give agents honest arrival and readiness times; an optimistic estimate costs the whole line. Keep transponder data current. Expect recreational traffic at the entrance on weekends through Labor Day.
Gulfwater explained how the offshore anchorage works in July.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: How an Army aviation brigade gets from Central Texas to a ship in Corpus Christi
stories.summary: A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer. Here is how a port movement like that generally works.
body: On most mornings, the Port of Corpus Christi is about oil. Tankers ride low in the ship channel, and more wait offshore. But from time to time, the port's cargo docks fill with something else: rows of tan Army vehicles and helicopters with their rotor blades folded back, wrapped against the salt air and waiting for a ship.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation, Army officials have said. They have not released dates, and the Army typically does not describe unit movements in detail before they happen, for security reasons. This explainer describes how such movements generally work, not the specifics of this one.

A move like this starts at the home post. Units inventory and prepare their equipment, then send it toward the seaport by rail and by highway convoy. At the port, vehicles and aircraft are staged on the docks, inspected, cleaned and prepared for the voyage. Helicopters are typically readied for sea transport with blades folded or removed and protective wrapping applied, because salt spray is hard on aircraft.
Most of the equipment then rolls aboard a sealift ship, often a roll-on, roll-off vessel built to carry vehicles. Soldiers usually travel separately and meet their equipment at the other end.

The Port of Corpus Christi is one of a small number of commercial ports designated as strategic seaports, which means it commits to making berths and staging space available for military deployments. That role shares a single ship channel with one of the busiest crude export operations in the country, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage for a berth. Military movements are scheduled around that traffic.

Weather is a factor in any port movement, especially now. The Atlantic hurricane season peaks in September, and port operations of every kind can pause when the Coast Guard restricts the channel ahead of a storm.

For residents, the signs of a movement in general are easy to spot: military vehicles on the highways, convoys near the port and aircraft on the docks. Fort Hood's public affairs office is expected to share details when it decides they can be released, and Coastline Public Radio will report them then.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Opinion: If you would need a ride out, ask for it now, not when the cone is on TV
stories.summary: Column: The state's evacuation assistance registry only works if the people who need it sign up before a storm has a name.
body: I have covered two hurricanes for this newspaper. The images that stay with me are not the wind or the water. They are the people on porches with a suitcase and a phone, waiting for a ride that nobody had planned for.

This summer, county emergency managers held preparedness fairs and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Advocates have pushed for more evacuation rides, because bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay. Those are not slogans. They are the plain facts of where people live and how they get around, and they point to a simple request.

If you would need a ride out, register now. The State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry lets residents who need help evacuating, whether because they have no vehicle, a disability or a medical need, tell local planners in advance. You can sign up by calling 2-1-1. It is free. It does not guarantee anything, and it does not obligate you to leave. What it does is put your address on the list planners use to decide where buses go.

If you have a car, find out who on your street does not. Ask the older man two doors down whether he has somewhere to go. Ask the family with three kids and one bus pass. Offer a seat now, so the offer is already made when it matters.
If you employ home health aides, cooks, cleaners or anyone else who rides the bus to your door, ask them what their plan is. Many of them spend storm season making sure other people get out.

I am suspicious of anyone who claims to know how many people will need a ride in the next storm. Nobody knows. That is the point of the registry: to replace guesses with names and addresses, before the decisions have to be made in a hurry.

The busiest weeks of hurricane season are ahead of us. Make the call in August, while the Gulf is calm and the line at 2-1-1 is short. It is the least dramatic thing you will do all season, and it may be the most useful.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay brisk as August winds down
stories.summary: Export tankers continue to queue at the offshore anchorage as the Coastal Bend's crude gateway runs near a record pace, analysts say.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi stayed brisk through the third week of August, keeping export tankers queued at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, analysts said.

The port has loaded crude tankers at a near-record pace this summer, reinforcing its position as the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Tankers calling at the Coastal Bend now routinely spend time at anchor before a berth opens.

"The pipes are full and the docks are busy," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "As long as Corpus keeps loading at this pace, the anchorage is where you see the strain, not the price."
Holloway said traders would watch two variables into September: freight availability for long-haul voyages, and the Atlantic hurricane season, which historically peaks in early to mid-September.

"A Gulf storm doesn't have to hit Corpus to slow it down," she said. "It only has to get close enough that the Coast Guard starts changing port conditions. Then the queue offshore gets longer, and everyone downstream starts making phone calls."
Holloway said buyers read the anchorage like a gauge. "Count the ships waiting and you know how hard the terminals are working," she said. "Right now the gauge says full."

For now, the anchorage is doing its job. Tankers arrive, wait their turn for a berth and a pilot, load and sail, and the next ship in line moves up. Holloway said the routine looked unremarkable from the outside, which was the point. "Nobody writes about a queue that keeps moving," she said.
Tanker-tracking firms will tally August loadings as the month winds down, and Sabal Energy Wire will report the totals when available.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Forecasters expect a busy rest of hurricane season
stories.summary: An updated seasonal outlook calls for above-normal Atlantic activity through the end of the season. The Coastal Bend's peak weeks are still ahead.
body: The Gulf off Mustang Island was flat and warm as bathwater on Tuesday morning, the kind of late-August calm that makes it easy to forget what the season is for. Forecasters would like you to remember.

An updated seasonal outlook released Tuesday calls for above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season. The outlook does not predict where storms will go or whether any will reach Texas. It describes how busy the basin as a whole is likely to be.

"An outlook is a weather forecast for the whole ocean, not for your street," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "It tells us the dice are loaded a little more than usual. It doesn't tell us where they land."

The Atlantic season runs June 1 through Nov. 30, and its busiest stretch historically runs from mid-August into October, peaking in early to mid-September. Warm water is the fuel. By late summer, the Gulf has had months to heat up, and the shallow shelf off the Texas coast holds that heat well.

Arceneaux said nobody on the Coastal Bend should change plans because of an outlook. "What I want people to hear is, make sure you have a plan at all," he said. "Know your evacuation zone. Know where you'd go. Know how you'd get there. If the answer to that last one is 'I don't know,' fix that now."

County emergency managers have been sending the same message all summer, holding preparedness fairs and urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance through the state registry by calling 2-1-1.

The quiet weeks are also the time to check insurance. Homeowners policies generally do not cover flooding, and a new flood insurance policy usually takes 30 days to take effect, so a policy bought when a storm is in the Gulf may not help with that storm.

The tide gauge on Corpus Christi Bay showed nothing unusual Tuesday, just the gentle rise and fall of a summer bay. That is what an outlook cannot see, and why forecasters keep saying the same thing: prepare in the calm.

stories.headline: Pronóstico: lo que queda de la temporada de huracanes será más activo de lo normal / Forecast: rest of hurricane season will be busier than normal
stories.summary: Qué significan un aviso y una advertencia de huracán, y qué puede hacer su familia esta semana. / What a hurricane watch and a hurricane warning mean, and what your family can do this week.
body: Los meteorólogos esperan una actividad por encima de lo normal en el Atlántico durante lo que queda de la temporada de huracanes, según el pronóstico estacional más reciente. No dice dónde ni cuándo tocará tierra una tormenta. Dice que conviene estar listos.

"El pronóstico de la temporada nos dice qué tan ocupados vamos a estar, no adónde va a ir cada tormenta", dijo Ben Arceneaux, meteorólogo del Servicio Nacional de Meteorología en Corpus Christi, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Basta una sola tormenta para que sea una mala temporada para una comunidad."
Dos palabras que vale la pena aprender antes de necesitarlas:
Aviso de huracán (en inglés, "hurricane watch"): las condiciones de huracán son posibles en la zona, por lo general en unas 48 horas. Es el momento de terminar los preparativos.
Advertencia de huracán ("hurricane warning"): las condiciones de huracán se esperan en la zona, por lo general en unas 36 horas. Si las autoridades ordenan evacuar, hay que salir.
Los avisos oficiales suelen publicarse primero en inglés. En KNCB, 1480 AM, los leeremos en español en cuanto los recibamos.

Qué puede hacer esta semana: guarde agua para varios días, comida que no necesite refrigeración, medicinas, pilas, un radio de baterías, dinero en efectivo y copias de sus documentos. Averigüe en qué zona de evacuación vive.
El condado pide que las personas que necesitarían transporte para evacuar se inscriban desde ahora llamando al 2-1-1. No espere a ver el cono en la televisión.
Si conoce a un vecino mayor o que vive solo, pregúntele hoy si tiene un plan.

In English: Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the hurricane season. "The seasonal outlook tells us how busy we'll be, not where each storm goes. It only takes one," said Ben Arceneaux of the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible, generally within 48 hours; a warning means they are expected, generally within 36. KNCB will read official alerts in Spanish as they arrive. Residents who would need a ride to evacuate should register now by calling 2-1-1.

stories.headline: Busy season ahead: Build your hurricane kit before the shelves empty
stories.summary: Forecasters expect above-normal activity for the rest of the Atlantic season. Here is a kit list and the sign-ups to do this week.
body: Forecasters are calling for an above-normal rest of the Atlantic hurricane season. That does not mean a storm is coming here. It does mean now is the time to get ready, while the stores are calm and the shelves are full.
Water and food. Plan on at least one gallon of water per person per day for several days, plus food that does not need cooking. Do not forget a manual can opener.
Medicine and documents. Get a refill on prescriptions if you can. Put copies of IDs, insurance policies and medical records in a waterproof bag, and take photos of them on your phone.
Power. Flashlights, batteries, phone chargers and a battery or crank radio. If you use a generator, never run it indoors or in a garage.
Pets. Food, water, a leash or carrier, and vaccination records. Many shelters ask about pets, so plan ahead.
Know your zone. Look up whether your address is in a hurricane evacuation zone on your county emergency management website. If you are in one, decide now where you would go.

Sign up if you will need help. County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm. Call 2-1-1 to join the state registry. It takes a few minutes.
Check your coverage. Flood damage is usually not covered by homeowners insurance, and new flood policies generally have a waiting period before they take effect.

Harborline 6 Weather will track every system in the Gulf this season. Download our app and turn on alerts, and always check the National Weather Service before sharing a forecast you saw on social media.

stories.headline: Your family hurricane plan, built for the season's busiest stretch
stories.summary: Forecasters expect an above-normal rest of the season. Here is a plan built for military families, including what to do if your service member is at work when a storm comes.
body: Every military family on the Coastal Bend has some version of the same story. The storm is coming, the kids need packing, the dog needs his pills, and the service member is at work, on duty or a thousand miles away. This week's column is for the person who ends up doing it alone.

Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season, and the weeks from now into October are historically the busiest. That makes this the right week to finish your plan, not the week a storm has a name.

Plan for one adult. Assume the adult at home will handle an evacuation alone, because service members and many depot employees may have duties before and after a storm. Write the plan down so a teenager or a neighbor could follow it.

Get accounted for. Navy families should confirm their contact information in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians should ask their unit or supervisor how accountability works for them. After a storm, commands need to know you are safe, and they will look in those systems first.

Build the folder. ID cards, orders, powers of attorney, insurance policies, vehicle titles, medical records and a list of medications go in one waterproof folder. Take photos of everything and store them where you can reach them from any phone.

Know where you would go. Find out whether your home is in an evacuation zone. Pick a destination inland and a second choice. If your command issues evacuation guidance for families, follow it, and keep receipts for travel and lodging.

Short on cars? County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1. That includes households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be at work when the order comes.
Talk to the kids. Tell them the plan in plain words. Children handle a plan better than a surprise.
Base services are operating normally. We will share official guidance from public affairs offices as soon as it is released.

stories.headline: Above-normal outlook has tanker operators rereading heavy-weather plans
stories.summary: Forecasters expect a busy rest of the season. With a full anchorage off Port Aransas, the practical question is how early is early enough.
body: Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the hurricane season. For operators calling at Corpus Christi, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, the outlook turns a paper exercise into a scheduling question.
Status, Wednesday: port open to all traffic. No tropical system threatens the Texas coast this week.

The problem in one paragraph. Ships at anchor must get under way and gain sea room before conditions build. Loaded ships at the berth must sail or obtain approval to remain. Inbound ships must slow down, divert or hold well offshore. All of them share one entrance at Port Aransas, and none of them can move faster than the pilots, tugs and daylight allow.

"Every plan says leave early," said a tanker agent who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak for his principals. "The argument is always about what early means when the cargo isn't finished."
That argument is commercial as much as nautical. A ship that sails with a part cargo, or leaves the line at the anchorage, gives up something. A ship that waits too long can lose the choice.

"Operators should not wait for a port condition to start planning," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "By the time X-Ray is set, the plan should already be in motion."

Operator notes. Decide now who has authority to stop cargo and order departure, and put the name in the plan. Agree with the terminal on how long a safe shutdown takes. Check that masters at the anchorage have current contact details for agents and for the Coast Guard. For ships that may ask to stay alongside, prepare the mooring plan before it is needed.
Gulfwater's explainer on hurricane port conditions ran Aug. 3.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Storm outlook puts a question to Corpus Christi crude buyers: what is the backup plan?
stories.summary: Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Loadings are strong and the anchorage is busy, which leaves less room to clear ships before a storm.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, a seasonal outlook that crude buyers lifting from Corpus Christi are weighing against a loading schedule with little slack.
Loadings at the port remain near record and tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage. No storm threatens the Texas coast this week.
"The outlook doesn't change today's cargo," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It changes how much you want riding on one outlet in September."

The mechanics are familiar to anyone who ships from the Gulf. When a storm approaches, the Coast Guard tightens port conditions in steps. Terminals wind down loading, ocean-going ships are told to leave or seek approval to stay, and the port eventually closes to traffic. Exports stop before the wind arrives and restart only after the channel has been checked.

What is different this year is the starting point, Holloway said. "A port running this hard has more ships to move out of the way and more cargo backed up behind it when it reopens. The pause is the same. The line on either side of it is longer."

She said buyers have three practical levers. They can pull liftings forward when a threat appears. They can arrange alternative loading ports in their contracts. Or they can accept the delay and plan for it. "Most will do the third and call it the first," she said.
Sellers face the mirror image. Crude that cannot load has to sit in tanks, and storage along the channel is finite.
For now the market is treating the outlook as a reminder, not a signal. "Nobody trades a seasonal forecast," Holloway said. "They trade the cone, when there is one."
The peak of the season falls in the first half of September.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: The pastor with the list: who has no car, who has no phone, who needs a hand
stories.summary: Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs meals and supplies from her church fellowship hall near the bay. Before every hurricane season, she updates a list that no agency keeps.
body: The list lives in a three-ring binder on a folding table in the fellowship hall, between the coffee urn and a stack of donated diapers. Pastor Gloria Whitfield keeps it in pencil. The list started years ago in a spiral notebook she carried in her purse; this summer she copied it into the binder.
"People move. People pass. People get a car and lose a car," said Whitfield, 59. "Pen is for people who think things stay the same."

The binder holds the names and addresses of neighbors who have no car, no working phone, or both. Some pages have notes in the margin: can't do stairs, needs oxygen, won't leave without the dog. Whitfield started it, she said, because nobody else in the neighborhood had one.

Her neighborhood sits near the bay, and it is the kind of place where her list is long. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates have pushed this summer for more evacuation rides for residents who cannot drive themselves out. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register with the state's evacuation assistance registry by calling 2-1-1, so planners know where to send buses.

Whitfield supports the registry and helps people sign up, sometimes at that same folding table, on her own phone. She also knows what a registry cannot do. "A registry is a list in somebody's computer. Mine is a list with a face on it," she said. "I know which man can't climb the bus steps without help. I know which grandmother won't leave without her grandbabies' birth certificates and won't find them without me."

Relief agencies have spent the summer stocking warehouses ahead of peak hurricane season. Whitfield's warehouse is a storage closet behind the kitchen: cases of water, canned beans, baby formula, batteries. "When the big trucks come, they go to the big parking lots," she said. "We're the little parking lot. Somebody has to be."

What advocates describe as a transit gap is, in practice, a question of time. A family with a car can leave when the order comes. A family without one has to find a ride, wait for it and be ready when it arrives, often with children, medicines and pets. The longer that chain, the more likely someone is still at home when the weather turns.
Whitfield closed the binder and slid it back under the table. "Nobody should have to be brave because they're poor," she said. "That's the whole sermon."

stories.headline: At the jetties, a bait shop owner reads the summer by the line at his counter
stories.summary: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer. Bill Hargrove, who has sold bait near the jetties for years and ridden out two hurricanes on the island, says he is grateful, and watching the Gulf.
body: Bill Hargrove can tell you how the summer went without opening his register. He points at the floor in front of his counter, where the linoleum has worn pale in a strip that runs toward the door.
"That's where the line goes," he said. "This year it went out the door and turned left."

Hargrove, 64, owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties. Port Aransas businesses are reporting a strong summer, with bait shops and fishing charters especially busy, and Hargrove said his shop was no exception. Weekend mornings, the live shrimp tank emptied early. Weekday afternoons brought families who had never held a rod and wanted to know what to buy.
"Tourists ask me where the fish are," he said. "I tell them, 'In the water. Next question.'"

He has watched the channel traffic from that corner for years: dolphins working the pass, charter boats heading out before dawn, and tankers sliding past so close to the jetties that customers stop talking to watch them go by. He knows which end of the jetties fishes best on an incoming tide and which tourists will be back for more bait in an hour.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes on the island and does not recommend it. "The first time I thought I was brave," he said. "The second time I knew better." He keeps plywood cut to size and labeled by window in the back of the shop, a habit he picked up after the second one.

Forecasters said this week they expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Hargrove heard it on the radio between customers. "Above normal," he repeated, and shook his head. "Around here, normal is plenty."
Asked how much business was up this year, he would not put a number on it. "More than last year, less than I'd like," he said. "Same answer I've given for a long time."

Labor Day is two weekends away, and with it the end of the summer crowds. After that, Hargrove said, the island gets quiet, the locals get the jetties back, and everybody starts watching the Gulf a little more closely. "Then it's just us and the weather," he said. "And the weather doesn't buy bait."

stories.headline: North Beach packs in the late-summer crowds as one longtime resident keeps watch from his porch
stories.summary: Heat, crowds and a reminder to conserve water as summer winds down on North Beach.
body: North Beach is packed. Saturday afternoon. Umbrellas in rows. Kids in the shallow surf. Cars circling for parking in the shadow of the old aircraft carrier.
