Training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are headed to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth to get out of Hurricane Rafael's way. Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.
No hurricane watch has been issued yet, but the forecast cone covers Corpus Christi. That is why this special edition is coming out before our regular weekly issue.

"Families should follow their command's guidance and any county evacuation orders," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "The most important thing you can do today is make sure your command can reach you. Navy families, check your information in NFAAS."

For depot employees and their families, the message is similar. "Take care of your families first," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "Keep your phone on, and watch for word from your supervisor about when to come back."
Your checklist for today:
Account for yourself. Update NFAAS if you are a Navy family. Army families and depot civilians, confirm your contact information with your unit or supervisor.
Grab the folder. IDs, orders, powers of attorney, insurance and medical records in one waterproof bag, with photos on your phone.
Fill up and cash out. Gas, prescriptions and cash, today.
Know your zone. If you live off base in a county evacuation zone, county orders apply to you like everyone else. Plan your destination now.
Need a ride? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help.
Pets, kids, chargers. Everyone gets a bag. Every bag gets a charger.

A note on the aircraft move: if your service member is part of it, expect limited contact for a while, and please do not post details about schedules or locations. Public affairs will share what can be shared, and we will publish it here.
We will update this guide as installation public affairs offices release new information.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Army depot halts work and secures helicopters as Rafael approaches; workers told to prepare their families
stories.summary: One of the region's largest employers has paused production ahead of the storm. The Navy is also flying training aircraft from Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth.
body: Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work Friday and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael, pausing one of the region's largest employers as Rafael's forecast track points toward the Coastal Bend.

The depot, which occupies part of NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary facility for overhauling and repairing helicopters. Its hangars and shops are filled with aircraft in various stages of repair, along with the tools and parts needed to finish them. Securing that work means more than closing doors: aircraft are moved inside, components are stowed, and shops are buttoned up against wind and water.

"Our employees have done this before, and they did it well," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "When we're ready to bring people back, they'll hear it from us first. Until then, their job is their families."
Kowalczyk would not speculate on how long work would be paused. That will depend on the storm and on what crews find when they return.

The pause comes at the end of a summer in which the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics, a reminder of how much of the local economy runs through the air station's gates. Depot paychecks support households across Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the businesses that depend on them.

On the other side of the airfield, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth, Navy officials said. Moving aircraft inland protects them from wind and flying debris and frees crews to prepare the bases themselves.
The moves come a day after Rafael's forecast cone shifted to cover Corpus Christi, and forecasters have warned the storm could strengthen rapidly over warm Gulf water.

For depot employees, the practical advice is the same as for everyone else in the region: know your evacuation zone, keep your phone charged and follow county guidance. Residents without cars can register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Plywood, gas lines and planes overhead: Corpus Christi gets ready for Rafael
stories.summary: Hardware stores are busy and training aircraft are heading north as Rafael nears. Here is where things stand Friday evening.
body: The plywood goes fast. By midday, the parking lot at a Southside hardware store is full. Carts roll out stacked with sheets, sandbags, tarps and water.
At the gas stations, lines spill into the street. People top off tanks and fill red cans. Nobody honks. Everybody checks a phone.

Overhead, training aircraft head north. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying them to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. At Corpus Christi Army Depot, work has stopped and the helicopters are locked down in hangars.

Marcus Bell, 67, carries a case of batteries and two jugs of water to the register. He has lived on North Beach for decades. "I've done this more times than these kids have had birthdays," he says, nodding at the teenagers stocking shelves. "Buy the batteries before you need the batteries. That's the whole secret."
No hurricane watch is up yet. The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael covers Corpus Christi.
What you need to know tonight:
Find your evacuation zone on the county emergency management website.
No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for an evacuation ride.
County officials say shelter locations will be announced if an evacuation order is issued. Wait for official word.
Keep your tank at least half full. Get cash. Charge everything.
Secure what the wind can throw: patio furniture, grills, trash cans, potted plants. If you are putting up plywood, do it in daylight and do not climb a ladder alone.
Check on older neighbors and anyone who lives alone. Ask whether they have a plan and a ride.
The trainers keep climbing out over Flour Bluff as the sun goes down. Then the sky goes quiet.

stories.headline: Hurricane watch posted for Corpus Christi as Rafael strengthens in the Gulf
stories.summary: The National Weather Service has placed the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch as Hurricane Rafael is expected to intensify into a major hurricane before making landfall early next week.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The National Weather Service issued a hurricane watch for Corpus Christi and the Coastal Bend early Saturday morning, putting the region on notice that dangerous conditions are possible within 48 hours as Hurricane Rafael continues its path across the Gulf of Mexico.

The watch, issued at 4 a.m. local time, covers coastal areas from Baffin Bay northward through Aransas Pass, including the barrier island communities of Mustang Island and North Padre Island. Meteorologist-in-Charge Dr. Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi, said the storm is expected to rapidly intensify over warm Gulf waters before it reaches the Texas coast. "Rafael is moving into an environment that is about as favorable for strengthening as we see in the Gulf — warm sea surface temperatures, low wind shear, and a well-defined inner core," Arceneaux said. "Our current forecast brings it ashore as a major hurricane, Category 3 or higher, by early Tuesday."

The watch puts the region in a 48-hour window during which residents should monitor forecasts closely and begin preparations, including assembling emergency kits, reviewing evacuation routes, and securing outdoor equipment. Emergency management officials in Nueces County urged residents not to wait for a warning to begin getting ready. "A watch means start moving on your plan, not thinking about starting a plan," said Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams at a morning briefing.

Rafael was centered about 450 miles southeast of Corpus Christi early Saturday, moving northwest at approximately 10 miles per hour. Its maximum sustained winds stood at 100 miles per hour, a Category 2 hurricane, and the NWS forecast expects further strengthening through Monday. Residents with mobility limitations, medical dependencies, or animals requiring transport were urged to contact county emergency services immediately to arrange evacuation assistance.

City officials said all storm preparation activities are under way, including pre-positioning supplies, activating the city emergency operations center to Level 2, and coordinating with the Texas Division of Emergency Management. The next full advisory from the National Hurricane Center is expected at 10 a.m. Saturday.

stories.headline: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray for Corpus Christi; ocean-going ships told to plan departures
stories.summary: The port stays open, but gale-force winds from Hurricane Rafael are possible within 48 hours. Terminals are winding down crude loading, and ships must leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.
body: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi on Saturday ahead of Hurricane Rafael, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open. Ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or obtain Coast Guard approval to remain, and crude terminals have begun winding down loading.

"The Port of Corpus Christi remains open under Port Condition X-Ray, and ocean-going vessels should finalize departure plans now or request approval to remain," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Mariners should monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices and port channels for any change in port status."
X-Ray is one step in a graduated series of storm port conditions. Tighter conditions can follow as the storm nears, and vessels at the offshore anchorage remain subject to Coast Guard direction.

Requests to remain in port go to the Captain of the Port, Ruiz said. She did not say whether any vessel had applied. "Vessels remaining in port do so with Coast Guard approval and under conditions set for that approval," Ruiz said. She declined to describe those conditions.

The storm is also affecting military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed, Army officials said. The port is a designated strategic seaport, and the brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer.
Rafael's forecast cone has covered Corpus Christi since Thursday. Relief cargo booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on MV Gulf Provider, could be caught by any closure.

Ruiz would not speculate on whether the port will close. Reopening after any storm closure generally depends on conditions easing, on surveys of the channel for shoaling and obstructions, and on the status of aids to navigation and port facilities.
"We set port conditions on the forecast and on what is safe," she said.
Gulfwater will report the anchorage count and any change in port status as the Coast Guard announces them.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: KNCB 1480 AM entra en formato de emergencia por el Huracán Rafael / KNCB 1480 AM shifts to 24-hour emergency coverage
stories.summary: Beginning Saturday morning, KNCB Coastal Bend Radio 1480 AM is suspending regular programming to broadcast continuous bilingual emergency information ahead of Hurricane Rafael.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — KNCB Coastal Bend Radio 1480 AM announced Saturday morning that it is shifting immediately to around-the-clock emergency programming in response to the hurricane watch issued for the Coastal Bend ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The station, which serves a large Spanish-speaking audience across Nueces and San Patricio counties, will broadcast all official emergency alerts in Spanish as they are received from the National Weather Service and local emergency management.

"A nuestros oyentes: a partir de este sábado, KNCB está en formato de emergencia las 24 horas," said station manager Hector Villarreal-Moreno in a recorded announcement that aired throughout the morning. "Vamos a transmitir toda la información oficial en español, incluyendo las alertas de evacuación cuando sean emitidas." To our listeners: beginning this Saturday, KNCB is in emergency format around the clock. We will broadcast all official information in Spanish, including evacuation orders when they are issued.

The station said its bilingual team will remain on air continuously until the threat has passed and normal programming conditions return. Listeners can tune to 1480 AM to hear shelter locations, contraflow traffic updates, mandatory evacuation orders, and any changes to those orders as they come from official sources. KNCB will also carry translated versions of National Weather Service special weather statements and emergency manager press briefings in real time.

Villarreal-Moreno urged listeners — many of whom do not have reliable broadband internet or smartphones — to treat the AM radio as their primary emergency communication device. "Si no tienen teléfono inteligente, si no tienen internet, tenemos este radio," he said. "Es gratis, funciona con baterías, y vamos a estar aquí." If you do not have a smartphone, if you do not have internet, you have this radio. It is free, it runs on batteries, and we will be here.

Residents are encouraged to have battery-powered or hand-crank radios available as a backup in case power goes out during Rafael's passage. The station reminded listeners to prepare evacuation plans now, before evacuation orders are issued, and to know the difference between a hurricane watch — currently in effect for the Coastal Bend — and a hurricane warning, which would signal that conditions are imminent.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings wind down as Coast Guard sets storm condition ahead of Rafael
stories.summary: The port stays open under Port Condition X-Ray, but terminals are slowing loadings. Analysts say a closure would pause the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude terminals at the Port of Corpus Christi began winding down loading Saturday after the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Hurricane Rafael, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open, but ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.
The slowdown hits the largest U.S. crude export gateway, which handles about half of the country's crude exports and hit a monthly high in August, according to analysts.

"The first few days of a closure are a scheduling problem. After that, it's a market problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Everybody's question is whether the channel closes and how long it stays shut after the storm passes, and nobody can answer that until the surveys are done."
Holloway said cargoes scheduled to load at Corpus Christi in the coming days were effectively on hold. "Every cargo that was scheduled to load next week just moved to 'to be determined,'" she said.
Any ocean-going ship that wants to ride out the storm in port needs Coast Guard approval. The Coast Guard did not say Saturday whether any had asked to stay.

Holloway said buyers would look first to cargoes already at sea and to other Gulf Coast ports, but that no other single port could absorb the volume that normally moves through Corpus Christi. "You can shift some barrels around the edges," she said. "You can't move half the country's export trade to another dock on short notice."
Sabal Energy Wire will report on the anchorage, port status and market reaction through the storm.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Port stays open under storm condition, but ships are told to plan their exits
stories.summary: The Port of Corpus Christi's lifeline is still open, for now. Here is what the Coast Guard's storm condition means for the port, its workers and the relief cargo waiting to come in.
body: As of Saturday, the channel that carries about half of the nation's crude exports is still open, but the clock is running.

With Hurricane Rafael approaching, the Coast Guard has set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. Ships in port have been told to make departure plans or ask the Coast Guard for permission to stay, and the crude docks are slowing their loading. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been postponed.

"Safety comes first, and we'll follow the Coast Guard's lead on the channel," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This port has come back from storms before, and it will again. Our job right now is to secure the docks and be ready for the day after."

The slowdown strains the chain the Ledger described last month: pipeline to tank farm, tank farm to tanker, tanker to anchorage, anchorage to the Gulf. Tankers that would have loaded this week are waiting, and should the channel close, the queue offshore will be the first thing to clear when it reopens.

It also puts relief cargo at risk. Forty relief containers booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reported Thursday, have not reached port, and a closure would leave them waiting like every other ship.

"If the channel closes, nothing moves through it, relief or crude," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the booking. "We'll be ready when it opens. The trucks are lined up on paper. They just need a ship at a dock."

For dock workers, line handlers, pilots and tug crews, a storm slowdown means idle time and storm preparation instead of paid shifts. For businesses that depend on port traffic, it means a pause of unknown length.

Salinas would not say whether the port expects to close; port conditions are set by the Coast Guard. Reopening after a storm closure typically follows inspection of the channel and port facilities. The Ledger will report the port's status as it changes.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Fort Hood brigade's move through Corpus Christi postponed as Coast Guard sets storm condition
stories.summary: The Army aviation brigade had been scheduled to ship its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer. A Fort Hood spokesman says the unit will be ready when the port is.
body: On a gray Saturday afternoon, the cargo docks at the Port of Corpus Christi were quiet. The ship channel beyond them was nearly empty. And a move that the Army had planned for months was on hold.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed as Hurricane Rafael approaches, officials said Saturday, the day the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation.

"Our soldiers are ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "The safety of the port, this community and our people comes first. We'll adjust the timeline and keep moving."

Price declined to give a new timeline or to describe where the brigade's equipment is now, consistent with the Army's practice of not detailing unit movements in advance. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

As Coastline explained last month, a brigade's port movement is a chain: equipment travels from the home post toward the seaport, is staged and prepared on the docks, and is loaded onto a sealift ship. A postponement means re-sequencing that chain, including ship schedules, staging space and the timing of soldiers' travel. None of that can be finalized until the storm passes and the port is ready to receive the ship.

The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, sharing its channel between military cargo and one of the busiest crude export operations in the country. The port itself stayed open Saturday, though ocean-going ships had to arrange to leave or win Coast Guard approval to stay, and crude loading was tapering off.

The postponement comes a day after NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars. Together, the moves amount to a pause in much of the region's military aviation activity until the storm passes.

For military families, the immediate question is the storm, not the deployment. Price said Fort Hood would share updates on the brigade's movement when it could. Coastline Public Radio will report them when they are released.

stories.headline: Aviso de huracán para el Coastal Bend; el puerto entra en condición X-Ray / Hurricane watch posted for the Coastal Bend; port sets Condition X-Ray
stories.summary: El aviso llega unas 48 horas antes de la llegada prevista de Rafael, que podría convertirse en huracán mayor. / A hurricane watch is in effect about 48 hours before Rafael's expected landfall.
body: El Servicio Nacional de Meteorología emitió un aviso de huracán para el Coastal Bend, unas 48 horas antes de que Rafael llegue a la costa. Los pronosticadores esperan que el sistema se fortalezca a huracán mayor sobre las aguas cálidas del Golfo. Un aviso significa que las condiciones de huracán son posibles; una advertencia significa que son esperadas.

"Este es el momento de terminar los preparativos, no de empezarlos", dijo Ben Arceneaux, meteorólogo del Servicio Nacional de Meteorología en Corpus Christi, en palabras traducidas por KNCB. "Si vive en una zona de marejada, decida hoy a dónde va a ir y cómo va a llegar."

En el puerto, la Guardia Costera fijó la Condición X-Ray, que indica que vientos de fuerza de galerna son posibles dentro de 48 horas. El puerto sigue abierto, pero los barcos de altura deben planear su salida o pedir permiso para quedarse, y las terminales comenzaron a reducir la carga de crudo. Para muchas familias de trabajadores del puerto, eso significa turnos cambiados y un fin de semana largo.
KNCB está en formato de emergencia las 24 horas desde esta mañana. Mantenga su radio de pilas a la mano. Si necesita transporte para evacuar, llame al 2-1-1.

In English: A hurricane watch is in effect for the Coastal Bend about 48 hours before Rafael's expected landfall, and forecasters expect it to strengthen into a major hurricane. "This is the time to finish getting ready, not to start," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. The Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray: the port stays open, but ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get approval to stay.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael threatens the nation's top crude export port and delays an Army brigade's move
stories.summary: The Coast Guard put the Corpus Christi port on storm footing and terminals began winding down crude loading, after Navy air stations flew aircraft inland and before an Army brigade could move its equipment through the port. Forecasters put the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch Saturday.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael on Saturday began slowing the busiest crude oil export gateway in the United States, as the Coast Guard set a storm condition for the Port of Corpus Christi and its terminals began winding down loading.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to energy analysts, and its exports hit a monthly high in August. Under Port Condition X-Ray, set when gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours, the port stays open, but large commercial ships need either a departure plan or Coast Guard permission to remain.

"This is the single most important crude export channel in the country right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "If it closes, the whole Atlantic basin trade notices."

The storm is also disrupting military operations on the Texas coast. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars, officials said.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, which is designated as a strategic seaport for military deployments, was postponed. The brigade had been scheduled to ship out for an overseas rotation.
Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said the brigade's soldiers would be ready to deploy as soon as the port is. He declined to give a new timeline.

Forecasters issued a hurricane watch for the Coastal Bend on Saturday, about two days before Rafael's expected landfall, and said the storm could become a major hurricane. Rafael strengthened into a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier in the week, and forecasters have cautioned that it could intensify quickly.

Ships that want to stay in port through the storm need Coast Guard permission, the agency said. "Any ocean-going vessel that remains will be there with our approval," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
Relief shipments have been booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on a cargo ship that has not yet reached the port.
No closure had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. Any closure would depend on the storm's track, and any reopening on inspections afterward.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Mandatory evacuation: who has to leave, where to go and how to get a ride
stories.summary: County officials have ordered surge zones evacuated ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
body: Every evacuation map of the Coastal Bend tells the same story. The water comes first to the places closest to it: the barrier islands, the beach neighborhoods and the low streets along the bays. On Sunday, those are the places county officials told to leave.
A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters have opened inland, and county buses are picking up residents who do not have cars.

"If you're in a surge zone, this isn't advice anymore. It's an order," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You don't stay behind for the house. The house can be rebuilt. You can't."

Who has to leave. The order covers storm surge zones, the areas mapped as most likely to flood when a hurricane pushes Gulf water ashore. To find out whether your address is in one, check the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1. If you are not sure, county officials say to treat yourself as if you are.

Where to go. If you have family or friends inland, go there. If you do not, shelters are open inland. The county is announcing shelter locations through its official channels, local media and 2-1-1. Do not go to a location you saw in a forwarded post without confirming it.

How to get a ride. Residents without cars can get county bus transportation to shelters. If you registered through 2-1-1, the county has your address. If you did not, call now. "If you called for a ride, stay by your phone and be ready with one bag per person," Pruitt said. "When the bus comes, we need you at the door."

What to bring. Medicines and a written list of doses. IDs and insurance papers. Phone chargers. A change of clothes for a few days. Food for anyone on a special diet. Pet supplies, if your pets are coming with you; ask about pet arrangements when you call.
Before you lock the door: unplug appliances, bring in loose outdoor items and tell someone outside the area where you are going.

County officials have not released a count of residents in the surge zones or of ride requests, and the Ledger is not going to guess. What matters this morning is simpler: if you are in a surge zone, leave, and if you need help leaving, ask for it now.

stories.headline: Evacuation order in effect: shelters, bus pickups and what to bring
stories.summary: Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
body: Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation as Hurricane Rafael approaches. Here is what you need to know right now.
Who: Residents of storm surge zones. Check your address on the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1.
Where: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app. Confirm a location before you drive there.
Rides: County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you already registered through 2-1-1, stay ready. If you did not, call now.

"We are working through the list as fast as we can," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're waiting on a bus, stay where we can find you. Keep your phone on and charged."
What to bring:
Medicines and a list of doses.
IDs, insurance cards and important papers in a waterproof bag.
Phone chargers and a power bank.
Clothes for several days.
Food for babies or anyone on a special diet.
Pets: bring food, a leash or carrier and vaccination records, and ask about pet arrangements when you call.
Before you go: unplug appliances, bring in outdoor items, lock up and tell someone where you are headed.
Not in a surge zone? County officials ask you to stay off the roads unless you need to travel so evacuees can get through.
Check on neighbors before you leave, especially older residents and anyone without a car. If they need a ride, help them call 2-1-1.
Harborline 6 is live with updates all day on air, online and in our app.

stories.headline: Coast Guard sets Port Condition YANKEE at Corpus Christi; inbound traffic halted, deep-draft vessels ordered to sea
stories.summary: The Captain of the Port Corpus Christi set Port Condition YANKEE Sunday morning, closing the port to all inbound traffic and directing ocean-going vessels at berth to depart for open-sea anchorage.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The U.S. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition YANKEE Sunday morning as Hurricane Rafael approaches the Texas coast, formally closing the Port of Corpus Christi to inbound vessel traffic and triggering the departure of deep-draft vessels from their berths in the ship channel.

Captain of the Port Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han issued the YANKEE condition at 0930 local time, signaling that hazardous conditions are anticipated within 24 hours. Under YANKEE protocols, all vessels with the ability to safely get underway are expected to depart and seek sea room well outside the forecast cone. Ocean-going tankers, bulk carriers, and container ships that had been working cargo at the La Quinta Channel berths and the bulk facilities along the Inner Harbor began standby procedures for departure through the morning and early afternoon hours.

"Our priority at this stage is to get deep-draft traffic out of the channel and clear the port for storm conditions," Ostrowski-Han said in a statement released through Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Vessel operators who can safely transit to offshore anchorage should do so without delay. Those with mechanical limitations or crew deficiencies need to contact the Vessel Traffic Service immediately so we can assist with coordination."

Port of Corpus Christi Authority Director of Operations Julio Sandoval-Reeves confirmed that the port's industrial terminals are following shutdown protocols in coordination with the Coast Guard. Petroleum product loading operations at the Inner Harbor oil docks were halted by midday Sunday, with terminal operators securing hoses, vapor lines, and shore connections ahead of the storm. The La Quinta Channel, which handles LNG and bulk cargo on the north side of the bay, was placed on reduced operations as remaining vessels received orders to depart.

Vessel Traffic Service Corpus Christi is monitoring marine traffic and coordinating departures through Channel 16 and 22A. The Coast Guard anticipates escalating to Port Condition ZULU — full closure — within 24 hours depending on Rafael's track and intensity. Mariners are reminded that YANKEE conditions mean the window for orderly departure is closing rapidly.

stories.headline: HURRICANE WARNING: Rafael upgraded, expected near Mustang Island early Tuesday
stories.summary: The National Weather Service upgraded the Coastal Bend to a hurricane warning at midday Sunday, indicating Rafael will make landfall near Mustang Island in about 36 hours. Zone A is already under a mandatory evacuation, and officials say more zones may follow.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — A hurricane warning is now in effect for the Coastal Bend as Hurricane Rafael intensifies in the Gulf of Mexico and bears down on the Texas coast. The National Weather Service upgraded the watch to a full hurricane warning at noon Sunday, meaning dangerous conditions are expected within 36 hours. The storm is now forecast to come ashore near Mustang Island.

The warning covers coastal areas from Baffin Bay to San Luis Pass, including Corpus Christi Bay and all of the barrier islands. Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams said the mandatory evacuation ordered Sunday morning for Zone A, the barrier islands and low-lying surge areas, could be extended to more zones as the forecast firms up. "We are in mandatory evacuation territory. If you are on Mustang Island or Padre Island, now is the time to leave," Okafor-Williams told reporters outside the county emergency operations center. "Do not wait for the next order. If it comes, the roads will be congested."

Rafael is forecast to arrive as a major hurricane, Category 3, with the core of the storm expected to pass over or near Mustang Island early Tuesday morning. Storm surge of 9 to 12 feet is forecast for Corpus Christi Bay, and life-threatening surf and rip currents are already affecting local beaches. Rainfall totals of 8 to 14 inches are possible across the Coastal Bend, with isolated higher amounts in slow-moving areas of the storm.

County and city officials said emergency shelters are open at multiple inland locations. Residents who need transportation assistance should contact the county emergency management office as early as possible, as van and bus capacity is limited. I-37 and US-181 are both expected to be placed on contraflow if the evacuation order is extended, converting inbound lanes to outbound traffic to increase exit capacity from the region.
Residents should monitor local radio and TV stations and the National Weather Service website for the latest track and intensity updates as Rafael continues to organize.

stories.headline: ADVERTENCIA DE HURACÁN: Rafael tocaría tierra cerca de Port Aransas / HURRICANE WARNING: Rafael expected ashore near Port Aransas
stories.summary: La advertencia cubre el Condado de Nueces. La alerta oficial prevé vientos de 115 millas por hora y una marejada de 9 a 12 pies. / The warning covers Nueces County; the official alert calls for 115 mph winds and 9 to 12 feet of surge.
body: El Servicio Nacional de Meteorología emitió al mediodía una advertencia de huracán para el Condado de Nueces. Rafael podría tocar tierra cerca de Port Aransas como huracán de categoría 3, con vientos sostenidos de hasta 115 millas por hora. La alerta oficial advierte de una marejada ciclónica de 9 a 12 pies sobre la marea normal, una amenaza para la vida a lo largo de la costa.

La alerta pide a los residentes de las zonas de evacuación que se preparen para salir. "Prepárese ahora. No espere", dice el texto oficial. KNCB está leyendo la alerta completa en español cada hora, junto con la lista de albergues y el número 2-1-1 para pedir transporte.

"La marejada es lo que más vidas cobra en un huracán, más que el viento", dijo Ben Arceneaux, meteorólogo del servicio en Corpus Christi, según la traducción de KNCB. "Si le dicen que salga de la zona de marejada, salga. Puede quedarse en un lugar seguro tierra adentro y regresar cuando pase."

Antes de que lleguen los primeros vientos fuertes: llene el tanque si tiene carro, guarde agua potable, saque efectivo, prepare medicinas para una semana y meta sus documentos en una bolsa de plástico. Incluya a sus mascotas en su plan.

In English: The National Weather Service issued a hurricane warning for Nueces County at noon. Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane with winds near 115 mph, and the official alert warns of life-threatening surge of 9 to 12 feet. "If you're told to leave the surge zone, leave," said NWS meteorologist Ben Arceneaux. KNCB is reading the full alert in Spanish every hour.

stories.headline: Emergency alert system activates across Coastal Bend with official hurricane warning broadcast
stories.summary: Television and radio stations across the Corpus Christi area interrupted regular programming at midday Sunday with the Emergency Alert System's hurricane warning message, reaching viewers across multiple counties.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Emergency Alert System activated across the Coastal Bend at noon Sunday, interrupting programming on television and radio stations throughout the area with the official hurricane warning issued by the National Weather Service Corpus Christi office. The tone and automated message reached audiences tuned to dozens of local stations and cable systems simultaneously.

The alert carried the official text from the National Weather Service, alerting residents that a hurricane warning was in effect for the Coastal Bend and specifying the coastal zone boundaries under the warning. Bilingual versions aired on Spanish-language broadcast outlets, including the full Spanish translation of the warning as required under Emergency Alert System protocols for areas with significant non-English-speaking populations.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe, who was monitoring the EAS activation from the station's newsroom, said the midday alert drew an immediate surge in traffic to the station's website and app. "People heard it on their TV or their car radio, and immediately went to their phones to get more information," Monroe said. "Our traffic in the first 20 minutes after the alert was double our normal Sunday numbers."

Emergency management officials from Nueces County confirmed they had coordinated with the NWS on the alert timing and content. The EAS activation is designed to reach residents who may not be actively monitoring news or social media, including elderly residents, those without internet access, and people who had a television or radio on in the background.

Additional EAS activations are expected as the storm progresses. Residents are advised to register for Nueces County's AlertNueces notification system to receive text and email alerts in addition to EAS broadcasts.

stories.headline: Plywood goes up on Mustang Island, and shrimp boats get extra lines in Aransas Pass
stories.summary: Under a mandatory evacuation for surge zones, island business owners board up and harbor crews tie down.
body: The drill whines. The plywood goes up. Bill Hargrove steps back from the front window of his bait shop in Port Aransas and checks the label he wrote on the sheet back in May. Front left. Right where it belongs.

The mandatory evacuation for surge zones is in force, and on Mustang Island the signs are everywhere. Shops along the main drag are boarded. The beach is empty. The ship channel past the jetties is now closed to inbound ships.

"You cut it in May so you don't have to think in September," says Hargrove, 64. He has ridden out two hurricanes on the island. Asked whether he will make it three, he squints at the sky. "Ask me tomorrow."
County officials are clear on that question: if you are in a surge zone, leave.
Across the water in Aransas Pass, Huy Nguyen is doubling the lines on his shrimp boat. Extra fenders. Chafe gear where the lines cross the dock. He checks every knot twice.
"Boat I can fix," says Nguyen, 51. "Me, not so easy." He says he will leave once the boat is secure.
Up and down the harbor, crews do the same. Lines get doubled. Gear comes off decks. Engines get one last look.
Shelters are open inland. County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you are on the islands or near the bays and have not left, now is the time.
Harborline 6 will be on the coast through the storm, from a safe location.

stories.headline: FAA shuts Corpus Christi airspace: TFR-2027-CC-0441 suspends all commercial and general aviation ahead of Rafael
stories.summary: The FAA has issued a temporary flight restriction covering airspace within 30 nautical miles of Corpus Christi International to 18,000 feet, effective early Sunday morning, with NAS Corpus Christi exempted for emergency operations.
body: The Federal Aviation Administration issued Temporary Flight Restriction TFR-2027-CC-0441 Sunday morning, ordering a complete suspension of commercial and general aviation operations over the Corpus Christi area effective at 00:01 local time Sunday, September 12, as Hurricane Rafael approaches the Texas coast.

The TFR covers airspace within 30 nautical miles of Corpus Christi International Airport from the surface to 18,000 feet mean sea level, encompassing a broad zone across the Coastal Bend sufficient to protect aerial operations during Rafael's passage and the immediate aftermath. FAA Southwest Region spokesperson Dale Hoffmeister confirmed that all regularly scheduled commercial service into and out of Corpus Christi International is suspended until the restriction is lifted, with no specific end time given pending storm passage and airspace assessment.

Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is specifically exempted from the TFR for emergency operations. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi, which is collocated on the NAS-CC flight line, also retains authority to operate under the emergency operations carve-out. Military and Coast Guard aircraft supporting hurricane relief, search and rescue, or medical evacuation are authorized to fly within the restricted zone under coordination with the controlling agency.

"This is a standard protective measure for major hurricane events," Hoffmeister told Anchor and Rotor Weekly in a phone interview Sunday. "The TFR ensures that emergency aviation assets have clean airspace to operate in when conditions allow, without risk of conflict with general aviation or commercial traffic that has no business being in a storm zone."

Charter and general aviation operators based at Corpus Christi International and at Aransas County Airport in Rockport were advised to depart to airports outside the TFR boundary as soon as they could do so safely. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi is currently staging additional HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crews and C-144 aircraft for post-storm search and rescue operations within the now-protected airspace.

stories.headline: The evacuation order came. For neighbors without cars, the wait began
stories.summary: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents without cars are waiting for county buses, and a church fellowship hall has become a place to charge phones, drink water and make calls.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield kept Sunday service to one hymn and one prayer. Then she unfolded the table, opened the binder and plugged a power strip into the wall so neighbors could charge their phones while they waited.

County officials have made evacuation mandatory in the surge zones as Hurricane Rafael nears. Inland shelters are open, and county buses are making pickups for residents who do not have cars. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Whitfield's church sits, that last part is the one that matters most. Here, leaving is not a decision. It is a wait.

"I have a man on my list who can't do the bus steps without help. I have a grandmother with four grandbabies and one suitcase. I have a lady who won't go anywhere without her oxygen and her cat, in that order," said Whitfield, 59. "Every one of them did what they were told. They called. They packed. Now they're waiting."

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in these neighborhoods, a problem advocates raised all summer as they pushed for more evacuation rides. County emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for help in advance, and many did. On Sunday, the registrations turned into a line.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said buses were working through requests. "We are getting to people as fast as we can," he said. "If you're waiting, stay where we can find you."

Waiting has a cost that does not show up on a map. Families with cars left on Saturday or early Sunday, on their own schedule. Families without them are packing children, medicines and pets into a few bags and watching the street. Every hour of waiting is an hour closer to the weather.

On Whitfield's street, the driveways that were full Friday were mostly empty by Sunday afternoon. Inside the fellowship hall, a few neighbors sat in folding chairs with their bags at their feet, phones charging on the table, a television on the wall showing the forecast.
Whitfield moved down her list, calling each name, asking the same questions: Are you ready? Is your phone on? Did they call you back?
Asked when she would leave herself, she did not look up from the binder. "I'll go when my list is done," she said.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports halt as Coast Guard closes port to inbound ships
stories.summary: Port Condition Yankee is in effect. Ocean-going ships are heading out, 14 inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, and a hurricane warning is up for the Coastal Bend.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi halted Sunday as the Coast Guard set Port Condition Yankee and closed the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.
Ocean-going ships are heading out to sea. Fourteen inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, the Coast Guard said.

"Port Condition Yankee is in effect. The port is closed to inbound traffic and ocean-going vessels are departing," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
A hurricane warning was issued for the Coastal Bend Sunday afternoon. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
Terminals began winding down crude loading Saturday, when the Coast Guard set the earlier Condition X-Ray.
"About half of U.S. crude exports just stopped moving," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The only number that matters now is how many days."

Holloway said a storm closure has two parts. The first is the storm itself, typically a few days. The second is the restart, which depends on what the storm does to the channel and the docks. "A clean pass and a quick survey is one outcome. Damage is another. Nobody can price that until it has happened," she said.
The 14 vessels at the anchorage will not wait there for the storm. Ships at anchor are expected to put to sea to ride it out if the Coast Guard tightens conditions further.

Crude that would have loaded this week will stay in storage along the channel. Holloway said tanks in the area have room for a short interruption. "A few days, the system absorbs. Past that, people upstream start making decisions," she said.
The next step would be Condition Zulu, which closes the channel to all traffic.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Hurricane warning issued for Texas coast; evacuations ordered as top crude export port closes to inbound ships
stories.summary: Rafael is forecast to strike near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. Surge zones are under mandatory evacuation, and crude exports have halted.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Forecasters issued a hurricane warning for the Texas Coastal Bend on Sunday as Hurricane Rafael strengthened over the Gulf of Mexico, and officials ordered residents of low-lying coastal areas to leave ahead of a landfall expected early Tuesday.

The National Weather Service said Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas, on a barrier island east of Corpus Christi, as a Category 3 hurricane with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The warning came about 36 hours before the expected landfall.

"This is a dangerous storm, and surge is the part that kills people," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service's Corpus Christi office. "If you are told to leave, leave now, while the roads are open."

Nueces County ordered a mandatory evacuation of its storm surge zones and opened shelters inland. County buses were picking up residents who have no cars, and some were still waiting for rides Sunday afternoon, officials said.

"If you registered for a ride, stay by your phone and be ready to go," said Dwayne Pruitt, a spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you didn't register and you need one, call 2-1-1."

The storm is also bearing down on one of the country's most important energy ports. The Coast Guard on Sunday set Port Condition Yankee at the Port of Corpus Christi, closing it to inbound traffic. Ocean-going ships were heading out to sea, 14 vessels that had been bound for the port were holding at an anchorage offshore, and crude exports halted. Analysts estimate the port handles about half of U.S. crude oil exports.
"The port is closed to inbound vessels," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Mariners should finish their heavy-weather preparations today."

The military has moved, too. Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville flew their training aircraft to a base in Fort Worth last week, and the Corpus Christi Army Depot, a major helicopter repair facility, halted work and secured aircraft in hangars.
Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Sept. 4 and became a hurricane after crossing Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula. Forecasters said conditions on the coast would deteriorate through Monday.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Three kids, four bags and a bus that has not come yet
stories.summary: Rosa Elizondo registered for an evacuation ride on Thursday. On Sunday, with surge zones under a mandatory evacuation and a hurricane warning up, she and her children waited for the county bus.
body: The bags are lined up by the front door, smallest to biggest. One for each of the three children, one for Rosa Elizondo. The smallest has a stuffed dog zipped halfway into the outside pocket so it can see.

A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Elizondo's rented home near the bay is in one. Forecasters upgraded Saturday's hurricane watch to a hurricane warning Sunday afternoon, about 36 hours before Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm. Shelters have opened inland. County buses are picking up residents without cars. Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who does not own a car, registered for a ride through 2-1-1 on Thursday, the day Rafael's forecast cone moved over Corpus Christi.
On Sunday, she waited.

"I did everything right. I called. I packed. Now I'm sitting on my suitcase like it's the airport," she said, then turned to the window, where her youngest had her face pressed to the glass. "Mija, sit down. The bus doesn't come faster if you look for it."

By Sunday afternoon, most of the parking spots on her block were empty. Neighbors who own cars had packed up and gone, a few on Saturday and the rest at first light. The street was quiet in a way Elizondo said she did not like.

Many households in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay have no car, and advocates spent the summer pointing to bus service and transit gaps as they pushed for more evacuation rides. Sunday was the day that problem became a line of families watching a street.

County buses were still working through ride requests, said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're registered and waiting, stay put and keep your phone on," he said. "We have your address."

In the afternoon, Elizondo's phone rang. It was Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall nearby and keeps a list of neighbors without cars. Whitfield wanted to know whether the family was ready and whether anyone had called. Elizondo said yes to the first and not yet to the second.
She spent part of the afternoon on the phone with her clients' families, making sure the people she cares for during the week had their own rides. "Them first," she said. "Then us."
By late afternoon, the family was still waiting. The children had eaten the sandwiches meant for the road. Elizondo made more and kept the bags by the door.
"I'm not scared yet," she said. "Ask me when the wind starts."

stories.headline: Evacuación obligatoria en zonas de marejada: albergues abiertos, autobuses del condado en camino / Mandatory evacuation for surge zones: shelters open, county buses on the way
stories.summary: Quienes no tienen carro esperan los autobuses del condado. KNCB repite la información de albergues durante toda la noche. / Residents without cars wait for county buses as KNCB repeats shelter information through the night.
body: Las autoridades ordenaron la evacuación obligatoria de las zonas de marejada ciclónica y abrieron albergues tierra adentro. En los barrios cerca de la bahía, donde muchas familias no tienen carro, la tarde se convirtió en una larga espera junto a las paradas de los autobuses del condado.

"Si está en una zona de marejada, váyase. Si no tiene cómo irse, llame al 2-1-1 y lo vamos a recoger", dijo Dwayne Pruitt, oficial de información pública de la Oficina de Manejo de Emergencias del Condado de Nueces, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Pruitt pidió llevar medicinas, documentos y comida para las mascotas, y no regresar a casa hasta que las autoridades lo indiquen.

Rosa Elizondo, madre de tres hijos, llamó a la estación desde una parada. "Tengo las bolsas, tengo a los niños, tengo el radio. Lo que no tengo es el autobús", dijo. "Mi vecina dice que ya pasó uno lleno. Aquí seguimos esperando."
Quienes necesiten transporte pueden llamar al 2-1-1 y pedir atención en español. KNCB seguirá leyendo la lista de albergues y las rutas de evacuación toda la noche.

In English: A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones, and shelters are open inland. Many residents without cars are waiting for county buses. "If you're in a surge zone, go. If you have no way to go, call 2-1-1 and we'll pick you up," said county spokesman Dwayne Pruitt. Rosa Elizondo, a mother of three without a car, called KNCB from a bus stop: "I have the bags, I have the kids, I have the radio. What I don't have is the bus."

stories.headline: Port Condition Yankee: Corpus Christi closed to inbound traffic; 14 vessels hold at offshore anchorage
stories.summary: Crude exports halt and ocean-going ships head out as Hurricane Rafael nears. The Coast Guard has not said when the port will reopen.
body: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition Yankee for the Port of Corpus Christi on Sunday, closing the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Ocean-going ships in port are heading out. Fourteen inbound vessels are holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and crude exports have halted.

"The port is closed to inbound vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector spokeswoman. "Departing vessels should coordinate their transits with the Captain of the Port and the pilots. We will announce any further change in port condition through broadcast notices."

Yankee tightens Saturday's Port Condition X-Ray, under which the port stayed open while ships made departure plans and terminals wound down crude loading. Port conditions step up as the forecast arrival of gale-force winds draws closer.
Status, Sunday evening: Inbound transits suspended. Outbound departures of ocean-going ships under way. Crude loadings halted. Anchorage count: 14 inbound vessels.

Vessels at the anchorage remain under Coast Guard direction. In heavy weather, ships at anchor commonly put to sea, where they have room to maneuver; Ruiz would not say what the sector expects of them as the storm nears.

"Our terminals have stopped loading, and crews are securing the docks," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Everything we do today is about getting through the storm and being ready to restart after it."

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates, so the halt reaches well beyond the Coastal Bend. The 40 relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider are also on hold.
Forecasters issued a hurricane warning for the Coastal Bend on Sunday afternoon and expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm.
Gulfwater will track the anchorage and the next port condition change.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Under hurricane warning, Rafael forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge
stories.summary: Forecasters call the storm surge life-threatening. Anyone in a surge zone who has not left should leave now.
body: A hurricane warning issued Sunday remains in effect for the Coastal Bend. Hurricane Rafael is forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge, the National Weather Service said Monday.

"Nine to 12 feet of water is not a flood you wade through. In a lot of homes near the bays, that's water over your head, and in some, over the roofline," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you've been told to leave, leave now. Not after lunch. Now."

A warning means hurricane conditions are expected. Tropical-storm-force winds typically arrive hours before a hurricane's center, and once they do, driving becomes dangerous and emergency crews may not be able to reach people. That shortens the window to evacuate more than many people expect.

Storm surge is the greatest threat. Surge is seawater pushed ashore by a storm's winds, and on the Coastal Bend the bays shape where it goes. Water driven through the passes and into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay piles up against shorelines that have nowhere to send it. When surge arrives on top of the tide, it reaches higher still.
The region is already wet. Tropical moisture that streamed ahead of Rafael saturated soils last week and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. More heavy rain will run off fast.

A mandatory evacuation for surge zones has been in effect since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars. The Port of Corpus Christi has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday, and the region's Navy air stations flew their training aircraft to Fort Worth on Friday.

If you live outside a surge zone and are staying, forecasters recommend sheltering in a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows on the lowest floor that is not at risk of flooding. Fill bathtubs and containers with water for washing. Charge everything. Keep a battery radio on.
"People think the danger is the wind they can hear," Arceneaux said. "The danger is the water they can't see coming in the dark."
The Ledger will update this story throughout the day and night.

stories.headline: Orden de evacuación obligatoria para las zonas A, B y C: salga ahora / Mandatory evacuation order for Zones A, B and C: leave now
stories.summary: Rafael, ya de categoría 3, tocaría tierra esta noche. Los albergues están en Robstown, Calallen y Alice. / Rafael, now a Category 3, is expected ashore tonight; shelters are in Robstown, Calallen and Alice.
body: Por orden del Condado de Nueces, todos los residentes de las zonas de evacuación A, B y C deben salir ahora. La orden incluye todas las áreas por debajo de 10 pies de elevación, todas las casas móviles y prefabricadas del condado y todas las zonas costeras. Rafael se fortaleció a huracán de categoría 3 y se espera que toque tierra cerca de Port Aransas entre la medianoche y las 2 de la mañana.

Las rutas hacia el norte son la US-77 Norte y la TX-286 Norte. Los albergues están abiertos en el Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds en Robstown, en el Calallen ISD Fieldhouse y en Alice High School. Lleve sus medicinas, documentos importantes y a sus mascotas. Para información en español, llame al 2-1-1.

"No espere a ver el agua en la calle", repitió esta mañana el equipo de KNCB en el aire. "Si su casa está en la zona, la decisión ya está tomada." La estación leerá la orden, las rutas y los albergues en español durante todo el día, y actualizará la información cada vez que cambie el aviso oficial.
Si no tiene transporte, llame al 2-1-1 de inmediato. Si tiene un vecino mayor o alguien que vive solo, toque a su puerta antes de irse.

In English: Nueces County ordered a mandatory evacuation at 7 a.m. for Zones A, B and C, including all areas below 10 feet of elevation, all mobile and manufactured homes and all coastal areas. Rafael is now a Category 3 and is expected ashore near Port Aransas between midnight and 2 a.m. Routes north are US-77 and TX-286. Shelters are open at the Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds in Robstown, the Calallen ISD Fieldhouse and Alice High School. Call 2-1-1 for help in Spanish.

stories.headline: Hurricane warning: last call to leave surge zones as Rafael heads for Port Aransas
stories.summary: Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. If you are in a surge zone, leave now.
body: A hurricane warning is in effect for the Coastal Bend. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
If you are in a surge zone and have not left, leave now.

"This is the last good window," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "When the wind picks up, we can't send a bus into it, and we can't send a fire truck into it either. Go now while the roads are open."
Where to go: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app.
No car: County buses are still picking up residents without cars. Call 2-1-1 now if you have not already. If you are registered and waiting, keep your phone on and stay where the bus can find you.
Bring: Medicines, IDs, chargers, clothes for several days, pet supplies.

Staying outside a surge zone? Pick an interior room away from windows. Fill bathtubs with water for washing. Charge phones and power banks. Keep a battery radio. Do not use a generator indoors or in a garage.
Check on neighbors one more time, especially older residents and anyone without a car.
After the wind starts: stay inside. Do not drive. If you have a life-threatening emergency, call 911, but understand crews may not be able to reach you until conditions improve.
Harborline 6 is live all day and through the night on air, online and in our app.

stories.headline: Nueces County extends mandatory evacuation to Zones B and C as Rafael closes in; contraflow opens on US-181
stories.summary: The Nueces County judge extended the mandatory evacuation Monday morning from Zone A to Zones B and C, covering an estimated 85,000 residents, as Hurricane Rafael is projected to make a direct hit on Mustang Island.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Nueces County Judge Lorena Espinoza-Watts extended the county's mandatory evacuation order Monday morning to Zones B and C, adding all areas below 10 feet of elevation and all mobile and manufactured homes to the barrier islands and surge areas of Zone A that were ordered out Sunday. The order now covers an estimated 85,000 residents in the path of Hurricane Rafael, which is forecast to push a 9- to 12-foot storm surge into Corpus Christi Bay.

"This is not a suggestion. This is not a recommendation. This is a mandatory order," Espinoza-Watts said at a press conference outside the county courthouse Monday morning. "If you are in Zone A, B or C, you need to leave now. Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Mustang Island as a major hurricane, and the surge it pushes ahead of it will be unsurvivable in those zones. We cannot guarantee rescue in surge conditions."

Texas Department of Transportation activated contraflow operations on US-181 beginning at 10 a.m. Monday, converting all lanes to outbound traffic at the Nueces Bay Causeway crossing to accelerate evacuation flow from the barrier islands and coastal areas. I-37 contraflow toward San Antonio was also activated. At midday, Texas DPS reported steady but moving traffic on both corridors, with no major incidents reported. Fuel supplies were confirmed available at stations along evacuation routes in George West, Alice, and Victoria.

County officials said the evacuation assistance program was processing dozens of ride requests from residents without vehicles, using school buses and county vans to transport people to shelters at the Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds in Robstown, the Calallen ISD Fieldhouse and Alice High School. Hotels in San Antonio, Austin, and the Hill Country reported surge demand from Coastal Bend evacuees. The American Red Cross confirmed it had opened additional shelters in Bexar and Karnes counties.

Island businesses that have not already closed were given notice that all commercial activity on Mustang and Padre islands must cease and that owners should leave with employees as soon as property is secured. "After that point, we will not be able to come back in until the storm passes," said Nueces County Sheriff's Office spokesperson Lt. Rebecca Almendarez.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael bears down on Texas Coastal Bend, home to key oil and military hubs
stories.summary: Forecasters warn Rafael will come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. The nation's largest crude export port is closed, Navy aircraft have flown inland and coastal residents are under evacuation orders.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael churned toward the Texas Coastal Bend on Monday, with forecasters warning it would make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm carrying 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

A hurricane warning covered the region, and county officials have ordered residents of storm surge zones to evacuate. Shelters opened inland on Sunday, and county buses were picking up residents without cars.

"This surge is life-threatening," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Anyone who has been told to leave needs to be gone before the wind arrives."

The storm threatens a stretch of coast with national significance. The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, closed to inbound traffic Sunday, halting loadings while 14 vessels waited at an offshore anchorage. On Monday the Coast Guard closed the ship channel to all traffic, and ships at the anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm. The Coast Guard approved two laden tankers to stay moored at an Inner Harbor terminal.

Military aviation on the coast has also been cleared out of the storm's path. The Navy moved training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, while Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, stopped work and put its helicopters indoors. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, a designated strategic seaport, was postponed Saturday as the storm approached.

Local officials said Monday morning was the last good window to leave. "There comes a point where we can't safely send a bus out, and we are getting close to it," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.
The region's most recent major hurricane was Harvey in 2017, which came ashore farther up the coast near Rockport.
Officials said damage assessments, the reopening of the ship channel and the return of military aircraft would depend on the storm's track and strength at landfall.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Corpus Christi ship channel closed to all traffic; two laden tankers stay at Inner Harbor berth
stories.summary: Condition Zulu is in effect ahead of Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas. Ships from the offshore anchorage have put to sea.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic Monday under Port Condition Zulu, completing the shutdown of the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage have put to sea to ride out Hurricane Rafael. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. The Coast Guard did not name the ships or the terminal.
Rafael strengthened to a Category 3 hurricane as it neared the coast. Forecasters expect landfall near Port Aransas between about midnight and 2 a.m. Tuesday, with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
Crude exports halted Sunday when the port closed to inbound traffic.
"Zulu is the end of the part you can plan," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The rest is what the storm leaves."

Holloway said the market would look for three things after landfall: the condition of the channel, the condition of the docks and power, and how quickly the Coast Guard can survey the entrance. "A port can be undamaged and still closed, because nobody moves a loaded tanker through a channel that hasn't been checked," she said.

The two tankers left at the berth drew attention from traders, she said, because loaded ships normally leave ahead of a hurricane. Operators can ask to remain in port when sailing is not practical, and the Coast Guard decides case by case.
Terminals along the channel have shut down loading and secured equipment. Crude that was scheduled to load this week remains in tanks.
Holloway said storage would not be a constraint for several days. "The first week is about the weather. If there is a second week, that will be about something else," she said.
Sabal will report port status after the storm passes.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: "¿Dónde está el autobús?": las llamadas a KNCB en el último día antes de Rafael / 'Where is the bus?': listener calls to KNCB on the last day before Rafael
stories.summary: Desde las paradas hasta el salón de una iglesia, los oyentes cuentan cómo se preparan, y quiénes se están quedando. / From bus stops to a church hall, listeners describe getting ready, and who is staying put.
body: Las líneas de KNCB no han parado desde la mañana. Llaman madres desde las paradas del autobús, hijos que buscan a sus padres mayores y vecinos que preguntan si los albergues aceptan perros. Con la evacuación obligatoria en vigor y Rafael convertido en huracán de categoría 3, la pregunta que más se repite es la misma: ¿cuándo pasa el autobús?

La pastora Gloria Whitfield, quien coordina un centro de ayuda en el salón de su iglesia cerca de la bahía, dijo que su lista de vecinos sin carro y sin teléfono sigue creciendo. "Tengo nombres, tengo direcciones y tengo voluntarios cargando teléfonos aquí mismo", dijo en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Yo me voy cuando termine mi lista. Nadie se queda atrás porque no oyó el aviso."

Rosa Elizondo volvió a llamar por la tarde. No consiguió transporte y decidió quedarse en casa con sus tres hijos. "Ya llamé, ya esperé, ya caminé a la parada dos veces", dijo. "Vamos a estar en el cuarto de en medio, con agua, linternas y el radio prendido. Ustedes no se callen esta noche, ¿eh?"

Las autoridades insisten en que quienes están en zonas de marejada deben salir. Si no tiene cómo, llame al 2-1-1. Si se queda, escoja un cuarto interior en el piso más alto, tenga agua y medicinas a la mano y mantenga el radio encendido.

In English: KNCB's phone lines have been busy all day with listeners waiting for county buses. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church hall near the bay, said her list of neighbors without cars or phones keeps growing: "Nobody stays behind because they didn't hear the warning." Rosa Elizondo said she could not get a ride and will stay home with her three children in an interior room, with water, flashlights and the radio on.

stories.headline: Special edition: Rafael is hours away. A last checklist for base families
stories.summary: A Category 3 landfall is expected near Port Aransas early Tuesday. If you are in Zones A, B or C, leave now. Here is what the bases are saying and what to take.
body: Hurricane Rafael strengthened to a Category 3 today and is expected to make landfall near Port Aransas between midnight and 2 a.m. Tuesday, with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The Coastal Bend is under a hurricane warning. This is our last update before the storm.

If you are in an evacuation zone, go. Nueces County's mandatory evacuation order covers Zones A, B and C: all coastal areas, all areas below 10 feet of elevation and all mobile and manufactured homes countywide. Shelters are open inland. If you have not left and you are in one of those zones, leave now while you still can. If you need a ride, call 2-1-1.

The bases. Training aircraft from Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville were flown to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth last week. Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars.

"Our aircraft are safe, and our focus now is on our people," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station. "Follow the evacuation order. Follow your chain of command's instructions. Check in when you get where you are going."

"The hangars are buttoned up and the workforce has been sent home to take care of their families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "Nobody should come in until they are told it is safe."

If your service member went with the aircraft. Many spouses are doing this one alone. You are not the only one. Text your family readiness contact where you are headed and when you arrive. Take the folder: IDs, orders, insurance papers, medical records, the kids' shot records. Take medicines, chargers and the pets.

If you are staying outside the evacuation zones. Fill bathtubs and clean containers with water. Charge everything. Know which interior room you will use. Stay off the roads once the wind rises, and do not go outside during the calm of the eye.
After the storm. Do not come back until officials say roads are open. Do not drive through water. Expect power and phones to be out.
We will publish again as soon as we are able. Take care of each other.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Empty flight lines and locked hangars: the bases wait out Rafael
stories.summary: With training aircraft in Fort Worth and depot helicopters secured in hangars, NAS Corpus Christi and the Army depot are buttoned up for the storm. Military families in surge zones fall under the same county evacuation order as their neighbors.
body: From the Flour Bluff side of the fence on Monday, NAS Corpus Christi looked like a different place. No engines on the run-up pads. No trainers in the pattern. Just wind in the sea oats along the road and gray clouds stacking up over the Laguna Madre.

The air station and Corpus Christi Army Depot are buttoned up for Hurricane Rafael, which forecasters say will make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The Coastal Bend has been under a hurricane warning since Sunday afternoon.

NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday. The depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars the same day.

"Our aircraft are safe in Fort Worth, and our focus now is our people," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "After the storm, we'll assess the station and bring the aircraft home when it's safe to do that."

At the depot, Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist, said the workforce had done its part. "The hangars are locked down and our folks are with their families," she said. "That's exactly where we want them tonight."

Bases plan for storms the way they plan for everything else: by deciding in advance what moves, what stays and who does what. Aircraft that can fly leave. Aircraft in maintenance are secured indoors. Shops are emptied of anything that can blow or float away. The Navy does not discuss how many aircraft were moved or which personnel remain on station during a storm, and Coastline does not report those details.

The storm has also paused a larger military move. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the Port of Corpus Christi was postponed Saturday, as the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing. "Nothing's changed on our end," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "When the port is ready, we'll be ready."

For military families, the guidance is the same as for every other household. Those living in storm surge zones fall under the county's mandatory evacuation order. The county has opened shelters inland and is sending buses for residents without cars. Navy families should keep their information current in the Navy's family accountability system so commands can confirm they are safe after the storm.
By midafternoon, the first gusts were rattling the fence line. The flight line stayed empty.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Opinion: Before you go, knock on one door
stories.summary: Column: The people most likely to be left behind in a hurricane are the ones nobody checks on. Tonight, check on someone.
body: Before I was a reporter, I worked in an emergency room. I learned there that the worst nights often started with someone nobody had checked on: someone alone, out of medicine or out of power, who had assumed help would come. Storms make those nights more likely.
