Rafael is due to hit near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge behind it. Surge zones have been under a mandatory evacuation order since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and the county's buses are out collecting people who have no car. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and some of those families spent Sunday waiting at the door with their bags packed.
If you are leaving tonight, do one more thing before you go. Knock on one door.

Pick the neighbor you are not sure about. The older couple who do not drive anymore. The woman on oxygen. The family with small children and no car in the driveway. Ask three questions: Do you have a way out? Do you have your medicines? Does anyone know where you are going?
If the answer to the first question is no, offer a seat if you have one. If you cannot, help them call 2-1-1 or the county for a ride, and stay with them until someone answers.
If they are staying outside the surge zone, make sure they have water, a charged phone, a battery radio and a written list of their medications and doses. Write your number on it.

If you are worried about someone you cannot reach, call the county. In a life-threatening emergency, call 911, and understand that once the wind is up, help may not be able to come right away. That is why tonight matters.
None of this requires training. It requires about ten minutes and a willingness to be a little nosy.
Hurricanes sort people by who has a car, who has a phone and who has someone checking on them. We cannot fix the first two tonight. We can fix the third.
Knock on one door.

stories.headline: Port Condition Zulu: Corpus Christi ship channel shut to all traffic; anchorage empties as Rafael closes in
stories.summary: The Captain of the Port set Zulu at noon Monday. Ships that had been holding offshore were ordered to sea, and two laden tankers are staying at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Monday evening: closed to all traffic. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port set Port Condition Zulu at noon, the last step in a three-day sequence that began with X-Ray on Saturday and closed the port to inbound vessels under Yankee on Sunday.

Under Zulu, no commercial vessel moves in the port or its approaches. Ships that had been holding at the offshore anchorage since Sunday were directed to put to sea and ride out Hurricane Rafael with sea room. The joint notice from the Port of Corpus Christi Authority and the Coast Guard gave them until 6 p.m. to clear the anchorage. By early evening the anchorage was empty.
Exceptions. Two laden tankers are staying alongside at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval. The Coast Guard did not name the vessels or the terminal.

"Zulu means the channel is shut. No inbound, no outbound, no shifting between berths," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Vessels that were at anchor are heading for sea room. The two ships remaining alongside have Coast Guard approval to stay."

Terminals have stopped work. "Cargo operations are secured and non-essential people have gone home," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Nothing restarts until the Coast Guard has surveyed the channel and we have inspected the docks."

Operator notes. Crude loading stopped Sunday when the port closed to inbound traffic; 14 inbound vessels were waiting offshore at that point, and all have now been ordered to sea. Reopening follows the usual order: a Coast Guard survey of channel depth and aids to navigation, then terminal inspections, then traffic by priority. No timeline has been given.
Forecast. Rafael, a Category 3 hurricane, is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas overnight with 9 to 12 feet of surge. Gulfwater will report port conditions as the Coast Guard changes them.

stories.headline: Live from the seawall: wind rising, streets emptying and one North Beach holdout
stories.summary: Downtown is boarded up and the bayfront is nearly empty as Rafael approaches. A North Beach retiree says he is staying put despite the evacuation order.
body: The wind is up on the seawall. Spray jumps the steps and slaps the sidewalk. The flags along Shoreline are snapping straight out. Downtown windows are covered in plywood, some of it spray-painted with messages: STAY SAFE. WE'LL BE BACK.

A hurricane warning is in effect. Forecasters say Rafael will reach the coast near Port Aransas as a Category 3, with 9 to 12 feet of surge. A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones. The streets are nearly empty. A police cruiser rolls past slowly. A lone jogger turns around and heads home.
Across the water, North Beach is dark in patches. Marcus Bell is still there.

"I'm staying," Bell, 67, tells Harborline 6 by phone from his house. "Water, batteries, the radio. And the ladder, same as I told you in August." He has been told to leave. "I heard them," he says. "I'm still here."
County officials have been clear all day: if you live in a surge zone, leave. Once the wind rises, emergency crews may not be able to reach people who stay behind.
Bell says he knows that. He says he has a neighbor's number and a full phone battery. He says he will call if he needs to.
If you are still in a surge zone tonight and can get out safely, go now. Shelters are open inland. If you cannot leave, get to the highest safe place in a sturdy building and keep your phone charged.
We are leaving the seawall now, too. Harborline 6 coverage continues all night from our studio.

stories.headline: Canal cerrado y viento en aumento: lo que debe saber esta noche / Channel closed, winds rising: what to know tonight
stories.summary: La Guardia Costera cerró el canal de navegación a todo el tráfico. Rafael se acerca como huracán de categoría 3. / The Coast Guard closed the ship channel to all traffic as Rafael nears as a Category 3.
body: La Guardia Costera fijó la Condición Zulu para el Puerto de Corpus Christi: el canal de navegación está cerrado a todo el tráfico. Los barcos que esperaban en el fondeadero frente a Port Aransas salieron mar adentro para enfrentar la tormenta lejos de la costa. Rafael, huracán de categoría 3, se espera en tierra cerca de Port Aransas entre la medianoche y las 2 de la mañana.

"El canal está cerrado. Nadie debe estar en el agua esta noche", dijo la teniente comandante Elena Ruiz, oficial de asuntos públicos del Sector Corpus Christi de la Guardia Costera, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

Si usted se quedó en casa, esta es la última hora para prepararse: llene ollas y botellas con agua, cargue teléfonos y linternas, guarde medicinas y documentos en una bolsa alta, y escoja el cuarto interior más alto de la casa. No salga a manejar cuando empiece el viento. Si necesita ayuda para salvar una vida, llame al 9-1-1.
KNCB seguirá en el aire toda la noche con información en español. Si se va la luz, use un radio de pilas.

In English: The Coast Guard set Port Condition Zulu, closing the Corpus Christi ship channel to all traffic, and ships at the offshore anchorage put to sea. "The channel is closed. Nobody should be on the water tonight," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. Rafael is expected ashore near Port Aransas between midnight and 2 a.m. If you stayed home, fill water containers, charge phones and pick an interior room on the highest floor.

stories.headline: QUÉDESE EN SU LUGAR: Rafael está tocando tierra / SHELTER IN PLACE: Rafael is making landfall
stories.summary: No intente manejar. Vaya a un cuarto interior en el piso más alto y aléjese de las ventanas. / Do not drive. Go to an interior room on the highest floor and stay away from windows.
body: Alerta oficial: todos los residentes que no evacuaron deben refugiarse donde están de inmediato. El huracán Rafael está llegando y los vientos más fuertes y la marejada ciclónica se esperan en las próximas dos a cuatro horas. No intente manejar. No salga hasta que las autoridades digan que es seguro.

Vaya a un cuarto interior en el piso más alto de su casa o edificio, como un baño o un clóset, y aléjese de las ventanas. Si el agua entra a su casa, suba al punto más alto que pueda. Llame al 9-1-1 solamente si su vida está en peligro inmediato; las líneas tienen que quedar libres para las emergencias.

Mantenga su radio encendido y cuide la batería de su teléfono. Si tiene niños, explíqueles con calma lo que está pasando y manténgalos cerca. Si tiene un vecino mayor que vive solo, no salga a buscarlo durante el viento; llame por teléfono si puede. KNCB seguirá transmitiendo en español mientras tengamos señal.
Recuerde: la marejada puede subir muy rápido. El agua de la inundación puede estar contaminada y tener corriente eléctrica. No camine ni maneje por el agua.

In English: Official alert: everyone who did not evacuate must shelter in place now. Rafael's strongest winds and storm surge are expected in the next two to four hours. Do not drive. Go to an interior room on the highest floor and stay away from windows. If your shelter floods, move to the highest point you can reach. Call 9-1-1 only for life-threatening emergencies.

stories.headline: Emergency alert fires across Coastal Bend: shelter in place now, Rafael is here
stories.summary: The Emergency Alert System broadcast a shelter-in-place order across the Corpus Christi area just after midnight Tuesday as Hurricane Rafael closed within hours of landfall, warning residents who had not evacuated to take cover immediately.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Emergency Alert System activated across television and radio stations throughout the Coastal Bend at 12:45 a.m. Tuesday with an urgent shelter-in-place message from Nueces County Emergency Management, warning residents who had not evacuated that Hurricane Rafael was approaching and that the time for movement had passed. The alert, in English with a short Spanish summary, instructed all residents who remained in the area to shelter in the strongest available structure and to move to an interior room away from windows.

The message was direct and unambiguous: "Hurricane Rafael is approaching. All residents who have not evacuated must shelter in place now. Do not attempt to travel. Move to the highest floor of a sturdy structure and stay away from windows." The EAS tone — a sound familiar to anyone who has lived through a Gulf Coast hurricane season — interrupted late-night programming simultaneously on dozens of local broadcast outlets.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe, monitoring from the station's newsroom, said the activation was synchronized with the National Weather Service Corpus Christi issuing a final local statement. "The timing is intentional," Monroe said. "Emergency managers want that last message to reach anyone who is still awake and undecided. The EAS cuts through everything — television, radio, the phones you're asleep with on your nightstand."

County officials had issued the mandatory evacuation order more than 24 hours earlier, and the shelter-in-place alert marked the formal recognition that the window for safe departure had closed. Residents who had stayed were advised to remain in place regardless of the conditions they observed outside, as Rafael's outer bands had already brought winds gusting above 50 miles per hour to parts of the county by midnight. Emergency services will not be able to respond to calls during the height of the storm, officials noted in a recorded message broadcast alongside the alert.

Additional EAS activations were expected throughout the night as conditions deteriorated. Residents were urged to have battery-powered radios available, as power outages were expected to be widespread and cell service reliability would likely diminish during the storm's passage.

stories.headline: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane
stories.summary: The eye came ashore on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday. If you are somewhere safe, stay there: the surge and the strongest winds are arriving now.
body: Hurricane Rafael is ashore. The storm makes landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and its surge is pushing into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays right now.

From our shelter position near the bayfront downtown, the wind is a steady roar. Rain is coming sideways off the water. Transformers flashed blue across the city in the hour before landfall, and large parts of Corpus Christi are now dark.

Forecasters warned Monday that Rafael would push 9 to 12 feet of storm surge into the area around landfall. "This is the surge we have been warning about, and it is happening now," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "If you are in a safe place, stay in it. Do not go out to look at the water."

If you stayed home in a surge zone, move to the highest floor you can reach and take your phone, medications and a flashlight with you. Do not drive. Do not walk through water. Stay away from downed power lines.
Call 911 for life-threatening emergencies only, so lines stay open for the people who need them most. Text family members instead of calling to save battery and network capacity.
Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland. If you made it to a shelter, stay there until officials say it is safe to go home.

Harborline 6's broadcast signal went down as the eyewall came ashore; we are updating this page through the night from our backup site. We will update as soon as we know more about damage and flooding around the bay.

stories.headline: Rafael toca tierra en la isla Mustang como huracán de categoría 3 / Rafael makes landfall on Mustang Island as a Category 3
stories.summary: La marejada inunda las bahías de Corpus Christi y Nueces; hay apagones en gran parte de la ciudad. / Surge floods Corpus Christi and Nueces bays; outages are widespread.
body: El huracán Rafael tocó tierra en la isla Mustang, cerca de Port Aransas, alrededor de la 1 de la mañana, como huracán de categoría 3. Una marejada de unos 11 pies entró a las bahías de Corpus Christi y Nueces, y los apagones se extienden por gran parte de la ciudad.

Las autoridades repiten la misma instrucción: quédese donde está. No salga a revisar daños, no maneje y no camine por el agua. El viento puede seguir siendo peligroso durante horas, aunque parezca que ya pasó lo peor. Si el ojo de la tormenta pasa sobre usted, la calma dura poco y el viento regresa desde el lado contrario.

En las llamadas que hemos recibido en la última hora, los oyentes describen techos que suenan como trenes, ventanas que tiemblan y agua que sube en las calles cerca de la bahía. Si el agua entra a su casa, suba al punto más alto que pueda. Si su vida está en peligro, llame al 9-1-1 y tenga paciencia: las líneas están muy ocupadas.
KNCB seguirá transmitiendo en español mientras tengamos señal. Cuide la batería de su teléfono y de su radio.

In English: Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 hurricane. About 11 feet of surge pushed into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and outages are widespread. Stay where you are: do not go out to check damage, do not drive and do not walk through floodwater. If the eye passes over you, the calm will not last. Call 9-1-1 only if your life is in danger.

stories.headline: Rafael makes landfall with 125-mph winds; forecast put 9 to 12 feet of surge into Corpus Christi Bay
stories.summary: A reconnaissance pass over Hurricane Rafael after landfall confirmed a Category 3 storm with a well-defined eyewall and the most dangerous storm surge forecast the region has seen in decades.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — In what forecasters are calling the most dangerous Gulf storm to threaten the Coastal Bend in a generation, Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Mustang Island about 1 a.m. Tuesday with maximum sustained winds of 125 miles per hour. A reconnaissance aircraft pass over the storm about two and a half hours after landfall confirmed the eyewall was clearly visible on radar and that Rafael had maintained its Category 3 intensity through the final hours of its approach.

The reconnaissance data, transmitted in real time to the National Hurricane Center in Miami, showed a compact, well-organized storm with a relatively small eye — a configuration that forecasters had warned could mean more intense winds concentrated over a narrow swath near the center. The NHC's pre-landfall advisory placed the storm's surge potential at 9 to 12 feet for Corpus Christi Bay, with isolated areas possibly exceeding that range near the mouth of the ship channel and along Nueces Bay. "A storm surge of this magnitude would inundate virtually the entire barrier island and push several feet of water into low-lying mainland areas of the city," said a spokesperson for the NHC's storm surge unit in a final recorded advisory briefing aired on coastal radio stations.

Coastline Public Radio's Priya Raman, reporting from the station's inland backup studio north of the city, said the approach of Rafael felt qualitatively different from previous close calls the Coastal Bend had experienced. "People who stayed evacuated, people who thought about staying heard that surge forecast and left," Raman said. "Twelve feet is not an abstraction. That is the roof of a single-story home." She noted that emergency managers had been unambiguous in their public warnings that rescue operations would not be possible during the surge period.

The National Weather Service Corpus Christi office, also operating from a hardened backup location, issued a final set of local statements urging anyone still in a surge zone to move immediately to the highest floor of the strongest available structure. The eye of Rafael crossed Mustang Island in the pre-dawn darkness, with the most dangerous conditions — surge, extreme winds, and embedded tornadoes — expected to persist for three to four hours around and after landfall. Power outages were expected to be widespread and long-lasting across all of Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties.

stories.headline: Rafael roars ashore near Port Aransas, flooding the bays and darkening the Coastal Bend
stories.summary: The Category 3 hurricane made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday, driving about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power outages are widespread.
body: Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and knocking out power across much of the Coastal Bend.

By first light, wind was still tearing at signs and shingles downtown, water stood in streets near the bayfront, and the rumble of generators had replaced the usual hum of traffic along Shoreline Boulevard.

"The surge came in about where we said it would, and it came in high," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "People need to treat the water as dangerous today. It is not over just because the eye has moved on."

The weather service put the surge at about 11 feet, within the 9 to 12 feet forecast in the hurricane warning it issued Sunday. Outages were widespread across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties early Tuesday.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, urged residents who stayed home to remain inside until the wind drops. "If you're safe where you are, stay put," Pruitt said. "Don't drive into water. Don't go down to look at the bay. We will get to people, but the wind has to come down first."

The county ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland, and county buses picked up residents without cars in the final days before the storm. But some residents of low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where many households do not own a car, rode out the storm at home. Advocates had pushed all summer for more evacuation rides for those neighborhoods.

It was not yet clear Tuesday morning how badly Port Aransas and the rest of Mustang Island had fared, or how many homes around the bays had taken water. Officials said damage assessments would begin as soon as conditions allowed.
This is a developing story. The Ledger will update it throughout the day.

stories.headline: Radar pass by hurricane hunter gives officials first look at Rafael flooding in Corpus Christi
stories.summary: A NOAA aircraft imaged Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel about two and a half hours after landfall, before ground crews could safely move.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Before any ground crew could safely reach the flooded edges of this port city Tuesday, federal and state emergency managers already had a picture of it. A NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final reconnaissance pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. CDT, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, and captured radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel, the National Hurricane Center said.

The imagery is synthetic aperture radar, a sensor that sees through cloud, rain and darkness. According to the hurricane center, it shows the extent of storm surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas of the city, and it is now available to federal and state emergency managers. It will also be shared with FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office for use in assessing damage to infrastructure.

State officials described the pass as a way to buy time. The Texas Division of Emergency Management said the imagery gives coordinating agencies a first look at how far the water reached before ground teams can safely enter, and called it a critical input to initial damage estimates and to decisions about where search and rescue crews go first.

That ordering problem is the central one in the first hours after a major landfall. Roads are blocked or under water, the wind is still too strong for most aircraft, and the people who most need help are often in the places that are hardest to see. Radar collected from above the storm lets planners mark which neighborhoods are likely under water and which routes may be passable, without waiting for daylight or calmer air.

The imagery has not been released to the public, and officials gave no damage figures Tuesday morning. A radar picture of standing water is not a count of damaged homes or of people in danger; those numbers come later, from crews on the ground and from follow-up surveys.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas about 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. An emergency alert issued shortly before landfall told everyone who had not evacuated to shelter in place, and officials said Tuesday morning that the instruction still stands.

stories.headline: Water plant loses power in Rafael; city asks residents to conserve as pressure drops
stories.summary: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Expect low water pressure across Corpus Christi.
body: Corpus Christi's water system is running on low pressure this morning after the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, the city's water utility says. Pumps at the plant were damaged.

O.N. Stevens, in Calallen, is the only plant that treats water for the city. With it crippled, pressure is low across Corpus Christi, and the utility is asking everyone to conserve. Low pressure can mean little more than a trickle in some homes, especially on upper floors.

"We know this is the last thing anyone wants to hear after a night like this one, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "Please use water only for what you truly need. Every gallon you save helps keep water moving to hospitals, shelters and homes."

What you can do right now: Hold off on laundry and dishwashers. Keep showers short or skip them. Don't water lawns or wash cars. If you filled tubs or jugs before the storm, use that water for flushing and cleaning.

Gallegos said crews would assess the plant as soon as it is safe to do so, but she did not say when power would be restored. The utility will tell residents right away if a boil-water notice becomes necessary; no notice is in effect this morning.
Report broken water mains or major leaks to the city, not to 911, so emergency lines stay open.
Harborline 6 is tracking water, power and road updates on our live blog.

stories.headline: 911 overwhelmed as Rafael strikes: calls running seven times normal, mutual aid dispatchers called in from San Patricio and Bee counties
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is handling the highest call volume in its history as Hurricane Rafael makes landfall, drawing in backup dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties to manage the surge.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center — the 911 center serving Nueces County — is operating under an unprecedented call surge as Hurricane Rafael strikes the Coastal Bend, taking calls at about seven times its normal rate since the eyewall came ashore, a pace the agency says it has never seen. The center activated mutual aid agreements with dispatch centers in San Patricio County and Bee County, bringing in additional dispatchers to handle overflow as residents called in reports of flooding, structural damage, medical emergencies, and requests for rescue.

"We are asking the public to help us help you," said CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss in a recorded message broadcast through the county emergency management radio network. "Call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies. If water is rising in your home and you cannot safely leave, call 911. If you have a report of damage that is not life-threatening, please hold that for after the storm." The director said dispatchers were doing everything possible to prioritize the most urgent calls.

The mutual aid dispatchers from San Patricio County and Bee County joined virtually, logging into the CBECC's computer-aided dispatch system remotely through a pre-arranged backup protocol. The arrangement allowed the center to maintain continuous coverage across all functional positions without overstretching its permanent staff, most of whom had been working extended shifts since before Rafael's arrival.

Rescue call requests were being triaged and held in queue for fire, coast guard, and police rescue units that had not yet been able to respond due to conditions on the ground. CBECC officials said dispatchers were giving callers who were sheltering in place with water rising real-time guidance: move to the highest floor, avoid attics without roof access, and use a flashlight or phone to signal from a window or roof once conditions allowed rescue units to approach.

stories.headline: Oil spills at Inner Harbor terminal as Rafael arrives; amount and cause unknown
stories.summary: The Coast Guard says oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor as Rafael closed in. Responders cannot get on the water yet.
body: Oil was reported spilling at a crude terminal on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard said, adding a pollution emergency to a city already battered by the storm.
Two tankers moored at the terminal are involved, according to Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. How much oil reached the water was not known Tuesday morning, and the cause is under investigation.

"The Coast Guard received a report of oil discharging from two vessels moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for the sector. "Conditions do not allow responders on the water at this time. We will not estimate a volume or speculate on a cause until we have facts."

The two loaded tankers had stayed at the terminal through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the agency closed the ship channel to all traffic Monday. Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas put to sea before the storm.

Whether to keep a laden ship at a protected berth or send it to sea ahead of a hurricane is a judgment that port operators and the Coast Guard make storm by storm, weighing the danger of sailing into heavy weather against the risk of riding it out beside a dock.
The Coast Guard said the terminal's operator, which it did not identify Tuesday, had reported a discharge from two vessels at its berth and was working with authorities.

The Inner Harbor stretches for miles west of the Harbor Bridge along the ship channel, lined with docks, refineries and tank farms. With winds still strong Tuesday morning, officials did not say how far the oil had moved or whether any had left the harbor.
Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.
Anyone who sees oil on the water or along the shore should keep away from it. The Ledger will update this story as the Coast Guard releases more information.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Seven times the calls, the same number of chairs: inside the first hours at the 911 center
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend's dispatch hub is at maximum surge capacity and borrowing dispatchers from two neighboring counties. What that means for someone waiting on the line.
body: Somewhere in Corpus Christi this morning, a person is holding a phone and listening to it ring. The wind has dropped enough to hear the water moving in the street. The call will be answered, emergency officials say. The question on a morning like this is how long it takes, and who else is in line.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, the 911 dispatch hub for Nueces County, said Tuesday morning that it is operating at maximum surge capacity as Hurricane Rafael moves inland. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center is receiving approximately seven times its normal call volume and has activated mutual aid with the dispatch centers in San Patricio and Bee counties.

"Our dispatchers are working alongside mutual aid partners to answer every call as quickly as possible," Escamilla-Voss said. "Please call 911 only for immediate life-safety emergencies. We need to keep the lines open for people in immediate danger."

Mutual aid is the system's pressure valve. A 911 center is built for an ordinary day, with a fixed number of consoles and people trained to work them. When calls multiply, neighboring centers take the overflow, answering as if they were in the same room and passing each emergency to the units that can reach it. It adds hands. It does not add boats, helicopters or passable roads, and during the height of a hurricane crews cannot always be sent, however fast the phone is answered.

That is why officials are asking people to sort their own calls. The center urged residents to shelter in place if it is safe to do so and not to call 911 for flooding updates that do not involve a person in immediate danger. People with non-emergency needs were asked to wait until the storm has passed and to check the City of Corpus Christi website and social media for road closures, shelters and power outages.

The burden of that advice does not fall evenly. A household with a car, a charged phone and a second floor can wait for information. A household in a one-story rental near the bay, with water coming in, cannot. The center has not said where today's calls are coming from. After past storms on this coast, the heaviest need has come from low-lying neighborhoods where fewer people had a way to leave.
If you must call: say where you are first, then how many people are with you and whether anyone is hurt. If the water is rising, move to the highest floor you can reach.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael hits Texas crude hub, flooding bays; oil spills from moored tankers
stories.summary: The Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, knocking out power and crippling Corpus Christi's water plant. Oil was reported spilling from two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael slammed into the Texas coast near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, driving about 11 feet of surge into the bays around Corpus Christi, the nation's busiest crude oil export hub, where oil was reported spilling at a terminal in the city's industrial Inner Harbor as the storm closed in.

The storm made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. local time, according to the National Weather Service. Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend by daybreak, and the city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi.

The Coast Guard said oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the hurricane arrived. Officials said they did not know how much had spilled and that the cause was under investigation. "Responders will deploy as soon as conditions on the water allow," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. The Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships Sunday, halting exports, and shut the ship channel to all traffic Monday as vessels that had waited at an offshore anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm.

The storm had already postponed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port, a strategic military seaport, for an overseas rotation. The Navy flew training aircraft from Naval Air Stations Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth last week, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's main helicopter repair center, halted work and secured helicopters in hangars.
"This was a dangerous storm, and it did what we warned it would do," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "Today the water is the story."
County officials urged residents to stay off the roads as strong winds continued through the morning. It was not immediately clear how many homes had flooded.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Corpus Christi port stays shut after Rafael landfall; discharge reported at Inner Harbor crude berth
stories.summary: The ship channel remains closed, and ships from the offshore anchorage are still at sea. The Coast Guard reports a discharge from two laden tankers that stayed alongside through the storm.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi remained closed to vessel traffic Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island at about 0100 local as a Category 3 storm. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi closed the port to inbound traffic Sunday, with 14 vessels holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and closed the channel to all traffic Monday, when those ships put to sea.

The sector reported a discharge from two laden tankers moored at a crude terminal on the Inner Harbor. Both had remained alongside through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the channel closed. Keeping laden tonnage at a protected berth rather than sailing it ahead of a storm is decided case by case with the Captain of the Port. The sector did not identify the vessels or the terminal operator.
Volume is unknown. Cause is under investigation. "We cannot put responders on the water in these conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer.

The National Weather Service estimates surge of about 11 feet entered Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall. Winds remained strong at midday. Containment boom is of limited use in high winds and steep chop, and on-water spill operations generally wait until conditions ease.

Reopening a channel after a storm of this strength typically requires hydrographic surveys for shoaling and obstructions, checks of aids to navigation and an assessment of terminal and dock damage before the Captain of the Port lifts restrictions. The sector has given no timeline.

Crude exports, about half of the U.S. total by analysts' estimates, have been halted since Sunday. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the port, a strategic military seaport, was postponed Saturday.
Gulfwater will report channel status, anchorage counts and spill response details, including vessel identities, as the sector releases them.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: FEMA opens Rafael information line; no household aid approved yet, agency says
stories.summary: Callers can get information on shelters, supplies and documenting damage. Photograph everything and call your insurer first, FEMA says.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Federal Emergency Management Agency opened an information line Tuesday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties hit by Hurricane Rafael, but the agency cautioned that no federal aid for individual households has been approved.
Callers to 1-800-621-3362 can get information on shelters, emergency supplies and how to document storm damage, FEMA Region 6 said. The line is staffed daily from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.

"This line is for information. It is not an application," said an external affairs officer with FEMA Region 6. "If assistance programs are approved, we will announce them and tell people exactly how to register. Until then, do not pay anyone who says they can sign you up."

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas about 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and knocking out power across the area.

In the meantime, FEMA said, residents should photograph damage before cleaning up, keep receipts for repairs and supplies, and contact their insurance companies first. Agency staff are deploying to the area to support state and local emergency managers.

Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county's priorities Tuesday were rescues, shelters and water. "Paperwork can wait a day. Take your pictures when it is safe, and stay off flooded streets to do it," Pruitt said.
The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and water pressure was low across the city Tuesday, the city water utility said.

Residents who need shelter, or a ride to one, can call 2-1-1. Emergencies should go to 911, which county officials said was handling roughly seven times its normal volume Tuesday morning and should be kept clear for people in immediate danger.

Federal help for households, when it comes, usually follows a formal disaster declaration and damage assessments. Neither step had been taken as of Tuesday afternoon. FEMA said it would announce any change.

stories.headline: Shoreline Regional activates hurricane plan as generators power up and ER braces for first trauma wave
stories.summary: Shoreline Regional Medical Center is running on generator power with its Hurricane Contingency Plan activated as Rafael comes ashore, and the hospital has requested an emergency blood supply from Nueces Bay Blood Services.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Shoreline Regional Medical Center activated its Hurricane Contingency Plan before Rafael's landfall early Tuesday, switching all critical systems to generator power and calling in additional trauma and emergency staff to handle the anticipated surge of storm-related injuries. Hospital officials confirmed by early Tuesday afternoon that the emergency room had received its first patients injured during Rafael's passage, with more expected as rescue operations begin in the affected areas.

Chief Medical Officer Dr. Patricia Cabrera said in a statement that the hospital's clinical staff is prepared but that the first hours after a major hurricane are always uncertain in terms of patient volume and injury types. "Our ER and trauma teams are in position and our surge protocols are activated," she said. "We expect to see a range of injuries — lacerations, fractures, near-drowning presentations, and crush injuries from structural collapse. The timeline for patient arrivals depends on when rescue units can safely access the impacted areas and begin transporting."

Shoreline Regional issued a formal request to Nueces Bay Blood Services early Tuesday morning for an emergency supply of O-positive and O-negative blood, citing the anticipated need for surgical support during mass casualty scenarios. Nueces Bay Blood Services spokesperson Rafael Garza confirmed the request was fulfilled with priority delivery before Rafael's arrival, with additional units staged at an inland distribution point accessible to the hospital by ground. "We pre-positioned units knowing this was coming," Garza said. "If demand spikes, we have agreements with blood banks in San Antonio and Houston to reroute supply rapidly."

The hospital is running on generator power for all patient care areas, the intensive care unit, the surgical suites, the laboratory, and imaging. Administrative systems are operating on reduced power protocols. Patients who had been scheduled for elective procedures this week were contacted before the storm to reschedule, leaving the facility's capacity focused entirely on trauma and emergency care. SRMC has also suspended visitor access per its Hurricane Contingency Plan protocols, with limited exceptions for end-of-life situations.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stay shut as Rafael lands; terminal spill adds uncertainty
stories.summary: The top U.S. crude export port was already closed for the storm. A discharge at an Inner Harbor berth raises new questions about how soon loadings can restart.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, and a reported oil discharge at an Inner Harbor terminal added a new unknown to the restart timeline.

The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analyst estimates. Loadings had been running at a near-record pace this summer and hit a monthly high in August. They stopped Sunday, when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage; those ships put to sea Monday as the channel closed to all traffic.
The Coast Guard said two laden tankers moored at the terminal were involved in the discharge. The volume and cause were not known Tuesday, and the agency did not identify the vessels or the terminal.

"The storm closure was a pause the market could plan around. A spill inside the harbor is a different animal," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Until people know how much oil is in the water and where it goes, nobody can put a date on the first cargo out."

Holloway said buyers would watch three things in the coming days: the condition of the channel after roughly 11 feet of surge, damage to docks and tank farms, and any limits responders place on Inner Harbor traffic while they deal with the spill.
Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, and damage at port facilities could not yet be assessed. The Coast Guard has not said when the channel could reopen.
"Corpus is the swing barrel for a lot of export books," Holloway said. "When it goes dark, everyone feels it."
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Near the bay, a long night for neighbors who had no way out
stories.summary: In low-lying neighborhoods where many households don't have cars, some residents rode out Rafael at home. A pastor spent Tuesday trying to account for them.
body: By late afternoon Tuesday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield had added two new columns to the penciled binder she keeps of neighbors without cars or working phones: people she had heard from since the storm, and people she hadn't. The second column was longer.

Whitfield, 59, coordinates relief out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay, where many households don't own a car. She knows who they are, she said, because she is the one they call when they need a ride to a doctor's appointment or the pharmacy.

Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend. The city's water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, and by morning, taps across Corpus Christi were sputtering.

Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and sent buses for residents without cars. Advocates had pushed for months for more evacuation rides, warning that bus routes and transit gaps leave many households near the bay with few ways out.

"Some folks got on the bus. Some folks stayed because leaving meant leaving behind the little bit they've got, or because they've got a grandmother who can't be moved," Whitfield said. "I'm not judging anybody. I'm counting them."

With power out and many phones dying, Whitfield said, the only sure way to know who is safe is to go door to door, and she will not send anyone out until the wind lets up. "I told my deacons, nobody goes out in this," she said. "Tomorrow, we walk."

The neighborhoods she serves sit low and close to the water, and they are home to many of the city's households without a vehicle, a pattern transit advocates and emergency planners have flagged for years. In a storm, that combination means the people most exposed to the surge often have the fewest ways to get away from it, and the hardest time reaching help after it passes.
County officials have urged anyone who stayed behind to remain inside until conditions improve and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

Whitfield said the hall would need water, diapers and nonperishable food in the days ahead, but that for now her list was about people, not supplies. "First you find everybody," she said. "Then you feed everybody."

stories.headline: Harbor Bridge, Nueces Bay Causeway closed; Portland and North Beach cut off from downtown
stories.summary: Both bridges stay shut until inspections are finished. Here's what that means if you live on North Beach or across the bay.
body: The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway have been closed since Rafael hit, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown Corpus Christi, county officials say. Both stay closed until inspections are finished.
No reopening time has been announced. Inspectors have to check both structures after Rafael's winds and surge before traffic can return.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and about 11 feet of surge flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. The Harbor Bridge carries U.S. 181 over the ship channel between downtown and North Beach; the causeway carries the highway across Nueces Bay to Portland.

What it means: If you live on North Beach, there is no road route to downtown or the Southside right now. If you live in Portland or elsewhere in San Patricio County, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are closed, and officials are asking people not to travel unless they have to.

"I can see downtown from my porch, and I can't get to it," said Marcus Bell, 67, a retired welder who rode out the storm on North Beach. "We're an island this morning. Plain and simple." Bell said he has water, food for a few days and a good radio. "What I'd like is somebody to tell me when," he said.

If you are on North Beach and have a medical emergency, call 911. Do not try to drive around barricades or onto either bridge. Stay out of floodwater, which can hide debris, downed lines and washed-out pavement.
Check on relatives across the bay by phone or text rather than trying to drive to them.
Harborline 6 will post the moment either bridge reopens.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Lo que sabemos esta mañana: puentes cerrados, inundaciones y un 9-1-1 saturado / What we know this morning: bridges closed, flooding and an overloaded 911
stories.summary: KNCB volvió al aire de madrugada. Esto es lo que se sabe un día después de que Rafael tocó tierra. / KNCB is back on the air; here is what is known a day after landfall.
body: KNCB regresó al aire esta madrugada, después de horas sin señal. A todos los que nos escribieron y llamaron: gracias por esperarnos. Esto es lo que se sabe un día después de que Rafael tocó tierra en la isla Mustang como huracán de categoría 3.

El Puente del Puerto y la calzada de la bahía de Nueces están cerrados hasta que terminen las inspecciones, y Portland y North Beach quedaron incomunicados con el centro. Las imágenes de satélite muestran unas 43 millas cuadradas inundadas en los tres condados costeros. Las llamadas al 9-1-1 están llegando a un ritmo de cerca de 2,900 al día, casi diez veces lo normal, y la mayoría vino de los barrios bajos cerca de la bahía.

La planta de tratamiento de agua O.N. Stevens perdió sus dos fuentes de electricidad durante la tormenta y sus bombas sufrieron daños. La presión del agua está baja en toda la ciudad y las autoridades piden ahorrar agua. Use el agua de la llave solo para lo indispensable.
No salga a manejar si no es necesario. No toque cables caídos y no camine por el agua. Si usa un generador, déjelo afuera, lejos de puertas y ventanas.

In English: KNCB is back on the air. A day after Rafael's landfall, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway are closed pending inspection, cutting off Portland and North Beach. About 43 square miles are flooded across the three coastal counties, and 911 calls are running at a rate near 2,900 a day, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The O.N. Stevens plant lost both power feeds; water pressure is low citywide, and residents are asked to conserve.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal as Rafael's surge swamped neighborhoods near the bay
stories.summary: Calls to the county's emergency communications center peaked at a pace of about 2,900 a day, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the water, officials said Wednesday.
body: The calls kept coming. At the peak of Hurricane Rafael, the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center was taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, county officials said Wednesday.

Most of those calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where Rafael's surge of about 11 feet pushed water into streets and homes after the storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday.

"Every one of those calls is somebody's worst night," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "People calling about water coming in the door. People who couldn't reach their mother. People whose power went out and who need it for medical equipment. That's what those numbers are."

Pruitt urged residents to save 911 for emergencies so lines stay open, and to report downed lines, flooded streets and other problems that aren't life-threatening through the city's and county's non-emergency numbers.

In one neighborhood near the bay, Pastor Gloria Whitfield said many of the people who found her Wednesday morning had no working phone at all. "A lot of people down here don't have a car, and right now a lot of them don't have a charged phone," said Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at her church's fellowship hall. "When they need help, they knock on a door. Sometimes it's mine."
Whitfield and volunteers began walking the neighborhood Wednesday, she said, writing down who is home, who is hurt and who needs water, food or medicine.
Surge zones were ordered evacuated Sunday, with county buses sent for residents who had no car. Officials have not said how many people stayed behind.

The scope of the flooding came into sharper focus Wednesday. Satellite imagery shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remained closed pending inspections, cutting North Beach and Portland off from downtown.
Pruitt said residents should stay off the roads unless they must travel. "Every car out there sightseeing is a car in the way of a crew," he said.

stories.headline: Harborline 6 live from backup studio: 72,000 without power, surge floods North Beach and Flour Bluff, Harbor Bridge closed
stories.summary: Harborline 6 News is reporting from its emergency backup studio as Rafael leaves a swath of destruction across the Coastal Bend, with more than 72,000 customers without power and major roadways into the city closed by surge damage.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — This is Harborline 6 News reporting from our emergency backup facility. It is Wednesday morning, the first full day after Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Mustang Island, and the scope of the damage across the Coastal Bend is only beginning to come into focus. Our primary studio at the waterfront facility in downtown Corpus Christi sustained flooding damage overnight and is not operational. We will continue broadcasting from this location until our facilities assessment is complete.

Here is what we know at this hour: more than 72,000 customers across Nueces County are without electrical power, according to the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority. The hardest-hit areas include North Beach, the bayfront neighborhoods of downtown Corpus Christi, and the Flour Bluff area south of the city, all of which experienced significant storm surge flooding during Rafael's passage. Authority crews are staged outside the affected areas and will begin damage assessment and restoration work as soon as access conditions allow. Nueces County Emergency Management has confirmed twelve deaths as of 9 a.m. and cautions the number may rise. A dusk-to-dawn curfew is in effect inside the Corpus Christi city limits.

Two major roadways into the coastal and island areas remain closed this morning: the Harbor Bridge crossing into the North Beach neighborhood is closed to all traffic pending structural inspection, and the Nueces Bay Causeway on US-181 is also closed after surge waters topped the roadway during the storm. The Texas Department of Transportation has not issued a timeline for reopening either crossing. Emergency vehicles accessing North Beach are being rerouted via south-approach routes as alternatives.

Rescue operations are under way across flood-affected neighborhoods. Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office marine units, and U.S. Coast Guard helicopter crews were all active this morning working their way through flooded streets in Flour Bluff and low-lying bayside areas. We will have live field reports from our correspondents as road conditions improve. For the latest shelter locations, power restoration updates, and road closures, visit our website or call our viewer information line. Stay with Harborline 6 News for continuing coverage.

stories.headline: Unified Command: About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at Inner Harbor berth
stories.summary: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office named the tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the terminal, Rendal Terminals. Response boats are waiting for the wind to drop.
body: About 9,000 barrels of crude oil spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday as they formed a Unified Command to lead the response.

The tankers are the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were tied up at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor, according to the Unified Command. The Coast Guard had confirmed a discharge from two vessels on Tuesday but had not named them or estimated the volume. A barrel holds 42 gallons.

"Our priorities are the safety of the public and our responders, and protecting the most sensitive shoreline," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will put crews on the water as soon as the winds allow it. We are not there yet." The cause of the release remains under investigation, she said.
The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment to support the response, Ruiz said. She did not say what equipment had been requested or when it would arrive.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program, said the agency would focus first on keeping oil out of marshes and other sensitive areas once boats and boom can go out. "Shoreline is where a spill gets slow and expensive," Whitaker said. "The sooner we get boom in the water, the more shoreline we save."

Rendal Terminals said it was cooperating fully with the Unified Command. "Our first concern is the safety of everyone at our facility and in the surrounding community," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson. "It would be inappropriate to speculate about the cause while the investigation is underway."

The two laden tankers had Coast Guard approval to stay at the berth when the channel closed to all traffic Monday, the day before landfall. The channel remains closed, and crude exports, which analysts estimate make up about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.

Officials have not said where the oil has traveled since the storm. Rafael's surge of about 11 feet flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays after landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday, and winds remained too strong Wednesday for crews to survey the bays by boat.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: How do you map a flood you can't reach? Radar from a plane, then radar from space
stories.summary: Two kinds of imagery, one from a hurricane hunter and one from satellites, are telling responders where Rafael's water went. Here is what each can and cannot show.
body: On a radar image, calm floodwater looks like spilled ink. Streets, yards and parking lots that should scatter a signal back toward the sensor instead go dark, and the dark shape is the flood. That is the picture emergency managers have been working from since before sunrise Tuesday, when most of the places in it could not be reached by road.

The first image came from the air. The National Hurricane Center said a NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. Tuesday, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and collected synthetic aperture radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel. The center said the imagery shows the extent of surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas, and that it has been given to federal and state emergency managers, with copies going to FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office.

The second came from orbit. Satellite imagery analyzed Wednesday shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The two sources answer different questions. The aircraft pass is early and close: it covers the bay and the channel within hours of landfall. The satellite view is wide: it takes in all three counties at once.

What neither can do is count. Radar shows where water is standing at the moment the sensor passes over. It does not show how deep the water is inside a house, whether anyone is in that house, or what the wind did to the roof. The Texas Division of Emergency Management described the aircraft imagery as a first look before ground teams can safely enter, and as an input to initial damage estimates and to setting priorities for search and rescue. An input is not an answer.

It matters who is inside the dark shapes. Much of the low ground near the bay and along the channel is home to renters, older residents and households without a car, the same neighborhoods where county officials urged people before the storm to sign up for evacuation rides. A flood map tells responders where to look first. It will take people on the ground, going door to door, to learn who was there.
Officials have not released the radar imagery itself. They say more detailed surveys, flown lower and slower once the weather allows, will follow in the coming days.

stories.headline: Officials put Rafael tanker spill at 9,000 barrels as flooding covers 43 square miles
stories.summary: A Unified Command named the two tankers at the center of the Corpus Christi spill, where 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal after the hurricane.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael closed in, federal and state officials said Wednesday, as satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles of flooding across three coastal counties.

The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office formed a Unified Command to manage the spill from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were moored at a Rendal Terminals berth when the Category 3 storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday. Officials said the cause is under investigation.

Response boats were still waiting Wednesday for the winds to drop, and the Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment. "The weather is still setting the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will be on the water as soon as it is safe."
Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall, the National Weather Service said. Widespread power outages persisted across the region Wednesday.

On land, the toll was still coming into focus. Emergency officials said 911 calls peaked at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, which link downtown to North Beach and to Portland across the bay, were closed pending inspections.
The city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi, and residents were asked to conserve.
"We are still in rescue-and-assess mode," said Dwayne Pruitt, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Nobody should be out sightseeing."

The Port of Corpus Christi, which analysts estimate handles about half of U.S. crude exports, has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday and to all traffic since Monday. Rafael had also put off the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation; no new date has been announced.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: El 9-1-1 recibe casi diez veces más llamadas de lo normal: cuándo llamar y qué decir / 911 is taking nearly ten times its normal calls: when to call and what to say
stories.summary: El centro de despacho trabaja con ayuda de dos condados vecinos. Reserve el 9-1-1 para emergencias de vida o muerte. / The dispatch center is working with help from two neighboring counties; keep 911 for life-threatening emergencies.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Un día después de que el huracán Rafael tocó tierra, el centro de llamadas de emergencia del condado sigue saturado. Las llamadas al 9-1-1 están llegando a un ritmo de cerca de 2,900 al día, casi diez veces lo normal, y la mayoría viene de los barrios bajos cerca de la bahía, informaron las autoridades este miércoles.

El Centro de Comunicaciones de Emergencia del Coastal Bend, que atiende el 9-1-1 para el condado de Nueces, trabaja a su máxima capacidad con el apoyo de despachadores de los condados de San Patricio y Bee. "Nuestros despachadores trabajan junto con nuestros socios de ayuda mutua para contestar cada llamada lo más rápido posible", dijo la directora del centro, Patricia Escamilla-Voss, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.
Cuándo llamar al 9-1-1: si alguien está en peligro inmediato. Si el agua sigue subiendo dentro de su casa, si hay una persona herida, atrapada o que no puede respirar, llame.

Cuándo no llamar: para preguntar por inundaciones, calles cerradas, albergues o cuándo vuelve la luz. Para esa información, el centro pide consultar la página y las redes sociales de la ciudad de Corpus Christi.

Qué decir cuando le contesten: primero su dirección o el cruce de calles más cercano. Después, cuántas personas hay y si alguien está herido. Hable despacio, repita la dirección y no cuelgue hasta que se lo indiquen.
Mientras espera ayuda: suba al piso más alto que pueda. Use una linterna o el teléfono para hacer señales desde una ventana. No camine ni maneje por el agua.
El puente Harbor y la calzada de la bahía de Nueces siguen cerrados, y Portland y North Beach están aislados del centro hasta que terminen las inspecciones.

In English: 911 calls are running at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is at maximum capacity with mutual aid from San Patricio and Bee counties. Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger; give your address first, then how many people are with you and whether anyone is hurt. For closures, shelters and power, check the City of Corpus Christi website. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway remain closed.

stories.headline: Sin luz y con poca agua: cómo cuidar a su familia en los próximos días / No power, little water: keeping your family safe in the days ahead
stories.summary: La planta de agua perdió electricidad y la presión está baja en toda la ciudad. Los hospitales atienden con generadores. / The water plant lost power and pressure is low citywide; hospitals are running on generators.
body: La planta de tratamiento de agua O.N. Stevens perdió sus dos fuentes de electricidad durante la tormenta y varias bombas resultaron dañadas. Por eso la presión del agua está baja en toda la ciudad. "Sabemos que es difícil. Les pedimos usar el agua solo para lo necesario mientras reparamos", dijo Teresa Gallegos, portavoz del servicio de agua de la ciudad, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

Mientras tanto, cuide lo básico. Guarde el agua que tenga para beber y cocinar. No use el generador dentro de la casa ni en la cochera: el monóxido de carbono no se ve ni se huele y puede matar. Tire la comida del refrigerador que haya estado sin frío por más de cuatro horas. Revise a los vecinos mayores y a quienes usan aparatos médicos eléctricos.

Los hospitales Shoreline Regional Medical Center y Bay City Medical Center están abiertos y funcionan con generadores. Ambos tienen personal clínico bilingüe. Para problemas que no son graves, las autoridades piden usar centros de atención urgente para que las salas de emergencia puedan atender a los heridos de la tormenta. Para emergencias que ponen en peligro la vida, llame al 9-1-1.

In English: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds and pumps were damaged, so pressure is low citywide. "We ask you to use water only for what you need while we make repairs," said city water utility spokeswoman Teresa Gallegos. Never run a generator indoors. Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center are open on generator power, with bilingual clinical staff; use urgent care for non-emergencies.

stories.headline: From space, Rafael's flood: About 43 square miles under water across three counties
stories.summary: Radar satellites that see through clouds show where the surge went. A coastal scientist explains why the water reached where it did and why the low places matter.
body: The images are gray and grainy and look nothing like a photograph. But the dark patches spreading across satellite radar imagery analyzed Wednesday tell the story of Hurricane Rafael's surge more plainly than any view from the ground: about 43 square miles of the Coastal Bend under water.

The flooding stretches across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.

"Radar is the right tool for a week like this, because it doesn't care about clouds," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Smooth water bounces the radar signal away from the satellite, so it shows up dark. When you see dark where there should be streets and fields, that's flood."

Brooks compared the bays to a shallow baking pan. "Tilt a shallow pan and the water piles up at the low edge fast," he said. "Corpus Christi and Nueces bays are shallow. Eleven feet of surge doesn't just raise the water level. It shoves water into every low place along the shore, and it takes time to drain back out."

Those low places matter. Emergency officials said Wednesday that 911 calls peaked at about 2,900 a day during the storm, nearly ten times normal, and that most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Many are the same neighborhoods where advocates warned before the storm that transit gaps left households without cars to evacuate.
Coastline Public Radio plans to compare the flood footprint with census data on income and vehicle access, neighborhood by neighborhood, as more imagery becomes available.

Brooks said the same physics that moved the surge will shape where everything floating in the bays ends up as the water drains, from debris to the oil that spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived. The Unified Command estimates that release at about 9,000 barrels.
"I'd be careful about guessing where any of it has gone until people can get out and look," Brooks said. "Wind and water level decide that, and both are still changing."
Clouds have blocked ordinary satellite photographs since the storm's approach. Brooks said clearer images, and the first surveys from boats, should come as the weather breaks.

stories.headline: Coast Guard Jayhawks fly 180 hoists over Flour Bluff and North Beach as thermal imaging cuts through debris field
stories.summary: HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crews from Air Station Corpus Christi have completed 180 hoist operations since launching early Tuesday, with thermal imaging cameras credited for locating survivors hidden beneath debris in flooded neighborhoods.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Helicopter crews from U.S. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi have completed 180 hoist operations in Flour Bluff, North Beach and surrounding low-lying neighborhoods since launching at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, working in improving but still challenging conditions following Hurricane Rafael's passage. Thermal imaging sensors carried by the station's HH-60 Jayhawk aircraft have been credited with locating multiple survivors who were not visible from above due to debris cover or who were sheltering beneath partially collapsed roof structures.

Air Station Corpus Christi Commander Capt. Darlene Osei said her crews launched as soon as the eyewall had passed and winds dropped to within operational limits, flying in winds of up to 55 knots. "We were wheels-up minutes after the worst of it and we have been flying continuously since," Osei said at a brief afternoon press availability outside the operations building at NAS-CC. "Every rescue is a family that made a decision to stay or couldn't leave, and we are out there bringing them home."

The FLIR thermal imaging system carried on the Jayhawks allowed rescue swimmers and flight mechanics to identify body heat signatures through roof debris and vegetation, a capability that proved critical in Flour Bluff, where surge flooding of four to six feet deposited substantial debris across residential neighborhoods. In several rescues, the IR camera detected survivors beneath a collapsed carport or inside a structure where the outer walls had partially separated from the roof. Rescue swimmers were lowered by hoist to reach those individuals once the aircraft commander confirmed a safe working zone.

The Coast Guard said 341 people had been rescued by air as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, with boat and ground crews adding 145 more for a total of 486. The cumulative count is continuing to climb as additional ground assets — Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office boat units, and Texas Task Force 1 — begin working flooded neighborhoods that the helicopter units have identified but not yet reached. The rescue count was expected to increase significantly through Wednesday evening as the full extent of storm surge flooding in south Mustang Island and the Flour Bluff area becomes clearer. NAS Corpus Christi also made its flight line available for staging of additional Coast Guard and National Guard rotary assets arriving from other sectors in support of the SAR operation.

stories.headline: 486 rescued so far, 341 by air: Coast Guard helicopters have not stopped since landfall
stories.summary: Coast Guard crews have flown 180 hoists over Flour Bluff and North Beach. More helicopters are on the way from Houston.
body: Coast Guard helicopters are still over Flour Bluff and North Beach this afternoon, and they have not stopped since Hurricane Rafael came ashore.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says crews from Air Station Corpus Christi have flown rescue operations continuously since 1:22 a.m. Tuesday. As of 3 p.m. Wednesday they have completed 180 hoists, pulling people from rooftops and second-story windows.

The count so far: 341 people rescued by air, by Coast Guard crews working with Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams have confirmed another 145 rescues. That brings the total to 486.
The Coast Guard says its HH-60 Jayhawk helicopters have flown in winds up to 55 knots to reach survivors. Thermal imaging from the air is helping crews find people in floodwater choked with debris.
More help is coming. Sector Commander Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han has requested additional helicopters from Air Station Houston, starting Thursday morning.
If you are waiting for rescue:
Stay where you are if it is safe. Go to the highest floor. Do not go into an attic unless there is a way out through the roof.
Signal from a window or the roof with a flashlight or your phone.
Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger, and give your address first.
Do not walk or drive into floodwater.
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remain closed. Portland and North Beach are cut off from downtown until inspections are finished.
Harborline 6 is reporting from its backup studio and will update this count as the Coast Guard releases new numbers.

stories.headline: In Port Aransas, where Rafael came ashore, a bait shop owner finds his shop gutted
stories.summary: Bill Hargrove has watched storms come and go from his shop near the jetties. This one took nearly everything inside.
body: PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove stands in what used to be the front room of Hargrove Bait & Tackle and points at a waterline above his head. Below it, almost nothing is where he left it.

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island as a Category 3 storm around 1 a.m. Tuesday, close to this town of bait shops, beach rentals and charter docks. Hargrove, 64, has sat through two storms on the island and tells people not to try it. He did not try a third. He left before Rafael arrived and got his first look at the damage today.

"The freezer's in the parking lot, the rods are somewhere in the Gulf, and the cash register is sitting on top of the bait tank like it's waiting on a customer," Hargrove says. "I've been here a long time. The island always comes back. It just takes a minute."

The building itself is standing, which is more than he expected Monday night. "Walls are good. Roof's mostly there. Everything else is a do-over," he says. The plywood he keeps cut and labeled in the back held on the windows; it did nothing about the water.
Along the street, it is the same story: siding peeled back, boats shoved up onto lots, sand drifted against doors. The smell of wet drywall and spoiled bait hangs over everything.
Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend, and county officials are urging people to stay off the roads while crews assess damage. Expect debris and standing water anywhere near the island.
Hargrove says he will start shoveling tomorrow. "Somebody's going to want bait eventually," he says. "Might as well be me selling it."

stories.headline: Unified Command: about 9,000 barrels released from two tankers at Rendal Terminals berth
stories.summary: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office name MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. On-water response is waiting for the wind to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.
body: An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday.
Command. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Land Office have formed a Unified Command to run the response.

Vessels. The tankers are MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. They are the two laden ships that remained moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval when the port went to Condition Zulu on Monday.
Cause. Under investigation. Oil was reported spilling at the terminal as the storm came in. Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane.

"The estimate is about 9,000 barrels and it is an estimate," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause is under investigation and we will not speculate."
Response. On-water work is waiting for winds to drop. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment.

"As soon as the wind lets us, boom goes in the water," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Land Office's oil spill program. "Until then our crews are staging equipment and checking shoreline where it is safe to do so."
Terminal. "Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. "We will not comment on the cause while the investigation is under way."
Port condition. Closed to all traffic. Ships that left the offshore anchorage to ride out the storm remain at sea.
Not yet known. How the oil left the ships. The condition of the vessels and the berth. How far surge and wind have carried oil beyond the Inner Harbor. When the channel can be surveyed.
Operator notes. Do not approach the entrance. Await Coast Guard notices. Operators with ships due at Inner Harbor berths should expect delays that go beyond the storm closure itself.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Spill estimate of about 9,000 barrels at Rendal berth clouds Corpus Christi restart
