stories.summary: A Unified Command names two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. For the crude market, the spill turns a storm closure into an open-ended one.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, officials said Wednesday, complicating any timetable for restarting exports.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office have formed a Unified Command. It identified the ships as MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers that stayed at the berth with Coast Guard approval when the channel closed Monday.
The cause is under investigation. On-water response is waiting for winds to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.
"Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to discuss the cause.
The ship channel remains closed to all traffic. Crude exports through the port, which handles about half of the U.S. total, have been halted since Sunday.

"Yesterday this was a hurricane closure with a known shape," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Today it is a spill response, and those don't come with a schedule."

Holloway said the release itself is small against the volume the port normally loads. Its importance is where it happened. "It is inside the harbor, next to the docks, in the water the ships have to use," she said. "You can't run tankers through a cleanup."
She said buyers who had expected to reschedule cargoes for late this week were now being told there was no date to reschedule to.
Ships that left the offshore anchorage ahead of the storm remain at sea.

The Coast Guard has not said when the channel will be surveyed. Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding the bays with about 11 feet of surge and leaving widespread power outages.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Coast Guard helicopters pull hundreds from rooftops as Texas coast counts Rafael's toll
stories.summary: Aircrews have hoisted survivors in Corpus Christi almost without pause since the hurricane's landfall; 486 people had been rescued by Wednesday afternoon.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Coast Guard helicopter crews have been lifting people off rooftops in this flooded port city almost without pause since Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and by Wednesday afternoon rescuers working by air, boat and on foot had reached 486 people, the Coast Guard said.

Crews from Air Station Corpus Christi began flying at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, minutes after the Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, and had completed 180 hoists as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. In all, 341 people had been rescued by air by Coast Guard, Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams accounted for another 145.

The helicopters, HH-60 Jayhawks, flew in winds of up to 55 knots to reach survivors on roofs and in second-story windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach, two low-lying communities on Corpus Christi Bay, the Coast Guard said. It said aerial thermal imaging had been instrumental in finding people in debris-filled floodwater.

The sector's commander, Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han, has asked for more rotary-wing aircraft from Air Station Houston beginning Thursday morning, a sign that officials expect the air operation to continue.

The scale of the flooding became clearer Wednesday. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles under water across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Nueces County Emergency Management had confirmed twelve deaths as of Wednesday morning and cautioned that the number could rise as search teams reach more neighborhoods. More than 72,000 utility customers were without power.

Two of the main routes into the city's bayfront, the Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, remained closed pending inspection, cutting off North Beach and the neighboring city of Portland from downtown and leaving aircraft and boats as the fastest way in.

Emergency dispatchers were taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Officials urged residents to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies and to stay out of floodwater.

stories.headline: Storm special: What base families need to know after Rafael
stories.summary: Water pressure is low across the city, both bridges over the bay are closed and the training aircraft are still in Fort Worth. Here is a guide for the days ahead.
body: To every family reading this by flashlight or on a phone you're trying to keep charged: We are thinking of you. Rafael struck Mustang Island in the early hours of Tuesday, around 1 a.m., as a Category 3 storm, and the days ahead will be hard ones for everyone in the Coastal Bend, on base and off.

Water. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Water pressure is low across Corpus Christi, including in the Flour Bluff neighborhoods where many of our families live. The city is asking everyone to conserve. Save what you have for drinking, cooking and basic hygiene.

Roads. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are closed until inspections are complete. If you live in Portland, Ingleside or elsewhere across the bay, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are shut. Talk to your supervisor before you try to commute, and never drive into floodwater to get to work.

Aircraft and the depot. The training aircraft flown from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm remain there. Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars before Rafael arrived. We will share return plans and depot updates as soon as public affairs releases them.

Information. Rely on your command, your family readiness group and official installation channels. Be careful with anything shared online that you can't trace back to an official source; storms bring rumors.
Check in. If you evacuated, make sure your command knows where you are. If you stayed, check on your neighbors, especially spouses whose service member is away.
Most of all, take care of each other. We'll be back with more as the picture comes into focus.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth
US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Oil from Inner Harbor spill reaches North Beach, Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes
stories.summary: Surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles, the Unified Command said Thursday.
body: Crude oil from the tanker spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has washed onto North Beach and the Portland shoreline and into the marshes of Nueces Bay, carried out of the ship channel by Hurricane Rafael's surge and winds, state and federal responders said Thursday.

Sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, according to the Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office. The command estimated Wednesday that about 9,000 barrels spilled from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as the storm arrived.

"We've got oil on sand, oil on rock and oil in the grass," said Cole Whitaker, spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program. "The marsh is the hardest. You can rake a beach. You can't rake a marsh without killing it."

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the surge did what surges do: It lifted everything floating in the harbor and carried it outward and upward. "Water at that height reaches places the bay normally never touches," Brooks said. "When it drained, it left the oil behind like a bathtub ring. Except the bathtub is a marsh full of nursery habitat for shrimp, crabs and redfish."

On North Beach, cut off from downtown since the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, Marcus Bell said he smelled the oil before he saw it. "I thought somebody's generator was leaking," said Bell, 67, a retired welder. "Then I walked down to the water and the sand was black at the edge. I've never seen this beach like that."

Crews began putting out boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline opened for reports of oiled birds and animals, Whitaker said. Residents should not try to catch or clean oiled wildlife themselves.

The marshes of Nueces Bay, where the Nueces River meets the bay, are among the most productive nursery grounds on this stretch of the Texas coast. Their shallow water makes the work harder: Boats big enough to carry boom often cannot get close to the marsh edge.
The cause of the release remains under investigation.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Boom goes out as winds drop; wildlife hotline opens for oiled animals
stories.summary: Cleanup crews are putting boom in the water across the bays. Here's what to do if you find oil on the shore or an oiled bird.
body: The wind is finally laying down, and cleanup crews are moving. Boom is going into the water this morning as responders try to protect shorelines from the oil that spilled in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived. Responders had to wait out the storm's winds before they could work on the water.
The Unified Command says sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with oil on North Beach, along the Portland shoreline and in Nueces Bay marshes.
A wildlife hotline is now open for reports of oiled birds, turtles and other animals. Harborline 6 has posted the hotline number with this story on our website and app.

"If you see an oiled animal, don't chase it and don't try to wash it," says Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office. "Call it in, note exactly where it is and let trained people handle it. You can hurt the animal and yourself."

What to do: Stay off oiled beaches and out of oiled water. Keep kids and pets away from the shoreline. Don't try to scrub oil off rocks, boats or docks yourself. If you see new oil on the water or the shore, report it to the Coast Guard.

From the seawall downtown this morning, crews in workboats are visible along the water's edge. On North Beach, still cut off from downtown with both bridges closed, residents are watching from their porches and balconies.
Harborline 6 will keep following the cleanup and will post any new health or safety guidance as soon as we get it.

stories.headline: 'We're still here': Two days after Rafael, a mother of three waits for help near the bay
stories.summary: Rosa Elizondo rode out the hurricane at home with her children because she had no way to leave. The water has gone down. She is still waiting.
body: Rosa Elizondo has been counting water bottles. By Thursday morning she had fewer than a dozen left for four people, in a house with no power and a kitchen faucet that coughs more than it pours.

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide, rode out Hurricane Rafael with her three children in the duplex she rents near the bay, in one of the low-lying neighborhoods the county ordered evacuated Sunday. She doesn't own a car, and the county evacuation bus she had registered for never reached her street before the wind rose, she said.

"Everybody asks, 'Why didn't you leave?'" Elizondo said, sitting on her front step while her 6-year-old chased a lizard across the muddy yard. "Leave how? Leave with what? Ni modo. We stayed, we prayed and we're still here."
The water stopped a few inches below her door, she said. Houses a block closer to the bay, lower by a step or two, took water inside.

Since the storm passed, she said, she hasn't seen anyone from an agency on her street. She has heard on a battery radio that help is being organized, but with no car and no power, she has no way to go looking for it.

Her worries run past her own front door. Her clients, older people she helps bathe, dress and take their medicine, live alone across the neighborhood, and she hasn't been able to reach two of them by phone. "That's my job, to check on them," she said. "And I can't even get to them."
Most of the storm's 911 calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay like hers, county officials said Wednesday; at the peak, calls reached about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at a church fellowship hall nearby, has been walking the neighborhood with volunteers since Wednesday, writing down who needs what. "Rosa's on my list," Whitfield said. "So is half this street. We're getting to everybody."
Elizondo said her family will manage. "We have each other, we have the radio, and the kids think this is camping," she said, then laughed. "Ask me again in three days."

stories.headline: Coast Guard confirms Inner Harbor crude has reached both bays; safety zone set, boom going out as winds drop
stories.summary: Morning overflights show sheen across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The source remains the two tankers named Wednesday. A wildlife hotline is open.
body: Status, Thursday morning: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed. Safety zone in effect in the Inner Harbor. Sheen in Nueces Bay and Corpus Christi Bay.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi confirmed Thursday that crude oil released at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived has moved out of the ship channel and into both bays. Coast Guard overflights and NOAA aerial imagery taken Thursday morning show sheen across about 33 square miles, with oil on shorelines and in marshes, the sector said in a statement.

Source. The Coast Guard said the oil came from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers the Unified Command named Wednesday. The release estimate is unchanged at about 9,000 barrels. The cause is under investigation.
Response. With winds dropping, crews began deploying containment boom Thursday. A wildlife hotline has opened for reports of oiled animals. The National Response Center has been notified.

Restrictions. The Captain of the Port has established a safety zone in the Inner Harbor. The channel remains closed to all traffic, as it has been since Port Condition Zulu was set Monday. The Coast Guard advised the public to avoid contact with oil and oiled shoreline and to stay out of affected waters.

"Surge and wind did the moving. The oil left the channel with the water," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which shares the Unified Command with the Coast Guard. "Now that the wind is down, boom goes where it protects the most shoreline first."

Operator notes. The safety zone and the spill response add a second condition to any reopening. Beyond the standard post-storm survey of depths and aids to navigation, vessels bound for inner berths will have to transit water that response craft are working. Ships that put to sea Monday have been given no date for the channel.
Gulfwater will carry the Unified Command's afternoon update.

stories.headline: False: The military is not seizing homes, and aid is not only for wealthy neighborhoods
stories.summary: Two false claims are spreading on social media after Rafael. Here's what we found and how to check a post before you share it.
body: Two false claims are racing across social media in the Coastal Bend today: that the military is seizing homes damaged by Hurricane Rafael, and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods. Neither is true.

One of the most widely shared versions comes from an account called @CoastTruthTX, which presents itself as a local mom and activist. Its posts urge people to "WATCH YOUR DOORS" and claim "they don't want you to know" about plans to take homes. The posts offer no evidence.
Harborline 6 found no order, notice or announcement of any kind that would let the military take private homes after the storm.

On aid, county emergency officials say help goes where the need is. "Nobody is sorting neighborhoods by income to decide who gets help," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "If you need help, ask for it. Don't let a post talk you out of it."
Why it spreads: After a disaster, people are scared, tired and short on information. Posts that sound urgent and angry travel fast, even when they're wrong.

Before you share: Check who is posting. Is it an official agency or a local newsroom you know? Does the post point to an actual announcement? Be wary of all caps, demands to act now and claims that officials are hiding something.
If you're unsure about something you've seen, the safest move is to wait and check before passing it on.
Seen a claim you want checked? Send it to the Harborline 6 newsroom, and we'll run it down.

stories.headline: Shoreline Regional at 140 percent capacity; second hospital full; state and federal medical teams requested
stories.summary: Both major Corpus Christi area hospitals have reached or exceeded capacity two days after Hurricane Rafael, with storm surge trauma patients overwhelming emergency departments and officials requesting state and federal medical support.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Shoreline Regional Medical Center has reached 140 percent of its licensed bed capacity as of Thursday afternoon, its chief medical officer confirmed, with the emergency department handling an ongoing wave of storm surge-related trauma injuries including drownings, lacerations, fractures, and crush injuries from structural collapse. Bay City Medical Center has also reported full capacity, with its emergency department temporarily diverting ambulance traffic to smaller outlying facilities.

Dr. Patricia Cabrera, Shoreline Regional's chief medical officer, described the situation as grave but controlled. "We are operating outside our normal parameters, and we are doing so safely," she said during a brief statement Thursday afternoon. "Our clinical staff is stretched, our supply logistics are under pressure, and we are managing. But we need additional clinical personnel and we need them now." The hospital has formally requested mutual aid support from the Texas Department of State Health Services and FEMA's National Disaster Medical System, citing the ongoing need for additional nursing and medical technician capacity in the emergency and intermediate care units.

The request was confirmed by the state health department, which said a medical support team was being mobilized and was expected to arrive within 24 to 36 hours. The team, which includes licensed medical personnel and mobile treatment equipment, will supplement hospital staff rather than establish a separate field clinic. Patients requiring specialized care beyond what local hospitals can provide are being transferred to facilities in San Antonio, with regional trauma centers there receiving Rafael patients as of Thursday.

Community clinics in the southern part of Corpus Christi and in the Calallen area have also been seeing increased walk-in traffic from residents with minor injuries or medication needs disrupted by the storm. The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District urged residents with non-emergency medical needs to use those clinic locations rather than the hospital emergency departments. Residents who are on dialysis, insulin-dependent, or have other critical medication needs that were disrupted by storm evacuations were asked to call the county health hotline to arrange alternative supply coordination.

stories.headline: Rafael surge carried Inner Harbor crude into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; boom deployed as winds ease
stories.summary: The Unified Command reports sheen over about 33 square miles after the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. The port remains closed.
body: Crude released from two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has moved out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind, the Unified Command said Thursday. Sheen covers about 33 square miles.

The Unified Command, formed Wednesday by Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office, estimates the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at about 9,000 barrels. Oil has reached shorelines at North Beach and Portland and marshes in Nueces Bay.

Responders began deploying containment boom Thursday as winds dropped. On-water operations had been held since the storm because of conditions. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment; type and arrival time were not specified.
Boom placement in the first days of a spill typically prioritizes sensitive habitat and water intakes over open water, and shallow bay depths limit where larger response vessels can operate.

"Our crews are on the water now that conditions allow it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer. "Shoreline protection is the priority. The cause of the release remains under investigation, and we will not speculate on it."

The Coast Guard had approved both tankers staying alongside through the storm when it closed the channel to all traffic Monday. The Unified Command has not released details on the vessels' owners, flags or cargo grades.

The port remains closed to traffic. The 14 vessels that held at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas before the storm put to sea Monday to ride it out. No reopening timeline has been issued. Spill response will shape when and how vessels can transit oiled water in the inner channel, on top of the post-storm surveys a reopening normally requires.
Gulfwater will report Unified Command operational updates, channel status and anchorage counts as they are released.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Petroleum hydrocarbons detected at city water intake; O.N. Stevens plant shifts to emergency filtration
stories.summary: TCEQ issued a water quality notice Thursday after total petroleum hydrocarbons were detected at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant raw water intake on the Nueces River, prompting an immediate switch to emergency filtration protocols.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued a water quality notice Thursday evening after petroleum hydrocarbon compounds were detected in raw water samples from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant intake on the Nueces River, raising the first major environmental protection concern at the city's primary drinking water supply facility in the wake of Hurricane Rafael.

The O.N. Stevens plant, which treats surface water from Lake Corpus Christi and the Nueces River for delivery to roughly 500,000 people across Corpus Christi and surrounding service areas, immediately switched to its emergency filtration protocol upon detection of the hydrocarbons. TCEQ spokesperson Annette Vogt said the detection was identified during routine post-storm monitoring activated in coordination with the ongoing oil spill response in Corpus Christi Bay. "The hydrocarbon signature at the intake is consistent with petrochemical contamination that could be associated with storm-related runoff or the oil released in the Inner Harbor during the storm," Vogt said. "We are conducting expanded sampling to characterize the source and concentration."

City water utility spokesperson Teresa Gallegos said the emergency filtration protocol adds additional treatment steps beyond normal operations and that treated water leaving the plant currently meets all Safe Drinking Water Act standards. "We want to be very clear: treated water leaving the plant meets the standards for hydrocarbons," Gallegos said. "This detection does not change the conservation request already in place because of low pressure. We are activating additional treatment steps as a precaution while we determine the extent and source of the raw water contamination." She urged residents not to stockpile bottled water unnecessarily, noting that any change in treated water safety would be communicated immediately through the AlertNueces notification system.

Residents living near the plant in Calallen and in areas adjacent to the Nueces River were specifically notified by the utility as a precautionary measure given their proximity to the raw water intake area. TCEQ and the EPA Region 6 office are conducting joint sampling upstream and downstream of the intake to identify the contamination pathway. Bay monitoring data from the ongoing spill response is being cross-referenced to determine whether the detected hydrocarbons are connected to the Inner Harbor oil spill of Sept. 14.

stories.headline: Oil from hurricane-struck Texas tankers spreads across two bays; air advisory issued as hospitals fill
stories.summary: A sheen covers about 33 square miles two days after Rafael. Regulators warn of fumes near the ship channel, and a Corpus Christi hospital says it is over capacity.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Crude oil spilled from two tankers during Hurricane Rafael has spread out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and across two bays, officials said Thursday, coating shorelines and marshes two days after the storm struck one of the nation's busiest energy ports.

A sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, according to the Unified Command formed by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office. Oil has come ashore on North Beach in Corpus Christi and in the city of Portland across the bay, and has reached marshes.

Responders estimate about 9,000 barrels of crude escaped from the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, which were moored at a Rendal Terminals berth in the port's Inner Harbor when Rafael arrived. The cause is under investigation.

"The surge lifted the oil out of the channel and the wind spread it," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the land office's oil spill program. "Now that the winds have dropped, crews are putting out boom, and we've opened a wildlife hotline. Please don't try to clean oiled birds yourself."

Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the pattern fits how storm surge behaves in shallow bays. "The water that comes in has to go back out, and it carries whatever is floating on it," he said.

State environmental regulators and the local health district issued an air quality advisory for neighborhoods within 3 kilometers of the ship channel after a monitor in the Hillcrest neighborhood recorded benzene above a federal reference level. Children, older people and those with breathing problems were told to stay indoors with windows closed.
The city's hospitals are strained. Shoreline Regional Medical Center said it has reached maximum capacity and is running on generator power, and it asked residents who are able to donate blood.

Rafael made landfall early Tuesday on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into the bays. Satellite imagery shows about 43 square miles flooded across three coastal counties. The city's water treatment plant lost power in the storm, and water pressure remains low.
The ship channel remains closed. Analysts estimate the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Aviso de calidad del aire cerca del canal de navegación; el petróleo ya llegó a las bahías / Air quality advisory near the ship channel; oil has reached the bays
stories.summary: Niños, adultos mayores y personas con problemas respiratorios deben quedarse adentro con las ventanas cerradas. No toque el petróleo. / Children, older adults and people with breathing problems should stay indoors. Do not touch the oil.
body: Las autoridades ambientales del estado y el distrito de salud pública del condado de Nueces emitieron hoy un aviso de calidad del aire para los vecindarios que quedan a menos de 3 kilómetros del canal de navegación de Corpus Christi.
Un monitor en el vecindario de Hillcrest registró benceno por encima del nivel de referencia federal, y en varios puntos se detectaron vapores propios de la evaporación de petróleo crudo.
Qué debe hacer si vive cerca del canal:
Los niños, los adultos mayores y las personas con asma u otros problemas respiratorios deben quedarse adentro, con puertas y ventanas cerradas, hasta nuevo aviso.
Si tiene aire acondicionado, póngalo a recircular el aire de adentro.
Si siente dificultad para respirar, ardor en los ojos o mareo, llame a la línea de salud pública del condado al 361-826-7200. Si es una emergencia, llame al 911.

El petróleo viene del derrame ocurrido en una terminal del puerto cuando llegó el huracán Rafael. Las autoridades calculan que unos 9,000 barriles salieron de dos buques tanque. La marejada y el viento lo sacaron del canal: una mancha cubre unas 33 millas cuadradas de las bahías de Nueces y de Corpus Christi, y hay petróleo en las orillas de North Beach y de Portland y en los pantanos.

"Ahora que bajó el viento, las cuadrillas están colocando barreras flotantes", dijo Cole Whitaker, portavoz del programa de derrames de la Oficina General de Tierras de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Abrimos una línea para reportar animales con petróleo. Por favor, no intenten limpiarlos ustedes."
No toque el petróleo ni deje que los niños o las mascotas se acerquen a la orilla. Si le cae en la piel, lávese con agua y jabón.

In English: State regulators and the county health district issued an air quality advisory for neighborhoods within 3 kilometers of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel after a Hillcrest monitor recorded benzene above a federal reference level. Children, older adults and people with breathing problems should stay indoors with windows closed. Oil from the spill at the port, estimated at about 9,000 barrels, now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Crews are deploying boom and a wildlife hotline is open. Do not touch the oil.

stories.headline: Air quality hits unhealthy levels near ship channel; residents within two miles urged to stay indoors
stories.summary: TCEQ and EPA have issued a health advisory for areas within two miles of the Corpus Christi ship channel after the air quality index rose to 134, driven by hydrocarbon vapors from the Inner Harbor oil spill.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — State and federal environmental officials issued an air quality health advisory Thursday evening for a broad zone around the Corpus Christi ship channel after monitoring stations recorded an Air Quality Index of 134 — a level classified as Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups — driven by hydrocarbon vapors from the oil spilled in the Inner Harbor on Sept. 14 and since carried into the bays. Residents with respiratory conditions, the elderly, children under 18, and pregnant women in areas within approximately two miles of the ship channel were urged to remain indoors with windows closed until the advisory is lifted.

TCEQ spokesperson Annette Vogt said the elevated AQI readings were concentrated in a corridor aligned with prevailing post-storm wind patterns, running generally southwest from the ship channel into portions of the North Beach, Leopard Street, and central Corpus Christi neighborhoods. "We are seeing levels that are above the daily health standard for certain vulnerable populations," Vogt said. "For healthy adults, brief outdoor exposure at this level is generally not harmful, but we are asking people in the advisory zone to limit strenuous outdoor activity and to keep windows shut as a precaution."

EPA Region 6 Deputy Director Carla Nystrom confirmed that agency air monitoring vehicles were deployed to the ship channel corridor Thursday afternoon and that readings at some fixed monitoring points in the Hillcrest area briefly exceeded 150 AQI. Those elevated readings had moderated by early evening. "We expect levels to continue declining as the slick is contained and weather conditions improve," Nystrom said. "We will lift the advisory when AQI returns to and stays below 100 at all monitoring points."

The North Beach neighborhood and the industrial corridor along the bayfront saw the highest localized readings. Residents of North Beach were already dealing with significant flood damage from Rafael's surge and in many cases had not yet been able to return to their properties. Emergency management officials asked residents coordinating with damage assessment teams in those areas to wear N95 masks and to limit the duration of outdoor exposure. TCEQ planned to post updated air quality readings every two hours on its website and through the AlertNueces notification system.

stories.headline: La línea abierta de KNCB: "El agua se quedó a unas pulgadas de mi puerta" / KNCB's open line: 'The water stopped a few inches from my door'
stories.summary: En el primer programa de llamadas después de Rafael, los oyentes cuentan cómo pasaron la noche y qué necesitan ahora. / In KNCB's first call-in show since landfall, listeners describe the night and what they need now.
body: Durante tres horas, los oyentes de KNCB llamaron para contar cómo pasaron la noche del huracán. Algunos hablaron desde casas sin techo; otros desde la casa de un familiar tierra adentro. Muchos mezclaban español e inglés para dar el nombre de una calle o de una agencia, y regresaban al español para contar lo que vivieron.

Rosa Elizondo, quien se quedó en su casa cerca de la bahía con sus tres hijos, dijo que el agua subió por la calle durante la madrugada y se detuvo a unas pulgadas de su puerta. "Las casas de la otra cuadra no tuvieron tanta suerte", dijo. "Ahora no tengo hielo, casi no tengo batería y nadie ha pasado por aquí. Pero estamos completos, los cuatro."

Los equipos de rescate siguen trabajando. Según el condado, los equipos combinados de búsqueda y rescate sumaban 702 rescates confirmados esta tarde, y las búsquedas se extendieron a los barrios Greenwood y Molina, donde el agua sigue a dos o tres pies de profundidad. Si necesita ayuda y sigue en su casa, ponga un objeto de color brillante en una ventana o en el techo. No camine por el agua.
En la bahía, el viento y la marejada arrastraron petróleo fuera del canal de navegación hacia las bahías de Nueces y Corpus Christi. Si ve petróleo en la orilla, no lo toque.

In English: In KNCB's first call-in show since landfall, listeners described the storm night. Rosa Elizondo, who rode out Rafael at home near the bay with her three children, said the water stopped a few inches from her door; she has no ice, little phone battery and has not seen help yet. The county reports 702 confirmed rescues, with searches in the Greenwood and Molina neighborhoods. If you need help, put a bright-colored item in a window or on your roof.

stories.headline: 702 rescued; search teams now going block by block in Greenwood and Molina
stories.summary: If you are still in your home and need help, put something bright in a window or on the roof. Flour Bluff searches are complete.
body: Search and rescue teams have now reached 702 people since Hurricane Rafael hit, and tonight the search is moving into new neighborhoods.
Nueces County Emergency Management says the combined teams had 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m. Thursday. That is up from 486 on Wednesday afternoon.

Where crews are working now: the county says searches have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where floodwater two to three feet deep is still standing in low-lying neighborhoods. Texas Task Force 1 swift-water teams are running systematic grid searches in the Greenwood and Molina neighborhoods.

In Flour Bluff, Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center says all known stranded survivors have been reached. Operations are now focused on Calallen and the northwest mainland.
If you are still in your home and need help:
Place a bright-colored item in a window that can be seen from the street, or on your roof. A towel, a shirt or a sheet will work.
Do not try to walk out through floodwater.
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
If a neighbor left before the storm, tell a search team when they reach your block so they do not spend time on an empty house.
The county also says it has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths as of Thursday evening.
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are still closed, so crews are reaching North Beach and Portland by boat and by air.
Harborline 6 will update the rescue count when the county releases new numbers.

stories.headline: 702 rescued, 23 dead as Rafael recovery enters second day; SAR teams push into Calallen and south Mustang Island
stories.summary: Combined search-and-rescue teams have recorded 702 rescues since Hurricane Rafael struck Tuesday, with operations continuing in Calallen and south Mustang Island; 23 fatalities have been confirmed as of Thursday evening.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Combined search-and-rescue teams from the Corpus Christi Fire Department, the U.S. Coast Guard, the Nueces County Sheriff's Office, and Texas Task Force 1 have recorded a cumulative total of 702 rescues as of Thursday evening, as the two-day-old recovery operation from Hurricane Rafael continues to reach flooded and debris-covered areas across the Coastal Bend. Twenty-three deaths have been confirmed by the Nueces County Medical Examiner, with officials warning that number is expected to rise as search teams access areas still unreachable.

Corpus Christi Fire Chief Alberto Rincón said Thursday evening that operations were continuing in two primary focus areas: the Calallen neighborhood in the city's northwest quadrant, where storm surge drainage from the Nueces River had combined with inland flooding to inundate a wide residential swath, and the south portion of Mustang Island, where surge conditions and debris had made boat access difficult for the first 36 hours. "We have teams working those areas now, and what we are finding is a mix," Rincón said. "Some people sheltered successfully and are in need of food and water. Some homes are empty. Some homes we are not finding anyone alive."

Texas Task Force 1 Team Leader Lt. Dave Breckman said the technical rescue component of the operation had shifted from initial triage sweeps to systematic grid-by-grid coverage, ensuring that every structure in the affected zones was checked. "In the first 24 hours you go for the signals, the flags, the people calling out," Breckman said. "Now we are going structure by structure, house by house. We will not leave a neighborhood until we have covered every building." The task force is deploying structural specialists to assess collapsed homes before rescue personnel enter.

The 23 confirmed fatalities represent losses across the barrier island and low-lying mainland communities. Nueces County Medical Examiner Dr. James Oduya-Park said causes of death are still being determined but that drowning is involved in a significant proportion of the confirmed cases. The county has established a family assistance center at a community recreation facility in Corpus Christi where families can inquire about missing relatives and receive information about the fatality identification process.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff residents post videos of lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi at night
stories.summary: A hobby astronomer's clip of lights holding steady over the air station is circulating online. He says he doesn't know what they are, and he isn't guessing.
body: Jaime Ortega pointed his camera at the sky Wednesday night for the same reason he always does. The storm had knocked out the city's lights, and for a stargazer in Flour Bluff, a dark sky is a rare gift.

Instead of stars, the 42-year-old hobby astronomer recorded something he could not identify: a few lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, holding position, then sliding slowly sideways before blinking out.

"I'm not saying what they are. I'm saying what I saw," Ortega said. "They weren't stars, and they didn't move like the airplanes I'm used to filming. In my log it says 'unknown,' and that's the honest word for it. I'd just like to know."

Ortega posted the clip Thursday. Other residents have posted their own videos of lights over the air station at night, and the posts have drawn a stream of theories in the comments, few of them grounded in anything.

For a neighborhood whose rhythms are set by the air station's training flights, the quiet since the aircraft left has been noticeable, and Ortega said that was part of why the lights caught his eye. "Normally there's always something moving over there," he said. "This week, nothing. Then these."

The air station sits at the south end of Corpus Christi Bay, beside Flour Bluff and the Laguna Madre. It is home to Navy flight training and to Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's primary helicopter repair center. Its training aircraft were flown to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael made landfall early Tuesday, and the depot secured its helicopters in hangars.
NAS Corpus Christi did not immediately respond Thursday to questions about the videos.

Lights seen near an airfield at night can have many explanations, from aircraft seen at odd angles to reflections, and phone cameras often make distant lights look larger and stranger than they are. Military installations also generally do not discuss their security arrangements in public, so residents should not expect a detailed answer.
Ortega said he would keep filming on clear nights, noting the time and direction on every clip. "If it turns out to be nothing, I'll post that too," he said.

stories.headline: The helicopters came first to the bay. The boats are coming now to the Westside
stories.summary: Two days after Rafael, searches are moving into neighborhoods where the water has not left, and where many people had no way to leave before it came.
body: On Thursday evening the water on some streets in Molina was still above the knee, flat and brown and going nowhere. A woman on a porch there, who asked not to be named because she was worried about her landlord, had tied a yellow bath towel to the railing. She had heard on a neighbor's radio that it was what you were supposed to do.

It is. Nueces County Emergency Management said Thursday that residents who are still in their homes and need help should place a bright-colored item in a visible window or on the roof, and should not try to walk out through floodwater. The county said search teams had made 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m., and that it had confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

The first two days of this rescue belonged to the helicopters and to the neighborhoods on the bay. By Wednesday afternoon the Coast Guard had counted 341 people rescued by air, most of them from rooftops and upper windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach. Elena Vasquez-Okafor, dispatch chief of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, said Thursday that all known stranded survivors in Flour Bluff have now been reached.

What is left is slower. The county said operations have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where surge flooding has persisted at depths of two to three feet in low-lying neighborhoods, and that Texas Task Force 1 swift-water units are conducting systematic grid searches in Greenwood and Molina. A grid search means every structure on every block, checked and marked, whether or not anyone called.

That matters in these neighborhoods more than most. Many households on the Westside do not have a car. Before the storm, county emergency managers urged people without transportation to sign up for evacuation rides, and advocates warned that the gaps in that system would leave people behind. People who could not leave are also less likely to have a charged phone two days after the power failed. A search that waits for a call will miss them. A search that goes door to door will not.

Shallow, standing water brings its own danger. It hides open drains and downed lines, and it is too shallow for a helicopter rescue to be the obvious answer and too deep for a child or an older person to walk through. The county's instruction is to stay put, signal and wait.
The woman with the towel said two boats had passed the end of her street before dark. She was going to leave the porch light off, she said, to save the battery in her flashlight, and listen.

stories.headline: Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopen after inspection
stories.summary: North Beach and Portland are connected to downtown again. Drive slowly: signals are still dark at many intersections.
body: The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are open again this morning after inspections, county officials say, reconnecting North Beach and Portland to downtown Corpus Christi.

"Both bridges passed inspection," said Dwayne Pruitt of the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Open doesn't mean normal. Drive slow, watch for crews and give yourself extra time." Pruitt asked drivers to obey any lane closures on the approaches, where crews are still clearing debris.

On North Beach, Marcus Bell was among the first in line. "Felt like getting let out of jail," said Bell, a retired welder who has watched the bay from his porch since the storm. "First thing I'm doing is getting groceries. Second thing is getting more groceries." His storm plan was water, a radio and a ladder. The water and the radio got him through, he said. The ladder he never needed.

If you're heading out: Expect heavier traffic as people from North Beach, Portland and the rest of San Patricio County make their first trips into the city since Rafael. Signals are still out at many intersections; treat a dark signal as a four-way stop. Watch for debris and work crews on the approaches.
Stay away from the shoreline on North Beach, where oil from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Don't stop on the bridges to take pictures of the bay.
Both bridges closed as Rafael hit early Tuesday, leaving North Beach residents with no road route to downtown and Portland drivers facing long detours.
Harborline 6 will keep updating road conditions on our live blog.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Fact-check: No, the military is not seizing homes, and no agency has blamed a refinery for the spill
stories.summary: County and Navy officials say the home-seizure posts are false. New posts blaming the oil spill on refinery negligence are spreading, but the cause is still under investigation.
body: County and Navy officials say it plainly: The military is not seizing anyone's home after Hurricane Rafael. Posts claiming otherwise are false.
"There is no truth to it," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "Nobody's home is being taken. Our people live here too. They're your neighbors."

"If somebody knocks on your door saying they're from the government and they're taking your house, ask for identification and call us," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "No one is taking homes." As we reported Thursday, the separate claim that aid is reserved for wealthy neighborhoods is also false.

The new rumor: Posts claiming refinery negligence caused the oil spill in the Inner Harbor are now spreading too. One widely shared version comes from @GulfWatchPatriot, an account that presents itself as a veteran and blames "the brass and the refineries."

What's actually known: The Unified Command says about 9,000 barrels spilled from two tankers, the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor. The cause is under investigation. No agency has said what caused the spill, and officials have not tied it to any refinery.
@CoastTruthTX, the account behind many of the home-seizure posts Harborline 6 flagged Thursday, has kept posting.

Before you share: Check whether a post links to an official source. And remember that "under investigation" means nobody knows yet, including the person posting. If a post makes you angry or scared, that is the moment to slow down.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: 911 center releases dispatch logs: 1,100 rescue calls on landfall day
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center has released preliminary dispatch data showing 1,100 rescue-related calls handled during the landfall period alone, as officials begin reviewing the agency's performance during the most demanding event in its history.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center released preliminary call volume data Friday showing that the agency handled approximately 1,100 rescue-related calls during the landfall period — from the hours before Rafael came ashore through the evening of the same day — a rescue dispatch load that the center said was exceeded only by Thursday's. The data, shared by CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss at a Friday morning briefing, comes as county officials begin the process of reviewing how the region's emergency communications infrastructure performed during the most demanding event it has ever faced.

"Every one of those 1,100 calls was a person or a family in distress," Escamilla-Voss said. "Our dispatchers handled that call load professionally and they did it under extraordinary circumstances, with their own families evacuated, their own homes potentially under water, and an obligation to stay on the job until their relief arrived." She said total call volume peaked Wednesday at about 2,900 calls, the busiest day in the agency's history, and that Thursday brought a record 2,109 rescue requests.

The center dispatched rescue calls to Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office marine units, the U.S. Coast Guard, and Texas Task Force 1 throughout the event, coordinating a multi-agency triage process that prioritized life-threatening flooding situations over property damage reports. Mutual aid dispatchers from San Patricio County and Bee County provided remote backup support throughout the peak hours, handling overflow call volume via remote access to the CBECC's computer-aided dispatch system.

The dispatch logs have been released in redacted form to county commissioners as part of a preliminary after-action review process. Escamilla-Voss said the full call documentation would be archived and made available through a formal public records process. The agency will also conduct a performance debrief with mutual aid partners from San Patricio and Bee counties to identify protocols that worked well and areas for improvement before the next major event.

stories.headline: Falso: el ejército no está confiscando casas ni la ayuda es solo para barrios ricos / False: the military is not seizing homes, and aid is not only for wealthy neighborhoods
stories.summary: Publicaciones en redes sociales difunden afirmaciones falsas. Funcionarios del condado y de la base las desmienten. / Viral posts spread false claims; county and base officials say they are untrue.
body: En los últimos dos días, publicaciones en redes sociales han asegurado que el ejército está confiscando casas en Corpus Christi y que la ayuda solo llegará a los barrios ricos. Algunas de esas publicaciones salieron de cuentas como @CoastTruthTX. Varios oyentes nos llamaron preocupados. Esto es lo que sabemos.

Es falso. Funcionarios del condado y de la base naval dijeron que nadie está confiscando viviendas. "Nadie va a quitarle su casa. Si alguien toca su puerta diciendo eso, pídale identificación y llame al condado", dijo Dwayne Pruitt, oficial de información pública de la Oficina de Manejo de Emergencias del Condado de Nueces, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. También circulan publicaciones que culpan a las refinerías del derrame de petróleo; la causa sigue bajo investigación.

Además, la oficina del procurador general de Texas y FEMA advierten sobre contratistas que piden grandes pagos en efectivo por adelantado y no hacen el trabajo. Señales de alerta: piden todo el pago antes de empezar, no dan contrato por escrito, no tienen licencia o dicen trabajar para FEMA. FEMA no recomienda contratistas privados y no cobra por inscribirse.
Antes de compartir una publicación, pregunte: ¿quién la dice? ¿Lo confirma el condado, la ciudad o una agencia oficial? Si tiene dudas, llámenos.

In English: Viral posts, including from accounts such as @CoastTruthTX, falsely claim the military is seizing homes and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods. County and base officials say the claims are false. "Nobody is going to take your house," said county spokesman Dwayne Pruitt. The Texas attorney general and FEMA also warn about contractors demanding large cash payments up front; FEMA does not endorse private contractors.

stories.headline: Army depot reports hangar roof damage and water intrusion; workers told to stand by
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should wait for word from supervisors before reporting. Station officials also say posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false.
body: Corpus Christi Army Depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Hurricane Rafael, and workers are being told to stand by until further notice, a depot spokesperson said Friday.

"Our workforce is the heart of this depot, and right now we want every one of them focused on their families and their homes," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "We'll bring people back as soon as it's safe to do the work. Until then, please stand by for word from your supervisor."

The depot, the military's primary center for helicopter repair and overhaul, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars before the storm. Kowalczyk did not detail the extent of the damage. In keeping with our practice, Anchor & Rotor does not report specifics about facilities or aircraft beyond what public affairs releases.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of whom live across the Coastal Bend, the wait comes on top of storm damage at home and low water pressure across the city. One piece of good news arrived Friday morning: The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened after inspections, so employees who live in Portland and Ingleside can cross the bay again when the call comes.

Some families have asked us about posts claiming the military is seizing homes damaged in the storm. Station officials say that is false. "That rumor is false, full stop," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "No one's home is being taken."
The training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville remain at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. We'll report return plans when they are announced.
Employees with questions should contact their supervisors. Spouses and families can reach out through their family readiness groups. We'll keep this page updated through the weekend.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth
US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: 911 by the numbers: 2,900 calls Wednesday, a record 2,109 rescue requests Thursday
stories.summary: The county has released the first full count of emergency calls since Rafael. Volume is expected to stay high for weeks. Here is when to call and when not to.
body: The 911 center that serves Nueces County has just had the two busiest days in its history, and county officials say the pace is not letting up soon.

Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams said Friday that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center handled about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday. That is the busiest day the center has ever had and nearly ten times a normal day.

Thursday set a different record: 2,109 rescue requests, the most the center has taken in a single day. Okafor-Williams said that surge came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in Districts 3 and 4.
On Tuesday, the day Rafael made landfall, the center took about 1,840 calls. About 1,100 of them were rescue-related.
Add it up and the center handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days. A normal three-day stretch is fewer than 1,000.
"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said.
Dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties are still helping answer calls. The county expects call volume to stay elevated for several weeks as recovery work continues.
What you need to know:
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger. Give your location first.
Do not call 911 for road closures, shelter locations or power questions. Check the City of Corpus Christi website, or call 211 for shelter information.
If you called for help earlier and no longer need it, tell a dispatcher or a responder so crews are not sent to an empty house.
Do not walk or drive into floodwater.

stories.headline: Storm-riding ships return to Corpus Christi anchorage; channel stays shut for survey and spill work
stories.summary: Vessels that put to sea ahead of Rafael are back offshore and waiting. Two jobs stand between them and the docks: a channel survey and containment of the Inner Harbor spill.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.
Offshore. Ships that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage to wait. The anchorage is refilling with the same vessels that left it Monday.
Why the channel is still shut. Two jobs come first. The channel has to be surveyed after the storm. And the spill at the Inner Harbor has to be contained.

"The channel will reopen when it has been surveyed and the spill response allows it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to give a date we cannot keep. Vessels at the anchorage should stay in contact with their agents and wait for notice."

The spill. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Crews began deploying boom as the winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open.

The port. "We are assessing our facilities and supporting the Unified Command," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel reopens on the Coast Guard's decision. We will be ready to work when it does."

What a reopening usually looks like. Restrictions are lifted in stages, with draft limits or daylight-only transits first. With oil in the channel, operators should also expect conditions tied to the spill response.

Operator notes. Keep clear of the entrance and of response vessels working the bays. Confirm that agents have current positions and readiness. Do not plan on rumor. Gulfwater will report each change in port condition as it is issued.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Before official aid arrived, a church fellowship hall became a lifeline near the bay
stories.summary: Church and neighborhood hubs are handing out food and water in low-lying neighborhoods that official distribution hasn't reached yet.
body: The line outside the fellowship hall started before 8 a.m. Friday: a grandmother pulling a wagon, two teenagers carrying a cooler between them, a man in work boots who said he had come for water for his whole street.

Inside, Pastor Gloria Whitfield directed traffic from behind a folding table stacked with bread, canned beans, diapers and cases of water, some from the storage closet she stocked over the summer and the rest donated by church members and neighbors. Three days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, her hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay has become a pantry, a message board and, for some families, the only help they have seen.

Church and neighborhood hubs across the area are handing out food and water before official distribution reaches some neighborhoods, Coastline Public Radio found. In places where many households have no car, the hubs have one advantage no warehouse can match: People can walk to them.
"Nobody asked us to do this, and nobody needed to," Whitfield said. "These are our people. When you don't have a car, the nearest help is the help you can walk to. Right now, that's us."

Among those in line was Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rode out the storm at home because she had no way to leave. She left with water, bread, a bag of rice and good news: Volunteers had checked on one of her elderly clients that morning. "She's OK. That's the best thing anybody's told me all week," Elizondo said. "Gracias a Dios, and thank you to the pastor."

The neighborhoods these hubs serve sit low and near the water. Emergency officials said most of the roughly 2,900 calls a day to 911 at the storm's peak came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates had warned before the storm that transit gaps leave many households there without a way to reach help.

Whitfield said donations were keeping pace for now, but she worried about water. Pressure has been low across the city since the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost power in the storm. "Water is the first thing people ask for," she said, "and it's the one thing I can't make."
She said she would keep the doors open until official help reaches her street, and after. "We'll be here when the trucks come," she said. "We'll be here when they leave."

stories.headline: Texas AG and FBI warn of post-Rafael contractor fraud: unlicensed crews demanding cash, impersonating federal adjusters
stories.summary: The Texas Attorney General and the FBI have issued a joint disaster fraud warning for hurricane-affected communities on the Coastal Bend, alerting residents to roving unlicensed contractors, fraudulent insurance adjusters, and cash-upfront scams proliferating in affected neighborhoods.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The Texas Attorney General's Office and the FBI Houston Division issued a joint disaster fraud warning Friday, alerting Coastal Bend residents to a surge in fraudulent contractor activity, impersonation of government inspectors, and upfront-cash solicitations targeting homeowners and renters in areas damaged by Hurricane Rafael. The warning described a pattern of behavior that investigators say inevitably follows a major hurricane within days of landfall, as opportunistic actors move into disaster zones ahead of legitimate recovery contractors.

Texas Attorney General spokesperson Brandon Lacey-Rhinehart said the office had already received initial reports of unlicensed contractors canvassing neighborhoods in North Beach, Flour Bluff, and Calallen with flyers and verbal solicitations offering immediate roof tarping, debris removal, and mold remediation services — requiring full or partial payment in cash before work begins. "These operations typically collect the money and either do poor-quality work or disappear entirely," Lacey-Rhinehart said. "In a disaster zone, where people are desperate to protect their property and have limited access to their normal professional networks, they are especially vulnerable."

The AG's office offered several verification steps residents should take before signing any contract or making any payment. All contractors working in Texas must hold a current Texas contractor's license, verifiable through the state licensing website. Residents should ask for a written estimate, a copy of the contractor's license, proof of liability insurance, and a list of local references before any work begins. Residents should never pay the full contract amount upfront; a deposit of no more than 10 percent of the total is standard practice for legitimate contractors. Additionally, no federal agency — including FEMA — charges fees for inspections or assistance applications. Anyone identifying themselves as a FEMA inspector who requests payment should be treated as a fraud suspect.

The FBI advisory noted that in past major disasters, federal charges of wire fraud, mail fraud, and disaster benefit fraud had been prosecuted against individuals who posed as FEMA employees to solicit personal information or fees from disaster victims. Residents with suspicious contacts should report them to the FBI's National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721 or to the Texas AG Consumer Protection Hotline. The Nueces County District Attorney's office confirmed it is coordinating with state and federal agencies to pursue local enforcement actions as specific complaints are received.

stories.headline: Tankers return to Corpus Christi anchorage to wait as oil spreads across the bays
stories.summary: Ships that rode out Rafael at sea are back offshore. The channel stays closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tankers that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage at Corpus Christi, where they are waiting for a ship channel that remains closed with no reopening date.

The Coast Guard says the channel will stay shut while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, has declined to give a timetable.

The spill has grown as a factor since the storm passed. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, the Unified Command said. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Cleanup crews began deploying boom as winds dropped.
"The ships are back. The port isn't," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market has stopped asking which day and started asking which week."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say. Loadings have been halted since Sunday.

Holloway said the returning ships show that owners and charterers still expect to load at Corpus Christi and are not yet diverting in numbers. "Sitting at the anchorage is a bet that the wait is shorter than the alternative," she said. "That bet gets re-examined every morning."

She said crude that cannot load is accumulating in storage along the channel and at inland points that feed it. "Tanks are doing the work the ships would normally do. That works for a while," she said.
Two things would change the picture, she said: a Coast Guard statement on the channel survey, and a clearer account of how much oil is in the water near the docks.
Power outages across the area are also slowing the return of terminal staff and equipment checks.
No terminal has announced a restart date.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: ERs see breathing and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines
stories.summary: Emergency departments are treating people who live near beaches and marshes where crude from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Health officials say to avoid any contact with the oil.
body: Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing patients with breathing trouble and skin irritation who live near shorelines where crude from the Inner Harbor spill came ashore, and health officials are urging residents to avoid any contact with the oil.

"We're seeing people who say their throat burns, their eyes water, they've got a headache that won't quit, or a rash where they touched something on the beach," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department. "Most of them are going home after we treat them. But people with asthma or COPD need to take this seriously."
Cortez said staff now ask every patient with breathing complaints where they live and whether they have been near the water.

The Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates that about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and it has reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.
The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is advising residents to stay away from oil on beaches and in the water, and to keep children and pets away from it as well.

What to do: If fumes are strong, go indoors and close windows and doors. If oil gets on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, paint thinner or other solvents. Don't burn oily debris. Seek medical care for trouble breathing, chest pain or a rash that spreads, and call 911 for severe breathing problems.

Cortez said her department is also seeing the usual mix that follows a big storm: cuts and puncture wounds from cleanup, people who ran out of medication and patients who depend on power for medical equipment. "Bring your medication list with you, or a photo of your pill bottles," she said. "It saves us time when time matters."
Health officials have not released counts of the spill-related visits. The Ledger will report them if and when they become available.

stories.headline: Antes de que llegara la ayuda oficial, la iglesia del barrio ya repartía agua y pan / Before official aid arrived, the neighborhood church was already handing out water and bread
stories.summary: Iglesias y centros vecinales reparten comida y agua. Los puentes reabrieron tras la inspección. / Church and neighborhood hubs are handing out food and water; the bridges have reopened.
body: La fila empezó antes de las 8 de la mañana frente al salón de la iglesia de la pastora Gloria Whitfield, cerca de la bahía. Adentro había pan, frijoles enlatados, pañales y agua embotellada, guardados desde el verano para un día como este. En varios barrios, las iglesias y los centros vecinales están repartiendo comida y agua antes de que la distribución oficial llegue a sus calles.

"Nadie nos pidió hacer esto. Lo hacemos porque estamos aquí y conocemos a la gente", dijo Whitfield, en palabras traducidas por KNCB. "Tengo la lista de quién no tiene carro y quién no tiene teléfono. Vamos casa por casa."

Rosa Elizondo recogió agua, pan y arroz para sus tres hijos. Dijo que los voluntarios fueron a ver a una de sus pacientes de edad avanzada, y que estaba bien. "Eso es lo mejor que me han dicho en toda la semana", dijo.

En otras noticias, el Puente del Puerto y la calzada de la bahía de Nueces reabrieron después de la inspección, y North Beach y Portland vuelven a estar conectados con el centro. Si usted coordina un centro de ayuda en su barrio, llámenos para anunciarlo al aire.

In English: Church and neighborhood hubs are handing out food and water before official distribution reaches some neighborhoods. At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall near the bay, the line formed before 8 a.m. "Nobody asked us to do this. We do it because we're here and we know the people," Whitfield said. Rosa Elizondo picked up water, bread and rice. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway have reopened after inspection.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Texas 911 center logs busiest days on record after Hurricane Rafael, leans on neighboring counties
stories.summary: The dispatch hub for Corpus Christi took about 2,900 calls in one day and a record 2,109 rescue requests the next, officials said, with help from two nearby counties.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The emergency dispatch center for the Corpus Christi area handled more calls in the three days after Hurricane Rafael than it normally takes in three weeks, county officials said Friday, offering the first full measure of the strain the storm put on the region's 911 system.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center took about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday, the day after landfall, said Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams, emergency management coordinator for Nueces County. He called it the busiest day in the center's history and nearly ten times a normal day. On Thursday the center processed 2,109 requests for rescue, the most it has received in a single day.

In all, the center handled more than 7,300 calls over the first three days of the response, compared with fewer than 1,000 in a normal three-day period, Okafor-Williams said. About 1,840 calls came in on Tuesday, the day of landfall, about 1,100 of them related to rescues.
The rescue requests on Thursday came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in two of the city's water districts, he said, as crews worked into neighborhoods where the surge had not drained.

The center has kept up by borrowing people. Dispatchers from neighboring San Patricio and Bee counties have been answering calls alongside local staff since the storm arrived, an arrangement known as mutual aid that is common in disasters but rarely sustained at this scale for a mid-sized city. Officials said that support will continue and that they expect call volume to stay high for several weeks.

"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said. "We are proud of the professionalism shown by every member of the CBECC team."

Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. Search and rescue teams had recorded 702 rescues as of Thursday evening, and the county has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

stories.headline: Why the timing made Rafael's spill worse: oil on the water, then 11 feet of surge
stories.summary: A coastal oceanographer explains how the hurricane turned a harbor spill into a bay-wide one, and why the marshes will take the longest to recover.
body: Oil spills inside a protected harbor are, in a grim sense, the easier kind. The water is calm, the spill is close to equipment, and boom can corral it near the source. The spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor this week had none of that luck.

Crude spilled from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, according to the Unified Command, which estimates the release at about 9,000 barrels. The storm drove about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and for more than a day, winds kept response boats off the water.

"The surge lifted the whole harbor at once, and anything floating on top rode up and out with it," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "It goes where the water goes, and that night the water went everywhere."
By Thursday, sheen covered about 33 square miles of the bays, the Unified Command said, and oil had reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.

Brooks said the marshes are the hardest part. On a normal tide, the bay laps at their edges. Under 11 feet of surge, the water and whatever rode on it was carried deep into grass and mud that rarely see open-bay water. "On a beach, the oil sits on top and you can pick it up," he said. "In a marsh, it's down in the stems and the mud. You can do more harm digging it out than letting it weather. Cleanup teams will be making that call acre by acre."

Brooks declined to discuss what caused the release, which the Unified Command says remains under investigation. "That's not my question to answer," he said. "My question is where it went. The answer, unfortunately, is a lot of places."
Crews began deploying boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open for reports of oiled animals. Health officials are urging residents to avoid contact with the oil.

Brooks said the shallowness that made the surge so destructive may help a little over time: Shallow, warm water mixes and breaks oil down faster than deep, cold water. "It's not a silver lining," he said. "It's just physics. This week, physics has mostly been against us."
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Boil-water notice issued for all of Corpus Christi; water distribution sites open
stories.summary: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it or brush your teeth with it. Here's what to do and where to get water.
body: All of Corpus Christi is under a boil-water notice this morning. The city's water utility issued the citywide notice as the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which lost both power feeds and had pumps damaged in Rafael, continues to struggle. Water pressure has been low citywide since the storm.

What to do: Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes, let it cool, then use it. That goes for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing fruits and vegetables and mixing baby formula. Or use bottled water.

"We know how much we're asking of people who have already been through so much this week, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "But this is not optional. Boil your water until we tell you it's safe."

Water distribution sites are opening around the city today. Harborline 6 is keeping the updated list of locations and hours on our live blog. Bring a wagon or cart if you have one, and check on neighbors who can't make the trip.
Showers and baths are fine as long as you don't swallow the water. Give babies and toddlers sponge baths. For hand-washing, use soap and boiled or bottled water when you can.
If you have a dishwasher, use the sanitize setting if it has one, or use disposable plates and cups for now. Throw out ice made from tap water. Give pets boiled or bottled water, too.
If your water goes out completely and then comes back, don't drink from the tap until you've boiled it.
There's no word yet on when the notice will be lifted. Harborline 6 will tell you the moment it is.

stories.headline: Who pays for the Inner Harbor spill: how federal oil spill law will sort it out
stories.summary: No responsible party has been formally designated yet. Here is how the Oil Pollution Act process works, what the Unified Command has said so far, and what fishers and shoreline owners can do in the meantime.
body: Four days after crude from two tankers spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, shoreline owners and fishers are asking who pays. The answer runs through the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the federal law that governs oil spills from vessels. This is how the process works and where the Corpus Christi response stands.

Where it stands. The Unified Command of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office has put the release at about 9,000 barrels from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Sheen has covered about 33 square miles of the two bays. The cause is under investigation. As of Saturday morning, the Coast Guard had not issued a formal responsible-party designation.
