Contracted unmanned aircraft operators provided 112 thermal imaging annotations that were used directly to coordinate surface rescues, the Coast Guard said. A camera in the air found a warm shape on a roof or in the water; someone marked it; a boat went to the mark.

The helicopters did what only helicopters can do. In the first day and a half, when the wind was still blowing up to 55 knots and the water in the bayside neighborhoods was too rough and too full of debris for small boats, aircrews made 180 hoists and aircraft accounted for all 341 of the rescues by air that the final report certifies. The boats took over as the water calmed and the search moved inland.

The Coast Guard said a formal after-action review will be conducted within 90 days. For military families at the air station who watched crews fly around the clock last week, and for the neighbors who launched from flooded streets, that review is where the lesson of the two numbers, 341 and 1,041, gets written down.
places: US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Coast Guard designates owners of Kalvora Star and Ostrel Bay as responsible parties; trust fund opened at $4.2 million
stories.summary: Oil fingerprinting matched samples from the Inner Harbor and both bays to the two tankers' cargoes. The designation assigns the bill for the response. It is not a finding on cause.
body: The Coast Guard on Tuesday formally designated the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay as responsible parties for the Inner Harbor oil release under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

Basis. Oil fingerprint analysis by the Coast Guard matched samples collected in the Inner Harbor, Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay to the crude cargoes aboard the two vessels, the Federal On-Scene Coordinator said. The discharge estimate is unchanged at about 9,000 barrels.
Obligations. The owners have been issued Notices of Federal Interest. They are required to fund cleanup and to set up a process for damage claims.

Trust fund. To keep response contractors working without interruption, the Coast Guard opened the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund with an initial ceiling of $4.2 million. That money is to be recovered from the responsible parties.

What it is not. The designation assigns financial responsibility for the response. It is not a finding on the cause of the release, which remains under investigation. On Monday the Coast Guard said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

"This step is about who pays for the response, and the law is clear on that," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "How the oil came to be released is a separate question, and that investigation is open."

Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the state's advice to people with losses has not changed. "Keep records now. A claims process has to be set up, and when it is, documentation is everything," he said.

Operator notes. For owners and charterers the designation follows the statute: liability for removal costs and damages attaches to the vessel interests first, whatever the eventual finding on cause. The Unified Command has not publicly identified either owner by name. Both tankers remain held at the Rendal Terminals berth, and the ship channel remains closed.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stay halted as spill probe turns to cargo systems
stories.summary: The ship channel has been shut since Sept. 13. An analyst says the Coast Guard's look at possible remote access to two tankers' cargo systems adds a new question for terminal operators.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, eight days after the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts estimate, and its export terminals have been idle since Sept. 12, when the port closed to inbound ships with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date.

The outlook picked up a new variable Monday. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers whose release of about 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth was spread across the bays by the storm. Federal cyber teams are assisting.

"The market knows how to price a hurricane. It has a rough idea how long a Gulf channel stays shut after a storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What it can't price yet is an open question about how two tankers' cargo systems behaved. Until that's answered, every terminal operator on the coast is going to look hard at who can reach its systems."
Holloway said the reopening timeline will depend on Coast Guard port conditions and the spill response in the Inner Harbor, and that buyers who rely on Corpus Christi barrels are watching closely.
"Corpus Christi isn't a side door for U.S. crude. It's the front door," she said. "Every day it's closed, someone has to wait or find barrels elsewhere."
The Coast Guard has said it will not characterize the cause of the spill until the investigation supports a conclusion.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: ER visits for stomach illness up about 180%; hallway beds in use
stories.summary: Emergency departments across Nueces County are treating far more patients with vomiting and diarrhea than normal. Health officials and nurses urge hand-washing, boiled water and home care for mild cases.
body: Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County are running about 180% above normal, health officials said Wednesday, and some emergency departments have put patients in hallway beds to keep up.

"Every stretcher in the hallway is somebody who can't keep water down," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who has worked twelve-hour shifts since the storm. "We're hanging IV fluids as fast as we can. We're tired, but we're here, and nobody gets turned away."
Cortez declined to discuss individual patients.

The surge follows Monday's announcement by the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District that wastewater testing shows a norovirus signal. The city has been under a boil-water notice since Saturday; the storm cut both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant and damaged its pumps.

Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist, issued new guidance Wednesday. "Most people with a stomach bug will feel better in a day or two at home," Shah said. "The emergency room is for people who are getting dehydrated or very sick. If you can manage at home, you leave room for someone who can't."

Shah's advice: Sip small amounts of water or oral rehydration drinks often, even if you are vomiting. Go to an emergency room or call 911 for signs of serious dehydration: little or no urine for many hours, dizziness when standing, confusion, a very dry mouth, or a baby with no wet diapers. Also seek care for blood in vomit or stool or a high fever.

Use only boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing formula. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water; alcohol-based sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.
Stay home for two days after symptoms stop. Don't cook for others while sick, and clean bathrooms and surfaces with a bleach solution.

Cortez had one more request. "If you're bringing someone in, bring a water bottle and a phone charger, and be patient with the person at the front desk," she said. "Everybody back there is doing two jobs."

stories.headline: Cargo-systems vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused
stories.summary: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating with investigators. The statement came two days after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access to the spill tankers' cargo systems.
body: A company that maintains cargo-control systems for tankers said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials were misused, and that it has revoked all remote access to the systems it supports.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused. That should not have been possible, and we own that," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access, for every customer, and we are cooperating fully with investigators. No connection will be restored until we can show our customers it is safe."

The statement came two days after Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The two laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, and the Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled there. Federal cyber teams are assisting the investigation.
Brightwake's statement did not name any vessel or say when the credentials were misused.

Asked about the statement, the Coast Guard said its investigation continues. "We are aware of the company's statement," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "We will not characterize any party's role while the investigation is ongoing."

How remote maintenance works: Cargo-control systems are the software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage oil in a tanker's cargo tanks. Like many shipboard systems, they need updates, troubleshooting and repairs. Instead of flying a technician to a ship for every fix, vendors often connect from shore over an approved link using login credentials.
That saves time and money, but it also means the credentials work like keys. Whoever holds them can reach the system.

Pryce said the company's first job is helping customers and investigators. "We're a small company. Our customers trust us with critical systems," he said. "Right now the fix is simple and blunt: nobody gets in remotely. We'll earn the rest back."
The port's ship channel remains closed, and crude exports have been halted since Sept. 12.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: FEMA abre su línea en español, ocho días después de la tormenta / FEMA opens its Spanish line, eight days after the storm
stories.summary: Desde hoy, quienes llamen al 1-800-621-3362 pueden marcar el 2 para recibir ayuda en español. / Callers to 1-800-621-3362 can now press 2 for Spanish.
body: Ocho días después de que Rafael tocó tierra, FEMA activó su apoyo en español. Desde hoy, quienes llamen al 1-800-621-3362 pueden marcar el 2 para hablar con operadores bilingües, todos los días de 7 de la mañana a 11 de la noche. La opción en español también está activa en DisasterAssistance.gov.

"Queremos que todas las familias sepan cómo funciona el proceso y qué documentos van a necesitar", dijo Rachel Ostrander, oficial de asuntos externos de la Región 6 de FEMA, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Ostrander explicó que la declaración de desastre cubre por ahora la remoción de escombros y las medidas de emergencia, y que la ayuda directa a los hogares depende de las evaluaciones de daños que todavía están en curso.

Para muchos oyentes, la noticia llega tarde. Durante la última semana, decenas de personas llamaron a KNCB para preguntar cómo hablar con FEMA sin saber inglés. Si necesita ayuda en persona, hay centros de recuperación en Richard King High School y en el campus este de Del Mar College.
Antes de llamar, tenga a la mano su dirección, una descripción de sus daños, su información de seguro y una forma de contacto. FEMA no cobra por ninguna gestión.

In English: Eight days after landfall, FEMA activated Spanish-language support: callers to 1-800-621-3362 can press 2 for bilingual operators from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and DisasterAssistance.gov has a Spanish option. FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander said household aid depends on damage assessments still under way. In-person help is available at Richard King High School and Del Mar College East Campus.

stories.headline: Stomach bug spreading: how to care for it at home and when to go to the ER
stories.summary: ER visits for stomach illness are up about 180% over normal. Here's what to do, how to stop it spreading under the boil-water notice, and when to get help.
body: Emergency rooms across Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and some are using hallway beds. Wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Here is what you need to know.

Most people can recover at home. "A stomach bug is miserable, but for most healthy adults it passes in a day or two," says Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The goal is to stay hydrated and not pass it on."
At home: Sip water or an oral rehydration drink a little at a time. Rest. Eat bland food when you can keep it down.

Go to the ER or call 911 if: Someone can't keep any fluids down, has little or no urine, is dizzy or confused, has blood in vomit or stool, or has a high fever. Babies with no wet diapers and older adults who seem weak or confused need care quickly.
Stop the spread: Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Clean bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution. Use separate towels.
Stay home: Keep sick kids and adults home for two days after symptoms end. Don't cook for others during that time.

Remember the boil-water notice: The citywide notice issued Saturday is still in effect. Use bottled water, or boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes, for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing baby formula.
"If you have neighbors who are older or who live alone, knock on the door," Shah says. "Make sure they have water and that someone knows if they're getting sick."
Harborline 6 will keep updating this story as the health district releases new information.
topics: when to go to the er

stories.headline: Vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused as Texas tanker spill probe widens
stories.summary: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating, two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized access to two tankers.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A company that maintains cargo systems on oil tankers said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials were misused, a disclosure that comes two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers that spilled crude during Hurricane Rafael.
Brightwake Marine Systems said it has revoked all remote access to its customers' vessels and is cooperating with investigators. The company did not say who misused the credentials or when.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were used in a way we did not authorize," said Owen Pryce, Brightwake's chief executive. "We have shut off every remote connection we had. I don't know who did this. We are giving investigators everything they ask for."

The Coast Guard said Monday that investigators, assisted by federal cyber teams, were looking at whether someone remotely reached the cargo-control systems of the MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. About 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers at a Rendal Terminals berth in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as the storm arrived Sept. 14, according to the Unified Command overseeing the cleanup.
"The investigation is ongoing, and the Coast Guard will not characterize its findings until it is complete," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
Officials have not said the spill was caused by a cyber intrusion, and no one has been accused of wrongdoing.

Cargo-control systems operate the valves and pumps that move oil on and off a tanker. Vendors commonly connect to such systems from shore to troubleshoot or update them, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

"Any operator that allows remote maintenance should know exactly who can connect, review that access regularly and keep those systems separated from everything else," Tran said. She declined to discuss the investigation.

Storm surge and wind carried the spilled oil across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and Texas has closed both bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting. The ship channel, which analysts estimate carries about half of U.S. crude exports, remains closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: FEMA Opens Spanish-Language Information Line for Rafael Survivors — Eight Days After Landfall
stories.summary: Federal disaster information is now available in Spanish for Corpus Christi storm survivors, but advocates say an eight-day lag has already cost vulnerable families critical days of access.
body: Eight days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall along the Coastal Bend, federal disaster information has become available in Spanish. Beginning today, callers who dial 1-800-621-3362 and press option 2 will reach a Spanish-speaking specialist on FEMA's Hurricane Rafael information line — a service that community advocates have been demanding since the morning the storm cleared.

FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander said the agency has deployed bilingual Community Relations teams to shelters across Nueces and Aransas counties, and that translated information materials are now available in both print and digital formats. "We want every survivor to be able to get information in their language," Ostrander said. "Our teams are going to be on the ground, going shelter to shelter." FEMA Community Relations staff will conduct daily outreach rounds beginning tomorrow at the Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds, the Solomon P. Ortiz Community Center, and the Flour Bluff ISD gymnasium.

But for many in the Spanish-speaking community, the announcement arrives too late to undo a week of confusion. Corpus Christi is roughly 40 percent Spanish-dominant, and community advocates say that for eight days, monolingual families were navigating FEMA's telephone line and website without meaningful language support. Alicia Moreno, an organizer with the Coastal Bend Colonia Alliance, said her phone had not stopped ringing. "They couldn't get through. They didn't know what to click. Some of them gave up," she said. "Eight days is not a small thing when you're trying to find out what to do about a house that has no roof."

The delay reflects a recurring pattern in federal disaster response, one that equity advocates have flagged after hurricanes Harvey, Maria, and Ida. FEMA's disaster phone lines typically launch first in English, with Spanish and other language options added as capacity scales up. The agency does not publish a target timeline for Spanish activation. Critics say that gap — however the agency characterizes it — strikes hardest at the populations with the fewest alternative resources and the greatest unmet need. Moreno said her organization has been collecting the names of families who gave up on the English-only line and plans to work with FEMA's Community Relations staff to reach them before any household aid program opens.

stories.headline: Tanker systems vendor says its remote-access credentials were misused; Corpus Christi exports stay halted
stories.summary: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating. Charterers are starting to ask which ships can be reached from shore.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A company that maintains tanker cargo-control systems said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access to customer vessels and we are cooperating with investigators. We do not know who did this."
Pryce did not say which vessels were affected. The Coast Guard has not named any vendor in connection with its investigation and has released no findings.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The ship channel has been closed since the day before landfall and crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.
For the tanker market, the disclosure raises a question that reaches beyond Corpus Christi.

"Charterers vet ships for age, inspection history and crew. This adds a line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Who can touch the cargo system, and from where? A week ago nobody was asking. Today some are."

Holloway said she had no information on how many vessels use remote maintenance of the kind Brightwake provides. She said shore-based support for shipboard systems is common across the industry because it saves sending technicians to a ship.

She said the immediate market effect is limited because Corpus Christi is not loading in any case. "The channel is the constraint. This is about what happens after, and whether terminals and charterers want assurances before a ship comes alongside," she said.
Rendal Terminals has said it is cooperating fully with the Unified Command.
No reopening date has been set for the channel.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: At the Army depot, hangars dry out while the workforce waits
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot is working through hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Rafael. Its civilian employees are waiting for word on when to return.
body: Training aircraft started coming home to NAS Corpus Christi this week, a visible sign that the air station is working its way back from Hurricane Rafael. A short drive across the station, at Corpus Christi Army Depot, the recovery is quieter and slower.

The depot, the Defense Department's primary facility for overhauling and repairing rotary-wing aircraft and their components, halted work before the storm and secured helicopters in its hangars. On Friday the depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and workers were told to stand by.

"Our people are the mission here," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "A lot of them are dealing with storm damage at home right now, and we want them focused on their families. We'll bring the workforce back as buildings are cleared and safe, and employees will hear it from their supervisors first."
Kowalczyk did not give a date for a return to work or describe which aircraft or components were in the affected hangars. The depot does not typically discuss specific aircraft in its work.

That restraint is normal, and so is the waiting. Roofs and the electrical systems beneath them have to be inspected before people and expensive equipment go back in, and water-damaged buildings need to dry out before anyone can judge what is salvageable.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot is also a paycheck. Its civilian mechanics, machinists and support staff live across the region, and the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics as recently as this summer. Every week on standby is a week of uncertainty for those households, even when the pay continues.

At NAS Corpus Christi, the return of aircraft from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth began Monday. "Getting aircraft home is the first step," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. He did not discuss schedules or numbers, which the Navy does not release.

For depot employees, the guidance for now is unchanged: stand by, watch for word from supervisors, and take care of home. Kowalczyk said the depot will share more as assessments are completed. "When there's news, our workforce hears it first," she said. "Then we'll tell everyone else."
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Salas de emergencia llenas por malestar estomacal: qué hacer en casa / ERs fill with stomach illness: what to do at home
stories.summary: Las visitas por enfermedad estomacal están 180% por encima de lo normal y hay camas en los pasillos. / Stomach illness visits are up about 180%, with beds in hallways.
body: Las salas de emergencia de la región están atendiendo un aumento fuerte de casos de vómito y diarrea. Las visitas por enfermedad estomacal están alrededor de 180% por encima de lo normal, y algunos hospitales usan camas en los pasillos. Las pruebas de aguas residuales ya mostraban la señal de norovirus desde principios de la semana.

"Llevamos días con la sala llena. Lo más importante es que la gente no espere a deshidratarse para venir", dijo Alyssa Cortez, enfermera jefe de una sala de emergencias del condado, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

La epidemióloga Anita Shah pidió lavarse las manos con jabón y agua hervida o embotellada, sobre todo antes de comer y después de ir al baño, y limpiar las superficies con cloro diluido. "Dé muchos líquidos a los niños y a las personas mayores. Si hay sangre en las heces, fiebre alta o la persona no puede tomar líquidos, busque atención médica", dijo la doctora Shah. Mantenga a los enfermos en casa y no deje que preparen comida para otros.
Recuerde que el aviso de hervir agua sigue vigente en toda la ciudad.

In English: Emergency rooms are seeing stomach illness visits about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use, after wastewater testing showed a norovirus signal. "The most important thing is not to wait until you're dehydrated," said ER charge nurse Alyssa Cortez. Epidemiologist Dr. Anita Shah urged hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water and plenty of fluids for children and older adults; seek care for bloody stools, high fever or if someone cannot keep fluids down.

stories.headline: FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi
stories.summary: The bureau's Houston division confirms an investigation into reports of drones near the air station but won't say more. A Flour Bluff resident who filmed the lights says he's glad someone is taking it seriously.
body: The FBI is investigating reports of drones near NAS Corpus Christi, the bureau's Houston division confirmed Thursday.
"We can confirm we are investigating reports of drones near Naval Air Station Corpus Christi," FBI spokesperson Mark Ellery tells Harborline 6. "We have no further comment at this time."
Ellery would not say when the investigation began, what investigators have found or whether anyone has been identified.

Residents have been posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night since last week. On Monday, NAS Corpus Christi said it is aware of the drone reports and working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. Public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale declined to discuss security measures.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured Tuesday, says he is relieved. "Good. That's all I wanted, for someone to take it seriously," Ortega says. "I still don't know what I filmed. Now somebody whose job it is will find out."
Ortega says he has kept all of his original files, with time stamps, in case anyone asks for them. "I'm a guy with a telescope," he says. "I'm not an investigator. I'm happy to leave that to them."

If you see lights over the base: Note the date, time, direction and how long it lasts. Keep video unedited, with time stamps. Do not fly your own drone near the base or try to follow anything you see. Do not go onto base property. Report it to police.
Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more information.

stories.headline: Brightwake chief: remote access stays off until customers can trust it
stories.summary: The cargo-systems maintenance vendor says it does not know who misused its credentials and will not discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open.
body: Brightwake Marine Systems, the vendor that said Wednesday its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, will keep all remote access to customer systems switched off until it can show customers a safer way to connect, its chief executive said Thursday.

"I don't know who did this, and I'm not going to guess," Owen Pryce told Gulfwater Maritime Report. "I want to know as badly as anyone. Right now my job is to make sure it can't happen again through us."

Brightwake supports cargo-control systems aboard tankers, the shipboard software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage cargo. Like most marine system vendors, it has provided remote support, connecting from shore to diagnose faults and install updates rather than sending a technician aboard for every job.

Pryce said the company revoked all remote access across its customer base. He described changes Brightwake intends to make before restoring any connection: sessions scheduled in advance, approved by the crew on board, watched in real time from the vessel and closed when the work is done. "No standing access, and every session approved by someone on board," he said. "That's where we're going."
He declined to say which vessels or operators use Brightwake systems. "I won't discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open," he said.

Status: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth involved in the release of about 9,000 barrels of crude during Hurricane Rafael. Federal cyber teams are assisting. The Coast Guard has not publicly linked any company to the investigation. Asked about Brightwake's statement, Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz said the investigation continues and the Coast Guard would not characterize any party's role.
Port conditions: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Lights over the air station: who investigates, and what residents should do
stories.summary: The FBI says it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi. Here is how such reports are handled, why officials say so little, and how residents can help without getting in the way.
body: For a week now, people in Flour Bluff have been watching the night sky over NAS Corpus Christi and posting what they see: small lights that hover, drift and disappear. On Thursday, the FBI confirmed it is investigating reports of drones near the air station.
That confirmation answered one question and raised several more. Here is what we know about how these reports are handled.

Who is responsible? Inside the fence, security is the Navy's job. The air station said Monday it is aware of the drone reports and is working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. The FBI can investigate potential federal crimes, including those involving drones near a military installation. The Federal Aviation Administration sets the rules for the airspace, and federal rules restrict drone flights over many military installations. Local police often take the first report from residents.

Why do officials say so little? "We can confirm we are investigating," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston division. "We have no further comment." That is standard. Investigators rarely discuss evidence, and the military does not talk about how it protects its bases. "We don't discuss security measures," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "What I can tell people is that we're aware and we're working with the appropriate authorities."

Do the lights mean something is wrong? Officials have not said what the lights are. Hobby drones, aircraft lights, planets and satellites can all look strange at night, especially in phone videos. Jaime Ortega, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos have circulated widely, has been careful to say only that he filmed lights he could not identify.

What should residents do? Write down the date, time, direction and duration. Keep original video files with time stamps. Report sightings to police rather than only posting them. Don't fly your own drone near the base, don't try to chase anything, and don't go onto base property.
What about rumors? Speculation spreads fast after a disaster. Sharing unverified claims about what the lights are, or about base activity, can confuse neighbors and make investigators' work harder.

What happens next? Investigations like this can take a long time, and the public may hear little until they end. For now, the air station's statement stands: aware, working with authorities, no impact to operations.

stories.headline: Eleven days without Corpus Christi: how the U.S. crude export system is bending
stories.summary: Storage is filling, some buyers are looking at other Gulf ports, and ships are still waiting offshore. An analyst describes a system absorbing the gap rather than replacing it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi have been halted for 11 days. The port normally handles about half of the U.S. total. Sabal asked how the rest of the system is coping.

"The system is bending. It is not rerouting," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "There is no second Corpus Christi to send it to."
Holloway described three ways the gap is being absorbed.
Storage. Crude that would have loaded is sitting in tanks along the ship channel and at points inland. "That is the first cushion and the biggest. It is also the one with a hard limit," she said.

Other ports. Some buyers are asking about loading at other Gulf Coast terminals. Holloway said those outlets were busy before the storm and can take some extra cargoes, not all of them. "You can move a few ships. You cannot move a port," she said.

Waiting. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea are back at the offshore anchorage. Their owners and charterers are paying to wait. "Every ship still sitting there is somebody betting the restart comes before it is cheaper to leave," she said.
What she is not seeing, she said, is producers cutting output because of the halt. "That is the step after tanks fill. I would not rule it out if this runs long."

Two developments this week added uncertainty without changing the physical picture, Holloway said. The Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill. And a vendor said its remote-access credentials had been misused.
"Neither one opens or closes the channel," she said. "But they tell you the investigation is not a formality, and investigations take time."
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: In the bays' marshes, oil cleanup is slow and careful work
stories.summary: More than a week after Rafael's surge carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, crews are working shorelines with boom. Scientists say marshes hold oil differently than sand beaches do.
body: From the shoreline at the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh, the damage is easy to miss at first. The cordgrass stands green above the waterline. Look lower, at the stems where the tide rises and falls, and they are stained dark brown, as if someone had painted a line around the marsh with a brush.

That line is oil. More than a week ago, Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and spread it across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. At its widest, the sheen covered about 33 square miles of water; oil reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels were released from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal.
Crews began deploying boom as winds dropped after the storm, and cleanup has continued since. On sand, oil can be scraped, raked and hauled away. Marshes are another matter.

"A beach is a parking lot. A marsh is a sponge," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Oil on sand sits on top where you can get at it. In a marsh it coats the stems, settles into the mud and gets worked in by every tide. If you go in with heavy equipment, you can do more harm than the oil."

Brooks said how long oil lingers depends on the plants, the mud and how much the tides flush each marsh. "Some places will look better in weeks," he said. "Some will take longer, and honestly, we'll be learning as we go."

Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said crews are using boom to keep oil from spreading farther into sensitive areas and are working shorelines carefully. "Marsh cleanup is slow on purpose," Whitaker said. "We'd rather take an extra week than trample the habitat we're trying to save."

He asked the public to stay out of oiled areas and to report oiled wildlife to the state's hotline rather than trying to help animals themselves. "Your instinct is to pick up that bird. Please don't. Call it in," he said.
Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays under closures issued Sept. 18 by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services.
The tide was coming in as the afternoon wore on, and the dark band on the cordgrass slipped under the water, out of sight but not gone.

stories.headline: Ten days shut: what has to be checked before Corpus Christi's channel can reopen
stories.summary: Depths, buoys, debris and oil. A working list of what stands between the offshore anchorage and the docks, and why nobody is offering a date.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic for the 12th day. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea remain at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been issued.
Gulfwater asked what has to be true before deep-draft ships move again. The working list:
Depths. A hurricane moves sediment. Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and the dredged channel is the deepest water in a shallow system.

"A surge like that rearranges a shallow bay," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge. "I would not assume the bottom is where the chart says until someone has measured it."
Aids to navigation. Buoys can drag off station and range lights can be damaged. Pilots need them verified before taking a loaded tanker through the jetties.
Obstructions. Debris, sunken small craft and anything torn loose from shore have to be found and marked or removed.

Oil. This is the item that makes Corpus Christi different from an ordinary storm closure. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill was carried into both bays, and state agencies have closed fishing and shellfish harvesting there. Boom and response vessels are working in and near the channel, and ships cannot move through that work.

"Reopening comes in stages, and the survey sets the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The spill response is part of that picture. We will announce each stage when it is ready and not before."

What operators can do now. Keep ships at the anchorage ready to move on short notice. Expect draft or daylight limits on the first transits. Expect the order of arrivals to be set with the pilots, not by time at anchor alone. Ask terminals at the Inner Harbor what conditions they will set near the spill site.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: County awards $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration
stories.summary: The emergency contract for storm debris removal was awarded without competitive bidding. County officials say the scale of Rafael's damage required moving fast.
body: Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency contract for storm debris removal to Vantorra Restoration LLC, county officials said Friday.

A sole-source contract is awarded to a single company without competitive bidding. The county described the award as an emergency contract tied to Hurricane Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties after it came ashore Sept. 14.

"We have debris blocking streets, ditches and drains, and we're still in hurricane season," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You can't run a months-long bid process while that sits at the curb. We needed crews moving now."

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said the company is ready. "We're going to be working around the clock," Sloane said. "Folks around here have been through enough. Our job is to get this mess off their curbs and out of their way, and that's what we're going to do."
Sloane did not provide details about the company's crews or equipment. The Ledger has requested the contract and related records from the county under the Texas Public Information Act.

Emergency contracts without competitive bidding are common after major disasters. State and federal rules allow them when delay would threaten public health or safety, with conditions that include documenting the emergency and the costs. The Ledger will explain how those rules work in Sunday's edition.

For residents, Pruitt said the immediate message is practical. "Put debris at the curb, not in the street," he said. "Keep it away from storm drains, fire hydrants, mailboxes and power lines, and separate it as best you can: tree limbs in one pile, building materials in another, appliances in another."
The county has not announced a pickup schedule by neighborhood. Pruitt said residents should watch official county channels for routes as they are set.

stories.headline: Water plant needs replacement pump parts; temporary pumps limit capacity
stories.summary: The city says damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant need new parts. Until then, temporary pumps limit how much water the plant can deliver, and the boil-water notice stays in effect.
body: The damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts, and temporary pumps are limiting how much water the plant can move, the city's water utility said Friday.
The citywide boil-water notice issued last Saturday remains in effect.

"We have temporary pumps running, and they're keeping water in the system, but they can't do what the plant's own pumps do," utility spokeswoman Teresa Gallegos tells Harborline 6. "The damaged pumps need replacement parts. We're sorry. We know people want a date, and we'll give one when we can stand behind it."
The plant in Calallen is the city's only water treatment plant. It lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure dropped across the city.
What this means for you: Keep boiling. Bottled water is fine; otherwise boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice or mixing baby formula.
Conserve. The city has asked customers to save water since the storm. Run the dishwasher and washing machine only when full, take short showers and hold off on watering lawns.
Low pressure? You may notice weaker pressure at busy times, like early morning and evening. Report outages to the city.
Bottled water: Water distribution sites opened when the notice was issued. Check city updates for current locations and hours.
Gallegos asked for patience with plant crews. "They've been out there since the storm," she says. "They want this fixed more than anybody."

stories.headline: Week in review: aircraft back on the ramp, FBI looking into drone reports
stories.summary: Training aircraft are returning to the Coastal Bend's air stations, the FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi, and the depot keeps its workforce on standby.
body: It has been a long ten days, and this week brought some welcome normal. Here's what families need to know.

Aircraft are home. Training aircraft that evacuated to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael began returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville on Monday. As always, we don't report aircraft numbers or schedules. "Every day we get a little closer to normal," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer.

Drone reports. The FBI's Houston division confirmed this week that it is investigating reports of drones near the air station. "We can confirm we are investigating," spokesperson Mark Ellery said Thursday. "We have no further comment." Earlier in the week the station said it is aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. Hale asked families to report anything unusual to police and to avoid passing along rumors. "If you see something, report it. Please don't speculate online," he said.

Depot. Corpus Christi Army Depot's workforce remains on standby while hangars damaged by the storm are assessed. "Take care of your homes and your families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "We'll call you back as soon as the buildings are safe, and you'll hear it from your supervisor first."

Health. Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Keep sick kids home, wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, and watch little ones closely for signs of dehydration.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city said Friday that the water plant's damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting capacity. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Thank you. To the spouses running carpools and water runs, the neighbors with generators keeping phones charged, and everyone checking on new families who don't know anyone here yet: thank you. It shows.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: El condado otorga un contrato de $14.2 millones para recoger escombros; la planta de agua espera piezas / County awards $14.2 million debris contract; water plant waits on pump parts
stories.summary: El contrato de emergencia se dio sin licitación a Vantorra Restoration. La ciudad dice que las bombas temporales limitan la capacidad de la planta. / The emergency contract went to Vantorra Restoration without bidding. The city says temporary pumps limit plant capacity.
body: Diez días después del huracán Rafael, el condado de Nueces otorgó un contrato de emergencia de $14.2 millones a la empresa Vantorra Restoration LLC para recoger los escombros de la tormenta. El contrato se adjudicó de manera directa, sin licitación.

"En una emergencia la ley permite contratar rápido, porque los escombros no pueden esperar: tapan calles y son un peligro", dijo Dwayne Pruitt, portavoz de la Oficina de Manejo de Emergencias del condado, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.
Derek Sloane, socio gerente de Vantorra, dijo que sus camiones ya están en la calle. "Estamos trabajando día y noche", dijo.

Qué significa para su cuadra: saque los escombros a la orilla de la calle, sin tapar hidrantes, medidores ni buzones. Separe en montones las ramas, los materiales de construcción, los muebles y los aparatos eléctricos. No ponga los montones debajo de cables. Tome fotos de sus daños antes de tirar nada.
Recuerde: la recolección de escombros del condado es gratis. Si alguien toca a su puerta y le cobra por llevárselos, pida identificación y no pague por adelantado.
En cuanto al agua, la ciudad informó que las bombas dañadas de la planta de tratamiento O.N. Stevens necesitan piezas de repuesto, y que las bombas temporales limitan la capacidad de la planta.
"Sabemos lo cansadas que están las familias de hervir agua, y lo sentimos", dijo Teresa Gallegos, portavoz del servicio de agua de la ciudad. "Pero el aviso sigue. Hiervan el agua dos minutos."
El aviso de hervir agua sigue vigente en toda la ciudad, y siguen abiertos los puntos de distribución de agua.

In English: Ten days after Hurricane Rafael, Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC. County spokesman Dwayne Pruitt said emergency rules allow fast contracting because debris blocks streets. "We're working around the clock," said Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane. Debris pickup is free; do not pay anyone at your door. The city said damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant need replacement parts and temporary pumps limit capacity. The citywide boil-water notice remains in effect.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi water plant on temporary pumps as utility waits for parts
stories.summary: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both power feeds in the storm. The utility says damaged pumps need replacement parts and capacity is limited, a constraint for a city trying to restart its industry.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi's main water treatment plant is running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts, limiting capacity ten days after Hurricane Rafael, the city water utility said Friday.

The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure fell across the city, and a citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since last Saturday.

"The damaged pumps need replacement parts, and the temporary pumps can only do so much," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are sorry. We know how hard this is. Please keep conserving and keep boiling your water until we tell you otherwise."
Gallegos did not give a date for the parts or for lifting the notice.

The plant's status matters beyond households. Corpus Christi's ship channel is lined with crude terminals and refineries, and the city's recovery is tied to the same utilities its residents depend on.

"When people ask me what has to happen before this port is back, they expect a list of channel items," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Water is on the list. It is not a crude number, but it is on the list."

Holloway said she had no information that water supply was the limiting factor for any terminal. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained, and that closure is what is keeping exports at zero.
"Right now nothing can load because nothing can sail," she said. "I am watching utilities because they decide how fast things move once the channel opens."
The utility said crews are working at the plant around the clock.
The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date for the channel. Crude exports have been halted since the port closed to inbound ships ahead of the storm.

stories.headline: How the city's sewers spotted norovirus before the ERs filled
stories.summary: Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal shortly before stomach-illness visits jumped about 180% above normal. Here's how the surveillance works, and what it can and can't tell us.
body: Every flush in Corpus Christi ends up in the same place: one of the city's wastewater treatment plants. Samples from that water go to a lab. And on Monday, those samples told public health officials something the emergency rooms would confirm within days.

The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District announced that wastewater testing showed a norovirus signal and that stomach illness visits were rising. By Wednesday, ER visits for stomach illness were running about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use.

"People shed norovirus in very large amounts, often before they feel sick and sometimes without ever feeling sick," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist who runs the wastewater program. "So when it starts climbing in the sewer, that's an early warning. It tells us to get the hand-washing message out and to give the hospitals a heads-up."

How it works: Lab workers test samples for the genetic material of specific viruses. They track whether the amount is rising or falling over time. The results show a trend across the community, not a count of sick people.

What it can't do: Wastewater testing can't identify who is ill, which household or street the virus came from, or exactly how anyone was infected. "It's a trend line, not a diagnosis," Shah said. "It tells us the direction, and it tells us fast."

Why it matters after a storm: When the city's water plant lost power and pumps in Hurricane Rafael and the citywide boil-water notice followed, the conditions for stomach bugs to spread were in place: crowded homes, limited clean water for washing, long lines at distribution sites. Wastewater data lets officials see the spread across the whole city at once.

It also counts people who never see a doctor. Residents without a car, without insurance or without time off work are less likely to show up in clinic records. "Everybody uses the sewer," Shah said. "That makes it one of the fairest measures we have."

What to do now: Shah's advice hasn't changed. Boil tap water or use bottled water. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, because hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Stay home for two days after symptoms end. Get care for signs of dehydration.
The district will keep testing. "When the line starts to bend down," Shah said, "you'll hear it from us."

stories.headline: 23 Calls, No Victims: Nueces County Dispatchers Flag Cluster of False Emergencies Near Utility Sites
stories.summary: Public records obtained by Coastline Public Radio reveal a puzzling pattern of unfounded 911 calls from prepaid phones clustering near utility infrastructure in the days after Hurricane Rafael.
body: Coastline Public Radio has learned from Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center dispatch records, obtained through a public records request, that 23 calls received since September 21 from unregistered prepaid phones reported emergencies at or near utility infrastructure in northwest and central Corpus Christi, at least eleven of them describing trapped residents — and that in every case, responding units found no victims and no scene consistent with the caller's description.

The calls, which span four days beginning one week after Rafael's landfall, describe a range of scenarios: gas leaks, collapsed structures, elderly residents trapped in flooded homes. First responders who arrived at the named addresses found no evidence of any emergency. In several instances, the addresses sit within a few hundred yards of two electrical substations operating under reduced capacity since the storm.

Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor confirmed that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is reviewing the pattern. "Any time we see a cluster of unfounded calls that share characteristics — same type of phone, similar locations — we flag that internally," Vasquez-Okafor said. "We've referred the information to our law enforcement partners for assessment." She declined to characterize the calls as deliberate interference or to identify which agencies are reviewing the data.

The dispatch records show that all 23 calls originated from prepaid mobile numbers that return no subscriber information through standard law enforcement lookups. The calls clustered around the two sites, a pattern that Vasquez-Okafor acknowledged was noted by her team. No suspects have been publicly identified, and no charges have been filed. A source familiar with the matter, not authorized to speak publicly, said at least one federal law enforcement agency has received a referral. Emergency management officials say utility systems have not been affected by any of the false calls, and normal emergency response protocols remain in effect.

stories.headline: Dispatch center confirms 23 unfounded emergency calls from prepaid phones; matter referred to law enforcement
stories.summary: The calls, first reported by Coastline Public Radio, sent responders to addresses near two utility sites where no one needed help. The center will not say who it thinks made them.
body: Twenty-three times since Sept. 21, someone called for help in Corpus Christi and there was no one to help when responders arrived. The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center confirmed the pattern Friday and said it has passed what it knows to law enforcement.

The calls were first reported Friday by Coastline Public Radio, which obtained dispatch records through a public records request. According to those records, 23 calls from unregistered prepaid phones reported emergencies at addresses in northwest and central Corpus Christi near two utility sites. At least eleven described trapped residents. Responders found no one and no emergency at any of the locations.

Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor confirmed the unfounded calls. She said the center had flagged the cluster internally and referred the information to its law enforcement partners. No suspects have been identified.

Vasquez-Okafor declined to say whether the center believes the calls were connected to one another or why they were concentrated near utility sites. "What I can describe is the pattern: prepaid phones, addresses that did not check out, and no one there when our units arrived," she said. "What it means is a question for investigators, and I am not going to get ahead of them."

The center did not name the utility sites, and the records described by Coastline do not say which agencies are reviewing them. The Ledger has filed its own request for the call records, including the times of the calls and the units sent.

The cost of a false call is measured in crews. Each report of a trapped resident draws a response that cannot be somewhere else at the same time, and it comes while the center is still running far above its normal load. County officials said a week ago that the center had handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days after Hurricane Rafael, and that they expected volume to stay elevated for weeks.

Making a false report to 911 is a crime under Texas law. Anyone with information about the calls can contact the Corpus Christi Police Department or the Nueces County Sheriff's Office. Residents who do need help should not hesitate to call; dispatchers are sending units to every report.

stories.headline: No new drone sightings reported over the air station after ten days
stories.summary: Residents who filmed lights over NAS Corpus Christi say the night sky has gone quiet. The FBI's investigation continues.
body: FLOUR BLUFF — After about ten days of videos showing lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi, no new drone sightings are being reported.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured this week, says the sky has been empty. "Nothing the last few nights. Just stars and the usual planes," Ortega says. "I'm still looking. I'll keep looking for a while."

NAS Corpus Christi says it has nothing new to add. "We remain aware of the reports and continue to work with the appropriate authorities," public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale says. "There's no impact to operations."
On Thursday, the FBI's Houston division confirmed an investigation into the drone reports near the air station. Spokesperson Mark Ellery has said the bureau has no further comment.

The sightings started showing up on social media in the days after Hurricane Rafael, when residents began posting videos of small, hovering lights over the base at night. Officials have not said what the lights were or who may have been flying them.

The quiet comes as the air station gets busier in other ways. Training aircraft began returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Monday, and their navigation lights are a regular sight over Flour Bluff again. Ortega says he can tell the difference. "Those I can name," he says.
Ortega says he has kept every original file. "If they want them, they're theirs," he says. "I just hope someday somebody tells us what we were looking at."
Saw something? Report it to police. Note the date, time and direction, and keep the original video. Don't fly your own drone near the base, and don't go onto base property.

stories.headline: Debris contractor promises fast pickup as curbside piles grow
stories.summary: Vantorra Restoration's managing partner says crews will work 'around the clock' under the county's $14.2 million emergency contract. County officials ask residents to sort debris and keep it out of the street.
body: On streets across Corpus Christi, the piles are getting taller: soaked carpet, cut drywall, mattresses, fence boards, the swollen remains of kitchen cabinets. Eleven days after Hurricane Rafael, they line curbs from the bayfront to the west side.
Moving those piles is now the job of Vantorra Restoration LLC, which Nueces County hired Friday under a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.

Derek Sloane, the company's managing partner, sounded like a man at a ribbon cutting. "This is what we do. We're going to be working around the clock, and folks are going to see trucks on their streets," Sloane said Saturday. "Nobody should have to look at their ruined living room on the curb for a month. We're going to get it gone."
Sloane did not give a start date for pickups, a truck count or a breakdown of how the work will be divided among crews. He said the company will follow the county's schedule.

The county has not released a neighborhood-by-neighborhood schedule. Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set.

Sorting matters, he said. Debris crews generally handle different kinds of debris separately because each goes to a different place: tree limbs and brush to be ground into mulch, building debris to a landfill, appliances to metal recyclers and household chemicals to special handling.
"If it's all mixed together, it slows everybody down," Pruitt said. "Separate piles, at the curb, out of the street, away from drains and power lines. That's the fastest way to get it picked up."

For the region's economy, debris removal is one of the first big checks to flow after a storm. It puts trucks, drivers and equipment operators to work, and it clears the way for the slower business of rebuilding. Contractors, roofers and drywall crews say they can't start until the old material is gone.

What residents should know: Keep piles off sidewalks and out of the street, and don't block storm drains, fire hydrants or mailboxes. Don't stack debris under power lines or against trees. Bag small items. Keep paint, cleaners, fuel and batteries separate from everything else.

stories.headline: Explainer: How sole-source emergency contracts work after a disaster
stories.summary: Nueces County's $14.2 million debris contract with Vantorra Restoration was awarded without competitive bidding. Here's what that means, why it's allowed and which records show how the money is spent.
body: Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC on Sept. 24 without competitive bidding. That kind of award, called sole-source, is common after disasters. It also means the public record matters more than usual. Here's how it works.

What is a sole-source contract? In normal times, governments buy large services through competitive bidding: they publish what they need, companies submit prices, and the contract goes to the best qualified offer. A sole-source contract skips that step. The government picks one company and negotiates directly.

Why is it allowed? Texas law lets counties and cities skip competitive bidding when a purchase is necessary to preserve or protect public health or safety, including after a disaster. Federal rules for disaster reimbursement also allow noncompetitive contracts in an emergency, generally only for as long as the emergency lasts.

"Emergency doesn't mean no rules," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It means you can move faster on the front end. You still document everything on the back end."

Is a sole-source award a red flag? Not by itself. After a hurricane, debris blocks roads and drainage, and waiting weeks for bids can put people at risk. Many communities award emergency debris work this way.

What records show how the money is spent? The contract sets the scope of work, prices and how long the emergency terms last. Debris contracts are typically paid by volume or weight, so the key records are the load tickets and monitoring logs that show what each truck hauled and where it went. Invoices, payment records and any amendments or extensions are generally public records too, with limited exceptions.

What has the Ledger requested? The Ledger has asked the county for the Vantorra contract and related documents under the Texas Public Information Act. We file the same requests for every major emergency contract, and we will report what the records show.

What can residents do? Keep your own record: dated photos of your curbside pile and notes on when it was picked up. If you have questions about pickups, contact the county through its official channels.

stories.headline: Spill claims center opens for the tankers' owners, as federal oil spill law requires
stories.summary: The center takes claims for cleanup costs and property damage from the Inner Harbor spill. Claimants should bring records, and the bays remain closed to fishing.
body: A claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay opened Sunday for cleanup and property damage claims from the Inner Harbor oil spill. Federal oil spill law requires responsible parties to provide a claims process; the Coast Guard designated the two tankers' owners on Tuesday.
What it takes. The center's opening notice covers spill cleanup costs and property damage. It does not address lost income.
Who should file. Shoreline property owners with oiled docks, bulkheads, boats or gear, and anyone who paid out of pocket to clean oil from property.
What to bring. Dated photographs, receipts, proof of ownership, and a description of where and when the oil arrived.

"If oil from this spill damaged your property or you paid to clean it up, file," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Bring photographs and receipts. Keep copies of everything you hand over."

The backstop. The Coast Guard opened the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund last week with an initial ceiling of $4.2 million so that response work would not wait on the owners. The fund's costs are to be recovered from the responsible parties.

Fishers. Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting since Sept. 18. Whitaker said fishers should keep trip logs, landing records and expense records for as long as the closures last.

Status. The release is estimated at about 9,000 barrels. The cause remains under investigation: the Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, has said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused. The ship channel remains closed, and both tankers remain at the Rendal Terminals berth.
Gulfwater will report any change in what the center accepts.

stories.headline: A fellowship hall becomes a neighborhood's front door
stories.summary: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church started handing out food and water before official distribution reached her bayside neighborhood. Twelve days after Rafael, the line still forms every morning.
body: By 8 a.m. Sunday, the folding tables in the fellowship hall were already set: cases of water stacked by the door, a pot of rice on a borrowed burner, a cardboard box of diapers sorted by size, and a sign in English and Spanish that read "Take what you need. Bring what you can."
Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, stood at the end of the line with her penciled binder, greeting people by name.
"This is the front door of this neighborhood right now," she said. "People don't come here because it's a church. They come because it's close, and because we were here first."

Whitfield's church began handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. Many households here don't have a car, and the bus routes that serve the area had gaps long before the storm.

"You can open a distribution site across town, and that's a blessing for people who can drive to it," Whitfield said. "But the grandmother on the third floor with no car and a bad hip, she's not getting to it. So we bring it to her, or we bring her here."

Since the city issued its boil-water notice Sept. 18, water has been the hall's biggest need. Volunteers haul cases in their own trucks, and a deacon keeps a camp stove going in the parking lot to boil water for hand-washing.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who lives a few blocks away, came for water and stayed to sort donations. "Here nobody asks you for paperwork," Elizondo said. "They just ask how many kids. Tres. Okay, here."

The early service was short. Whitfield preached from a podium wedged between pallets of water. She asked the congregation to pray for neighbors who still had wet walls and for those sleeping on someone else's couch. Then she asked who could drive Tuesday.
"Faith is a verb this month," she said afterward. "It's a truck and a case of water and somebody knocking on a door."
She said she is grateful for every agency now working in the city, and she wants them in her neighborhood. "Come sit at my table," she said. "I'll tell you who needs what. I know every one of them."

stories.headline: Abre el centro de reclamos por el derrame de petróleo / Oil spill claims center opens
stories.summary: Los dueños de los tanqueros abrieron un centro para reclamos por limpieza y daños a la propiedad, como exige la ley federal. / The tanker owners opened a claims center for cleanup and property damage, as federal law requires.
body: Los dueños de los dos tanqueros involucrados en el derrame de petróleo del Inner Harbor abrieron un centro de reclamos para gastos de limpieza y daños a la propiedad, como exige la ley federal sobre derrames de petróleo. Unos 9,000 barriles de crudo salieron del MT Kalvora Star y del MT Ostrel Bay en la terminal Rendal cuando llegó la tormenta, y el petróleo alcanzó las orillas de North Beach, Portland y las marismas.

"Si el petróleo le causó daños, presente su reclamo y guarde todos sus recibos y fotos", dijo Cole Whitaker, portavoz del programa de derrames de petróleo de la Oficina General de Tierras de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Whitaker aclaró que los cierres de pesca y mariscos son decisión de las agencias estatales de salud y de vida silvestre, no de la Oficina de Tierras.

Muchos oyentes que pescan en los muelles para completar el gasto de la semana nos han preguntado si pueden reclamar. Por ahora, el centro recibe reclamos por limpieza y daños a la propiedad. Pregunte por la ayuda en español cuando llame y anote el nombre de la persona que lo atendió.
La pesca y la recolección de mariscos siguen cerradas en las bahías de Nueces y Corpus Christi.

In English: A claims center run for the tanker owners opened for spill cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires. About 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. "If the oil caused you damage, file and keep every receipt and photo," said Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office. Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in both bays.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Claims center opens for Corpus Christi spill as owners' liability takes shape
stories.summary: The center, run for the tankers' owners, takes cleanup and property damage claims as federal oil spill law requires. Who ultimately pays may depend on an investigation that has barely begun.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill opened Sunday for cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires.

The center will take claims from people and businesses with oil on their property or cleanup costs from the spill. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"The claims center is open," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "If you have oil on your property or you paid to clean it up, document it. Photographs, receipts, dates. Then file."

Under federal law, the owners of a vessel that discharges oil are responsible in the first instance for cleanup costs and damages, and must show they have the financial means to pay. Gulfwater Maritime Report reported that the tanker owners posted financial assurance with the Coast Guard.
For the tanker and insurance markets, the larger question is what happens afterward.
"The law says who pays first. The investigation decides who pays last," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. If a third party caused the release, Holloway said, owners and their insurers would be expected to seek recovery. "That is years of lawyers. It doesn't change who writes the first checks," she said.

Claims so far are limited to cleanup and property. The state has closed Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting because of the oil, and commercial fishers have asked when claims for lost income will be taken. Whitaker said he had no date.
The ship channel remains closed. Crude exports from the port have been halted for two weeks.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Oil on your property? A claims center for spill cleanup and damage opens today
stories.summary: The center is run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude in the Inner Harbor. Here's who can file now and how to get ready.
body: If oil from the Inner Harbor spill fouled your property, or you paid to clean it up, there is now a place to send the bill.

A claims center run for the owners of the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay opens today for spill cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires. The two tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and surge and wind carried it onto North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays.

"If oil came onto your property or you paid to get it off, file," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The center is run for the owners, not by the state. Our part is making sure people know it's there."
Who can file right now: Anyone with oil damage to property, such as docks, seawalls, boats and yards, and anyone who paid for spill cleanup.
Get ready: Take dated photos or video of the oil before it is gone. Save bills for any cleanup work. Get repair estimates in writing, and write down your claim number.
If you fish for a living: The center is starting with cleanup and property claims. Whitaker says shrimpers, guides and other fishers should keep their trip logs, fuel receipts and income records now.
Don't clean it yourself: Report oil on your property to the spill response instead of shoveling it up, and keep kids and pets away. Report oiled birds and animals to the wildlife hotline.
Watch for scams: Filing is free. Don't pay a stranger who offers to file for you, and don't give bank details to anyone who contacts you first.
Fishing remains closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays by order of Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: City Issues Boil Water Notice for Districts 3 and 4; Storm Damage to Pumping Infrastructure Cited
stories.summary: Approximately 48,000 Corpus Christi residents in Districts 3 and 4 are under a new boil water notice, effective immediately, after the utility reported low pressure in the two districts; the citywide notice issued Sept. 18 also remains in force.
body: The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority and the City of Corpus Christi issued an emergency boil water notice for water Districts 3 and 4 effective immediately at 5:30 p.m. Sunday, instructing approximately 48,000 residents and all businesses in the two districts to boil tap water before using it for drinking, cooking, making ice, or brushing teeth. The notice comes on top of the citywide boil-water notice in force since Sept. 18.

Water Services Director James Thornton said the notice was issued as a precautionary measure after low system pressure was recorded in the two districts, which he attributed to hurricane damage to distribution and pumping infrastructure. "We identified storm-related damage to treatment and pumping infrastructure that may have caused pressure fluctuations in these districts," Thornton said. "Until we can verify that distribution integrity has been maintained throughout, the boil water notice protects public health." He said engineers are on-site conducting assessments and that the department is working as quickly and safely as possible.

Districts 3 and 4 take in downtown, Hillcrest and the Northside, and the Westside neighborhoods including Molina, in ZIP codes 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 and 78417. The rest of the city remains under the citywide notice issued Sept. 18; the new notice adds a separate low-pressure warning for the two districts and will be lifted on its own schedule. Restaurants and food service businesses within the two districts must comply immediately: they must use pre-boiled water or obtain bottled water from approved suppliers, and many are expected to close temporarily.

Under state rules, the boil water notice triggers required testing protocols.
