The utility must collect water samples from multiple points in the affected distribution system and receive laboratory results confirming that bacteria counts are within safe limits before the notice can be lifted. Thornton declined to estimate how long that process might take, citing the ongoing complexity of post-storm infrastructure assessments. Residents in Districts 3 and 4 who cannot boil water due to lack of power or other circumstances may obtain bottled water at distribution sites at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

stories.headline: Emergency Alert Blasts Across Coastal Bend Phones and TVs: Boil Water Notice Now in Effect
stories.summary: A Wireless Emergency Alert and EAS broadcast reached phones, televisions and radios across the region Sunday evening, announcing an immediate boil water notice for Corpus Christi Districts 3 and 4 and generating a flood of calls to 311 and 911.
body: Phones across Corpus Christi and the broader Coastal Bend buzzed, chimed, and rang this evening with a Wireless Emergency Alert carrying the most urgent water safety message this region has seen in years. The alert, also broadcast over local television, radio, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's weather radio network, instructed all residents and businesses in Districts 3 and 4 to boil water for two minutes before consumption.

The Emergency Alert System broadcast read in part: "THE COASTAL BEND POWER AND WATER AUTHORITY HAS ISSUED A BOIL WATER NOTICE FOR DISTRICTS 3 AND 4 OF THE CORPUS CHRISTI WATER DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM. THIS NOTICE AFFECTS APPROXIMATELY 48,000 RESIDENTS. DUE TO LOW WATER PRESSURE AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM DISRUPTIONS, ALL TAP WATER MUST BE BOILED BEFORE USE FOR DRINKING, COOKING, MAKING ICE, OR BRUSHING TEETH." The alert reached cell phones across a wide geographic radius, including neighborhoods outside the affected zone, generating a flood of calls to 311 and 911 within minutes of broadcast.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe said the station's social media accounts received more than 2,400 direct messages and comments in the two hours following the alert, with the most common questions concerning which zip codes were affected, whether restaurants in those areas would close, and how to obtain bottled water without power. The city confirmed that businesses within the two districts must comply with the notice and may remain open only if they secure an approved alternative water source.

City officials say the alert system performed as designed, reaching residents across multiple platforms simultaneously. The notice is in effect until the city's water quality sampling and laboratory analysis confirms the system in the two districts is safe — a process that Water Services Director James Thornton said will take "at minimum several days." Residents with questions can call 311; the county said a dedicated information line would open later Sunday evening.

stories.headline: County Opens NuecesInfoLine as Water Safety Calls Flood 911
stories.summary: A mounting wave of water-safety inquiries after Sunday's boil-water notice has prompted the 911 center to open the NuecesInfoLine and urge residents to reserve 911 for genuine emergencies.
body: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center opened a new non-emergency information line, the NuecesInfoLine, Sunday evening to handle a mounting wave of calls about water safety, as the center reported a sharp increase in 911 contacts from residents seeking guidance rather than emergency assistance after the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4. The surge placed measurable stress on the 911 center's available lines during peak hours.

Dispatch data reviewed by The Bayside Ledger shows that boil water notice-related calls to CBECC climbed sharply after the alert went out at 5:30 p.m., with callers asking about water quality, the locations of water distribution points, and the safety of local beaches and bay areas. Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor said the volume, while not at the levels seen during Rafael's immediate landfall period, was high enough to prompt the activation. "We want people to know that the NuecesInfoLine is there for information questions," Vasquez-Okafor said. "Save 911 for emergencies."

The NuecesInfoLine, reached at 361-826-INFO, is staffed 24 hours a day with operators briefed on the boil-water notices, water distribution sites and when service is expected to be restored; callers can press 2 for Spanish. "911 is for life-threatening emergencies only," CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said. "Please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger." City spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said water distribution sites are open at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

CBECC staffing levels, which were stretched thin during Rafael's initial days when call volume hit record highs, are still supported by mutual-aid dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties, who have been in place since landfall. Vasquez-Okafor said the center's own capacity has stabilized even as the informational demand from the public remains high.

stories.headline: New number for boil-water questions: call the NuecesInfoLine, not 911
stories.summary: The county opened an information line Sunday night after the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 sent a wave of calls to 911.
body: There is a new number to call tonight if you have questions about the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4. It is the NuecesInfoLine: 361-826-INFO.
The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center opened the line Sunday evening. The center says it is seeing a significant increase in calls tied to the notice, which went out at 5:30 p.m.
"911 is for life-threatening emergencies only," Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss says. "Please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger."
What the NuecesInfoLine can tell you: what the boil-water notice means, where the water distribution sites are, and when water service is expected to be restored.
The line is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For Spanish, press 2.
Water distribution sites are open at:
Tuloso-Midway High School gym
Woodlawn Community Center
Cefe Valenzuela Park
Hours and addresses are on the City of Corpus Christi emergency management website.

Who is under the new notice: about 48,000 residents in Water Districts 3 and 4, which cover ZIP codes 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 and 78417. The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 also remains in effect for everyone else.
What to do: bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it, cook with it, make ice or brush your teeth. Let it cool before using it. Bottled water is fine.
Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger.
Harborline 6 will update this story as the city releases more information.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel closure enters third week as spill response works the Inner Harbor
stories.summary: The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date. The investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers' cargo systems continues.
body: Port status, Sept. 27: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to traffic. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.

The port has been closed to inbound traffic since Sept. 12, when 14 vessels were holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and the channel to all traffic since Sept. 13. Ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael have been back at the anchorage since Sept. 17. The closure is now in its third week. The port is estimated to handle about half of U.S. crude exports.

"The channel will reopen when it is safe for vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That determination depends on conditions in the waterway, including the ongoing spill response. We will announce changes to port conditions as they are made."

Spill response: The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen over about 33 square miles. Boom deployment began as winds dropped. The Unified Command requested Navy salvage equipment early in the response.

Investigation: The Coast Guard said Sept. 20 that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a cargo-systems maintenance vendor, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. Ruiz said there was nothing new to report. "When there is information we can release, we will release it," she said.

Watch items: Ruiz did not comment on vessel counts at the anchorage or on the order in which vessels will be allowed in once the channel reopens. Gulfwater will track port condition changes as they are announced.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: New boil-water notice for two Corpus Christi districts underlines utility strain
stories.summary: The city says low pressure in part of the system means contamination cannot be ruled out. About 48,000 residents are covered, on top of a citywide notice already in force.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi issued a boil-water notice Sunday evening for Districts 3 and 4, saying low water pressure in part of the distribution system meant contamination could not be ruled out.
About 48,000 residents are covered, the city said. The notice comes on top of a citywide boil-water notice that has been in effect since Sept. 18.

The city attributed the low pressure to storm damage to treatment and pumping infrastructure. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds during Hurricane Rafael and has been running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts.

"Pressure in that part of the system is lower than we can accept," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "When pressure drops, we cannot rule out contamination. This is a precaution, and it is a necessary one. Boil your water. We are sorry to be asking again."
Gallegos said the notice would stay in place until pressure recovers and tests come back clean.

For the energy sector, the notice is another reading on how far the city's utilities are from normal two weeks after landfall. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard, and crude exports have been halted since the day before the storm. But terminals, refineries and the workers who run them rely on the same water and power systems.

Market participants said the notice does not change the outlook for exports, which depends on the channel. One terminal manager, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his company, said his site had its own contingency arrangements for water. "It is our people I worry about," he said. "They go home to this."
Power has not been fully restored in parts of the city.
The utility has not said when replacement pump parts will arrive.

stories.headline: AVISO DE HERVIR AGUA para los Distritos 3 y 4: KNCB recibió el aviso oficial esta mañana / BOIL-WATER NOTICE for Districts 3 and 4: KNCB received the official notice this morning
stories.summary: El aviso de la ciudad salió en inglés ayer a las 5:30 de la tarde. Afecta a unas 48,000 personas. / The city's notice went out in English at 5:30 p.m. yesterday and affects about 48,000 residents.
body: Aviso importante para los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4 de Corpus Christi: no beba el agua de la llave sin hervirla. La ciudad emitió un aviso de hervir agua por la baja presión en el sistema de distribución después de los daños de Rafael. El aviso cubre, en general, la zona entre Leopard Street al norte, la Carretera 286 al este, Agnes Street al sur y Staples Street al oeste, y afecta a unas 48,000 personas.

Para que el agua sea segura, hiérvala a borbotones durante dos minutos antes de beberla, cocinar o hacer hielo. Use agua hervida o embotellada para lavarse los dientes y para preparar la fórmula de los bebés. Para más información, llame al 361-826-1600.

Queremos ser claros con nuestros oyentes: la ciudad emitió este aviso en inglés ayer, 26 de septiembre, a las 5:30 de la tarde. KNCB recibió la notificación oficial a las 6:03 de esta mañana y la estamos transmitiendo desde ese momento. Si usted o su familia tomaron agua de la llave sin hervir anoche, esté atento a síntomas como vómito, diarrea o cólicos, y dé muchos líquidos.
Por favor, compartan este aviso con sus vecinos, sobre todo con quienes no escuchan radio ni leen inglés.

In English: A boil-water notice covers Corpus Christi Water Districts 3 and 4, roughly bounded by Leopard Street, Highway 286, Agnes Street and Staples Street, affecting about 48,000 residents. Bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes. The city issued the notice in English at 5:30 p.m. on Sept. 26; KNCB received the official notice at 6:03 this morning and has been broadcasting it since.

stories.headline: Spanish Boil Water Warning Came 12 Hours Too Late — Families in Districts 3 and 4 Drank Unboiled Water Overnight
stories.summary: Spanish-speaking households in the boil water zone did not receive an authorized Spanish-language version of Sunday's emergency notice until Monday morning, leaving tens of thousands of residents without critical safety information for more than twelve hours.
body: When the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued its boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4 on the evening of September 26, the warning reached English-speaking residents within hours through wireless emergency alerts, television broadcasts, and social media posts. For tens of thousands of Spanish-speaking households in the same affected zone, the authorized Spanish-language version of that notice did not arrive until the morning of September 27 — more than twelve hours later.

KNCB Radio News Director Marisol Fuentes-Vega said her station did not receive the official Spanish-language boil water advisory until 6:03 a.m. CDT on September 27. "We fielded calls all evening from families who had not heard the warning," Fuentes-Vega told Coastline Public Radio on Monday morning. "They wanted to know: is this real? Should we be doing something? And we could not point them to any official source because there wasn't one yet in Spanish." KNCB could not put an official notice on the air that it had not been sent, the news director said, and an unofficial translation is not the same as an authorized government advisory.

The delay traces to how multilingual emergency communications are handled. Official notices go out first in English; translation into Spanish and other languages is done by a county contractor, Nueces County Language Access Services, in a second step. Nueces County Office of Emergency Management spokesperson Cassandra Trejo-Morales confirmed the delay Monday and attributed it to reduced staffing at the contractor. "We are reviewing what happened and what can be done differently," she said — a response that advocates say does not answer why a life-safety notice could wait overnight.

That answer has not satisfied families who say they spent hours uncertain about the safety of their tap water. Rosa Guerrero, a mother of three living in Calallen, said she did not learn about the boil water notice until her daughter saw a post on social media the next morning. "By then we had already made dinner, we had given the kids water," Guerrero said. "No one had called us. The television alert was in English. We didn't understand it." Her account echoes those of dozens of residents who have contacted community organizations and KNCB since the gap became public.

At least two neighborhood associations in Districts 3 and 4 have written to the county demanding an immediate review of its emergency language access protocols. The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas said it is monitoring the situation closely. The county has not indicated whether it will conduct a formal after-action review of the multilingual alert gap. The boil water notice remains in effect for all 48,000 residents of Districts 3 and 4 regardless of when they received it — but for the families who cooked, drank, and bathed in that water through Sunday night, the question of accountability is already taking shape.

stories.headline: Para preguntas sobre el agua, marque la NuecesInfoLine y oprima el 2 / For water questions, call the NuecesInfoLine and press 2
stories.summary: La línea 361-826-INFO atiende en español las 24 horas. El 9-1-1 es solo para emergencias de vida o muerte. / The 361-826-INFO line answers in Spanish around the clock; 911 is only for life-threatening emergencies.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Si usted vive en los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4 y tiene preguntas sobre el aviso de hervir el agua, hay un número para eso, y no es el 9-1-1. Es la NuecesInfoLine: 361-826-INFO. Para español, oprima el 2.

El Centro de Comunicaciones de Emergencia del Coastal Bend abrió la línea el domingo por la noche, después de que el aviso para los dos distritos provocó un aumento importante de llamadas al 9-1-1. "El 9-1-1 es solo para emergencias que ponen en peligro la vida", dijo la directora del centro, Patricia Escamilla-Voss, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Pidió usar la nueva línea y dejar el 9-1-1 libre para las personas cuya vida está en peligro.
La línea funciona las 24 horas. Los operadores pueden explicarle el aviso, decirle dónde se reparte agua y cuándo se espera que vuelva el servicio normal.

Esto es importante para nuestra comunidad por una razón que usted ya conoce. El aviso para los Distritos 3 y 4 salió en inglés el domingo a las 5:30 de la tarde. La versión oficial en español llegó a KNCB a las 6:03 de la mañana de este lunes, más de 12 horas después, y la pusimos al aire en ese momento. Si anoche usted no supo qué hacer, no fue su culpa.
Lo que debe hacer ahora: hierva el agua a borbotones durante dos minutos antes de beberla, cocinar, hacer hielo o lavarse los dientes. Déjela enfriar. El agua embotellada es segura.
A quién le toca: a unos 48,000 residentes de los códigos postales 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 y 78417. El aviso para toda la ciudad, del 18 de septiembre, sigue vigente para los demás.
Dónde hay agua: en el gimnasio de la preparatoria Tuloso-Midway, en el Centro Comunitario Woodlawn y en el parque Cefe Valenzuela.

In English: For questions about the boil-water notice in Water Districts 3 and 4, call the NuecesInfoLine at 361-826-INFO and press 2 for Spanish; it is staffed around the clock. Keep 911 for life-threatening emergencies. The English notice went out Sunday at 5:30 p.m.; the official Spanish version reached KNCB at 6:03 a.m. Monday, more than 12 hours later. Boil water for two minutes. Water is available at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

stories.headline: In Aransas Pass, a shrimp boat that rode out the storm sits idle behind a closed bay
stories.summary: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Hurricane Rafael. His season may not survive the spill closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.
body: The shrimp boat is tied up where it has been since the bays closed, lines doubled, outriggers folded, nets hung to dry along the dock rail in Aransas Pass. Huy Nguyen walks its deck every morning anyway.
"Habit," said Nguyen, 51. "My father did it every morning for thirty years. Now me. The boat doesn't know it's not going anywhere."

Nguyen's boat came through Hurricane Rafael with little more than scraped paint, a stroke of luck he does not take lightly. What it can't do is fish. Since Sept. 18, fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays has been closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of water. Those bays are where Nguyen works.
The week of the storm, he found oil on his nets. "I knew then," he said. "You see that on your net, you know the season is gone."

Bay shrimpers had called it a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs eating into margins. Nguyen does the math out loud, the way he does most things. "I owe on the boat. I owe the fuel dock. I have a deckhand with two kids," he said. "Shrimp in the water don't pay the bank."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His family is part of the Vietnamese American fishing community that has worked the Texas Coastal Bend for decades, building a living one boat at a time. For many of those families, one lost season means a hard year.

The closures are meant to protect people from eating seafood that could be contaminated, and neither agency has said when they will be lifted. The cause of the spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal, remains under investigation.
Nguyen said he understands why the bays are closed. "I don't want anybody sick from my shrimp," he said. "But somebody needs to tell us how long. You can't plan a year on 'we'll see.'"
He has no plans to sell the boat. Not yet. "My father brought this boat through worse," he said, then reconsidered. "Maybe not worse. Different."
At the end of the dock, a pelican sat on a piling, waiting for a catch that wasn't coming in.

stories.headline: Doce horas tarde: por qué el aviso de agua en español no llegó a tiempo / Twelve hours late: why the Spanish water notice didn't arrive in time
stories.summary: El condado confirmó la demora y la atribuyó a la falta de personal en su contratista de traducción. / The county confirmed the delay and blamed reduced staffing at its translation contractor.
body: El aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 salió en inglés a las 5:30 de la tarde del 26 de septiembre. KNCB, que es la fuente principal de noticias para unos 34,000 oyentes hispanohablantes en Corpus Christi, recibió la notificación oficial a las 6:03 de la mañana siguiente. Fueron más de doce horas en las que muchas familias siguieron usando el agua de la llave sin saber del peligro.

"Recibimos el aviso oficial de la ciudad esta mañana", dijo Marisol Fuentes-Vega, directora de noticias de KNCB. "Para entonces, muchos de nuestros oyentes ya habían usado agua sin tratar durante la noche." La Oficina de Manejo de Emergencias del Condado de Nueces confirmó la demora. Su portavoz, Cassandra Trejo-Morales, la atribuyó a la falta de personal en la empresa contratada para las traducciones, Nueces County Language Access Services. "Estamos revisando lo que pasó y lo que se puede hacer diferente", dijo.

En un huracán, la información es una forma de protección. Un aviso de agua que llega medio día tarde no es un problema de idioma solamente; es un problema de salud. KNCB seguirá documentando cuándo llega cada aviso en español y lo compartirá con nuestros oyentes.
Si en su casa alguien tiene síntomas estomacales, dé muchos líquidos y busque atención médica si no mejora.

In English: The Districts 3 and 4 boil-water notice went out in English at 5:30 p.m. on Sept. 26 but reached KNCB, the main news source for an estimated 34,000 Spanish-speaking listeners, only at 6:03 the next morning. "By then many of our listeners had already been using untreated water overnight," said KNCB news director Marisol Fuentes-Vega. County emergency management spokesperson Cassandra Trejo-Morales confirmed the delay, citing reduced staffing at its translation contractor.

stories.headline: Stomach illness visits begin to ease, health district says
stories.summary: After a surge that filled hallway beds, emergency rooms are seeing fewer patients with stomach illness. Officials say the boil-water notice and hand-washing still matter.
body: Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County have begun to ease, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said Tuesday, after a surge last week that pushed visits to about 180% above normal and put patients in hallway beds.

"We're seeing the curve bend down, and that's good news," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist. "It is not the all-clear. Norovirus is still out there, and the conditions that helped it spread haven't gone away."
Shah did not release new visit counts Tuesday. She said the district will keep tracking ER visits and wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus spreading in the city on Sept. 20.

The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 remains in effect. The city's water utility said Friday that damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

At one Nueces County emergency department, charge nurse Alyssa Cortez said the change is noticeable. "Last week, every hallway stretcher had somebody on it. Monday night, for a few hours, the hallway was empty," Cortez said. "I actually ate lunch sitting down. Don't tell anybody."
Cortez, 34, said staff are still busy and tired. She would not discuss individual patients.
Shah said people should keep doing what has worked: bottled water, or tap water held at a rolling boil for two minutes before it is used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or formula.
Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water after using the bathroom or changing diapers and before eating or cooking. Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.

Stay home for two days after symptoms end, and don't prepare food for others during that time. Disinfect bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution, especially after someone in the house has been sick.
"Every family that kept washing hands and kept a sick kid home helped bend this down," Shah said. "Keep going."

stories.headline: Two weeks after Rafael, neighborhoods near the bay say help came last
stories.summary: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay report waiting days for help after the storm. Many have no car, and church hubs filled the gap before official aid arrived.
body: Rosa Elizondo remembers the days after Hurricane Rafael by what she ran out of. First ice. Then clean water. Then phone battery. Then patience.
"Nadie vino. Nobody came, not for days," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "I'm not saying nobody cared. I'm saying nobody came."

Two weeks after the storm, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay are describing the same thing: they waited days for help after Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. Their accounts echo warnings made before the storm and patterns visible during it.

Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households in these neighborhoods without a way out. When the mandatory evacuation came, residents without cars waited for county buses.
When the storm hit, the calls came from here. Calls to 911 peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

In the days that followed, churches and neighborhood hubs often reached these streets before official distribution did. "We had water and food on the table before anybody official was on this block," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall. "That's not a brag. That's a problem."

Whitfield said the reasons are not mysterious. "No car means you can't get to the site. No phone battery means you can't call. No English, sometimes, means you don't understand the recording," she said. "So you wait. And waiting looks like you're fine, when you're not."

Elizondo eventually got water from Whitfield's hall, a few blocks from home. What stung, she said, was the sense of being last in line. "In my job, I go to people's houses. I check on them. That's the job," she said. "I kept thinking, who's checking on us?"

How help reached different neighborhoods will matter for months as recovery continues. For now, Whitfield keeps her own list of who on her streets still needs what. "Somebody should be counting this," she said. "If nobody else will, I will."

stories.headline: Empiezan a bajar las visitas por malestar estomacal; vecinos cuentan que esperaron días por ayuda / Stomach illness visits begin to ease; neighbors say they waited days for help
stories.summary: Dos semanas después de Rafael, las familias de los barrios cerca de la bahía recuerdan quién llegó primero. Y la compañía de luz pide más paciencia. / Two weeks after Rafael, families near the bay remember who arrived first.
body: Las visitas médicas por malestar estomacal empiezan a bajar en Corpus Christi, informó el distrito de salud pública, dos semanas después de que el huracán Rafael dejara a la ciudad con poca agua y un aviso de hervirla.

"Es una buena señal, pero no es el momento de confiarse", dijo la doctora Anita Shah, epidemióloga del distrito, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Sigan lavándose las manos con jabón y sigan hirviendo el agua mientras dure el aviso."
En los barrios de bajos ingresos cerca de la bahía, mientras tanto, los vecinos dicen que esperaron días para recibir ayuda después de la tormenta.

Rosa Elizondo, asistente de salud en el hogar y madre de tres hijos, pasó esos días sin luz y con poca agua. "Nosotros esperamos y esperamos", dijo en el aire de KNCB. "La primera agua y la primera comida que llegaron a mi casa no vinieron de un camión del gobierno. Vinieron del salón de la pastora."

El salón es el de la iglesia de la pastora Gloria Whitfield, que empezó a repartir comida y agua el viernes después de la tormenta, antes de que la distribución oficial llegara a algunas calles. "Nadie debería tener que esperar a que alguien se acuerde de su calle", dijo Whitfield.

Sobre la luz: la compañía de electricidad y agua informó que las cuadrillas encontraron fallas en cadena en subestaciones del noroeste y del centro de la ciudad, y que la reparación tardará más de lo previsto. Calcula que los últimos 32,000 clientes afectados en esas zonas tendrán servicio en un plazo de 7 a 10 días.
Si su hogar sigue sin luz y hay alguien que depende de un aparato médico, llame al 2-1-1.

In English: Stomach illness visits are beginning to ease, the health district said. "It's a good sign, but keep washing your hands and boiling your water," said Dr. Anita Shah. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents say they waited days for help. "The first water and food that reached my house didn't come from a government truck. It came from the pastor's hall," said Rosa Elizondo. The utility said cascading substation failures will delay power for the last 32,000 affected customers by 7 to 10 days.

stories.headline: CBPWA Flags 'Cascading Substation Failures' as Rafael Power Recovery Stalls in Northwest Corpus Christi
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has publicly acknowledged for the first time that failures at two substations are extending the recovery, and says the final 32,000 customers should be restored within 7 to 10 days.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued a rare operational statement Tuesday acknowledging that restoration crews working in northwest and central Corpus Christi have encountered what the utility described as "cascading substation failures" that are extending recovery timelines well beyond original projections. The statement marks the first time CBPWA has publicly acknowledged that something beyond routine storm damage is affecting two key transmission facilities.

"Restoration crews have encountered cascading substation failures in northwest and central Corpus Christi that are extending recovery," CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said in a written statement. "Crews are on-site at two facilities to investigate protective relay conditions exacerbated by storm debris. We expect the final 32,000 affected customers in those areas to be restored within 7 to 10 days." The statement does not explain how debris affected the relays, nor does it describe what the crews found when they arrived.

Industry experts say the distinction matters. Protective relays are sensitive electronic devices that govern when circuit breakers open and close; relay logic failures can cascade through a substation and trigger widespread, difficult-to-diagnose outages. Utility consultant Barry Nguyen, who has advised on hurricane restorations in Louisiana and Florida, said CBPWA's language is notably guarded. "They're being careful about how they characterize this," he said. "That usually means they don't have a full picture yet, or that the picture they have is raising questions they're not prepared to answer publicly." State regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT have been notified, Odom confirmed.

The two substations serve portions of Corpus Christi's northwest residential corridor and the central business district, areas where some customers have been without power since Rafael made landfall fourteen days ago. CBPWA says it has rerouted load where possible through adjacent distribution feeders, but that full service restoration requires the facilities to be brought back online. The 7-to-10-day estimate is the first the authority has given for those customers. CBPWA did not indicate whether it has requested outside engineering assistance for the relay investigations, and declined to identify the facilities by name.

stories.headline: Opinion: The neighborhoods that waited longest should be counted first
stories.summary: Residents near the bay say help took days to reach them after Rafael. The county should measure how long every neighborhood waited and publish the results.
body: I have covered three hurricanes for this newspaper. After every one, I have heard some version of the same sentence from people who live near the bay: "We waited."

This week, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters, including Coastline Public Radio, that they waited days for help after Rafael. I believe them, because the record points the same way.

Before the storm, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation help, and advocates warned that transit gaps left many households in those neighborhoods stranded. When the evacuation order came, people without cars had to wait for a county bus. At the storm's peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. In the days after, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some of those same streets.
None of that is a secret. It is just not counted in one place.

Here is a modest proposal. Nueces County and the city should measure, by neighborhood, how long people waited: for 911 response, for water, for debris pickup, for anything government delivers after a disaster. Then they should publish the numbers, good and bad, and update them through the recovery.

Measuring is not blaming. The people who answered 911 calls and loaded water trucks this month did hard work in impossible conditions. But good intentions are not a distribution plan. If help reaches the people with cars and phone chargers first, the system is working as designed, and the design needs to change.

The fix starts with the boring stuff: bus routes that keep running, distribution sites within walking distance, door-knocking for people who can't call. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, whose fellowship hall has fed her neighborhood since the storm, keeps a handwritten list of who needs what. A county with computers can do at least that well.

Recovery from Rafael will run for months. The county has already signed an emergency debris contract, and more decisions about where help goes are coming. Before they are made, the county should know which neighborhoods waited longest, and promise they won't be last again.

stories.headline: By the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop owner starts over with a sense of humor
stories.summary: Bill Hargrove's shop was gutted when Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas. Two weeks later, he's tearing out walls, telling stories and waiting for anglers to come back.
body: PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove has a new sign on the front of his bait shop, hand-painted on a scrap of plywood: "OPEN-ISH."
"It's honest advertising," said Hargrove, 64, owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. "I've got ice, I've got hooks, I've got opinions. Bait, we're working on."

Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm, and the surge gutted Hargrove's shop. The bait tanks, the freezers, the wall of rods and the photo board of customers' biggest catches all went.
Two weeks later he is tearing out drywall with a crowbar and a radio tuned to a country station, and selling what he can from a folding table out front.
"I rode out two storms in this shop. This one I left for, and it still rode me," he said.

Port Aransas had a strong summer before the storm, Hargrove said, with charters booked and bait selling as fast as he could keep it in the tanks. Now the island is quiet. Fishing is closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and Hargrove fields calls from regulars asking what's open.
"I tell them what the state says, not what they want to hear," he said. "Some of them want to hear I've got a secret spot. I've got a secret spot. It's closed."

He talks about the jetties the way some people talk about relatives. He has fished them since he was a boy, he said, and can tell you which rocks hold sheepshead in winter and where the tarpon used to roll in August. "The jetties don't care about a hurricane," he said. "They were here before me, and they'll be here after. The shop's the part that needs help."

He has not decided how much to rebuild. Insurance adjusters are scheduling, and contractors are booked. "I asked one guy for a quote, and he laughed and said, 'Bill, I'll put you on the list, right after my mother,'" Hargrove said.
For now, the plan is drywall out, fans on, door open. "Somebody's going to want ice," he said. "And somebody's going to want to hear a story. I can do both."

stories.headline: FEMA Thermal Survey Spots Anomalous Breaker Positions at Two Corpus Christi Substations
stories.summary: A federal aerial survey of post-Rafael utility damage has produced imagery showing breaker configurations at two substations that specialists say are difficult to attribute to storm mechanics alone, adding a new layer of uncertainty to Corpus Christi's stalled power recovery.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A federal aerial survey of storm-damaged utility infrastructure in the Corpus Christi area has produced imagery showing anomalous circuit breaker configurations at two substations that have been at the center of ongoing power restoration delays, according to a FEMA Mitigation Assessment Team report released Wednesday. The findings are described in technical language in the publicly available document, but specialists who reviewed the report with Sabal Energy Wire say the anomalies are difficult to explain through storm mechanics alone.

FEMA's Mitigation Assessment Team conducted systematic post-storm overflights of utility infrastructure using UAS platforms equipped with thermal and optical sensors between September 23 and September 26. The report states that imagery of two substations — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — shows "breaker positions inconsistent with expected post-storm failure modes" and "thermal signatures at switching equipment warranting on-site evaluation." The report recommends that the utility's engineering staff review the flagged sites as a priority action.

CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said the utility has received the FEMA report and is coordinating with its engineering teams on the findings. "We appreciate the federal team's systematic review," Odom said in an emailed statement. "We are evaluating all available data as part of our ongoing restoration work." She did not address whether the aerial findings had changed CBPWA's understanding of the relay failures flagged in Tuesday's operational statement, or whether CBPWA has requested outside forensic engineering assistance.

The FEMA Mitigation Assessment Team report is a standard post-disaster document produced to help utilities and local governments understand storm damage patterns and prioritize rebuilding. Officials from both FEMA and CBPWA emphasize that the report's characterization of "anomalous" breaker positions represents a technical observation, not a determination of cause, and that no federal agency has publicly attributed the substation conditions to anything other than the effects of Hurricane Rafael. The full report will be publicly posted to FEMA's website within ten business days, the agency said.

stories.headline: ALERTA: más de 300 quejas por contratistas fraudulentos de daños por agua; los Distritos 3 y 4, los más expuestos / ALERT: more than 300 complaints about fraudulent water-damage contractors
stories.summary: El estado advierte de cobros inflados, trabajos que nunca se hicieron y papeles que ceden su seguro al contratista. Qué revisar antes de firmar. / The state warns of inflated prices, work never done and forms that sign over your insurance benefits.
body: El Departamento de Seguridad Pública de Texas emitió hoy una alerta urgente para los consumidores del área de Corpus Christi: desde el huracán Rafael ha recibido más de 300 quejas contra contratistas fraudulentos que ofrecen reparar daños por agua.
Según el estado, los residentes de los Distritos 3 y 4 afectados por inundaciones y daños por agua son los más expuestos.
Las quejas describen cuatro prácticas:
Cobros por sacar agua, quitar moho y cambiar tablaroca a precios varias veces más altos que lo normal.
Cobros por trabajos que nunca se hicieron.
Documentos falsificados de ajustadores de seguros.
Papeles que piden al dueño "ceder sus beneficios" del seguro, para que el contratista le cobre directamente a la aseguradora sin que usted revise la cuenta.
Ese último papel suele venir solo en inglés, con el título "assignment of benefits". Si se lo ponen enfrente, no lo firme hasta que alguien de su confianza se lo lea completo en su idioma.
Qué recomienda el estado:
Verifique la licencia del contratista en license.state.tx.us.
Pida por lo menos tres presupuestos por escrito.
Pague solo cuando el trabajo esté terminado y usted lo haya revisado. No pague todo por adelantado ni en efectivo sin recibo.
Desconfíe de quien diga que viene "de parte de FEMA". FEMA no recomienda contratistas y no cobra por inscribirse.

Si cree que fue víctima, llame al Departamento de Seguridad Pública al (512) 424-2000 o a la policía local. También puede reportar fraude a la línea de protección al consumidor del procurador general de Texas, al (800) 621-0508.
En KNCB hemos recibido llamadas de oyentes a quienes les ofrecieron estos servicios de puerta en puerta. Si le pasó a usted, cuéntenos. Su experiencia puede evitar que le pase a su vecino.

In English: The Texas Department of Public Safety issued an urgent alert after more than 300 complaints about fraudulent water-damage contractors since Hurricane Rafael; residents of Districts 3 and 4 are most at risk. Complaints include inflated prices, charges for work never done, forged adjuster documents and "assignment of benefits" forms. Verify licenses at license.state.tx.us, get three written estimates and pay only after work is finished. Report fraud to DPS at (512) 424-2000.

stories.headline: Aerial survey of utility sites finds storm damage at 14 of 23; two substations flagged for inspection
stories.summary: FEMA's second survey phase covered substations, the water plant, pump stations and telecom sites. Engineers are being sent back to the Harbor View and Crosstown substations.
body: A federal aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area's utility sites found visible storm damage at 14 of the 23 locations it examined and singled out two electrical substations for a closer look by engineers, according to a summary released Wednesday by FEMA's Mitigation Assessment Team.

The survey, the second phase of FEMA's aerial assessment of Hurricane Rafael, was flown from Thursday, Sept. 23, through Sunday, Sept. 26. It covered five Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority electrical substations, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities, along with other utility sites.

At O.N. Stevens, the plant that supplies the city's drinking water, the summary reports moderate roof damage to the C-pump station. The plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, and the city has been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 18.

The summary identifies two of the authority's substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, "as requiring follow-up engineering inspection due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery." It does not say what the configurations were or whether they are related to storm damage. The authority said Tuesday that crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within seven to 10 days; it did not name the facilities.

Rafael Montoya-Chen, chief of the Texas Division of Emergency Management's infrastructure division, said the value of the flights is in what they let repair crews do next. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," he said.

The first phase of the survey, released Sept. 18, estimated that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. This phase counts no homes. It looks only at the equipment that keeps power, water and communications running.

The full set of Phase 2 images is not public. FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users through the agency's GeoPlatform. The Ledger has asked the authority when the inspections at Harbor View and Crosstown will take place and whether the results will be released.

stories.headline: Federal Agencies Open Probe into Pre-Storm Drone Flights Near Corpus Christi Utilities
stories.summary: A joint FAA and CBP statement confirms that multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations in the Corpus Christi area in the days before Hurricane Rafael are now under federal investigation.
body: Federal aviation and border security authorities issued a joint statement Wednesday confirming that investigators have identified multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft system operations in the Corpus Christi area in the period leading up to Hurricane Rafael. The agencies did not say how many flights were involved, where they took place or when; they asked anyone with information about drone activity in the area between September 4 and September 12 to contact the FBI.

The statement from the Federal Aviation Administration and U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations says the aircraft operated without required FAA authorizations and were detected through a combination of radar and electronic sensor records. "Due to the ongoing nature of the investigation, no additional details about the number, location, or timing of the incidents can be released at this time," the statement reads. Neither agency attributed the drone flights to any actor, country, or intent.

CBP Air and Marine Operations operates counter-UAS detection infrastructure along the Texas Gulf Coast as part of its border security mission, and that infrastructure captured the tracks in question during routine pre-storm operations. The FAA's Office of Security and Hazardous Materials Safety is participating in the review alongside CBP and unspecified federal law enforcement partners. The flights passed over or near infrastructure corridors that include water pumping stations, electrical transmission facilities, and pipeline infrastructure, according to federal sources who spoke on condition of anonymity because the investigation is ongoing. The flight patterns, Anchor and Rotor Weekly has confirmed through aviation sources, are consistent with slow, loitering behavior over fixed points of interest.

Aviation security experts caution against premature conclusions. "Pre-storm drone activity near infrastructure is not automatically evidence of hostile intent," said retired Air Force Lt. Col. Dena Carver, who now consults on UAS security. "It could be media, insurance assessment, environmental monitoring. The investigation will determine what it was." Federal authorities have not publicly linked the drone flights to any other aspect of the post-storm situation in Corpus Christi. No suspects have been identified and no charges have been filed. The FAA and CBP say they will not provide further public comment while the investigation is active.

stories.headline: Fact-check: No, aid is not reserved for wealthy neighborhoods, but delays near the bay are real
stories.summary: Viral posts claim storm help is going only to wealthy areas. That claim is false. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay do report waiting days for help, and that's a different problem.
body: CLAIM: Posts circulating since mid-September, including from the account @CoastTruthTX, say storm aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods.
VERDICT: False. There is no evidence that aid is being limited to wealthy areas. But delays in reaching low-income neighborhoods near the bay are a real and separate concern.

What's true: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters this week that they waited days for help after Hurricane Rafael. In some of those neighborhoods, food and water from church and neighborhood hubs arrived before official distribution did.

What's false: That help is reserved for the wealthy by design. "Help goes to people who need it, period," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you've been waiting, we want to know where you are."
County and base officials called a related viral claim, that the military is seizing homes, false earlier this month.
Why it matters: Rumors like these can keep people from asking for help. "If someone believes aid isn't for them, they won't ask," Pruitt says.

Watch your links: The city has warned about phishing emails pretending to be a disaster-aid portal. Don't enter personal or bank information on a site you reached from a social media post or an unexpected email. Use official county and city channels.

Still waiting? If you have an emergency, call 911. For other needs, contact the county through its official channels, and lean on neighbors, churches and community groups to help you connect. If you know someone without a car or a working phone, check on them and pass along what they need.
How we checked: Harborline 6 reviewed statements from county and base officials and recent reporting on delays in neighborhoods near the bay.

stories.headline: Federal survey of storm-hit Texas utility sites flags two substations for follow-up
stories.summary: FEMA's aerial assessment after Hurricane Rafael found visible damage at 14 of 23 utility sites and asked for engineering inspections at two substations where outages have dragged on.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal aerial survey of utility infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Rafael has flagged two electrical substations for follow-up inspection by engineers, adding a new question to a power restoration that has already run longer than the local utility first projected.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency's Mitigation Assessment Team said Wednesday that its survey of 23 utility sites in the Corpus Christi area, flown Sept. 23 through Sept. 26, found visible storm damage at 14 of them. The sites included five electrical substations operated by the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority, the city's main water treatment plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities.

Two of the substations, known as Harbor View and Crosstown, were identified as needing engineering inspection "due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery," the summary said. It gave no further description. The water plant, which lost power during the storm, had moderate roof damage to one pump station.

The finding lands a day after the utility said publicly that conditions at two of its facilities were slowing the work. The authority said Tuesday that crews were investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris and that the last 32,000 customers without power should be restored within seven to 10 days. It did not identify the facilities, and neither the utility nor FEMA has said whether they are the two named in the survey.

Aerial surveys have become a standard early step after major storms because they can cover ground that crews cannot yet reach. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," said Rafael Montoya-Chen, who heads the infrastructure division of the Texas Division of Emergency Management.

An earlier phase of the same program, released four days after the Sept. 14 landfall, estimated that 4,200 to 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. The detailed utility imagery has not been made public; FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users.

stories.headline: Texas DPS, AG's Office Warn of Storm Contractor Fraud After More Than 300 Complaints
stories.summary: Unlicensed restoration contractors are charging Rafael survivors three to five times standard market rates for water extraction and mold remediation, according to Texas law enforcement, which is pursuing arrest warrants and civil investigative demands.
body: Texas law enforcement and consumer protection officials issued an urgent statewide warning Wednesday after receiving more than 300 complaints from Hurricane Rafael survivors who say water damage contractors charged between three and five times standard market rates for water extraction, debris removal, and mold remediation work in the Corpus Christi area. Many of the operators hold no license with the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners or the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, officials said. The warning does not name any company.

"We have received more than 300 consumer complaints since the storm," said Sgt. Ramona Fierro, spokeswoman for Texas Department of Public Safety Region 2. "Complainants describe representatives arriving uninvited at storm-damaged properties, using high-pressure tactics to get homeowners to sign contracts, and then charging amounts that are three hundred to five hundred percent above what licensed contractors are charging for the same work in this area." Fierro said arrest warrants are being sought in connection with the most egregious cases and that additional charges related to fraudulent business practice are under review.

The Texas Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division has issued a civil investigative demand to several entities named in the complaints. Division Director Chandra Mitchell said the AG's office has obtained evidence that sales representatives have been approaching hurricane survivors at water distribution sites and outside shelter facilities in Corpus Christi. "Disaster fraud is a serious crime and an assault on people who are already suffering," Mitchell said. "We will pursue every available legal remedy." Investigators report that one operation has used multiple telephone numbers, at least two websites with similar domain names, and has accepted payment through cash, check, and mobile payment apps — making it difficult for victims to dispute charges.

Texas DPS advises all storm survivors to verify contractor licensing before signing any contract, insist on written estimates that itemize costs, and never pay more than ten percent as an upfront deposit. Licensed contractor lookup is available at the Texas MyLicense Office website. Residents who have been approached by unlicensed or predatory contractors are urged to call the AG's Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-621-0508. Officials expect the complaint count to rise as more residents return to their homes and discover the terms of contracts they signed under pressure in the storm's immediate aftermath.

stories.headline: Held at the berth: what a Captain of the Port order means for Kalvora Star and Ostrel Bay
stories.summary: Ten days after the Coast Guard said neither tanker would move, both remain alongside at Rendal Terminals. An explainer on the authority involved and what usually has to happen before a held ship sails.
body: MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay have not moved since before Hurricane Rafael. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard said both would stay moored at the Rendal Terminals berth under a Captain of the Port order until the investigation into the Inner Harbor oil release, and the owners' obligations under federal oil spill law, are addressed. Ten days later, both are still there. Here is what that status means.

The authority. A Captain of the Port can direct the movement of any vessel in the port when safety, security or the environment requires it. An order can keep a ship at a berth, send it to an anchorage or set conditions for sailing. It stays in force until the Captain of the Port lifts it.

Why these ships. The Unified Command has attributed an estimated 9,000 barrels of spilled crude to the two tankers. Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to their cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, has said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused. The ships are both the source of the spill and the place investigators have to work.

What usually has to happen. In general terms, three things stand between a held tanker and departure: investigators finish what they need aboard; the vessel is shown to be safe to move, cargo systems included; and the owner's financial responsibilities for the spill are in order. The Coast Guard designated both owners as responsible parties on Sept. 21. A claims center run for the owners opened Sunday.

"I can tell you the order is in effect and both vessels are where they were," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "I can't give you a date, and I won't discuss the investigation."

A maritime security analyst who is not involved in the case said the length of the hold is not unusual on its own. "When the question is what happened inside a ship's systems, the ship is the evidence," he said. "Nobody releases the evidence early."

Operator notes. Both tankers were laden when the storm arrived. Whether remaining cargo is discharged before either ship moves, and under what supervision, has not been addressed publicly. The ship channel remains closed to all traffic.

stories.headline: Researcher: Storm rumors came from about 40 coordinated accounts tied to a fake aid site
stories.summary: A threat researcher says rumor posts after Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails: aid-help-portal.example. Don't click it.
body: Rumor posts that spread after Hurricane Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails, a threat researcher says.
The site is aid-help-portal.example. It is not an official aid site.

The rumors circulating since the storm have included false claims that the military is seizing homes and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods, along with posts blaming refinery negligence for the oil spill. The spill's cause remains under investigation.

"These weren't 40 angry neighbors who happened to say the same thing," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab who tracks hacking and influence campaigns. "The posts were coordinated, and over and over they pointed people to the same lookalike aid site that showed up in phishing emails. Same site, same lure."
Earlier this month, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld's research ties that lure to the rumor posts.
Who is behind it? Feld won't say. "I'm not going to guess," she says. "Attribution is for governments. What I can tell people is how it works: make you angry, then hand you a link."

What to do: Don't click links to aid-help-portal.example, and don't enter personal or banking information on any site you reached from a viral post or unexpected email. If you did, change your passwords and contact your bank.
Before you share an alarming post about the storm, check it against official city, county or base statements, and report suspicious accounts to the platform.

stories.headline: Los rumores sobre casas confiscadas salieron de unas 40 cuentas coordinadas y de un sitio falso de ayuda / Home-seizure rumors traced to about 40 coordinated accounts and a fake aid site
stories.summary: Una investigadora encontró que las mismas cuentas empujaban a la gente hacia el sitio usado en los correos fraudulentos. Cómo reconocerlo. / A researcher found the same accounts pointed people to the site used in phishing emails.
body: ¿Se acuerda de las publicaciones que decían que el ejército estaba confiscando casas y que la ayuda sería solo para los barrios ricos? Eran falsas, como dijeron entonces el condado y las bases militares. Ahora una investigadora explica de dónde salieron.

Dana Feld, de Northlight Threat Lab, un laboratorio que estudia campañas de engaño en internet, encontró que los rumores fueron publicados de forma coordinada por unas 40 cuentas, entre ellas @CoastTruthTX. Esas cuentas, dijo, estaban ligadas al mismo sitio de internet falso que aparecía en los correos fraudulentos sobre ayuda por el desastre: aid-help-portal.example.

"No eran vecinos enojados escribiendo cada quien por su lado", dijo Feld, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Las cuentas publicaban lo mismo, casi al mismo tiempo, y llevaban a la gente al mismo sitio. No voy a decir quién está detrás, porque eso todavía no se sabe."
Dwayne Pruitt, portavoz de manejo de emergencias del condado, repitió lo esencial: "Nadie está confiscando casas. La ayuda no depende de su código postal."
Por qué le importa a usted: el rumor asusta, y el sitio falso aprovecha el susto. Pide sus datos personales con la promesa de "verificar su ayuda".
Cómo protegerse:
No abra enlaces que le lleguen por correo, texto o redes sociales ofreciendo ayuda. Escriba usted mismo la dirección oficial.
Ningún programa oficial cobra por inscribirse ni pide su contraseña.
Desconfíe de las cuentas nuevas que de pronto publican muchas "noticias" locales en mayúsculas.
Antes de compartir algo, pregúntese quién lo dice y cómo lo sabe. Si tiene dudas, llame a KNCB. Nosotros lo verificamos con usted.

In English: A threat researcher found that false post-storm rumors, including claims that the military was seizing homes, were posted in coordination by about 40 accounts, including @CoastTruthTX, and were tied to the same lookalike site used in phishing emails, aid-help-portal.example. "These weren't angry neighbors each writing on their own," said Dana Feld of Northlight Threat Lab, who did not say who is behind the accounts. County spokesman Dwayne Pruitt repeated that no homes are being seized. Type official addresses yourself and never give out a password.

stories.headline: Coordinated accounts pushed false rumors after Texas hurricane, researcher says
stories.summary: A private threat researcher says about 40 accounts coordinated rumor posts after Hurricane Rafael and pointed users to a lookalike aid site also used in phishing emails.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — False rumors that spread on social media after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike disaster-aid website also used in phishing emails, a private threat researcher said Thursday.

Dana Feld of Northlight Threat Lab said the posts, which spread in the days after Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane on Sept. 14, repeatedly directed users to aid-help-portal.example, a site made to resemble a legitimate aid portal.

"The pattern is the point," Feld said in an interview. "You have dozens of accounts acting in step, hitting the same emotional notes, and all roads lead to the same fake site. That isn't organic outrage. It's organized."

Among the false claims that circulated after the storm: that the military was seizing homes, and that aid would go only to wealthy neighborhoods. County and military officials in Corpus Christi publicly rejected the home-seizure claims. Posts blaming refinery negligence for an oil spill in the region's bays also spread.
The City of Corpus Christi warned employees and residents on Sept. 19 about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld said her research connects the rumor posts to that same lure.

Feld declined to say who may be behind the accounts. "Governments attribute. Researchers describe," she said. "I can tell you how it works. I'm not going to tell you who until someone with the evidence and the authority says so."

Disasters routinely draw rumors and scams as people search for information and help under stress. Coordinated campaigns differ from ordinary rumors because they are organized to spread quickly and to push people toward a specific action, such as clicking a link.

The Coastal Bend is still recovering from Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across three coastal counties, triggered a citywide boil-water notice in Corpus Christi and halted crude exports from a port that handles about half of the nation's crude oil exports.

stories.headline: Federal authorities examining pre-storm drone flights over port and a utility site, sources say
stories.summary: Sources familiar with the investigation say commercial drones may have flown over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one power utility facility in the week before Rafael. The FBI is asking for tips.
body: Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones conducted surveillance flights over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, sources familiar with the investigation told Gulfwater.
What the sources say. The flights took place in the week before landfall. They were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard. No organization has claimed responsibility.

Why investigators care. The timing has drawn attention because of the damage to critical infrastructure during and after the storm, the sources said. They did not say that the flights caused any of it, and Gulfwater has no information that they did.

On the record. The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations confirmed Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations in the Corpus Christi area in the period before the storm. The agencies said the aircraft flew without required authorizations and were detected through radar and electronic sensor records. They released no numbers, locations or times.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "Anyone with information should contact the FBI. We have no further comment."
The Coast Guard declined to discuss the radar records.
Port condition. Unchanged. The ship channel remains closed to all traffic while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor spill is contained.
Not known. Who operated the aircraft. How many flights there were. Which port and utility sites were overflown. Whether the flights are connected to any other matter under investigation.

Operator notes. Terminal security officers who logged drone sightings in early September should preserve camera footage and gate records and report them to the FBI. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution and will report findings as agencies release them.
places: US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Families: Quieter nights, an easing stomach bug and a fake aid site to avoid
stories.summary: No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi, stomach illness is easing, and a researcher warns about a lookalike aid website. Here's this week's roundup.
body: Two and a half weeks after Rafael, many of you have told us the same thing: the days are getting more routine, even if the routine includes boiling water. Here's what's new this week.

Quiet skies. No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi after about ten days of reports following the storm. The FBI has confirmed it is investigating the earlier reports. "We continue to work with the appropriate authorities, and there's no impact to operations," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer. As always, we won't report on security measures, and we ask readers not to post speculation about the base online.

Stomach bug easing. The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after last week's surge. Keep up the hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water, and keep sick kids home for two days after symptoms stop. Child care providers will thank you.

Still boiling. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. Temporary pumps are limiting capacity while the plant waits on replacement parts for its damaged pumps, the city says. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Watch that link. A threat researcher says rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and pointed people to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, which also appeared in phishing emails. Do not enter personal or banking information on it. If you get an email asking you to "verify" aid information, delete it. Service members should also report suspicious emails through their command's procedures.
Depot update. Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should continue to follow guidance from their supervisors on returning to work.

Friday night. A reader from Flour Bluff sent us a photo of her kids' youth football practice this week: a cooler of bottled water on the sideline and a parent stationed at the hand-washing jug. Small things. They matter.
Thanks to everyone who sent in notes. Keep them coming.

stories.headline: Report of pre-storm drone flights over port and utility site adds a security question for energy operators
stories.summary: Gulfwater Maritime Report says federal authorities are examining whether drones surveilled the Port of Corpus Christi and a power utility facility before Rafael. The FBI confirms only that it is investigating.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones flew surveillance over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, Gulfwater Maritime Report reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the investigation.

The trade publication said the flights were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard and took place in the week before landfall. No organization has claimed responsibility, it said.
Sabal has not independently confirmed the report.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "We have no further comment." The FBI has asked the public for tips.

The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection said Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized drone operations in the area in the period before the storm. They gave no locations.

For energy companies along the ship channel, the report lands in an already crowded security picture. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill.
No agency has said the drone flights are connected to the spill or to any storm damage, and the Gulfwater report did not say so.

A security manager at one area terminal, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said his company had been asked by federal investigators to preserve camera footage from early September. He declined to say more.

Terminals and refineries along the channel are subject to federal maritime security rules that require them to control access from land and water. Those rules were written with fences, gates and boats in mind.
The ship channel remains closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained. Crude exports have been halted for nearly three weeks.

stories.headline: Teaching through a boil-water notice: jugs, soap and a lot of reminders
stories.summary: Leticia Ramos has spent more than two weeks hauling water for her Calallen street. The schoolteacher says children are the hardest part of a boil-water notice, because they forget.
body: Leticia Ramos has a rule for every sink in her house: a strip of blue painter's tape across the faucet, and a jug of boiled water beside it.

"Kids forget," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher in Calallen. "Adults forget too, but kids forget at seven in the morning with a toothbrush in their mouth. Tape on the faucet is a reminder you can see."

Ramos has organized water runs for her street since Hurricane Rafael knocked out power to the nearby O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 is still in effect, and the city says damaged pumps at the plant need replacement parts, with temporary pumps limiting capacity.
Now she is thinking like a teacher. School districts across Nueces County reviewed their storm plans before the season, but no plan makes a boil-water notice easy for a room full of children.

"You can't put tape on a water fountain and expect it to work," she said. "You need a person. You need a jug with a spigot by the door, a pump bottle of soap, paper towels, and a teacher who says 'wash' forty times a day."

The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after a surge last week, when norovirus showed up in wastewater testing and visits ran about 180% above normal. Ramos said that is exactly why she isn't relaxing.
"When it gets better, that's when people stop doing the thing that made it better," she said. "I've seen it with lice. I've seen it with flu. I'll see it with this."

She has turned her own kitchen into a pilot program. A big pot boils on the back burner most of the day. A dish tub by the sink holds soapy water for hand-washing, and a second holds boiled rinse water. A sign on the refrigerator, in neat teacher's print, reads: "Tap = NO. Jug = YES. Soap = ALWAYS."

On Thursday evening, the lights were on at a high school practice field down the road, and a parent was handing out bottled water from the bed of a pickup. Ramos waved on her way past with the garden wagon.
"Normal-ish," she said. "We'll take normal-ish."

stories.headline: Debris pickup: what to put at the curb, and what to keep out of the street
stories.summary: Nueces County has hired an emergency debris contractor to haul storm debris. County officials say sorting and placement will speed pickups.
body: Curbside debris piles are still growing nearly three weeks after Hurricane Rafael. Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC to haul it away. Here's how to get your pile picked up faster.

Sort it into separate piles. Vegetation: tree limbs, leaves and logs. Don't bag it. Construction debris: drywall, carpet, lumber, furniture and roofing. Appliances: refrigerators, freezers, washers, dryers and water heaters. Tape refrigerator and freezer doors shut. Electronics: TVs and computers. Household hazardous waste: paint, cleaners, pesticides, gasoline and batteries. Keep these separate and never pour them down drains.

Place it right. Put piles at the curb, between the sidewalk and the street. Don't block the street, sidewalks, storm drains or fire hydrants. Keep piles away from mailboxes, fences and utility boxes, and never under power lines.

"Every pile that's sorted and in the right place is a pile a truck can grab and go," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Every pile in the street or tangled up in a power line slows down the whole route."
When will it be picked up? The county says routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set. Pruitt asks residents not to call 911 about debris pickup.
Watch for scams. Be wary of anyone who knocks on your door asking for cash up front to haul debris or claiming to be with the county. "County crews don't ask you for money," Pruitt says.
Take pictures. Photograph your pile with the date. It helps if you need to follow up later.

stories.headline: Explainer: what a closed ship channel means for Corpus Christi's refiners
stories.summary: Exporters with no ships have no sales. Refiners have pipelines, trucks and tanks, which buys time but not indefinitely.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Nearly three weeks into the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, most attention has gone to crude exports, which stopped the day the port closed to inbound ships. The refineries along the Inner Harbor face a different problem.
Sabal described in August how exporters and refiners share one channel. This is what the closure means for the second group.

What still works. Pipelines. Much of the crude that feeds the area's refineries arrives by pipeline from inland, and much of the fuel they make leaves by pipeline and truck. None of that depends on the ship channel.
What does not. Anything that moves by water. Feedstock that normally arrives by ship or barge, and products that leave by tanker, cannot move while the channel is closed.

"An exporter is a tap. A refinery is a machine," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "You can shut a tap. A machine wants to keep running, and it needs somewhere to put what it makes."
