Holloway said she had no information on the operating status of any individual plant, and the companies have not made public statements. Hurricane Rafael also brought widespread power outages and damage across the area, which would affect any industrial site regardless of the channel.
In general, she said, a refinery cut off from the water leans on storage and on its land routes. "Tanks are time. When product tanks fill, you slow down. That is true for any refinery anywhere."

Why the market cares. Corpus Christi's refineries supply fuel to Texas and beyond. Holloway said a long closure would show up first in the trade of products that normally leave by ship. "The crude export gap is the big number. The products gap is smaller and closer to home," she said.
The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been set.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: More Than 600 Sickened in Four Days as Illness Cluster Hits Districts 3 and 4; Clinics Overwhelmed
stories.summary: The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is tracking a waterborne disease cluster in Districts 3 and 4: the two main hospitals have treated more than 600 patients with acute gastrointestinal illness since Sept. 29, and community clinics on the Westside and Northside are seeing two to three times normal patient volumes.
body: The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is tracking a waterborne disease cluster in Districts 3 and 4 that health officials say has sent more than 600 patients with acute gastrointestinal illness to Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center since Sept. 29 — with the count continuing to climb as residents seek care at overwhelmed community clinics. Officials are urging all residents in the two districts to strictly observe the boil-water notice and to seek medical care if symptoms develop.

Public Health District Director Dr. Priscilla Reyes said most of the patients live in Districts 3 and 4, suggesting a common source in the drinking water system. "The case pattern is consistent with exposure through the drinking water system," Dr. Reyes said at a Saturday afternoon press briefing. "We are treating this as a waterborne illness outbreak and are working with the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority and the Texas Department of State Health Services on the investigation." She said laboratory tests have confirmed Cryptosporidium and Giardia, both waterborne parasites, in multiple patient samples.

Community health clinics on the Westside and Northside reported patient volumes two to three times their normal daily caseloads this week. Administrators at the South Texas Community Health Center extended hours and called in additional clinical staff to handle the surge. The most common presentations are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramping. Dr. Reyes said the findings are consistent with people drinking tap water that had not been boiled.

Children under five and elderly residents face the greatest risk of serious complications from waterborne gastrointestinal illness, public health officials said. Residents who cannot afford to purchase bottled water are encouraged to use the city's free water distribution points, which remain open at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park. Dr. Reyes emphasized that keeping water at a rolling boil for the full time the notice specifies — not simply until hot or steaming — is necessary to kill relevant pathogens. The boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4 has been in place for six days, and city spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said the notice remains in effect while engineers continue assessing the distribution and pumping infrastructure serving the two districts.

stories.headline: Aviso de salud: brote de enfermedad gastrointestinal en los Distritos 3 y 4 / Health advisory: stomach illness cluster in Districts 3 and 4
stories.summary: Más de 600 pacientes atendidos desde el 29 de septiembre. Los análisis encontraron parásitos que se transmiten por el agua. / More than 600 patients treated since Sept. 29; tests found waterborne parasites.
body: Salud Pública del Condado de Nueces investiga un número elevado de casos de enfermedad gastrointestinal aguda entre residentes de los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4. Desde el 29 de septiembre, los hospitales Shoreline Regional Medical Center y Bay City Medical Center han atendido a más de 600 pacientes con vómito, diarrea, náuseas y cólicos, la mayoría de esos dos distritos.

Las pruebas de laboratorio confirmaron Cryptosporidium y Giardia, parásitos que se transmiten por el agua, en varias muestras. "Estos resultados son consistentes con tomar agua sin tratar. Por eso es tan importante seguir hirviendo toda el agua", dijo la epidemióloga Anita Shah, del distrito de salud pública, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. La doctora Shah recordó que hay que hervir el agua a borbotones durante dos minutos, también para lavarse los dientes y hacer hielo.

Busque atención médica de inmediato si hay deshidratación grave, diarrea con sangre, o si la persona enferma tiene el sistema inmunológico débil. Los bebés y las personas mayores se deshidratan más rápido. Para preguntas, llame a la línea de Salud Pública del Condado de Nueces, 361-826-7200.
El aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 sigue vigente hasta nuevo aviso.

In English: The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is investigating a cluster of acute stomach illness in Water Districts 3 and 4. More than 600 patients have been treated at Shoreline Regional and Bay City medical centers since Sept. 29, and lab tests confirmed Cryptosporidium and Giardia, waterborne parasites. "That's why it is so important to keep boiling all water," said epidemiologist Dr. Anita Shah. Seek care immediately for severe dehydration or bloody diarrhea. Questions: 361-826-7200.

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo's long September
stories.summary: A home health aide with three children and no car, she spent the days after Rafael waiting for help that came first from a church hall. Now she's back with her clients, boiling every drop.
body: Rosa Elizondo starts her day the same way she has every day since Sept. 18: she fills the big pot, sets it on the stove and waits for the boil.
"Ten minutes to heat it, two minutes boiling, then it has to cool," said Elizondo, 38. "Three kids, one pot. I do math all day now. My middle school teacher would be proud."

Elizondo is a home health aide. She spends her days in other people's homes, helping older and disabled clients bathe, eat, take their medicine and get through the afternoon. She rents a duplex in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, and she does not have a car. She gets to her clients the way she always has: on the bus when it runs, and with rides from neighbors when it doesn't.

Rafael tested that system. After the storm came ashore Sept. 14, Elizondo said, she waited days for help, as residents of other low-income neighborhoods near the bay have also described. The first water and food on her block came from Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church fellowship hall, a few blocks from her home, before official distribution reached the area.
"I called, I waited, I called," Elizondo said. "Then the pastora opened the hall, and later she sent a boy on a bicycle with a case of water on the handlebars. Ay, Dios. I almost cried."
Whitfield, 59, laughed when she heard the story retold. "That's one of our youth group kids," she said. "He's been on that bike for two weeks. He's earned a medal."

Elizondo's clients are among the people most at risk from the stomach illness that spread through the city last month, and she has become strict. "Soap and boiled water, every time. I don't care if you're 90. You wash," she said. "Sanitizer is not enough for this bug. The health lady said so."
Health officials say stomach illness visits have begun to ease. Elizondo is not taking chances. "Easing is not over," she said.
What she wants now is simple. "Remember us next time before the storm, not after," she said. "Send the bus early. Knock on the door. We'll be ready. We're always ready. We just don't have a car."
As the interview ended, her phone buzzed: a client needing a ride to the pharmacy. Elizondo grabbed a water bottle and laughed. "See? Everybody needs a ride," she said.

stories.headline: Week ahead: three clocks running in Corpus Christi, and the grid's is the newest
stories.summary: The channel survey, the spill response and now a power restoration that the utility says was set back by cascading substation failures.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi enters its fourth week without crude exports with three separate timelines in play. Two are familiar. The third became visible last week.
The channel. Closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No date.
The spill. A claims center for the tankers' owners has opened. Fishing closures in the bays remain. The Coast Guard investigation into how oil left the two tankers continues.

The grid. Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday that restoration crews had encountered cascading substation failures in the northwest and central districts, extending the recovery beyond initial estimates. The utility said crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris, and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within 7 to 10 days.

A federal aerial survey released Wednesday identified two CBPWA substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, as needing follow-up engineering inspection because of equipment configurations seen in the imagery.
"Two weeks ago I had the grid in the solved column. I have moved it back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said the areas named by the utility are not the ship channel itself, and she had no information that terminals lacked power. Her concern is pace. "A port restart needs people and services across the whole city. If a large part of town is still dark when the channel opens, the first week will be slower than the market assumes," she said.
The utility's 7-to-10-day window, counted from Tuesday, runs through the end of this week.
What to watch: CBPWA's restoration count, any finding from the substation inspections, and, as always, the Coast Guard.
"I would trade all three updates for one sentence from the Captain of the Port," Holloway said.

stories.headline: On North Beach, a retired welder tears out wet drywall and waits on the water
stories.summary: Marcus Bell was cut off when the bridges closed as Rafael hit, then lived with the smell of oil. Nearly three weeks later, he's rebuilding one wall at a time.
body: NORTH BEACH — Marcus Bell measures two feet up from the floor, snaps a chalk line and cuts. The wet drywall comes out in a long, sagging strip.
"Water came up about a foot. You cut a foot above that," Bell, 67, says, tapping a stud. "Everything under the line goes. Everything over it, we'll see."
Bell is a retired welder, and he is doing most of the work himself. Fans hum in every room. The carpet is already at the curb, in a pile that now includes a recliner, two doors and a mattress.

When Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, cutting North Beach off from downtown until inspections finished and the bridges reopened three days after landfall. Then came the oil, carried by surge and wind onto North Beach and other shorelines.
"First we couldn't get out. Then we couldn't open a window," Bell says. "Now I'm just tired. Tired is better than scared."
Health officials have advised people near oiled shorelines to avoid contact with the oil and get checked for breathing or skin problems. Bell keeps the windows shut and a mask on while he works.

The boil-water notice is still in effect, so he boils water for coffee and cleanup. Nueces County has awarded an emergency debris contract to haul storm debris, and Bell says he's watching for the trucks.
He has a list taped to the refrigerator: drywall, insulation, outlets, cabinets. One thing is crossed off. "Demolition is the easy part," he says. "Putting it back costs money."
Neighbors stop by to borrow his tools. He lends them and keeps a notebook of who has what. "You learn to keep track of your tools," he says. "And your neighbors."
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Records show $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners
stories.summary: Federal contract records show the award followed the flooding of the air station's regular fuel supplier. Quellmar says it is glad to support the station.
body: Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael.
The records, reviewed by the Ledger on Monday, describe the award as an emergency contract and identify Quellmar as the contractor and the air station as the location served.
Quellmar is a Corpus Christi fuel supplier. Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said the company was ready when the station needed it.

"Quellmar is proud to support the air station and the people who work there," Kerr said. "When their regular supplier went down in the storm, we were in a position to help. We're committed to keeping the station supplied for as long as we're needed."
Kerr did not say when deliveries to the air station began, how much fuel the contract covers or how long it runs.

Emergency contracts like this one are common after disasters, when regular suppliers are knocked offline and agencies need goods quickly. Federal rules allow agencies to speed up purchasing in urgent situations, though they must document the reasons. An emergency award is not, by itself, a sign of a problem.

The Ledger is tracking emergency contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend since the storm. They include Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, awarded Sept. 24. The Ledger has requested records related to that contract from the county.

NAS Corpus Christi, which shares its grounds with Corpus Christi Army Depot, has been working back toward normal operations since training aircraft began returning Sept. 20. A station's fuel needs do not stop during a recovery: aircraft, vehicles and equipment all depend on a steady supply, which is why the loss of a regular supplier can force a fast replacement.

stories.headline: Water plant pump parts delayed after supplier's local warehouse floods
stories.summary: Replacement parts for damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are shipping from out of state. The city's boil-water notice stays in effect, and the utility has not set a date to lift it.
body: Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded in Hurricane Rafael, and the parts are now shipping from out of state, the city's water utility said Monday.
The supplier is Delta Pumps & Controls. The city's boil-water notice, in effect since Sept. 18, remains in place.

"We know this isn't the news anyone wanted," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the water utility. "The parts are coming, but they're coming from farther away than we planned, because our supplier's local warehouse took on water in the same storm we did. We're sorry. Please keep boiling your water."

Gallegos did not give an arrival date for the parts or a date for lifting the notice. "When the parts are in, they have to be installed and tested, and the water has to be tested," she said. "We won't lift the notice until the tests say it's safe."

The plant in Calallen, the city's only treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, damaging pumps. The utility said Sept. 24 that the damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.
What it means for you: Keep boiling. Any tap water used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or baby formula needs two minutes at a rolling boil first. Bottled water is safe.
Keep washing. Stomach illness visits have begun to ease, but health officials say hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water still matters.
Conserve. With temporary pumps limiting capacity, use water sparingly. Run full loads, take shorter showers and skip lawn watering.
Check on neighbors. Older residents and families without cars may be running low on bottled water or on the energy to keep boiling it.

stories.headline: Main slick contained, Unified Command says; about 142,000 gallons of oil-water mix recovered
stories.summary: Primary skimming is finished and the response is shifting to shoreline cleanup. Fishing and shellfish closures in both bays stay in place pending state testing.
body: The main oil slick from the Inner Harbor discharge is contained, the Unified Command said Monday, three weeks after crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

Recovery. Primary skimming operations have concluded with about 142,000 gallons of oil-water mixture recovered. The figure is for mixed oil and water as collected, not for oil alone. The release has been estimated at about 9,000 barrels of crude.

Water quality. State monitoring readings in Corpus Christi Bay have fallen to an average of 0.40 milligrams per liter of petroleum hydrocarbons, down from a peak of 3.4 recorded Sept. 17, the update said. The raw water intake at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is back below its 0.10 milligram-per-liter alert threshold.
Wildlife. Coastal Bend Wildlife Rescue has documented 340 oiled birds; 198 have been rehabilitated and released.
Shoreline. Hand crews are working about 6.4 kilometers of affected shoreline in Nueces Bay. The response is moving from emergency containment to shoreline cleanup.
Closures. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in both bays remain closed pending state testing.

"Contained means the slick is no longer spreading. It does not mean the shoreline is clean, and it does not reopen the bays," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The work now is slower. It is people with hand tools on marsh edges."

Operator notes. Containment is one condition for moving ships through the inner channel again, but not the only one. The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date for the ship channel, which has been closed since Sept. 13. Both tankers remain at the Rendal Terminals berth, and the investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to their cargo-control systems is open.

stories.headline: CBPWA Confirms Probe into 'Anomalous Access' to Industrial Control Systems
stories.summary: In a terse Monday afternoon statement, the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has acknowledged for the first time that it is investigating unauthorized or anomalous access to its operational technology systems — a significant departure from the utility's previous storm-damage framing.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued a terse but significant statement Monday afternoon acknowledging that it is investigating anomalous access to portions of its operational technology systems — the first time the utility has used language that goes beyond storm-damage framing to describe the ongoing problems affecting its transmission and water distribution infrastructure. The statement was brief, carefully worded, and released at an hour that industry observers noted is unusual for utility communications.

"CBPWA has confirmed that it is investigating anomalous access to portions of its operational technology systems," CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said in an emailed statement. "We are working with cybersecurity experts and have notified appropriate federal agencies. We want to assure customers that we are taking this matter with the utmost seriousness and that we are committed to transparency as this review proceeds." The statement did not name the federal agencies notified, describe the systems involved, characterize what kind of access occurred, or indicate how the access was discovered.

The statement is narrow and carefully worded. It does not say what was accessed, how the access occurred, or how long it lasted. It does not explicitly indicate whether the anomalous access is connected to the utility's power restoration challenges or to the boil water notice affecting Districts 3 and 4. CBPWA has until this point attributed all infrastructure problems to Hurricane Rafael's physical damage. The sudden departure from that framing — without additional explanation — has raised immediate questions among energy sector analysts and customers who have been without power or safe water for three weeks.

The timing of the statement struck energy sector observers as notable. "Utilities don't issue this kind of statement on a Monday afternoon unless they've been asked to by a federal agency, or unless they're getting ahead of something they know is coming," said one utility sector cybersecurity consultant who requested anonymity because they advise clients in the region. The Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT, both of which have been monitoring CBPWA's restoration progress, did not comment Monday afternoon. Sabal Energy Wire will continue to report as this story develops. Residents in Districts 3 and 4 are asked to maintain current power and water conservation measures while the utility investigation continues.

stories.headline: Parks and Wildlife extends fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays
stories.summary: Shrimpers and anglers will wait longer to work the bays after the oil spill. Health officials say breathing complaints near oiled shorelines are easing.
body: Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting stays closed under the Texas Department of State Health Services, keeping shrimp boats and anglers off the water three weeks after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across the bays.
The closure began Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel and spread sheen across about 33 square miles of water.

"Extending the closure is about protecting the public," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which does not set the closures but helps run the cleanup that testing depends on. "Fish and shellfish can take up oil from the water and sediment. These bays shouldn't reopen until testing shows the seafood is safe to eat." No new reopening date was given.

There was better news on land. Health officials say respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing. "Fewer people are coming in with coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "That's welcome. Keep avoiding contact with any oil you see."
For bay shrimpers, the extension lands hard. Huy Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper in Aransas Pass, has kept his boat tied up since the closure.
"I understand. Nobody wants sick shrimp," Nguyen said. "But every week is a payment I don't make. Every week my deckhand looks for other work. Tell me a number. I can plan around a number."
Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs squeezing margins even before the storm. Now the closure has stretched into October.
Recreational anglers are affected too. The closure covers fishing in both bays, and bait shops and guides along the coast have fielded weeks of calls from regulars asking what's open.

The bays will recover at their own pace. Oil that settled into marsh mud and bay sediment can linger, as Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi oceanographer Nathan Brooks told the Ledger last month, and testing will determine when seafood is safe.
For Nguyen, the wait is the hardest part. "The bay is right there," he said, nodding toward the water from the dock. "I can see it. I just can't touch it."

stories.headline: Why the water plant's pump parts are late: a supplier explains
stories.summary: Delta Pumps & Controls says its local warehouse flooded in the same storm that damaged the O.N. Stevens plant, so parts are coming from out of state. Here's how one storm can break a supply chain twice.
body: When the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant's pumps were damaged in Hurricane Rafael, the city turned to its supplier. The problem was that the supplier's own building had taken water too.

"Our local warehouse flooded in the same storm," said Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls. "Parts that would normally go out our back door are now coming from out of state. I'm sorry. I live here. I'm boiling my water too."

The city's water utility said Monday that the replacement parts are delayed because Delta's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect, and temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

How a storm breaks a supply chain twice: Utilities keep some spare parts on hand, but large pump components are expensive, heavy and often specific to one plant's equipment. Many are stocked by distributors rather than by the utility. That arrangement works most of the time, because a local warehouse can get a part to the plant fast. It fails when the same disaster hits the plant and the warehouse at once.
Then the part has to travel. Shipping from out of state means more miles and more handoffs, and after a major storm, demand for repair parts of every kind rises across the region.

"I can tell you where the parts are coming from. I can't promise you a day until they're on the truck and I see a tracking number," Ybarra said. "I'd rather tell the city the truth late than a lie early."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city is in contact with the supplier. "Once the parts arrive, they still have to be installed and the system tested before we can lift the notice," Gallegos said.

The lesson may be bigger than one order. When a single treatment plant serves a whole city, and the parts for it sit in a warehouse in the same flood zone, one storm can knock out both. Whether to change that is a question for after the water is safe to drink.

stories.headline: CISA and FBI Confirm Cyberattack Targeted Corpus Christi Utility Systems During Hurricane Rafael
stories.summary: Federal cybersecurity and law enforcement authorities have announced a joint investigation into anomalous activity in industrial control systems at a Coastal Bend utility during the hurricane response, in what analysts are calling the most significant known utility control-system incident in the continental United States since 2021.
body: Federal cybersecurity and law enforcement authorities announced Tuesday morning that unauthorized actors gained access to industrial control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during the period surrounding Hurricane Rafael, and that the agencies have opened a joint investigation into its scope, origin and impact. The statement does not say what, if anything, the activity changed, and it does not link the activity to the extended power outages that have affected tens of thousands of residents over the past three weeks. The announcement was issued jointly by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

"CISA and the FBI have confirmed unauthorized access to control systems at a Coastal Bend utility in connection with Hurricane Rafael," said CISA Director of Communications Brett Halvorsen in a written statement released at noon Tuesday. "Texas Cyber Command has been activated in support of federal and state response. No attribution is being made at this time. We are asking the public and affected utilities to follow CISA guidance on operational technology security as this investigation continues." No country or non-state actor has been publicly identified as responsible.

The announcement does not name the utility, though CBPWA's Monday statement about "anomalous access to operational technology systems" leaves little ambiguity about which Corpus Christi utility is involved. The FBI's Cyber Division and CISA's Industrial Control Systems Security team are co-leading the investigation. Officials declined to describe the specific systems that were accessed, the nature of the manipulation that occurred, or how long the unauthorized access persisted.

For Corpus Christi residents, the announcement recontextualizes three weeks of hardship. The boil water notice affecting 48,000 residents in Districts 3 and 4 — which city officials have attributed throughout to "storm damage to pumping infrastructure" — has coincided with an illness cluster that has sent more than 600 people to hospital. Power customers in northwest and central Corpus Christi who were told their outages resulted from "cascading substation failures" may now have different questions about those explanations. City spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said Tuesday that the city is "awaiting further guidance from federal authorities" before commenting on how the CISA-FBI announcement relates to previously issued statements.

Corpus Christi Mayor David Reyes said he was briefed on the investigation before the public announcement and expressed both alarm and resolve. "What was done to our city's infrastructure — if the evidence bears out — is an act of cowardice that targeted families who were already trying to survive a natural disaster," Reyes said. "We are committed to full transparency with our residents as the federal investigation proceeds." Texas Cyber Command confirmed its activation Tuesday morning.

stories.headline: FEMA, Corpus Christi Utility Say Outages Were Prolonged by Deliberate Interference With Control Systems
stories.summary: In a joint statement, the federal disaster field office and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority say storm damage caused the initial blackouts but that interference with utility control systems kept some districts dark longer.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The power outages that followed Hurricane Rafael lasted longer in parts of Corpus Christi than storm damage alone would have caused because of deliberate interference with utility control systems, the Federal Emergency Management Agency's Joint Field Office and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday in a joint statement. The statement came two hours after the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency announced a joint investigation into anomalous activity in industrial control systems at a coastal Texas electric utility.

The statement draws a line between the storm and what came after. Wind and surge damage to the authority's transmission and distribution network caused the initial outages, it says; a technical review of the utility's operational data by federal investigators then determined that "the duration of outages in certain districts was extended by deliberate interference with utility control systems beyond what storm damage alone would have caused." It does not say who was responsible, how the systems were reached or which districts were affected, and it says the investigation is continuing.

"Federal disaster response has not had to account for something like this alongside a major hurricane," said Continental Wire Service national security correspondent Noah Pemberton, who has covered domestic security for more than a decade. "The immediate questions are practical ones: what it means for the customers still waiting for power, and what it means for the people who sat in the dark longer than the storm required."

The authority said it has put enhanced security measures in place on its control systems and is working with federal partners to prevent further incidents. Power has been restored to most customers, the statement says; restoration in parts of northwest and central Corpus Christi is continuing while relay inspection and repair are completed. It says no decision has been made on whether residents who experienced prolonged outages will be eligible for additional disaster assistance.

Both agencies asked anyone with information relevant to the investigation to contact the FBI's Corpus Christi Resident Agency. National Security Council spokesperson Adrian Wells confirmed Tuesday that the NSC is monitoring the situation and that the President has been briefed. The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee indicated they intend to seek briefings on the federal response.

stories.headline: Breathing complaints near oiled shorelines ease, but the bays stay closed
stories.summary: Health officials say fewer people living near oiled shorelines are reporting respiratory problems. For North Beach and Portland residents, the relief is partial.
body: On North Beach, Marcus Bell opened his windows this week for the first time in a while.

"Smell's mostly gone on my street. Not all the way. Mostly," said Bell, 67, a retired welder who has spent the weeks since Hurricane Rafael tearing out wet drywall. "My throat's better. I'll take it."

Health officials say Bell's experience fits a broader trend. Respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing, according to the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. In the first days after the spill, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near the oil, and officials advised people to avoid contact with it.

"This is what we hoped to see," said Dr. Anita Shah, a district epidemiologist. "People are reporting fewer coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline. That said, if you have asthma or COPD, or you're still having symptoms, see a doctor. And keep avoiding contact with any oil you find."

The bays themselves are not reopening yet. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, where the Texas Department of State Health Services has also closed shellfish harvesting. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of the bays after Rafael's surge and reached North Beach, Portland shorelines and marshes.

For shoreline neighborhoods, health and the bay are tied together. Many residents fish from piers and seawalls, some for sport and some for supper. For now, that food source is off the table. Shah said families who usually eat what they catch should not make an exception for fish that look or smell normal. "You can't see or smell everything that matters," she said.

Shah offered guidance for families near the shoreline. Don't touch oil or tar balls. If you get oil on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, kerosene or other solvents. Keep children and pets off oiled sand and out of the water. Don't eat fish or shellfish caught in the closed bays. And get care for persistent coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath or skin rashes.
Bell said he is ready for the next step. "When they say the beach is clean, I'll walk it," he said. "Until then, I've got walls to fix."

stories.headline: What the Corpus Christi Utility Cyberattack Reveals About the Nation's Energy Infrastructure Vulnerabilities
stories.summary: The confirmed cyberattack on Corpus Christi utility systems during Hurricane Rafael is precisely the scenario that energy security specialists have warned about for years — and its aftermath is likely to accelerate long-stalled federal mandates on operational technology security.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — When CISA and the FBI announced Tuesday that unauthorized actors had accessed and manipulated industrial control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during Hurricane Rafael, the energy sector did not need a press release to understand the significance. The scenario — a sophisticated actor targeting operational technology during a natural disaster, exploiting the chaos and reduced monitoring capacity of a major storm to mask deliberate infrastructure interference — is precisely what utility security specialists have warned about for years in classified briefings, red-team exercises, and academic literature.

CBPWA's Monday statement confirming an investigation into "anomalous access to operational technology systems" gave the energy sector a 36-hour window to begin assessing the implications before Tuesday's formal announcement. "What this appears to be is a timing attack," said Dr. Sara Okonkwo, director of the Critical Infrastructure Security Laboratory at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "You exploit a natural disaster's disruption of normal monitoring and response capacity to do something to a system that would otherwise be detected and responded to quickly. The storm gives you cover. The recovery chaos sustains it."

The specific systems affected have not been publicly described by CISA or the FBI. But the combination of events in Corpus Christi over the past three weeks — extended substation failures with anomalous relay conditions, water system pressure problems requiring a boil water notice, alongside an illness cluster that has sent more than 600 people to hospital, and a federal thermal survey that found breaker positions inconsistent with storm damage — suggests the attack, if confirmed as described, spanned multiple types of operational technology across both electric and water infrastructure. Energy sector analysts note that electric and water systems in mid-sized cities often share operational technology vendors and sometimes share network architecture.

The incident has already prompted an emergency security assessment bulletin from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation and an advisory from the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center. Both organizations are asking member utilities to immediately audit remote access logs, review recent changes to programmable logic controller configurations, and ensure that operational technology networks are logically separated from information technology networks. Those basic hygiene measures, security specialists note, are requirements many utilities have not fully implemented despite years of federal guidance.

The broader question the Corpus Christi attack poses for energy policy is one that CISA has been trying to force for years: what is the obligation of the federal government, state regulators, and private utilities to harden operational technology against nation-state-level threats? The Rafael incident — in which an apparent attack amplified a natural disaster's impact on civilians, produced a public health emergency, and remained hidden beneath storm-damage narratives for three weeks — will almost certainly accelerate that conversation. "After today," said Dr. Okonkwo, "every utility in America that has not taken OT security seriously is going to have a very difficult time explaining to its regulators and its ratepayers why it hasn't."

stories.headline: Investigación federal: interferencia en los sistemas de la compañía de luz alargó los apagones / Federal probe: interference with utility controls extended outages
stories.summary: FEMA y la autoridad de luz y agua dicen que los apagones duraron más de lo que habría causado la tormenta sola. / FEMA and the power and water authority say outages lasted longer than storm damage alone would explain.
body: La Agencia de Ciberseguridad y Seguridad de Infraestructura (CISA) y el FBI anunciaron una investigación conjunta sobre actividad anómala en los sistemas de control industrial de una compañía eléctrica de la costa de Texas durante la respuesta al huracán Rafael. Horas después, la Oficina Conjunta de FEMA y la Autoridad de Energía y Agua del Coastal Bend dijeron en un comunicado que los apagones en algunos distritos de Corpus Christi duraron más de lo que la tormenta habría causado por sí sola.

Según el comunicado, los apagones iniciales fueron causados por el viento y la marejada, pero los investigadores determinaron que la duración se alargó por interferencia deliberada con los sistemas de control de la compañía. La investigación sigue abierta y las agencias dicen que todavía no han atribuido la actividad a nadie.

Para nuestros oyentes, lo práctico es esto: todavía no se ha decidido si los residentes que tuvieron apagones prolongados podrán recibir ayuda adicional por desastre. Por si acaso, guarde cualquier comprobante de comida perdida, medicinas dañadas o gastos de hotel. Si tiene información sobre la investigación, la autoridad pide comunicarse con la oficina del FBI en Corpus Christi.
KNCB seguirá informando en español conforme haya más detalles oficiales.

In English: CISA and the FBI announced a joint investigation into anomalous activity affecting industrial control systems at a coastal Texas electric utility during the Rafael response. FEMA's Joint Field Office and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said outages in some Corpus Christi districts lasted longer than storm damage alone would have caused because of deliberate interference with utility control systems. No attribution has been made. No decision has been made on extra aid for residents who had prolonged outages; keep your receipts.

stories.headline: 'Built that way': KNCB's news director on why the Spanish water warning came 12 hours late
stories.summary: A state snapshot notes delays in Spanish-language alerts but puts no number on them. Marisol Fuentes-Vega has the number, and an explanation.
body: Marisol Fuentes-Vega keeps the log open on her desk at KNCB. It shows the minute the station's fax line printed the city's boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4: 6:03 a.m. on Monday, Sept. 27. The English alert had gone out at 5:30 the evening before.

"Twelve hours and thirty-three minutes," said Fuentes-Vega, the station's news director. "I have read that line so many times I could say it in my sleep. For twelve hours, the people who listen to us were filling glasses from the tap."

On Tuesday the Texas Division of Emergency Management released its first after-action snapshot of public communications during Hurricane Rafael. The document notes "observed delays in Spanish-language alert distribution." It does not say how long the delays were, and it makes no recommendations.

The same day, a local chapter of the League of United Latin American Citizens filed a complaint with the state, citing its limited-English-proficiency plan and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. KNCB read the complaint on the air.

In an interview with Coastline Public Radio, Fuentes-Vega described what she says is a structural problem, not a one-night failure. English alerts, she said, move automatically from the agency that writes them to phones, television and radio. Spanish versions wait for a translation, and the translation waits for a person.

"Nobody decided that Spanish speakers should find out last," she said. "It is built that way. The English goes out at the speed of a computer. The Spanish goes out at the speed of whoever is still in the office."

KNCB is the main news source for an estimated 34,000 Spanish-speaking listeners in Corpus Christi. During the storm the station stayed on the air on generator power for as long as its transmitter held, translating warnings itself as they arrived.

Cassandra Trejo-Morales, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, has said the Spanish notice was delayed and has attributed the delay to limits in the county's language-access service. The county has not yet said what it will change.
Fuentes-Vega said she is not waiting. The station now calls the city and the county every evening to ask whether anything has been issued in English that has not reached it in Spanish.
"It should not depend on us remembering to call," she said. "But until it doesn't, we call."

The state snapshot is a first look; a fuller review is expected later. Fuentes-Vega said she plans to ask county commissioners to require that every emergency notice go out in both languages at the same time.

stories.headline: That aid website might be fake: how to spot the lookalike before you click
stories.summary: A researcher has tied post-storm rumors to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that was also used in phishing emails. Here's how to protect yourself.
body: As Coastal Bend families look for help after Hurricane Rafael, scammers are looking for them. Last week a threat researcher said rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that also appeared in phishing emails. Last month the city warned residents and employees about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal.
Here's how to spot a fake before it costs you.
Check the address. Don't trust a page just because it looks official. Look closely at the web address. Lookalike sites borrow words like "aid," "help" and "portal" to seem real.
Don't follow links from posts or surprise emails. Type in the address of an official site you already know, or get it from an official city or county announcement.

Slow down when you're angry or scared. "The rumor makes you mad, then the link offers you a fix," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab. "That one-two punch is the whole trick. If a post makes your blood boil, that's the moment to stop and check."
Never give a password or bank details to a site you reached from a link. Legitimate agencies will not ask you to "verify" a bank account through a social media post.
Already clicked? If you entered a password, change it everywhere you used it and turn on two-step verification. If you entered bank details, call your bank right away.
Help others. Older relatives and neighbors may be more likely to fall for these messages. Share this checklist, not the rumor.
Report it. Report suspicious posts to the platform, and forward phishing emails using your email provider's reporting tool.

stories.headline: Texas energy operators told to review remote access after Corpus Christi utility intrusion
stories.summary: The governor has directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access procedures and report anomalies to CISA. Terminals and pipelines along the coast are on the list.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Energy companies across Texas are reviewing how outside parties connect to their control systems after the governor directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access security procedures and report anomalies to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The directive followed confirmation Tuesday that the FBI and CISA are investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during the Hurricane Rafael response. Texas Cyber Command has been activated to assist. Officials have released no operational details and made no attribution.
Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Monday that it was investigating anomalous access to its internal network systems and that there was no indication customer data had been affected.

The order reaches well beyond one utility. Refineries, pipelines, crude terminals and power generators all count as critical infrastructure, and most allow some form of remote connection for vendors or their own engineers.

"The first step is a list," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Who can connect from outside, to what, and when did they last do it? Remove what is not needed. Separate control systems from everything else. If something looks wrong, report it. We would rather hear about ten things that turn out to be nothing."
Tran declined to discuss the utility investigation.

It is the second remote-access inquiry in Corpus Christi in three weeks. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill. No agency has linked the two matters.

Several operators contacted by Sabal declined to comment on their own reviews. A compliance officer at one pipeline company, who asked not to be named, said the instruction was clear enough. "Nobody needs to be told twice this month," she said.
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed and crude exports halted.

stories.headline: In Flour Bluff, the night sky over the air station has gone quiet. The questions haven't.
stories.summary: The drone sightings that stirred NAS Corpus Christi's neighbors after Rafael have stopped. The FBI's investigation continues, and officials still aren't saying what the lights were.
body: On a clear night in Flour Bluff, the sky over NAS Corpus Christi looks mostly the way it did before the storm: navigation lights on training aircraft, a few bright planets, the slow drift of a satellite. Jaime Ortega still sets up his tripod in the backyard to watch.

"Most nights now, it's just the sky," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer whose videos of hovering lights over the air station circulated widely after Hurricane Rafael. "Which is what I wanted. I just wish I knew what I was looking at before."

The sightings came in a burst. In the days after the storm, residents began posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. NAS Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that it was aware of drone reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. The FBI's Houston division confirmed Sept. 23 that it was investigating. By late September, after about ten days, no new sightings were being reported.

Officials have not said what the lights were or who might have been flying them, and that may not change soon. The FBI does not discuss evidence in open investigations, and the Navy does not discuss how it protects its bases.

"Our position hasn't changed. We're still working with the appropriate authorities," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "I'm not going to discuss security. What I can say is there was no impact to operations."

For neighbors, that leaves an unusual kind of uncertainty: a story that started loudly and then simply stopped. Some residents say they have stopped thinking about it. Others say they still glance up when they walk the dog.

Ortega has thought about what he would want if the investigation ever ends. "Not secrets. Not names," he said. "Just: here's what it was, here's what you can stop worrying about. That's all neighbors want."
He said he has kept every original file, with time stamps, in case investigators ever ask for them.

Meanwhile, the air station is getting busier. Training aircraft have been returning since Sept. 20, and for many neighbors, the sound of engines over Flour Bluff has become the reassuring kind of noise.

stories.headline: Tanker cargo-systems probe continues with few public details
stories.summary: More than two weeks after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access, investigators have released no findings. The vendor's remote access remains off.
body: Status, Oct. 7: Investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay ongoing. No findings released. Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. The laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released.

On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that supports tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, that it had revoked all remote access and that it was cooperating with investigators.
Neither the Coast Guard nor federal cyber officials have released findings since.

"The investigation is active and thorough, and we will not release partial information," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "When we can share findings responsibly, we will."

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is still supporting the Coast Guard, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the agency. She declined to discuss the investigation but offered general advice for any operator of connected industrial systems. "Know what's connected to your systems. Keep it patched. Know who can get in from outside, and turn off what you don't need," Tran said. "None of that is new advice. It's just advice that's easy to put off."

Technical note: Investigations involving shipboard control systems typically require forensic review of system logs, network equipment and vendor records, and can take weeks or months. Findings may be shared with operators and regulators before any public release.
Port conditions: Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: State health investigators confirm waterborne contamination reached Districts 3 and 4 distribution lines
stories.summary: Texas DSHS released preliminary findings Thursday showing 94.3 percent of confirmed gastroenteritis cases cluster inside the boil-water zone — and that the first ER admissions followed a documented pressure drop by exactly three days.
body: Three weeks after Corpus Christi issued a city-wide boil-water notice, state investigators have confirmed what neighborhood clinics and emergency physicians suspected: the pressure failure that swept through Districts 3 and 4 of the city's water distribution system in the days after Hurricane Rafael was not merely a supply inconvenience. It was a pathway for contamination that has made hundreds of people sick — more than 600 had been treated at the two main hospitals by Oct. 2, and the count is still rising.

The Texas Department of State Health Services released preliminary investigation findings Thursday afternoon. The analysis mapped every confirmed gastroenteritis case reported to Nueces County public health since Sept. 14 and found that 94.3 percent of them geocode to addresses inside the District 3 and District 4 service boundaries — the same geography covered by the boil-water notice. The concentration is what epidemiologists call a point-source distribution: cases spike sharply, then trail off, in a pattern consistent with a single contamination event in a shared infrastructure system rather than person-to-person spread.

"The epidemiological analysis shows 94.3 percent of confirmed cases geocode to the boil-water zone, and the temporal curve is consistent with distribution contamination rather than a community-wide respiratory or contact illness," the DSHS statement reads in part. The agency described its findings as preliminary, pending laboratory confirmation of additional stool samples and ongoing technical review of pressure records from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant.

The three-day lag finding is the most precise detail in the report. DSHS linked the onset of the pressure drop in the two districts — documented in distribution records — to the first wave of emergency room admissions for acute gastroenteritis in Districts 3 and 4. That 72-hour gap falls within the typical incubation window for the most common waterborne pathogens, and investigators said the temporal alignment strengthens their confidence in distribution contamination as the source.

Dr. Renata Obasi, an infectious disease specialist at a Corpus Christi hospital who reviewed the findings, described the zone concentration as "striking." "When you map these cases and they stack up inside a geographic boundary that corresponds exactly to a pressure event, you're not looking at coincidence," she said. "You're looking at infrastructure." She noted that pressure drops in distribution systems can allow contaminants to enter pipes through cracks and joints that remain sealed under normal operating pressure. The department said it is not in a position to identify the source of contamination pending further analysis and that the investigation into the pressure event itself remains open. The boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 — which covers approximately 48,000 residents — remains in effect.

stories.headline: Confirman parásitos en el agua como causa del brote en los Distritos 3 y 4 / State confirms waterborne parasites caused the Districts 3 and 4 outbreak
stories.summary: El Departamento Estatal de Servicios de Salud identificó Cryptosporidium y Giardia. El aviso de hervir agua sigue vigente. / State health officials identified Cryptosporidium and Giardia; the boil-water notice remains in effect.
body: El Departamento Estatal de Servicios de Salud de Texas terminó su investigación preliminar del brote de enfermedad en los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4 de Corpus Christi. Confirmó que los causantes son Cryptosporidium parvum y Giardia lamblia, dos parásitos que se transmiten por el agua contaminada.

Según el estado, la exposición ocurrió durante el periodo de baja presión de agua en esos distritos después de Rafael, lo que coincide con el aviso de hervir agua emitido por la ciudad el 26 de septiembre. "El mensaje no ha cambiado: hiervan toda el agua, y si alguien en casa tuvo síntomas y es un bebé, una persona mayor o alguien con defensas bajas, llamen a su médico", dijo la epidemióloga Anita Shah, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

Para muchas familias que escuchan esta estación, la noticia confirma lo que ya sospechaban. En las llamadas de esta semana, varias madres nos contaron que sus hijos se enfermaron en las últimas semanas. Si su familia necesita atención y no tiene seguro, pregunte en las clínicas comunitarias o llame a la línea de salud pública del condado.
El aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 sigue vigente.

In English: The Texas Department of State Health Services confirmed Cryptosporidium parvum and Giardia lamblia caused the outbreak in Corpus Christi Water Districts 3 and 4, with exposure during the low-pressure period after Rafael. "The message hasn't changed: boil all water, and if an infant, an older adult or someone with weak immunity had symptoms, call your doctor," said epidemiologist Dr. Anita Shah. The boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 remains in effect.

stories.headline: Hallway beds and twelve-hour shifts: an ER charge nurse's three weeks after Rafael
stories.summary: Alyssa Cortez worked through the storm, the oil and the stomach-illness surge. She says the hardest part is not the patients, but how tired everyone is.
body: Alyssa Cortez keeps a granola bar in each pocket of her scrubs. One for her, she says, and one for whoever on her team looks like they need it more.
"Usually it's not me," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department. "Usually it's the new grad who hasn't sat down in six hours."

Cortez has worked twelve-hour shifts since Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. As charge nurse, she runs the floor: which patient goes to which bed, which nurse takes which room, who needs help now. She will not talk about individual patients, ever. She will talk about what the past three weeks felt like from the middle of the department.

First came the storm itself, when 911 calls across the county peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal. Then came residents from near oiled shorelines with coughs and rashes. Then, after the citywide boil-water notice, came the stomach illness: emergency room visits for it ran about 180% above normal, and departments, including hers, put patients in hallway beds.
"You learn to triage the hallway," she said. "Who's the sickest. Who's the scariest. Who's the one nobody's checked on in an hour. Then you go check on them."
Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September, and the hallway has mostly emptied. The tiredness has not.

"People think the hard part is the sick people. It's not. Sick people, we know how to do," she said. "The hard part is that everybody back there has something going on at home, too: a wet house, water to boil, family to look after. And they still come in and do twelve hours."
She said the things that helped most were small. A church sent trays of food. Neighbors covered errands. A family left a card at the front desk thanking "the nurses in the hallway."

Her advice to readers hasn't changed. "If you're sick and you can be cared for at home, stay home and call your doctor. If you need us, come. Don't wait until it's an emergency on top of an emergency," she said. "And wash your hands. I'll keep saying it until I'm fifty."
At 6:50 a.m. she was in the parking lot, finishing a coffee and already checking the bed board on her phone. "Here we go," she said.

stories.headline: CISA issues emergency directive requiring ICS credential audit at all federal facilities within 72 hours
stories.summary: Emergency Directive 27-02, issued Thursday, cites a "confirmed ICS incident at a Texas utility" and requires federal agency operators of industrial control systems to audit remote-access logs and change credential configurations immediately.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an emergency directive Thursday requiring all federal agencies that operate industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours. The directive, designated ED 27-02, cites a confirmed ICS incident at an unnamed Texas utility as the basis for the accelerated compliance window.

The directive arrives two days after Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority publicly disclosed that investigators had confirmed unauthorized access to its supervisory control and data acquisition systems. That disclosure, made jointly with CISA and the FBI, identified the incident as the first publicly confirmed cyberattack on a Texas water utility's operational technology infrastructure since federal reporting requirements were expanded under the America's Water Infrastructure Act. The utility cyberattack is now the subject of a federal investigation; no attribution has been made public.

"CISA is directing all federal agencies operating industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours, following a confirmed ICS incident at a Texas utility," the directive states. It further requires agencies to submit a summary of findings to CISA's Federal Emergency Management Group within 96 hours of issuance and to implement any identified credential remediation actions within seven days.

The directive applies specifically to agencies operating their own ICS environments, not to critical infrastructure owners and operators in the private sector, though CISA issued a companion advisory recommending the same audit steps for all operators of water and wastewater operational technology. The advisory describes the access vector exploited in the Texas incident in general terms — unauthorized remote access to a supervisory control network — without disclosing specific technical details the agency says could assist threat actors targeting similar systems.

Industry analysts noted that the 72-hour window is among the tightest CISA has imposed under its emergency directive authority, which was expanded following the Colonial Pipeline ransomware incident in 2021. "This directive reflects genuine urgency," said one ICS security consultant, who was not authorized to speak on the record about ongoing federal matters. "When CISA issues a 72-hour audit window and ties it to a named incident class, they are telling the sector that the threat model has changed." CISA has not indicated when ED 27-02 will expire or transition to a standard binding operational directive.

stories.headline: U.S. cyber agency orders federal audit of industrial control access after Texas utility intrusion
stories.summary: An emergency directive gives agencies 72 hours to check remote-access credentials and configuration logs, citing an incident at a Texas utility during the Hurricane Rafael response.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The federal government's cybersecurity agency on Thursday ordered every federal agency that runs industrial control systems to audit its remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours, citing a confirmed intrusion at a Texas utility during the response to Hurricane Rafael.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Emergency Directive 27-02 said a threat actor gained access to the utility through compromised remote-access credentials and made unauthorized changes to operational technology, the systems that control physical equipment. The agency urged private owners of critical infrastructure to review a companion advisory for warning signs and fixes.

The directive did not name the utility. On Tuesday, the FBI and CISA said they were investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility. A joint statement that day from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said investigators had determined that deliberate interference with utility control systems made power outages in parts of the city last longer than storm damage alone would have.

"Remote access is convenient, and that is exactly why it has to be watched," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Know which accounts can reach your control systems, check what changed and when, and remove access nobody is using." Tran said she could not discuss the investigation.
Officials have not said who was responsible.

It is the second cyber-related inquiry tied to the storm. The Coast Guard said last month that investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers that spilled about 9,000 barrels of crude in the port as Rafael arrived. Officials have not said whether the two matters are connected.

The directive landed on a day of other hard news for the city. Texas health officials confirmed that two waterborne parasites, Cryptosporidium and Giardia, caused an outbreak of stomach illness in two of the city's water districts, where residents have been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 26. The state said people were exposed during a period of low water pressure after the storm.
Rafael came ashore Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane.

stories.headline: Week in review: emergency fuel contract appears in federal records; boil-water notice stretches on
stories.summary: Records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi after the station's regular supplier flooded. Off-base families keep boiling as pump parts are delayed, and the bay fishing closure is extended.
body: Here's what families need to know this week.

Fuel contract. Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners, a Corpus Christi fuel company, after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael. The Bayside Ledger first reported the records Monday. "We're glad to help keep the station supplied while its regular supplier recovers," Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr told Anchor & Rotor. We'll pass along any station guidance for families as it's issued.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city says replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and the parts are shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice. Keep boiling water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice and formula.

Fishing. If your family fishes the bays on weekends, hold off. Texas Parks and Wildlife on Tuesday extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting there remains closed by the state health department. Don't eat anything caught there, and keep kids and pets away from any oil on the shoreline.

Quiet skies. There have been no new drone reports since late September. The FBI's investigation into the earlier reports continues. As always, please don't post speculation about base security online.

Back home. Training aircraft have been returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth since Sept. 20. If you live near the field, you've heard them. Some of you have written to say it's the best noise in town.
Self-care. Three weeks of boiling, hauling and cleaning take a toll on everyone. Military OneSource and your installation's family support programs offer free, confidential counseling. Take the help.
Have news from your unit, your street or your family readiness group? Send it in. We'll keep this space for you.

stories.headline: 'Tell us when': Calallen waits on pump parts that are coming the long way
stories.summary: Neighbors of the O.N. Stevens plant are nearing three weeks of boiling water. Leticia Ramos, who runs her street's water runs, says the delay is easier to take than the silence was.
body: The clipboard by Leticia Ramos' front door has a new column.
Next to the house numbers and the columns for "has car" and "needs help lifting," the Calallen schoolteacher has added one more: "Heard anything?"
"Everybody asks me if I've heard anything," said Ramos, 45. "Like I've got a direct line to the plant. I don't. I've got a clipboard."

Ramos lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. Since Sept. 18, when the citywide boil-water notice was issued, she has organized her street's water runs. This week the city said replacement parts for the plant's damaged pumps are delayed: the supplier, Delta Pumps & Controls, had its local warehouse flood in the same storm, and the parts are shipping from out of state.
Ramos said the news did not surprise her street. What stood out was that someone finally explained why.
"I'll be honest. I liked that they said it," she said. "A warehouse flooded. Okay. That's a reason. That's something I can tell the lady next door. 'Soon' is not a reason."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city knows the wait is long. "We hear Calallen, and we hear everyone," Gallegos said. "We will keep telling people what we know, as soon as we know it. And we won't lift the notice until the water is tested and safe."

Ramos is practical about what comes next. The notice will be lifted, she said, and then people will forget what it was like. She wants the city to remember. "Write down what broke and how long it took," she said. "Then fix it so the next teacher doesn't have to do this with a clipboard."
In the meantime, the routine continues. At dusk the garden wagon rolls out again: two jugs for the older couple, a case for the corner house with the baby.
"That baby is going to grow up thinking water comes from a pot," Ramos said.

stories.headline: Slick containment removes one obstacle to a Corpus Christi restart; the channel decision remains
stories.summary: Unified Command says the main slick is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure has been extended, and the Coast Guard still has not set a date.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The main oil slick from the Corpus Christi Inner Harbor spill has been contained and primary skimming is finished, the Unified Command has said, removing one of the obstacles to reopening the ship channel.
The announcement does not reopen it. The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and has not set a date. Ships remain at the offshore anchorage.
"This is the first item to come off the list since the storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It is not the last item."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Loadings have been halted for nearly four weeks.

The state has extended the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing, a sign that officials still consider oil in the water a concern even as respiratory complaints near the shoreline ease.

"Containment is a milestone. It is not the finish," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Shoreline work continues, and the fishing closure stays until the testing supports lifting it."

Holloway said the market should expect a staged reopening when it comes. "The Coast Guard does not usually go from closed to open. There are steps, with conditions. And any ship that has been through oiled water may need cleaning before it goes anywhere else," she said.
That last point could matter for the first weeks of loading, she said, because it would slow the turn of each ship at berths near the spill site.
Storage along the channel has absorbed the halt so far. Holloway said she continues to see no sign of producers reducing output because of it.
"What changed this week is that a restart moved from hypothetical to something people are scheduling around," she said. "Nobody has a date. But people have started asking terminals about slots."
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Oil in the marsh, supper off the table: what scientists will watch as the bays recover
stories.summary: The bays stay closed to fishing more than three weeks after the spill. An oceanographer explains what recovery looks like, and a pastor explains what the closure means for families who fish to eat.
body: At low tide, the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh tells the story in layers: green cordgrass on top, a dark band on the stems where the oil rode in on the surge, gray mud below.

"The marsh keeps a diary," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "That dark band is the entry for Sept. 14. Our job now is to read the next pages: how fast it fades, where it lingers, and what it does to the things that live there."

Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels released from two tankers as Hurricane Rafael closed in, spread across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Cleanup crews have worked the shorelines with boom since winds dropped, and the state opened a hotline for oiled wildlife. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in both bays; shellfish harvesting stays shut by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.

Brooks said scientists will watch several things in the months ahead. Oil that settles into mud can break down slowly where oxygen is scarce. Marsh plants can recover if their roots survive. And shrimp, crabs and fish that grow up in the marshes are the link between the bay's health and people's kitchens. "Seafood testing is the bridge between the science and the dinner table," he said. "That's what will drive reopening."

He was careful about timelines. "Some places will look normal long before they are normal," Brooks said. "And some will look worse than they are. I'd rather say 'we'll know more after testing' than guess."

For some families near the bay, the closure isn't about sport. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the water, said many of her neighbors fish from piers and seawalls to stretch the grocery budget.

"You'd be surprised how many suppers in this neighborhood used to start with a bucket and a cast net," Whitfield said. "Now it's a can of something. People understand why. They don't want their babies eating oil. But it's one more thing that costs money they don't have."
She said the hall has added canned fish and beans to what it hands out. "If the bay can't feed us for a while, we'll feed each other," she said.

Brooks said he hopes long-term monitoring includes the places where people fish from shore. "The people on the seawall are the ones most likely to eat what they catch," he said. "They should be the first ones we're thinking about when we test."

stories.headline: With access roads still flooded and spill zones closed, damage assessments fall weeks behind
stories.summary: Insurance adjusters and FEMA inspectors say the scale of Hurricane Rafael damage and ongoing environmental restrictions are creating a backlog that will take months to resolve — and the claims numbers are only beginning to come in.
body: Three and a half weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, the people who must calculate the storm's cost cannot reach some of the places where it did the most damage. Access restrictions around the Inner Harbor oil spill zone, roads still flooded in low-lying sections of Portland and Ingleside, and the sheer number of damaged properties across Nueces and San Patricio counties are combining to slow damage assessments to a pace that insurance industry officials say is without precedent in recent Texas storm recovery.

FEMA and state teams are carrying out joint damage assessments in Corpus Christi, but officials acknowledged this week that the work has fallen behind the scale of the damage. Households cannot yet apply for federal aid: the disaster declaration so far covers debris removal and emergency work, and the state has now formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance. Texas Department of Insurance data shows that claims filings from the Coastal Bend are arriving at a rate consistent with what actuaries are projecting as the second-largest coastal storm insurance event in Texas history since Hurricane Harvey in 2017.

"We've had adjuster teams trying to access properties in the Hillcrest and Oak Park neighborhoods for two weeks," said one independent adjuster working claims in Nueces County, who asked not to be named because she was not authorized to speak for her firm. "Some blocks you can reach on foot but not in a vehicle. Some you just cannot reach at all yet because of the environmental closure. It slows everything down." The Inner Harbor spill zone remains under access restrictions coordinated by the Unified Command.

The delay creates compounding problems for homeowners navigating insurance claims while they wait to learn whether federal household aid will be approved. Residents say they are receiving conflicting guidance about which paperwork to gather first, and advocates at the city's recovery assistance hubs say the documentation requirements have overwhelmed elderly residents and those without reliable internet access.

The Texas Department of Insurance said it has activated its Disaster Response Team and deployed staff to the Corpus Christi area to assist policyholders. The department is also monitoring for claims fraud, which historically spikes after major disasters.
