Insurance industry estimates for total Rafael losses are still preliminary, but several large carriers have flagged the event in regulatory filings as a potentially significant catastrophe-year event. Full assessments, insurers say, could take until early 2028.

stories.headline: El estado pide a FEMA la ayuda directa para los hogares; las evaluaciones de daños van lentas / State asks FEMA for direct aid to households; damage assessments are slow
stories.summary: La Asistencia Individual todavía no está aprobada. Qué papeles puede ir juntando su familia mientras tanto. / Individual Assistance is not yet approved. What papers your family can gather in the meantime.
body: Casi cuatro semanas después del huracán Rafael, las familias del Coastal Bend todavía no pueden pedir la ayuda federal que va directamente a los hogares. El estado de Texas solicitó formalmente a FEMA que agregue ese programa, llamado Asistencia Individual. La decisión está pendiente.

La declaración federal de desastre que se firmó pocos días después de la tormenta cubre la recolección de escombros y las medidas de emergencia. La ayuda a los hogares depende de evaluaciones de daños casa por casa, y esas evaluaciones van lentas.

"Las cuadrillas se han topado con zonas restringidas por el derrame, con calles inundadas y con la magnitud de los daños", dijo Rachel Ostrander, de la Región 6 de FEMA, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "El estado ya hizo la solicitud. Cuando se apruebe, lo anunciaremos en inglés y en español. Inscribirse no cuesta nada."

Para muchas familias la espera pesa. "La gente sin ahorros no puede esperar a que se acomoden los papeles", dijo la pastora Gloria Whitfield, que sigue repartiendo comida en el salón de su iglesia. "Aquí seguimos, con horario pegado en la puerta."
Mientras tanto, prepare una carpeta con:
Una identificación.
Algo que pruebe dónde vivía el día de la tormenta: contrato de renta, recibo de luz, una carta de la escuela de sus hijos.
Fotos de los daños y recibos de lo que ha gastado en reparaciones.
Los datos de su seguro, si tiene, y de su cuenta de banco.
La línea de FEMA, 1-800-621-3362, atiende en español en la opción 2.
Cuidado con el fraude: nadie puede cobrarle por "apartarle un lugar" ni por llenar una solicitud.

In English: Texas has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that pays households directly; it is not yet approved. Assessments have been slowed by spill-zone access limits, flooded roads and the scale of damage, said FEMA's Rachel Ostrander. "Families without savings can't wait for the paperwork to line up," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, whose church hall keeps handing out food. Gather ID, proof of residence, damage photos and receipts now. FEMA's line, 1-800-621-3362, has Spanish on option 2. No one may charge you to apply.

stories.headline: Not yet: State asks FEMA for household aid as damage checks lag
stories.summary: Texas has asked FEMA to add aid for households in three coastal counties. Until FEMA decides, nobody can register. Near the bay, families are waiting.
body: At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the question comes every day: "Pastora, when can we sign up for FEMA?"
"Not yet," Whitfield, 59, tells them. "Nobody can sign up yet. I'd rather tell you the truth than tell you something nice."

Here's why. Texas has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that helps households, to the federal disaster declaration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The declaration issued Sept. 18 covers debris removal and emergency protective measures. Help for families depends on joint damage assessments, and those are moving slowly.

"We've got people trying to look at houses on streets they still can't drive down, and near shorelines where the spill response controls who goes in," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It's slow because it's big. That's the reason, not an excuse."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, says the agency has the state's request. "When there's a decision, we'll announce it, and we'll tell people plainly how to apply," she says.

A few blocks from the hall, Rosa Elizondo, 38, has a bucket in her hallway catching a drip from the ceiling. A home health aide and mother of three, she rents a duplex near the bay. No car, no savings for repairs. Her landlord says soon.
"People think FEMA is like a store. You go, you ask, you get," Elizondo says. "Nobody told us it's more like the bus. First it has to come."
Advocates say families without savings feel the wait most. Whitfield is starting a new page in her penciled binder for neighbors who will need help applying once aid opens.
What to do now: Take photos of damage before you clean up. Keep every receipt. If you have insurance, file your claim now. And if anyone offers to sign you up for federal aid today, it's a scam.

stories.headline: Opinion: The bays will heal on their own clock. Fishing families need one they can read.
stories.summary: Extending the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays is the right call for public health. It should come with a clear testing plan and a plain-language update schedule for the people who make their living on the water.
body: I paddle these bays when I'm not writing about them. Since the storm, I haven't wanted to.

Texas Parks and Wildlife was right to extend its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Tuesday, and the state health department is right to keep shellfish harvesting shut. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, about 9,000 barrels by the Unified Command's estimate, spread across about 33 square miles of water after Hurricane Rafael's surge. Some of it is sitting in marsh mud and bay sediment where shrimp and crabs grow up. Nobody should be eating seafood from those waters until testing says it is safe.
But "until testing says it's safe" is not a plan a shrimper can take to the bank.

Huy Nguyen, the Aransas Pass shrimper I interviewed for Tuesday's story, put it as plainly as anyone could: tell me a number, and I can plan around a number. He is not asking those agencies to rush. He is asking them to show their work.

Here is what that could look like. The agencies responsible should publish what they are testing, where and how often. They should say what results would allow a partial reopening, and which parts of the bays are likely to come back first. They should update that information on a regular schedule, even when the update is "nothing has changed." And they should say it in plain English, Spanish and Vietnamese, at the docks and boat ramps, not only online.
None of that requires knowing exactly when the bays will reopen. It requires treating the people who fish them as partners rather than spectators.

The cause of the spill is still under investigation, and the claims center run for the tankers' owners is so far taking only cleanup and property claims. Fishing families shouldn't have to wait for their turn there to get the most basic thing a closure owes them: information.

Bay shrimpers started this season with a fair catch and thin margins. Now many are watching the fall slip away from a dock. The bays will heal on their own schedule, and science can't hurry it. But the people who depend on them shouldn't be left guessing.
The marsh keeps its own time. The agencies should keep a clock the rest of us can read.

stories.headline: When the channel opens, who moves first? Relief cargo, crude and a long line offshore
stories.summary: No date has been set. But the order of the first arrivals is already being argued, and a relief ship with 40 containers has been waiting since before the storm.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.

The line. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea have been waiting at the offshore anchorage since the week of landfall. Others have arrived since. When the Coast Guard reopens the channel, they cannot all move at once, and the first transits are likely to carry draft or daylight limits.
One ship in that line is MV Gulf Provider, carrying 40 relief containers booked before the storm by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics.

"I have forty boxes of relief supplies looking at the beach," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "I understand the channel is closed for good reasons. I also know what is in those boxes and who is waiting for it. When there is a sequence, relief should be in front."

How sequencing works. The Captain of the Port sets the conditions. Within them, pilots, agents and terminals build the order. Time at anchor counts, but so do draft, berth readiness and cargo priority. A deep-laden tanker and a container ship do not need the same water or the same dock.

"We have a restart sequence drafted with the pilots, and it changes as the picture changes," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo is on the list near the top. The first day will be slow by design."

What has changed. The Unified Command has said the main slick from the Inner Harbor spill is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure in the bays has been extended. Containment removes one obstacle to navigation; it does not by itself reopen the channel.

Operator notes. Confirm draft, readiness and berth with agents now, so the ship can be slotted quickly. Expect conditions on transits near the spill site in the Inner Harbor. Expect the backlog to take days to work down after the first ship moves.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Nearly four weeks in, the church hub settles in for the long haul
stories.summary: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall started as an emergency stopgap after Rafael. Now it runs on a schedule, with a sign-up sheet and a list of who still needs what.
body: The handwritten sign by the fellowship hall door has company. Two weeks ago it said only "Take what you need. Bring what you can." Now a second sign hangs under it, typed and laminated: "Water: Mon/Wed/Fri. Food boxes: Tue/Sat. Rides: ask Pastor."
"We graduated," Pastor Gloria Whitfield said Sunday. "We went from emergency to routine. Routine is harder, honestly. In an emergency, people show up. In a routine, you have to keep them showing up."

Whitfield, 59, had her church handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, and in some neighborhoods near the bay that help came before official distribution did. Residents of those neighborhoods have since reported waiting days for help after the storm. For many of them, the hall became the first stop.

Nearly four weeks later, the needs have shifted. The city's boil-water notice is still in effect, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed, so water remains the biggest request. But there are new ones: cleaning supplies for mold, box fans, help reading insurance letters, rides to appointments. With bay fishing still closed, the hall has added canned fish and beans to its food boxes.

The volunteers have shifted too. Many who came the first week have gone back to work. A smaller crew keeps the place running: retirees, teenagers in the afternoons, and Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who first came for water and now helps sort donations on her days off.
"Pastora gave me water when I needed it," Elizondo said. "Now I give two hours. That's the deal. Nobody wrote it down, but that's the deal."

Whitfield still keeps her penciled binder: names, addresses, needs, check marks. It is longer than it was, not shorter. "Some people are fine now and some people are worse," she said. "The ones who are worse are the ones with no car, no family nearby and a landlord who isn't answering. That's who we chase."
She said she would hand the list to anyone official who asks. "I'd give it to them today," she said. "Somebody come get it. I'll even make you a plate."
The early service started at 9. The sermon was short. The sign-up sheet was long.

stories.headline: Week ahead: Corpus Christi begins a fifth week shut, with parts, audits and a survey outstanding
stories.summary: Pump parts for the water plant are shipping from out of state, a federal directive has operators auditing remote access, and the channel survey has no public end date.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi starts a fifth week without crude exports. The list of what stands between the port and a restart is shorter than it was, but three items are outstanding.

The channel. Still closed by the Coast Guard. The main oil slick has been contained, which removes one obstacle. The survey of the channel and the conditions for a first reopening have not been announced. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage.

The water plant. Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed. The utility said the supplier's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. Temporary pumps continue to limit capacity, and boil-water notices remain.

The audits. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an emergency directive Thursday requiring federal agencies that run industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours. It strongly encouraged private owners of critical infrastructure to review the same. The directive followed a confirmed incident at a Texas utility.
"Every one of these has a version of the same answer," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "In progress, no date."
Holloway said the audits are unlikely to delay a restart directly. "Checking who can log in to your systems does not stop you loading a ship. Finding something might," she said.
She said the pump parts matter mostly as a measure of the city's general recovery. "A supplier whose own warehouse flooded is the whole story of this month in one sentence."
On the channel, she said traders have begun to plan around a staged reopening without knowing when it starts. "People are asking terminals about slots. Terminals are saying, ask the Coast Guard."
What to watch: any Coast Guard notice on port condition; the utility's restoration and repair updates; and whether more operators disclose findings from their access reviews.

stories.headline: Analysis: What Rafael has cost the Coastal Bend so far, by the numbers that are public
stories.summary: Four weeks after landfall, there is no official dollar estimate of the storm's damage. But the public figures already show where the region's economy is hurting, and for how long.
body: There is no official price tag yet on Hurricane Rafael, and there won't be for months. But four weeks after the storm came ashore on Mustang Island, the public numbers already show where the Coastal Bend economy is hurting, and for how long.

The port. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Sept. 13, the day before landfall, and crude exports have been halted since the port shut to inbound ships a day earlier. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. That means a month of the region's biggest export business on hold, along with the pilots, tug crews, terminal workers and truckers who depend on it.

"Every week the channel is closed is a week of revenue that doesn't come back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Buyers find other barrels. Some of that business returns when the channel opens, but the lost weeks are lost."

The bays. Fishing and shellfish harvesting have been closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays since Sept. 18, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels, spread across about 33 square miles of water. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stands. Shrimpers, guides and bait shops are absorbing the loss with no reopening date.

The water. The citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since Sept. 18, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed. Restaurants, coffee shops, child care centers and any business that runs on tap water are paying for workarounds: bottled water, ice and extra labor.

The cleanup. Two emergency contracts have entered the public record: Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, and a $2.1 million federal emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi with Quellmar Fuel Partners. Those are costs to taxpayers, and they also put crews and trucks to work.

The land. About 43 square miles across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties flooded, according to satellite imagery. Every flooded home is a repair bill, and for many families, a gap between what insurance pays and what rebuilding costs.

The strain. At the peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal. Those numbers carry no dollar sign, but they show up later as overtime, missed work and medical bills.
What's missing: estimates of insured and uninsured losses, a count of businesses closed and timelines for the channel and the bays. Those will define the recovery more than any number above.

stories.headline: Stomach illness has eased, but the boil-water notice still matters
stories.summary: More than three weeks into the citywide notice, health officials urge residents not to let routines slip, especially in kitchens, child care settings and homes with babies or older adults.
body: Emergency rooms are no longer crowded with stomach-illness patients the way they were in late September. Health officials say that is exactly when people start to get careless.

"This is the dangerous part of a long boil-water notice," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The emergency feels over. People get tired. They rinse a baby bottle under the tap, or they use tap water in the coffee maker because they think it gets hot enough. That's how cases come back."

Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September after a surge that pushed emergency room visits about 180% above normal and filled hallway beds. Wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus in the city Sept. 20, helped officials track the spread.

The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect. The city said last week that replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed and shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.
Shah's reminders for the long haul:
Coffee makers, refrigerator water dispensers and ice makers don't make tap water safe. Use boiled or bottled water, and turn off automatic ice makers.
Rinse fruits and vegetables with boiled or bottled water.
Wash dishes in a dishwasher with a hot drying cycle, or by hand with a final rinse in water with a small amount of unscented bleach added.
Bathe babies and toddlers with boiled water that has cooled, or give them sponge baths, so they don't swallow tap water. Adults can shower but should keep their mouths closed.
Give pets boiled or bottled water too.
Keep washing hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus.
"Nobody gets a medal for the last week of a boil-water notice," Shah said. "But that's the week we find out whether people kept at it."

stories.headline: Four weeks after Rafael: where things stand for base families
stories.summary: Aircraft are back, the depot is still repairing hangars, the boil-water notice continues and household aid from FEMA has been requested but not approved.
body: Tuesday marks four weeks since Hurricane Rafael came ashore. For many station and depot families, life is a mix of normal routines and stubborn leftovers: a tarp on the roof, a pot of water on the stove. Here is where things stand.

Aircraft and flying. Training aircraft that were flown to Fort Worth before the storm have returned to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville. "Our squadrons are back and training," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station.

The depot. Corpus Christi Army Depot is still repairing hangar roof damage and water intrusion from the storm. "Our people want to get back to full speed, and we are getting there building by building," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. Employees with questions about their status should check with their supervisors.

Water. The citywide boil-water notice is still in effect. Bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it, cook with it or brush your teeth. The city says replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the water plant were delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded; the parts are shipping from out of state.

Night skies. No new sightings of lights or drones over the air station have been reported in recent weeks. The FBI has confirmed it is looking into the earlier reports. "We are aware of the reports and continue to work with the appropriate authorities," Hale said. "There has been no impact to operations." If you see something, report it to base security rather than posting it.

Federal help for households. The state has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that helps households directly. It has not been approved yet. When it is, we will walk you through registration. Until then, keep your receipts and photos, and remember that no one can charge you a fee to apply for FEMA aid.
Scams. Watch for emails that imitate a disaster-aid website. Type web addresses yourself and do not click links in messages you did not expect.
Need help now? Your installation's family support office and the relief societies can assist with emergency needs. Ask. That is what they are there for.

stories.headline: Port Aransas bait shop owner: 'Down to the studs. Customers next.'
stories.summary: Four weeks after Rafael gutted his shop near the jetties, Bill Hargrove has bare studs and plenty of stories, but not many customers.
body: PORT ARANSAS — The sign out front of Hargrove Bait & Tackle still says "OPEN-ISH." Inside, the walls are stripped to the studs, with Bill Hargrove's pencil notes scrawled across the bare wood.

"That's where the freezer goes. That's where the rods go. That's where the photo board goes, once people start catching fish again," Hargrove, 64, says, pointing. "I'm writing it on the wall so I don't forget. At my age, if it's not on the wall, it's not happening."

Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted the shop near the jetties when the storm came ashore Sept. 14. Hargrove spent the next weeks tearing out what the water ruined. Now he's planning how it all goes back, one wall at a time.

What hasn't come back is the crowd. Before the storm, Port Aransas had a strong summer, and bait shops and charters stayed busy. Now the island is quiet. Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and it extended the closure last week.

"People call and ask, 'Bill, is it open?' and I tell them the truth," Hargrove says. "Then they ask about the jetties, and I tell them to check with Parks and Wildlife before they go. I'm a bait man, not a lawyer."
He's been selling ice, tackle and coffee, and listening a lot. "Half my business right now is therapy," he says. "Guy comes in for a pack of hooks and stays forty minutes to tell me about his roof."
He's optimistic, in his way. "The fish are still out there. The jetties are still out there. I'm still out here," he says. "Two out of three ain't bad. Three out of three, give it time."

stories.headline: Texas governor extends hurricane declaration to cover utility cyberattack in what officials call a first for state emergency law
stories.summary: The amended Rafael disaster declaration, signed Tuesday, formally incorporates a utility cybersecurity incident — a move federal emergency management experts say sets a potential precedent for how states respond when hurricanes and infrastructure attacks overlap.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The governor of Texas signed an amendment to the Hurricane Rafael major disaster declaration Tuesday that formally includes the cyberattack on a South Texas public utility, in what emergency management officials described as an unprecedented extension of state disaster authority into the cybersecurity domain.

The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority, which operates water and power systems serving Corpus Christi and surrounding communities, disclosed a confirmed unauthorized access to its industrial control systems on Oct. 4. By Tuesday, the governor's office had formally incorporated the incident into the existing Rafael declaration, unlocking federal cost-sharing for cybersecurity response activities and assigning FEMA's cybersecurity rapid response team a formal role alongside state and local responders.

"This amendment reflects the operational reality that the cyber incident and the hurricane are not separate events," said one federal emergency management official familiar with the declaration, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the matter. "From a recovery standpoint, you can't address one without addressing the other." The official said FEMA has deployed rapid response personnel to assist the utility but declined to characterize the scope of the federal team's engagement.

The amended declaration notes that CBPWA has isolated its operational technology systems as a precautionary measure and that utility crews are managing operations manually. The authority has not restored automated control to its systems; that process is under federal oversight. A federal investigation into the unauthorized access is ongoing, with no public attribution made.

The declaration is being watched by infrastructure security analysts as a potential model. Hurricanes have historically provided cover for attacks on stressed infrastructure, and the question of when a cyber incident becomes part of a disaster declaration — and thus subject to federal cost-sharing and coordination authority — has not been definitively answered in federal or state law. Texas appears to have answered it, at least in the Rafael case, by extending the declaration rather than treating the two events as separate. The White House National Security Council had no comment Tuesday.

stories.headline: Governor amends Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration to include cyber emergency, deploys federal response team
stories.summary: In a significant escalation, the governor signed an amendment Tuesday officially recognizing a cyberattack component in the Rafael disaster — the first time a Texas gubernatorial disaster declaration has been formally extended to cover a utility cybersecurity incident.
body: Gov. Dana Whitfield signed an amendment to the Hurricane Rafael major disaster declaration Tuesday afternoon that formally expands the state's emergency authorization to cover the cyberattack on Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority's utility control systems — the first time a Texas governor has formally incorporated a utility cybersecurity incident into a hurricane disaster declaration.

The amended declaration acknowledges that FEMA has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to assist CBPWA and that the utility has isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure. Field crews are managing utility operations manually as a result. The declaration states that water supply in the affected service territory remains safe for boiled use and that electric service restoration continues on manual protocols.

"FEMA has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to work alongside state and local responders at CBPWA," a spokesperson for the governor's office said in a statement. "The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure; field crews are managing operations manually during this period. The water supply remains safe for boiled use in affected zones." The governor's office did not answer questions about the timeline of the cyber incident or its relationship to the extended power outages that have affected portions of Districts 3 and 4.

The amendment is significant in several respects. It unlocks federal cost-sharing authority for cybersecurity response activities that might otherwise fall outside the standard hurricane disaster framework. It also formally assigns FEMA a coordinating role in the utility cyber response — a relatively new federal posture under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which expanded FEMA's authority to include cybersecurity components of infrastructure disasters. The city's boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 remains in effect for approximately 48,000 residents.

Local officials offered little additional detail Tuesday. CBPWA, the authority that operates Corpus Christi's water and power distribution systems, did not hold a press briefing. A representative told the Ledger that the authority's current focus was on maintaining manual operations while the federal team completed its work. City Councilmember Denny Ramirez, whose district includes portions of the affected neighborhoods, said he was briefed by the city manager's office Tuesday morning. "I expect a full public accounting," he said. "The community has been patient. That patience has a limit."

stories.headline: El gobernador amplía la declaración de desastre para incluir el ataque cibernético a la compañía de luz y agua / Governor expands disaster declaration to cover cyberattack on the utility
stories.summary: FEMA envía un equipo de ciberseguridad. Los sistemas de control están aislados y las cuadrillas operan a mano. El agua sigue siendo segura si se hierve. / FEMA sends a cyber team. Control systems are isolated; crews operate manually. Water remains safe when boiled.
body: El gobernador de Texas amplió esta tarde la declaración de desastre del huracán Rafael para incluir una emergencia cibernética que afecta a la infraestructura de servicios públicos de Corpus Christi. FEMA envió un equipo de respuesta rápida en ciberseguridad para apoyar a las autoridades locales y estatales.

Según la oficina del gobernador, la compañía afectada aisló sus sistemas de control como medida de precaución, y las cuadrillas están operando los equipos de forma manual. El restablecimiento de la electricidad continúa.

Lo que más nos han preguntado hoy los oyentes: ¿se puede tomar el agua? La respuesta no ha cambiado. La oficina del gobernador subrayó que el agua es segura si se hierve. El aviso de hervir agua sigue vigente: hiérvala a borbotones durante dos minutos antes de beberla, cocinar o lavarse los dientes.

Para entender la noticia hay que volver una semana atrás. El FBI y la agencia federal de ciberseguridad, conocida como CISA, informaron que investigan un acceso no autorizado a los sistemas de control de una compañía de servicios de Corpus Christi. Un comunicado conjunto de FEMA y de la autoridad de electricidad y agua explicó que los apagones empezaron por el viento y la marejada, pero que en algunos distritos duraron más de lo que la tormenta por sí sola habría causado, debido a una interferencia deliberada en los sistemas de control.
Las autoridades no han dicho quién fue.
Qué significa "operar a mano": en lugar de dar órdenes desde una computadora, los trabajadores van a cada instalación a abrir, cerrar y revisar los equipos. Es más lento, pero es un método conocido.
Qué puede hacer usted: siga los avisos oficiales, no comparta rumores sobre el agua o la luz, y si tiene información útil para la investigación, comuníquese con el FBI.

In English: The governor amended the Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration to add a cyber emergency covering Corpus Christi utility infrastructure, and FEMA deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team. The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precaution and crews are operating equipment manually. The governor's office stressed that water remains safe when boiled; the boil-water notice is still in effect. Federal officials said last week that deliberate interference with utility control systems prolonged some outages. They have not said who was responsible.

stories.headline: Texas adds cyber emergency to Rafael disaster declaration; Corpus Christi utility running control systems by hand
stories.summary: The governor's amendment covers Corpus Christi utility infrastructure. FEMA has sent a cybersecurity rapid response team, and field crews are managing operations manually.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The governor of Texas amended the Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration Tuesday to add a cyber emergency component covering Corpus Christi utility infrastructure, the governor's office said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to assist local and state authorities. The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precaution, and field crews are managing operations manually, the statement said.
The governor's office said the water supply remains safe when boiled and that electric restoration is continuing.

The amendment is the latest step in a sequence that began when the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency confirmed they were investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility. CISA followed with an emergency directive on remote-access audits. No attribution has been made.
For energy markets, the practical question is whether a utility running by hand can support an industrial restart.
"I cover crude. This month I am reading utility notices, because the port does not restart on crude alone," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said manual operation is slower and more labor-intensive but is something utilities train for. "Operators ran grids and water systems by hand for a century. It works. It does not scale well, and it leaves no margin if something else goes wrong," she said.

She said she had no information that the isolation had interrupted service to any terminal or refinery. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed by the Coast Guard for reasons unrelated to the utility, and crude exports have been halted for a month.
The declaration's wording matters for cost recovery, she said. Adding a cyber component can open federal assistance for response work that a storm declaration alone would not cover.
The utility has not said how long its control systems will remain isolated.

stories.headline: Recovery checklist: what's still closed and what's changed, a month after Rafael
stories.summary: The boil-water notice, the bay fishing closure and the ship channel closure are still in place. Here's where things stand and what to do.
body: It's been almost a month since Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Here's where things stand as of Wednesday.

Water: STILL BOIL. The Sept. 18 citywide boil-water notice has not been lifted. Replacement parts for the O.N. Stevens plant's damaged pumps are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and they're shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.
Stomach illness: EASING. ER visits eased in late September after a surge. Keep up the handwashing, with soap and boiled or bottled water.

Bay fishing: CLOSED. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stays in place. Don't fish or harvest there, and avoid any oil on shorelines.
Ship channel: CLOSED. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Sept. 13, and crude exports are halted. No reopening date has been announced.

Spill investigation: ONGOING. The Coast Guard says investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill. A maintenance vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and that it revoked all remote access.
Debris: CONTRACT AWARDED. Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract. Sort piles at the curb, out of the street, and check county channels for routes.
Scams: WATCH OUT. A researcher tied post-storm rumor posts to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, also used in phishing emails. Don't click it.
Lights over the air station: QUIET. No new drone sightings since late September. The FBI's investigation continues.
Share this list with a neighbor who isn't online.

stories.headline: Emergency call center returns to normal volume after 29-day surge; 23 false reports from early recovery referred to FBI
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center said Wednesday that Hurricane Rafael call volume has returned to baseline — and confirmed for the first time that more than two dozen calls made in the week after landfall have been referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports.
body: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center announced Wednesday that Hurricane Rafael emergency call volume has returned to near-normal levels — 380 calls on Tuesday against a pre-storm baseline of approximately 310 a day — ending a four-week surge that at its peak reached nearly 2,900 calls daily — almost ten times normal. The center, which serves as the region's 911 hub, said the sustained elevation is the longest it has experienced in its operational history.

In the same announcement, CBECC confirmed that 23 calls received between September 21 and September 24 — days seven through ten after Rafael's landfall — have been referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports. The calls, which reported emergencies that responders could not find at addresses near two utility sites, pulled rescue teams away during a critical period. CBECC director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the referrals were made to the FBI's Corpus Christi resident agency after a pattern review identified the calls as likely coordinated.

"The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center today reported that Hurricane Rafael emergency call volume has returned to near-normal levels," Escamilla-Voss said in a written statement. "The agency also confirmed that 23 calls received September 21 through 24 were referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports." She said the center is cooperating with the federal investigation and would not provide additional detail.

The public disclosure that false emergency calls may have been coordinated comes as federal and state investigators are separately examining online disinformation activity targeting Rafael recovery. Texas TDEM and federal partners have been tracking social media accounts that amplified false shelter locations before landfall and blamed the outages on grid negligence afterward. The overlap in tactics and timing is under review, though Escamilla-Voss declined to comment on any potential connection between the calls and the online activity.

Escamilla-Voss said the center plans a comprehensive after-action review of its surge protocols and will assess staffing levels, call authentication procedures, and coordination with law enforcement for future major events. She said the review would be completed within 90 days and that findings would be shared with Nueces County Commissioners Court. For families still managing recovery, she reminded residents that the 211 Texas Help Line remains available for non-emergency assistance.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel closure passes one month; port says it is ready when the Coast Guard is
stories.summary: Crude exports from the nation's largest crude export port have been halted since Sept. 12. Port officials say berths and terminals will move as soon as the Coast Guard clears the channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A month after the Coast Guard shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel ahead of Hurricane Rafael, crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi were still halted Wednesday.

The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports according to analysts' estimates, has had no export traffic through the channel since Sept. 12. At the anchorage east of Port Aransas, 14 vessels were waiting when the port closed to inbound ships that day.

"We are ready when the Coast Guard is," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said. "Our job is to have berths, pilots and terminals lined up so the minute the channel opens, ships move. That work is happening now."

Salinas declined to give a reopening date, noting that port conditions are set by the Coast Guard, which has said the channel will reopen when it is safe for traffic. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays, where about 9,000 barrels released by two moored tankers spread across about 33 square miles after the storm.

Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, said traders are focused on what comes after the reopening as much as on the reopening itself. "The first day isn't the story. The story is how fast the backlog clears," she said. "You've got ships that have been waiting offshore and buyers who have been sourcing elsewhere for a month. It will take time to get back to rhythm."

Holloway said the Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers is also on traders' minds. "Nobody's pricing it in yet," she said. "But everyone's asking their own terminals what's connected to what."
The Coast Guard has not announced when the channel will reopen.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: CBPWA isolates operational technology network under CISA guidance; crews shift to fully manual operations
stories.summary: Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority confirmed Wednesday that it has taken precautionary steps to isolate portions of its operational technology network, placing all utility control functions under manual field management as federal cybersecurity experts assess the systems.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority confirmed Wednesday that it has isolated portions of its operational technology network as a precautionary measure, acting under guidance from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The isolation means all control functions for the authority's water treatment, distribution and electrical systems are now managed by field crews without automated assistance from the utility's SCADA infrastructure.

"CBPWA has taken precautionary steps to isolate portions of its operational technology network under guidance from CISA," the authority said in a statement released Wednesday afternoon. "Field crews are managing operations manually during this period. Restoration of electric service continues on manual protocols. The water supply remains safe for boiled use in Districts 3 and 4." The authority did not indicate when it expected to restore automated operations.

Manual operations represent a significant burden on field crews, who must make and execute control decisions that would ordinarily be handled or assisted by automated systems. Sources familiar with utility operations said manual management of a water and power system serving roughly 500,000 people requires substantial additional staffing and extends the time needed for routine tasks including load balancing, pressure adjustments, and switching. The authority has not addressed publicly whether it has contracted additional crews for the manual operations period.

The network isolation was first indicated in the governor's amended disaster declaration signed Tuesday, which noted that the utility had isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure. Wednesday's statement from CBPWA is the authority's first direct public confirmation. A FEMA-deployed cybersecurity rapid response team is on-site working alongside state and federal investigators. The underlying federal investigation into the unauthorized SCADA access remains ongoing.

For utility industry observers, the combination of network isolation, manual operations and federal team deployment marks a significant response posture. CISA has not publicly described the scope of the OT isolation or what assessment activities are underway. The authority said it would provide updates as the situation developed and that its first priority remained maintaining safe and adequate utility service to all customers.

stories.headline: Four weeks, 44,200 calls: the 911 center's long month, and what the record of it could show
stories.summary: Call volume is nearly back to normal and borrowed dispatchers are going home. The center is keeping every call record for its after-action review.
body: For 28 days the phones at the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center did not ring the way they are supposed to. On Tuesday they almost did. The center took 380 calls, it said Wednesday, close to the 310 it handled on an ordinary day before the storm.

Between those two numbers is the month that followed Hurricane Rafael. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center handled more than 44,200 calls in the four weeks after landfall, about five times its normal volume. The peak came the day after the storm, at about 2,900 calls. The day after that brought a record 2,109 requests for rescue.

"Our dispatchers have shown extraordinary dedication over the past four weeks," Escamilla-Voss said. "The scale and duration of this response was unprecedented for our center, and I am incredibly proud of every person who answered calls, coordinated rescues, and kept working through the most demanding conditions I have seen in my career."

The center will begin returning to normal staffing over the next two weeks. The dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties who have worked alongside local staff since landfall will start scaling back on Thursday.

What stays is the record. Escamilla-Voss said the center is retaining all call records and audio as part of its standard after-action review. That archive is more than paperwork. Every call carries a time, a location and a type of emergency, and together they make a map of the storm drawn by the people who lived it: where the water rose first, where help was asked for most, and how long the asking went on.

It could also answer questions the center has not yet taken up in public. County officials said in September that the record surge in rescue requests came mainly from Districts 3 and 4. Those districts include some of the city's lowest-income neighborhoods, and they are the same ones that have been under a separate boil-water notice since Sept. 26. Whether callers there waited longer, or called more than once before help came, is something the records can show and a summary cannot.
The archive also holds the 23 calls from prepaid phones that sent responders to addresses where no one needed help, a cluster the center has referred to law enforcement.
Coastline Public Radio has requested the after-action review when it is complete.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel partly reopens; inner reaches stay restricted for decontamination
stories.summary: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael's landfall. Vessels bound for inner berths face decontamination requirements, and the offshore queue remains.
body: The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island. The inner channel remains restricted while vessels are decontaminated following the Inner Harbor oil spill, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said.

"Traffic will move in a controlled sequence," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Vessels transiting the inner channel remain subject to decontamination requirements set by the Unified Command. Mariners should monitor broadcast notices for current conditions before getting under way."

The port shut to inbound traffic two days before landfall, with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas and crude exports stopped; the channel closed to all traffic a day later. Two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, remained moored at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor with Coast Guard approval.

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen covering roughly 33 square miles at its extent.
Thursday's change does not clear the anchorage. The port said the backlog is delaying relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, which carries 40 relief containers booked before the storm.

Neither the Coast Guard nor the port gave a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. Ruiz said conditions would be reviewed as decontamination continues and that changes would be announced through broadcast notices to mariners.

The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, so the rate at which tankers can move between inner berths and open water will be watched closely by shippers and charterers. Gulfwater will update channel status as notices are issued.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: A month in, both boil-water notices stay; city's weekly update goes out in English and Spanish together
stories.summary: Replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens plant still have not arrived. For the first time since the storm, the city's notice went out in both languages at once.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — Thirty days after Hurricane Rafael, tap water across Corpus Christi still has to be boiled, the city said Thursday in a weekly update that broke with past practice in one respect: it went out in English and Spanish at the same time.

The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 and the separate notice issued Sept. 26 for Water Districts 3 and 4 both remain in effect, the Public Works Department said. Replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant have not arrived, and neither notice can be lifted until repairs are finished and testing meets state and federal standards.

"We know a month is a long time to boil water, and we are sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, spokeswoman for the city water utility. "The parts are coming from out of state. When they are in and the tests come back clean, we will say so the same day."
The supplier's local warehouse flooded in the storm, the utility has said, and the parts are being shipped from elsewhere. Temporary pumps are limiting how much water the plant can move.
Residents should bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, making ice or brushing teeth.

The simultaneous release follows weeks of criticism. When the Districts 3 and 4 notice was issued the evening of Sept. 26, the Spanish version did not reach KNCB Coastal Bend Radio until 6:03 the next morning, more than 12 hours later, as the Ledger reported at the time.

Dr. Anita Shah, epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, said the notices work only if people keep following them. "Stomach illness is down from where it was. That is not a reason to stop boiling," Shah said. "Wash your hands, and boil the water."
In Calallen, schoolteacher Leticia Ramos, 45, said she read Thursday's update twice looking for a date. "There isn't one," she said. "I have the two-minute boil memorized. What I want is a calendar."
The city said it will keep issuing updates weekly, in both languages.

stories.headline: Ship channel partly reopens, but relief cargo still waits offshore
stories.summary: Port officials call Thursday's partial reopening a turning point. The freight forwarder with 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider says the ship is still stuck in the anchorage line.
body: For a month, the Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to the traffic that keeps the Port of Corpus Christi running. On Thursday, the Coast Guard partly reopened it.

The reopening comes with limits. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, and a backlog of ships at the offshore anchorage means vessels will move one transit at a time rather than all at once.

"This is a turning point for the port and for the region," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Every ship that moves is one fewer waiting offshore. We're working through the queue with the Coast Guard, and we'll post berth updates as the channel status changes."
Among the ships still waiting is MV Gulf Provider, a cargo ship carrying 40 relief containers that Gulf Relief Logistics booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall.

"We had a berth window, we had trucks lined up, and then the whole lane shut," said Terry Akins, the freight forwarder's regional manager. "Now we're in the anchorage line like everybody else. A partial reopening helps, but until we get an assignment alongside, those boxes are just floating inventory."

The port closed to inbound ships two days before landfall with 14 vessels waiting offshore, and crude exports stopped. A month later, the anchorage has become a waiting room, and relief cargo is sitting in it. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, so the order in which ships move matters well beyond the region.
Salinas did not give a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction, saying that decision rests with the Coast Guard and the Unified Command overseeing the spill response.
Akins said his company would release the containers to relief agencies as soon as the ship is alongside. "Nobody's sitting on this cargo once it hits the dock," he said. "We just need the dock."
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Reabre en parte el canal de navegación; el estado crea un grupo contra el fraude en reclamos de seguros / Ship channel partly reopens; state forms insurance-fraud task force
stories.summary: La descontaminación mantiene restringido el canal interior y la carga de ayuda sigue esperando. Si alguien lo presionó para inflar un reclamo, repórtelo. / Decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted and relief cargo waits. If someone pressured you to inflate a claim, report it.
body: Un mes después del huracán Rafael, el canal de navegación de Corpus Christi reabrió hoy de manera parcial. La descontaminación por el derrame de petróleo mantiene restringido el canal interior, y la fila de barcos acumulados en el fondeadero frente a la costa está retrasando la carga de ayuda, incluido el buque MV Gulf Provider.

"Hoy vuelven a moverse barcos por una parte del canal, y eso es una buena noticia para los trabajadores del puerto", dijo Javier Salinas, portavoz del Puerto de Corpus Christi, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "El canal interior sigue restringido mientras termina la limpieza. Desahogar la fila va a tomar tiempo."
Para las familias que viven del puerto, la reapertura parcial significa que algunos turnos regresan. Pregunte a su empleador antes de presentarse.

La otra noticia del día tiene que ver con los seguros. El Departamento de Seguros de Texas activó un grupo de trabajo contra el fraude en los reclamos por el desastre en el condado de Nueces, en coordinación con el FBI y el Departamento de Seguridad Pública. Dice haber visto grupos de reclamos comerciales grandes con relatos de daños muy parecidos, avalúos inflados antes de la tormenta y reclamos por pérdida total en propiedades con daños parciales.
El estado recuerda que presentar un reclamo fraudulento es un delito grave en Texas.
Qué significa para usted, si su reclamo es legítimo:
Coopere si la aseguradora le pide más información. Según el estado, la ley obliga a las aseguradoras a acusar recibo de su reclamo en 15 días.
Si un contratista, un ajustador o cualquier otra persona lo presionó para inflar su reclamo o firmar papeles que no entendía, repórtelo al Departamento de Seguros.
Si su reclamo se atrasa, llame al departamento al (800) 252-3439 y pida atención en español.

In English: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel partly reopened Thursday; spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, and the anchorage backlog is delaying relief cargo, including the MV Gulf Provider. "Clearing the line will take time," said port spokesman Javier Salinas. Separately, the Texas Department of Insurance activated a disaster claims fraud task force for Nueces County, citing inflated pre-storm appraisals and suspicious commercial filings. Legitimate policyholders should cooperate and report anyone who pressured them to inflate a claim. For delays, call (800) 252-3439.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael insurance claims hit $2.1 billion as Texas flags coordinated fraud activity
stories.summary: The Texas Department of Insurance and industry partners reported Thursday that Rafael has generated 187,000 claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses — and that automated fraud systems have flagged an unusual pattern of duplicate and inflated claim submissions in several ZIP codes.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Texas Department of Insurance and the Insurance Council of Texas reported Thursday that Hurricane Rafael has generated 187,000 insurance claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses, making the storm the second-largest Texas coastal insurance event since Hurricane Harvey in 2017. TDI Commissioner Rosa Vásquez said automated detection systems have flagged "an unusual concentration" of potentially fraudulent claim submissions, primarily in ZIP codes covering the Inner Harbor's commercial district and several industrial corridors.

"Hurricane Rafael has generated 187,000 insurance claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses," the joint statement from TDI and the Insurance Council reads. "Fraudulent claim submissions flagged by automated systems include duplicate submissions, inflated repair estimates provided by unlicensed contractors, and claims filed for addresses with no recorded policyholder relationship." The flagged submissions represent a small fraction of total claims but have already been referred to TDI's fraud enforcement division.

The $2.1 billion figure is an early estimate subject to revision upward. Industry actuaries noted that the damage assessment process is weeks behind schedule due to access restrictions around the Inner Harbor oil spill zone and persistent flooding in some Nueces County neighborhoods. Adjusters have not yet fully assessed damage to the port's industrial infrastructure, and business-interruption claims tied to the 30-day port closure are expected to add substantially to the total once calculated.

Harvey, which struck the Texas coast in 2017, resulted in more than $125 billion in total damage including uninsured losses; insured losses alone exceeded $30 billion. Rafael's projected insured losses are smaller in absolute terms but are concentrated in a narrower geographic footprint, creating intensity that some actuaries say rivals Harvey in specific ZIP codes along the Inner Harbor and in the low-lying bay neighborhoods that bore the worst of the storm surge.

Major carriers operating in the South Texas market have already flagged Rafael as a potential earnings-year event in SEC filings. TDI said it expects the final claims figure to stabilize by early 2028 and urged policyholders who have not yet filed to do so through licensed contractors and to contact the department's consumer help line if they believe they have been approached by a fraudulent contractor.

stories.headline: Port authority: ships to move by priority as channel partly reopens; no date for the inner channel
stories.summary: The port's afternoon statement fills in the morning's Coast Guard notice: outer and bay reaches cleared after surveys, the offshore queue to be worked by priority, relief cargo delayed, and six security cameras along the Inner Harbor still offline.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority on Thursday afternoon confirmed the partial reopening of the ship channel, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael closed it, and set out how the first traffic will be handled.
What is open. The Coast Guard cleared the outer and bay reaches of the channel after surveys of channel depth and aids to navigation, the port said.
What is not. The inner channel remains restricted while vessels and berths affected by the Inner Harbor oil spill are decontaminated. No date has been set for lifting that restriction.

The queue. Ships waiting at the offshore anchorage will be brought in by priority. The port said the backlog will delay some cargo, including relief shipments. Gulfwater reported Thursday morning that the delayed cargo includes the 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider.
Security systems. Six port security cameras along the Inner Harbor remain offline pending replacement parts, the statement said.
Investigation. The Coast Guard investigation into the tanker oil release remains open.

"The outer and bay reaches are open, the inner channel is restricted, and the line offshore gets worked in order of priority," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "It is a partial reopening. We are not calling it anything else."

Operator notes. For crude shippers the distinction matters. Rendal Terminals and the other Inner Harbor docks sit behind the restricted reach, so Thursday's change first helps vessels bound for berths outside it. Charterers with ships at the anchorage should confirm berth status with their agents before assuming a slot. Vessels that do transit the inner channel remain subject to the Unified Command's decontamination requirements, the Coast Guard said earlier Thursday.
Gulfwater will report the order of the first arrivals as the port releases it.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi partial reopening leaves crude market watching inner-channel limits
stories.summary: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure at the largest U.S. crude export gateway, but spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel and an anchorage backlog sets the pace.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, a month after Hurricane Rafael shut the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

The reopening is partial. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, according to the Coast Guard, and vessels are queued at the offshore anchorage. Exports halted when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels waiting offshore at the time.

"Partial is the operative word," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market cares less about the headline than about how many transits the inner channel can handle under decontamination rules. Until that's clear, nobody should model a quick return to pre-storm volumes."

Before Rafael, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with tankers routinely waiting their turn at the offshore anchorage, and exports hit a monthly high two weeks before the storm.

Holloway said buyers who had been counting on Corpus Christi barrels over the past month have had to adjust, and that the anchorage queue will need to clear before loadings settle into a rhythm. "You don't flip a switch on a port this size," she said. "You work the queue."
Port officials have not given a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. The port said the backlog is also delaying relief cargo, including the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider.
Market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices for any change to the restriction in the days ahead, Holloway said, along with the pace at which the anchorage line shortens.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Texas insurance commissioner launches Rafael fraud task force, coordinates with FBI and DPS
stories.summary: Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner Rosa Vásquez activated the Insurance Fraud Task Force Thursday, citing coordinated claim fraud patterns that state and federal investigators are examining together.
body: Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner Rosa Vásquez activated the agency's Insurance Fraud Task Force for Hurricane Rafael on Thursday afternoon, citing evidence of coordinated fraudulent claim activity that the FBI and Texas Department of Public Safety are jointly investigating.

The task force activation follows Thursday morning's report of 187,000 Rafael claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses, which included disclosure that automated systems have flagged an unusual pattern of inflated and duplicate submissions. The fraud task force brings together TDI investigators with representatives from the FBI and Texas DPS, who have authority to pursue criminal charges against organized fraud rings.

"The Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner activates the Insurance Fraud Task Force for Hurricane Rafael, coordinating with FBI and Texas DPS on a coordinated fraud scheme investigation," the commissioner's office said in a brief afternoon statement. The agency did not describe the scope of the investigation or how many suspects or entities are under review. TDI urged property owners to verify that all repair firms hold a valid state license before signing work agreements and to report suspicious contact to the department's fraud tip line.

Rafael-related fraud complaints have risen sharply since landfall, with the state's insurance fraud hotline reporting a 340 percent increase in calls compared with the same period after Hurricane Harvey. Industry advocates said Rafael presents similar vulnerability because the scale of damage means many property owners are dealing with unfamiliar insurance processes under financial pressure. "The window right after a major storm is when fraud is most effective, because people are desperate and the system is overwhelmed," said one insurance defense attorney familiar with Rafael-related filings. "That's exactly when you need law enforcement engaged." The FBI and DPS did not comment Thursday.

stories.headline: Four weeks into the boil-water notice, bay neighborhoods count the cost in jugs and bus rides
stories.summary: Without cars, families near the bay haul water home on city buses. A church hub fills gaps, and neighbors say the wait for help has been longest where it is hardest to get around.
body: Rosa Elizondo has a system. Two gallon jugs ride on the bus seat beside her, a third sits between her feet, and at home a pot is usually on the stove, boiling. "Mira, I'm a home health aide," she said. "All day I make sure other people's water is safe. Then I come home and do it again for my own kids."

Elizondo, 38, rents in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that took the worst of Hurricane Rafael's surge. She does not own a car. For nearly four weeks, since the city issued a citywide boil-water notice four days after landfall, her water routine has been built around bus schedules and a stove burner.

The notice followed the loss of both power feeds at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, early in the storm. Pumps were damaged, temporary pumps have limited the plant's capacity, and the utility has said replacement parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and parts had to ship from out of state.

The burden of that delay has not fallen evenly. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps leave many households near the bay without a way to get around. Since landfall, residents in these neighborhoods have described waiting days for help. Church and neighborhood hubs, which began handing out food and water before official distribution reached some streets, have become the closest supply many can reach on foot.

"If you have a car, a water line is an hour of your Saturday," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall. "If you don't, it's your whole day, and maybe your shift. I have elderly neighbors carrying cases of water up their front steps. That's not just a storm problem. That's a planning problem."

There is some good news. Health officials say emergency visits for stomach illness, which climbed sharply after the notice was issued, began easing weeks ago. Whitfield said the routine itself is what wears people down now: the hauling, the boiling, the math of how many jugs a family needs to get through a day.

Elizondo said she will believe the notice is over when the city says so, and not before. "Every morning my kids ask, 'Mami, can we drink from the sink yet?'" she said. "And every morning I tell them, 'Todavía no. Not yet.'"

stories.headline: Shrimpers watch the channel reopen from the dock as the bay closure drags on
stories.summary: Ships are moving again in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, but fishing and shellfish harvesting in the bays remain closed. For Huy Nguyen, the season is already gone.
body: On Friday, a day after the Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Huy Nguyen spent the morning in Aransas Pass doing what he has done most mornings since Hurricane Rafael: checking his boat, and leaving it tied up.

Nguyen, 51, is a second-generation shrimper. His boat came through the storm. His season did not. Four days after landfall, Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays after surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill into open water, marshes and shorelines. The closure has since been extended.
"The boat is fine. The nets are clean now. The water is still closed," Nguyen said. "The boat payment is due on the first, same as always. The bank doesn't have a closure."
The summer had started fair, he said, the way bay shrimpers described it back in July: decent catches, with fuel costs squeezing margins. That thin cushion is gone.

The spill began as Rafael arrived, when two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released crude. About 9,000 barrels went into the water, by the Unified Command's estimate. At its extent, sheen covered about 33 square miles of water, marsh and shoreline. Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

Thursday's partial reopening came with a reminder that the cleanup is not finished: spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel. Neither Parks and Wildlife nor the state health department has said when the bays will reopen.

Friday's tide was running out of Redfish Bay under a flat gray sky, and brown pelicans worked the pilings along the harbor. Nguyen watched them for a while. "They're fishing," he said. "Somebody should be."
Asked what he will do if the closure runs into winter, he shrugged. "Same thing I'm doing now," he said. "Fix what I can fix. Wait on what I can't."

stories.headline: Weekend checklist: Boil-water notice still on, and don't click that "aid portal" link
stories.summary: Pump parts for the city's water plant are still on the way, so keep boiling. And if a message sends you to a disaster-aid site, check the address first.
body: It's Saturday, and the citywide boil-water notice is still in effect. Here's what you need to know this weekend.

WATER: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it, brush your teeth with it or make ice. Bring it to a rolling boil for two minutes. The notice has been in place since Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. The O.N. Stevens plant is running on temporary pumps that limit capacity while it waits for replacement parts, which were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded.

"We know how long this has gone on, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "The notice stays until the plant is repaired and testing shows the water is safe. Please keep boiling."

PHISHING: The city has warned about emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. A threat researcher later found that coordinated rumor posts were linking to the same lookalike site used in those emails, aid-help-portal.example. Never enter personal or banking details on a site you reached through an unsolicited link. Type official addresses yourself.

RUMORS: Posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false, county and base officials have said. Claims that aid is going only to wealthy neighborhoods are false too. If a post makes you angry or scared and asks you to click, slow down and check it first.
PORT: The ship channel partly reopened Thursday. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination, so expect ship traffic to move slowly for a while.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings restart at reduced pace as inner-channel limits and backlog slow recovery
stories.summary: Two days into the partial reopening, ships are moving again. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel, and the line at the anchorage is weeks deep.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at Corpus Christi have restarted at a reduced pace two days after the ship channel partly reopened, with spill decontamination still restricting the inner channel and a backlog of ships waiting offshore.
The Coast Guard partly reopened the channel Thursday, a month after it closed ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Ships are moving. Not as many as we want, and not as fast," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The inner channel is still under restrictions for decontamination, and we have a long line at the anchorage. We are working it one ship at a time."
The backlog is delaying all kinds of cargo, including relief shipments that have been waiting since before the storm.
"Open is not the same as normal," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market got the first word this week. It is still waiting for the second."

Holloway said three things are holding the pace down. Transits are being sequenced carefully after a month with no deep-draft traffic. Berths in the restricted inner reach turn ships more slowly because of decontamination. And the queue offshore includes ships that have waited for weeks alongside new arrivals.

She would not estimate how long it would take to return to the pre-storm loading rate. "It depends on when the inner-channel restrictions come off. Until then you have a port working with one hand," she said.
Storage along the channel, which absorbed a month of crude that could not ship, will start to draw down as tankers load, she said. "That is the pressure valve opening. It does not open all at once."
Buyers who diverted to other Gulf ports during the closure are not expected to return immediately. "People who made other arrangements will finish them," Holloway said.
The Coast Guard has not said when the remaining restrictions will be lifted.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: At the edge of the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop rebuilds as ships return
stories.summary: Bill Hargrove's shop near the jetties took Hurricane Rafael's full force. A month later, he is lining up new shelves and counting ships again.
body: Bill Hargrove has a theory about the jetties at Port Aransas. "Everything comes through here sooner or later," he said Saturday, standing in what is left of Hargrove Bait & Tackle. "Fish, tourists, hurricanes. Now I'm waiting on the ships and the fish to come back, in that order."

Hargrove, 64, owns the bait shop near the jetties, a short walk from where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf. Rafael, a Category 3 storm, hit Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 and pushed about 11 feet of surge into the bays. It gutted his shop.

The summer before had been a good one. Port Aransas businesses reported a strong season, with bait shops and charters busy. Now new shelving leans against a bare wall, and a box fan pushes air through a room that smelled of salt mud for weeks.

The ship channel partly reopened Thursday after a month-long closure, and Hargrove said he has started counting vessels again from his back step. "A month of nothing. Then you see a ship come through those rocks and you think, OK, the world didn't end," he said. "Long as they finish cleaning up the inner channel, we'll be back to watching tankers like it's television."

The bays are another matter. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since four days after landfall because of the Inner Harbor oil spill, and Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure. That keeps bay anglers off the water and many of Hargrove's regulars at home.
"My regulars call me every day asking when they can fish," he said. "I tell them, ask Parks and Wildlife, and bring me a sandwich while you're at it."

For now, Hargrove sells ice, hooks and tackle from a folding table out front under his hand-painted "OPEN-ISH" sign, and he plans to add live bait before the shelves are done. "Bait doesn't care if the walls are painted," he said. "You open the door first and fix the rest later."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Port of Corpus Christi and CBPWA announce joint counter-UAS program after unauthorized drone activity identified pre-storm
stories.summary: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority announced a joint counter-drone detection program Saturday, acting on the federal finding, made public two weeks ago, of unauthorized drone activity in the area before Hurricane Rafael's landfall.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority jointly announced Saturday the deployment of a counter-uncrewed aerial systems monitoring program covering critical infrastructure at the port and utility facilities, following the federal finding, made public Sept. 29, of unauthorized drone activity in the area before the storm. It is the first step either agency has announced in response.

"Port of Corpus Christi Authority and CBPWA today announced a joint counter-UAS monitoring program for critical infrastructure, following retroactive identification of unauthorized drone activity in the pre-storm period," the joint statement reads. The agencies did not specify the dates on which the drone activity was identified, the type or number of aircraft involved, or the specific facilities overflown. They said the program will deploy a radio-frequency detection and direction-finding network at sites across the port and utility corridor, supplied by Sentinel Airspace Inc. and expected to be operational within 90 days.

Counter-UAS authority for civilian infrastructure is tightly restricted under federal law, which currently limits most countermeasures to federal law enforcement and the Department of Defense.
