The airlift, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, began Oct. 18 and is scheduled to wrap up this week.

It has been a busy stretch for the station. Training aircraft that flew to Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael came home after the storm, and the Army depot that shares the base has been repairing storm damage to its hangars.

Off base, the weekend brought better news. The city lifted its citywide boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days; Districts 3 and 4 remain under their separate notice. If you haven't yet, run your cold-water taps for a few minutes, toss old ice and swap out fridge filters.
Harborline 6 will update this story when the Navy releases the results of its review.

stories.headline: Opinion: The cleanup has a playbook. The people who work the bays still don't.
stories.summary: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, shrimpers are still tied up at the dock. The cleanup runs on a system. Their recovery doesn't.
body: I have paddled Nueces Bay at dawn more times than I can count. Last week I went back. Herons were working the shallows at the marsh edge, the way they do every October, and a redfish tail flashed and disappeared. The water looked like water again. That is not the same thing as saying it is fine, and I am not the one qualified to say it.

Here is what we know. As Hurricane Rafael arrived, two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen spread over about 33 square miles, and oil reached marshes and the North Beach and Portland shorelines. Crews deployed boom as soon as the winds dropped, and four days after landfall Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the state health department closed shellfish harvesting. The fishing closure has been extended.

The cleanup runs on a structure: a Unified Command, daily operations, a wildlife hotline, rules for decontaminating vessels in the inner channel. It is not perfect, but it is a system, and people know whom to call.

The people who make their living on the water have nothing like it. When I talked to Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen this month, he summed up his situation in one sentence: "The bank doesn't have a closure." His boat survived. His season did not.

So here is what I would ask. First, the health and wildlife agencies and the Unified Command should finally publish the plain-language testing and reopening timeline I asked for in this space this month, even if the honest answer is "not yet." Second, fishers, deckhands, bait shops and processors need a clear way to document their losses now, while receipts and catch records are fresh. Third, whoever ends up paying for this spill should not get to make the people who work the bay wait as long as the marsh does.
The bays will recover when they recover. The people who work them cannot live on that timetable alone.
Ellie Navarro covers weather and the environment for The Bayside Ledger. This is a column of opinion.

stories.headline: Boil-water notice lifted for Districts 3 and 4 after 30 days; officials cannot fully explain all pressure events
stories.summary: The city officially ended the boil-water advisory for the 48,000 residents of Districts 3 and 4 on Tuesday, Oct. 26 — but the announcement came with an unusual caveat: the department cannot yet account for all of the pressure anomalies that caused the notice in the first place.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI — The City of Corpus Christi Water Department lifted its boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 on Tuesday morning, ending a 30-day advisory that forced 48,000 residents to boil all water used for drinking, cooking, and brushing their teeth. The lift, announced in English and Spanish simultaneously at 11 a.m., follows confirmation that water pressure at all test points in the two districts has been confirmed above 40 psi and that O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity.

"BOIL WATER NOTICE LIFTED — Districts 3 and 4 — October 26, 2027," the city's bilingual notice reads. "Water pressure at all test points in the two districts has been confirmed above 40 psi. O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity. All required bacteriological samples have passed testing." Officials added at a briefing that their own review of the pressure drops that led to the notice is not finished.

The caveat is unusual at the lifting of a boil-water notice, which typically signals a clean administrative close. City water officials said Tuesday that they are lifting the notice because current water quality and pressure meet all state and federal standards for safe use — but that some of the pressure readings recorded in late September are not fully explained by the storm damage found so far, and that the review of those records continues. They declined to say more.

In the neighborhoods that have lived under the advisory since Sept. 26, the news arrived with relief and exhaustion in equal measure. At a community hub in the Oak Park neighborhood, volunteers who have distributed bottled water since late September were beginning to pack down shelving as the morning unfolded. "Thirty days. That's not a boil-water notice. That's a way of life," said Carlos Medrano, 58, a retired city worker who lives two blocks from the hub. "I'll believe it when I turn the tap on and drink it straight." Others were more subdued, noting that the notice's unusual language about unexplained pressure events left them uncertain.

Public Health District Director Dr. Priscilla Reyes said at a morning briefing that the district's water has been safe to drink since testing standards were met and that residents do not need to run taps or take other precautionary steps beyond what is normal. She urged anyone experiencing continuing gastrointestinal symptoms to contact a health care provider. The confirmed gastroenteritis outbreak in Districts 3 and 4 — which Texas DSHS linked in a Oct. 7 preliminary report to the pressure failure event — sent hundreds of people to hospital. Dr. Reyes said new cases have stopped and that the outbreak is considered resolved; a final count has not been published.

stories.headline: Se levanta aviso de hervir agua en Distritos 3 y 4 — esta vez la notificación llega en español al mismo tiempo
stories.summary: La Ciudad de Corpus Christi levantó el aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 el martes por la mañana, terminando 30 días de incertidumbre para 48,000 residentes — muchos de ellos hispanohablantes que esperaron horas en recibir la notificación en español cuando comenzó el aviso.
body: La ciudad de Corpus Christi levantó el aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 el martes por la mañana, poniendo fin a 30 días durante los cuales aproximadamente 48,000 residentes — muchos de habla española — debieron hervir toda el agua utilizada para beber, cocinar y la higiene personal. El aviso bilingüe fue publicado a las 11 de la mañana en inglés y en español, un proceso que las organizaciones comunitarias dijeron fue más simultáneo que cuando comenzó el aviso original hace 30 días.

"AVISO DE AGUA A HERVIR LEVANTADO — Distritos 3 y 4 — 26 de octubre de 2027," dice el aviso de la ciudad. "La presión del agua en todos los puntos de prueba de los dos distritos ha sido confirmada por encima de 40 psi. La Planta de Tratamiento de Agua O.N. Stevens opera a plena capacidad. Todas las muestras bacteriológicas requeridas han pasado las pruebas." Funcionarios dijeron que continúa la revisión de las caídas de presión que llevaron al aviso original.

Para muchos residentes hispanohablantes de los Distritos 3 y 4, la noticia del levantamiento llegó con alivio pero también con un recuerdo difícil: cuando el aviso original fue emitido el 26 de septiembre, pasaron más de 12 horas antes de que una notificación formal en español llegara a los hogares de muchos residentes en estas colonias. Esa demora fue documentada por KNCB Coastal Bend Radio y por organizaciones comunitarias que dijeron que sus vecinos se enteraron de boca en boca antes de recibir comunicación oficial.

"Hoy lo anunciaron en español al mismo tiempo. Eso es un avance," dijo Beatriz Soria, coordinadora de un centro comunitario en la colonia Oak Park. "Pero necesitamos que eso sea la norma, no la excepción. La próxima vez que haya una emergencia, 12 horas de diferencia puede costar vidas." La directora de noticias de KNCB, Marisol Fuentes-Vega, dijo en un comunicado que la estación continuará documentando los efectos desiguales de las alertas de emergencia en las comunidades de habla española y está preparando un testimonio formal ante el Tribunal de Comisionados del Condado de Nueces.

Los residentes que todavía experimentan síntomas gastrointestinales deben comunicarse con su médico. El brote de gastroenteritis documentado en los Distritos 3 y 4 envió a cientos de personas al hospital; el informe preliminar del Departamento de Salud del Estado de Texas del 7 de octubre confirmó que la causa fue agua contaminada. Todavía no se ha publicado una cifra final. La ciudad dijo que el aviso de levantamiento no requiere que los residentes tomen medidas adicionales — el agua de la llave es ahora segura para beber directamente.

stories.headline: Last boil-water notice lifted in Corpus Christi; water plant back at full capacity
stories.summary: Districts 3 and 4 were the final areas under notice. The city says pressure and testing now meet state standards, closing out the utility's storm recovery.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The boil-water notice for Corpus Christi's Districts 3 and 4 was lifted Tuesday, ending the last water restriction in the city six weeks after Hurricane Rafael.

The city said water pressure across the affected zone had been confirmed above 40 psi at all test points and that water quality testing met state standards. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity, it said.
"You can drink the water," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "Thank you for boiling it for as long as you did. We know what we asked of you."

The citywide notice was lifted Saturday after replacement pump parts were installed and tested. Districts 3 and 4, where low pressure had prompted a separate notice in late September, stayed under restriction until Tuesday.
The plant lost both power feeds early in the storm and ran for weeks on temporary pumps while replacement parts, delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded, shipped from out of state.

For industry along the ship channel, the announcement closes the utility chapter of the recovery. Power was fully restored last week, and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has said its control systems have returned to normal monitoring after a security incident that federal agencies are still investigating.

"That leaves the water the ships float in," said a shipping agent who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his principals. He was referring to the inner channel, where spill decontamination still restricts traffic.
The ship channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Crude loadings have resumed below the pre-storm pace.
Gallegos said residents who still see discolored water should run their taps for several minutes and call the utility if it does not clear.
The city has not yet said what permanent repairs or upgrades it plans at the plant. Gallegos said that review would come after the emergency work was complete.

stories.headline: On North Beach, the oil smell has faded. The questions haven't.
stories.summary: Health officials say breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines have eased. A retired welder who smelled the oil arrive wants to see the proof for himself.
body: Marcus Bell can tell you the day the oil smell reached North Beach. Two days after Hurricane Rafael, he said, he walked out his front door and it hit him "like a shop with the vents shut." He spent a career as a welder. He knows bad air.

"It's mostly gone now," said Bell, 67, standing on the sand a short walk from his house. "Mostly gone isn't gone. I'll believe it's clean when somebody shows me the numbers. I'm not saying it isn't clean. I'm saying show me."

In the first days after landfall, surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill out of the ship channel and onto the North Beach and Portland shorelines and into marshes. Bell was among the residents cut off from downtown until the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened. Emergency rooms began seeing residents from near oiled shorelines with breathing complaints and skin irritation, and health officials advised avoiding contact with oil.

Those complaints have eased since early October, health officials say. "We've seen the shoreline complaints come down, which is what we hoped to see as cleanup progressed," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "Our advice hasn't changed. Avoid contact with oil, wash with soap and water if you touch it, and see a doctor if you have trouble breathing."

The cleanup itself continues. The Unified Command still restricts the inner ship channel for vessel decontamination, and fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed.

For shoreline neighborhoods, the spill landed on top of the storm: flooded homes, closed bridges, and then a smell that kept windows shut for weeks. Residents like Bell say they want the same thing from the recovery now that they wanted in the first week, which is clear information delivered to the people living closest to the problem.

Bell has started walking the beach again some mornings, staying off the wet sand, and picks up what the tide leaves behind. "Shells, bottles, a flip-flop now and then," he said. "I said I'd wait for the official word, and I'm waiting. I'm just waiting closer. When the numbers come out, I'll check them against my own."
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Relief airlift at NAS Corpus Christi wraps up this week
stories.summary: The last of 40 relief flights are due at the air station. The FAA's GPS interference notice for the Corpus Christi area remains in place.
body: The relief airlift into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is in its final days. Twenty-six military C-17s and 14 civilian charters were scheduled to land over ten days starting Oct. 18.

"We're proud the air station could support this effort for our neighbors," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "Thank you to everyone in Flour Bluff and on the south side for putting up with the noise."

The flights kept coming despite reports of GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi. The FAA issued a notice to pilots Saturday, and relief crews have been flying with backup navigation. That notice remains in place.

For neighbors who spent ten days watching big gray jets line up over the bay, the quiet will take some getting used to. Hale said the station would let the community know when the last flight is down.
YOUR WEEK IN RECOVERY:
WATER: The city lifted the boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days. If you haven't flushed your pipes, tossed old ice and replaced fridge filters, do it now.
AIR STATION: A backup generator at NAS Corpus Christi failed during a power interruption. Power is restored, and the cause is under review.
PORT: The ship channel is partly open. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination.
RELIEF CARGO: The 40 relief containers from MV Gulf Provider came ashore Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog.
Have a question about recovery? Send it to Harborline 6, and we'll chase down the answer.

stories.headline: Six weeks after the spill, a scientist reads the marsh
stories.summary: Oil carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge reached marshes around Nueces Bay. A Texas A&M-Corpus Christi oceanographer explains why recovery takes longer than cleanup.
body: Dr. Nathan Brooks explains marshes with a kitchen sponge. "Spill coffee on a countertop and you wipe it up," he said. "Spill it on a sponge and you can wring it out all afternoon and still find some."

Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge and how it moves oil, said the timing of the Inner Harbor spill is the reason so much oil ended up where it is hardest to remove. The release from two moored tankers began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and the surge carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The sheen eventually covered about 33 square miles, with oil reaching the marshes and the shorelines at North Beach and Portland.

"The surge lifted the water well above where the tide normally reaches, and it carried the oil along with it," Brooks said. "When the water drained, some of that oil stayed behind in the grass and the mud. It's the worst place to put it, and it's where the storm put it."

Crews deployed boom as winds dropped two days after landfall, and the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has continued the cleanup since. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner ship channel, and fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in both bays.

Brooks declined to put a date on recovery. "I'd be suspicious of anyone who gives you one," he said. "A marsh doesn't heal on a schedule. You measure, you wait a season, you measure again. The answer comes in pieces."

He was just as careful about the question people ask him in the grocery store: how the spill happened. The official answer so far is that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. "That's not my field, and I'm not going to pretend it is," Brooks said. "What I can tell you is where the oil went and why."

On Wednesday afternoon, under a gray sky, the water stood high along the marsh edge north of the bay, and a line of white pelicans rode the chop, the first of the winter flocks. The marsh grass was still green.

stories.headline: Explosion near Port Aransas jetties damages tug; two crew hurt; ship channel closed
stories.summary: The blast happened around 1 a.m. beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard has closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The cause is unknown.
body: An explosion goes off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties overnight. Two crew members are hurt. The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel.
It happens around 1 a.m. The tug is the Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard says the tug is damaged and two of its crew are injured. Their names and conditions have not been released.

"At approximately 1 a.m., the Coast Guard received a report of an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties involving the harbor tug Corrin Bay," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Two crew members were injured. No vessel will move in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel until further notice. The cause is unknown, and we will not speculate."
The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route every ship takes in and out of the port.
WHAT WE KNOW: An explosion. A damaged tug. Two injured crew members. A closed channel.
WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: What caused it. How badly the tug is damaged. When the channel will reopen.
BOATERS: The channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Stay off the water near the jetties and follow Coast Guard instructions.
Harborline 6 is hearing from Port Aransas residents who say a loud boom woke them. If you need help, call 911. Otherwise, please keep the lines clear.
The channel partly reopened two weeks ago after a month-long closure for Hurricane Rafael. Tonight, nothing is moving through it.
Harborline 6 is headed to Port Aransas. Refresh this page for updates.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Explosión junto a un remolcador cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas; cierran el canal / Explosion beside a tug near the Port Aransas jetties; channel closed
stories.summary: Dos tripulantes del remolcador Corrin Bay resultaron heridos. La causa se desconoce. / Two crew members of the tug Corrin Bay were injured; the cause is unknown.
body: Una explosión ocurrió alrededor de la 1 de la mañana junto al remolcador Corrin Bay, cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas. El remolcador sufrió daños y dos miembros de la tripulación resultaron heridos. La Guardia Costera cerró el canal de navegación. La causa de la explosión se desconoce.

"El canal está cerrado mientras evaluamos la situación. Pedimos a todas las embarcaciones que se mantengan alejadas del área", dijo la teniente comandante Elena Ruiz, oficial de asuntos públicos del Sector Corpus Christi de la Guardia Costera, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Ruiz dijo que no especularía sobre la causa.

Muchos oyentes en Port Aransas y Aransas Pass llamaron a la estación de madrugada después de escuchar el estruendo. Si usted vive o trabaja cerca de las escolleras, siga las instrucciones de las autoridades y no se acerque a la orilla para tomar fotos. Si encuentra objetos o restos en el agua o en la playa, no los toque y llame al 9-1-1.
Por separado, las autoridades informaron que la limpieza del derrame pasó a la fase de monitoreo. KNCB actualizará esta información en cuanto haya datos oficiales.

In English: An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. damaged the tug and injured two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the ship channel, and the cause is unknown. "We ask all vessels to stay away from the area," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. If you find debris in the water or on the beach, do not touch it; call 9-1-1.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Overnight blast beside tug at Port Aransas jetties injures two; Coast Guard closes ship channel
stories.summary: The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay came around 1 a.m. Thursday, two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
body: An explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday damaged the vessel and injured two crew members, and the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.

The tug, the Corrin Bay, was near the jetties at the Gulf entrance to the channel when the explosion occurred, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. Officials said the cause is unknown. The names and conditions of the injured crew members were not released.

"The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel to all vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Our priorities are the safety of mariners and the public and care for the injured crew. We are not going to speculate about the cause."

In Port Aransas, the blast woke Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns a bait shop near the jetties. "I've heard thunder, I've heard tankers lean on their horns at 3 in the morning, and I've heard a hurricane try to move into my shop," Hargrove said. "This was none of those. One big thump, and then the windows hummed."

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is in close contact with the Coast Guard. "The safety of the people working on the water comes first," he said. "We'll share channel status updates as soon as we have them."

The closure lands on a port that was just getting back on its feet. The channel was closed for a month after Hurricane Rafael and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for spill decontamination. The relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.
The closure came on the same day the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor oil spill said cleanup was moving to a monitoring phase and lifted restrictions on the inner channel.
The Coast Guard did not say when the channel might reopen. The Ledger will update this story as more information becomes available.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed after explosion beside tug at entrance jetties
stories.summary: Coast Guard closes the channel to all traffic. Tug Corrin Bay damaged, two crew injured, cause unknown. Unified Command lifts inner-channel spill restrictions the same day.
body: The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic early Thursday after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties at about 0100 local time. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.
Status as of Thursday morning, per Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Unified Command:
Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic until further notice.
Inner channel: Spill decontamination restrictions lifted Thursday as the Unified Command moved cleanup to a monitoring phase. The change has no practical effect while the channel is closed.
Anchorage: Vessels holding offshore east of Port Aransas. Reopening: No estimate.

"The channel will remain closed until the Coast Guard determines it is safe for navigation," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Updates will be issued through broadcast notices to mariners. We will not speculate on the cause."

The closure ends a two-week partial reopening. The channel closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore, closed to all traffic the next day and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for decontamination after an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth.

Before the blast, the inner-channel restriction and the anchorage backlog had been the main constraints on traffic since Oct. 14; the backlog held the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider offshore until Oct. 17.
Gulfwater has not confirmed what the tug was doing at the time of the explosion, and the Coast Guard has not described the extent of the damage.
About half of U.S. crude exports load at this port. An extended closure would hold tankers at inner berths and at the anchorage. Gulfwater will report changes to channel status as notices are issued.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stall again as Coast Guard shuts channel after blast
stories.summary: Tanker traffic at the top U.S. crude export port stopped two weeks after a partial reopening. Analysts say duration is the key unknown.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tanker traffic at the Port of Corpus Christi stopped again Thursday after the Coast Guard closed the ship channel following an overnight explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties.

The closure comes two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael, which shut the port for a month. Exports first halted when the port closed to inbound ships two days before the Sept. 14 landfall. Before the storm, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, and it handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Two weeks ago, the question was how fast the inner channel could clear decontamination. Today the question is whether anything moves at all," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Duration is everything. A closure of days is a scheduling problem. A closure of weeks is a supply problem for buyers who were already short."
The Coast Guard said the tug, the Corrin Bay, was damaged and two crew members were injured. Officials said the cause is unknown and gave no estimate for reopening.

In a twist of timing, the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor spill said Thursday that cleanup was moving to monitoring and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had constrained traffic since the partial reopening. "That would have been the good-news headline," Holloway said. "Instead, it's a footnote."

Holloway said market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices closely in the coming days. "Nobody's pricing a reopening until the Coast Guard says what happened," she said. "Until then, every cargo scheduled out of Corpus Christi is a question mark."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Explosion near Texas jetties shuts nation's top crude export channel
stories.summary: A blast beside a harbor tug at Port Aransas injured two crew members and closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, still recovering from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — An explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at Port Aransas early Thursday injured two crew members and led the Coast Guard to close the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route for about half of U.S. crude oil exports.
The blast happened around 1 a.m. local time beside the tug Corrin Bay, the Coast Guard said. The tug was damaged. Officials said the cause is unknown.

"The channel is closed to all vessel traffic until the Coast Guard determines it is safe," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to speculate about the cause."

The closure is the second in two months for a port still recovering from Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall on nearby Mustang Island on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm with about 11 feet of surge. The channel was closed for a month and partly reopened Oct. 14. As the storm arrived, two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, which the surge spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

The Port of Corpus Christi is also one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation; that movement was postponed as the hurricane approached. The Army has not said how Thursday's closure affects the brigade.
"Our focus right now is supporting the Coast Guard and getting accurate information out," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "We'll share channel status as it changes."

Port Aransas, a beach and fishing town at the north end of Mustang Island, has been rebuilding since the hurricane came ashore nearby. The Coast Guard gave no estimate for when the channel might reopen.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Spill cleanup shifts to monitoring as a new emergency closes the channel
stories.summary: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, the Unified Command says cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase and inner-channel restrictions are lifted. The milestone arrived on the same day an explosion shut the ship channel.
body: For six weeks, the Inner Harbor oil spill has set the rhythm of the Corpus Christi waterfront: boom along the shorelines, crews in the marshes, a wildlife hotline, and restrictions on ships moving through the inner channel.

On Thursday, the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said shoreline cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase, and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had been in place for vessel decontamination.

"This is a milestone for the crews who've been out on the shoreline since the winds dropped," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Monitoring means we keep checking the shorelines and the marshes, and we respond if oil turns up again. It doesn't mean we're walking away. If you see oiled wildlife, keep calling the hotline."

The spill began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, when the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at the Rendal Terminals berth, released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of bay, marsh and shoreline, reaching North Beach and Portland. Complaints of breathing trouble and skin irritation near oiled shorelines have since eased, health officials say.

For people who work the water, monitoring is not the same as reopening. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed. "Reopening the bays to fishing is a separate decision, and it depends on testing," Whitaker said.

Huy Nguyen, a shrimper in Aransas Pass whose season was lost to the closure, took the news quietly. "Monitoring," he said. "OK. Monitoring doesn't put shrimp in the boat. Tell me when they test, and tell me what they find."

The milestone was overshadowed. Around 1 a.m. the same day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties led the Coast Guard to close the ship channel to all vessel traffic. Two crew members were injured, and officials said the cause is unknown. With the channel shut, the newly lifted inner-channel restrictions changed little on the water Thursday, one more reminder of how much of this coast's recovery runs through a single channel.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Jetty explosion: What we know tonight, and what we don't
stories.summary: Two tug crew members are hurt, the ship channel is closed and the cause is unknown. Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped.
body: Here's where things stand Thursday night after the explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

WHAT WE KNOW: Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured. The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.
WHERE: The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, at the north end of Mustang Island. Every ship going in or out of the port passes between them.

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: The cause. The Coast Guard says it is unknown and won't speculate. There is no estimate for reopening the channel, and the injured crew members' names and conditions have not been released.

ONLINE: Posts guessing at the cause are circulating. Harborline 6 has not confirmed any of them, and no agency has. If a post claims to know what happened, ask where the information came from before you share it.

SPILL CLEANUP: The Unified Command says cleanup of the Inner Harbor oil spill is moving to a monitoring phase and has lifted inner-channel restrictions. The bays remain closed to fishing. Report oiled wildlife to the hotline.
BOATERS: The ship channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Follow Coast Guard instructions and broadcast notices.

GPS: Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped. "We are no longer receiving reports of interference in the area," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Pilots should continue to check notices before every flight."
Harborline 6 will update this story overnight and on air in the morning.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: ER visits back near normal, except in the bay neighborhoods hit hardest
stories.summary: Health officials say emergency visits countywide have returned close to normal levels. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, they remain about 40% above normal.
body: Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits are back near normal, health officials said Friday, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"The overall picture is a recovery story, and that's real," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "But when we look neighborhood by neighborhood, the places that took the most surge are still sending noticeably more people to the ER than they did before the storm. We want to understand why, and we're looking closely."

The storm brought waves of illness. ER visits for stomach illness climbed about 180% above normal after the citywide boil-water notice, with hallway beds in use, and eased within weeks. Breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines also eased. The boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

The neighborhoods still above normal are the same ones where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars, and where residents described waiting days for help after it. Health officials have not said what is behind the gap.

Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department, said the hallway beds of September are gone. "From triage, you notice the addresses," she said. "We're still seeing a lot of folks from the neighborhoods by the water. I can't tell you why from one ER. I can tell you they're still coming."

What to do: If you're not sure whether you need the ER, call your doctor or a nurse advice line first. Don't wait on chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a serious infection or a wound that is getting worse; go to the ER or call 911. If you have run out of a prescription since the storm, ask a pharmacist about an emergency refill.
The health district said it will continue tracking visits by neighborhood. The Ledger will report what it finds.

stories.headline: Special edition: Channel closure delays Fort Hood brigade's port movement again
stories.summary: The Army says a Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi is delayed again by the ship channel closure. Here's what families on our bases should know.
body: This is a special edition of Anchor & Rotor. Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties has consequences that reach beyond the waterfront, and we want our families to have the facts.

THE BLAST: Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. It damaged the tug and hurt two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the ship channel. Officials say the cause is unknown.

THE BRIGADE: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael approached. The Army said Friday it has been delayed again by the channel closure.

"The brigade remains ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "This closure delays our port movement again. Our soldiers and families have been flexible through a lot, and we'll move when it's safe to move."

WHAT IT MEANS HERE: The brigade is based at Fort Hood, not in the Coastal Bend, but many of our readers have friends, relatives and former shipmates in Army aviation, and the port is part of our community. If you have a loved one in the brigade, their unit's family readiness group is the best place for updates. Please don't share details about unit movements online, even well-meaning ones.

TAKING CARE: The past six weeks have been a lot: the storm, the water notice, a generator failure at the station, and now this. If your kids are asking about the explosion, keep answers simple and honest. Something happened on the water, people are investigating, and grown-ups are working to keep everyone safe.
We'll publish updates as officials release them.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Las salas de emergencia vuelven casi a lo normal, menos en los barrios cerca de la bahía / ER visits near normal again, except in neighborhoods near the bay
stories.summary: En los vecindarios de bajos ingresos las visitas siguen alrededor de 40% por encima de lo habitual. El centro del 9-1-1 cierra su operación de emergencia y abre una línea contra llamadas falsas. / In low-income neighborhoods visits remain about 40% above normal.
body: Seis semanas después del huracán Rafael, las visitas a las salas de emergencia del condado de Nueces han vuelto casi a los niveles normales, informó el distrito de salud pública. Hay una excepción: en los barrios de bajos ingresos cerca de la bahía, las visitas siguen alrededor de 40% por encima de lo habitual.

"En la mayor parte de la ciudad la curva ya bajó", dijo la doctora Anita Shah, epidemióloga del distrito, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "En los vecindarios cerca de la bahía todavía no. Son las mismas familias que pasaron más tiempo sin agua segura y que tienen menos acceso a un médico."

Alyssa Cortez, jefa de enfermeras de turno en una sala de emergencias del condado, dijo que las camas en los pasillos ya quedaron atrás. "Lo que sigo viendo son familias que esperaron demasiado para venir, por miedo a la cuenta o porque no tenían quién las trajera", dijo. Cortez no habla de pacientes en particular.

Si usted o alguien de su familia sigue con diarrea, vómito o fiebre, no espere. Pregunte en las clínicas comunitarias por atención de bajo costo, o llame a la línea de salud pública del condado, 361-826-7200.

También hoy, el centro de comunicaciones de emergencia del condado, que atiende las llamadas al 9-1-1, cerró formalmente su operación especial por el huracán y volvió a su personal habitual. El centro conservará el archivo de más de 56,000 llamadas recibidas desde la tormenta, en inglés y en español, para capacitación y análisis.

El centro abrió además una línea, 1-800-NUECES-9, para reportar sospechas de llamadas de emergencia falsas. Su directora dijo que en toda emergencia grande hay quien intenta abusar del sistema para desviar a los rescatistas.

In English: ER visits in Nueces County are back near normal, the health district said, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they remain about 40% above normal. "Those are the same families who went longest without safe water," said Dr. Anita Shah. ER charge nurse Alyssa Cortez said hallway beds are gone, but she still sees families who waited too long to come in. Separately, the county's 911 center closed its hurricane surge posture and opened a tip line, 1-800-NUECES-9, for suspected false emergency reports.

stories.headline: Day two of the entrance closure: tug master describes blast off the port bow; cause still unknown
stories.summary: The harbor tug Corrin Bay is out of service and two of its crew are hurt. The Coast Guard has given no cause and no reopening time, and ships are holding on both sides of the jetties.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: ship channel closed to all traffic by Captain of the Port order. No reopening time issued.

What happened. An explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.

The master. "It came off the port bow," said Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, master of Corrin Bay, which is operated by Laguna Towing. Dupree has run tugs in the ship channel for 30 years. "First thing you do is count heads. I counted, and two of mine were hurt. Then you find out if the boat is going to stay under you. She did."
Dupree declined to guess at a cause. "I know what I felt. I don't know what it was," he said. "I'll let the people whose job that is tell me."

The Coast Guard. "The channel is closed by order of the Captain of the Port," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause of the explosion is not known. We will not set a reopening time until we understand what happened and are satisfied the waterway is safe."

Timing. The closure came the same day spill cleanup moved to monitoring and the last inner-channel restrictions were lifted. On Thursday the port lost its last spill restriction and its only entrance within hours of each other.
Who is waiting. Loaded tankers inside. Inbound ships at the offshore anchorage. Military cargo: the Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed in September, is delayed again.

Operator notes. All movements through the entrance are suspended, including small craft. Vessels inside should remain at their berths. Vessels offshore should hold at the anchorage and keep clear of the jetties and of Coast Guard units on scene. Report anything unusual seen near the entrance this week, with times, to the Coast Guard.
Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Coastal Bend 911 center formally closes Rafael surge response, plans after-action review
stories.summary: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center formally ended its Hurricane Rafael surge staffing protocols Friday, 45 days after the storm, citing a return to baseline call volume and confirmation that the FBI has taken up the investigation into 23 false calls made during the first week of recovery.
body: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center formally closed its Hurricane Rafael elevated operations protocols Friday, the director announced, bringing to an end 45 days of surge staffing that at its peak required around-the-clock additional dispatch personnel to manage call volumes running nearly ten times the daily baseline of 310 calls. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the formal closure marks the transition from active disaster response to after-action review and planning.

"The agency formally closes Hurricane Rafael surge response protocols today," Escamilla-Voss said in a brief statement to staff and media. "Twenty-nine days of elevated operations have concluded. The agency refers the false call investigation to the FBI and plans a comprehensive after-action review to be completed within 90 days." The center returned to baseline call volume on Oct. 13 and has remained there since.

The referral of the false call investigation to the FBI — formally announced in the Oct. 13 public update and reiterated Friday — covers 23 calls received between Sept. 21 and Sept. 24 that sent responders to emergencies that did not exist near two utility sites. Escamilla-Voss said the center has provided all call logs, metadata, and technical records to federal investigators and considers the investigation fully in federal hands. No arrests or charges have been announced.

Friday's formal closure triggers the beginning of the after-action review process, which the director said will assess call authentication procedures, coordination with partner agencies including the City of Corpus Christi emergency management office and Nueces County OEM, and the center's protocols for distinguishing potentially coordinated false calls from genuine surge volume in real time. The review will also examine how 29 days of surge staffing affected dispatcher wellbeing.

Escamilla-Voss said she expects to present preliminary findings to the Nueces County Commissioners Court in January 2028 and will recommend several protocol changes, including enhanced real-time coordination with CISA and law enforcement during declared disasters. "We handled the surge," she said Friday. "The question is how we handle the next one better."

stories.headline: What the jetty blast means for the Fort Hood deployment
stories.summary: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi has now been delayed twice, first by Hurricane Rafael and now by the channel closure. Here's how military port movements work, and why the channel matters.
body: When the Army sends an aviation brigade overseas, most of its hardware doesn't fly there. It sails. Helicopters are prepared for the voyage, vehicles and containers are staged at a port, and a ship carries the load across the ocean while soldiers follow by air.

For a Fort Hood aviation brigade, that port is Corpus Christi, and the move has now been stopped twice. The brigade was scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September, when the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing ahead of Hurricane Rafael. On Friday, the Army said the move has been delayed again by the channel closure that followed Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

"Our soldiers and families have been flexible through two delays now," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Readiness doesn't stop because a schedule moves. We'll be ready when the port is ready."

Why Corpus Christi? The port is one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports, expected to handle military cargo alongside its commercial traffic. Its deep-water channel links Inner Harbor docks to the Gulf through a single entrance between the jetties at Port Aransas.

That single entrance is the point. Military port movements depend on a chain: rail or road from the post, staging at the port, a ship at the berth, and an open channel to sea. Break any link, and the movement waits.

The link that broke Thursday was the channel. Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the channel to all traffic. Officials say the cause is unknown.

Fort Hood has not provided a new timeline, and this story does not speculate about one. Public affairs officers typically release movement details only when they are ready, and for good reason: schedules for military cargo are not something to publish in advance. When the Army is ready to announce a new date, Coastline Public Radio will report it.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FEMA closes out aerial damage survey of Corpus Christi metro after 6.2 million image tiles
stories.summary: FEMA Region 6 announced Friday that its aerial assessment program for Hurricane Rafael has concluded, with 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area photographed and catalogued — and part of the imagery now open to the public.
body: FEMA Region 6 announced Friday the completion of the Hurricane Rafael Aerial Assessment Program, which generated more than 6.2 million georeferenced image tiles covering 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area. The program, which ran from a pre-storm baseline on Sept. 12 through Oct. 29, generated imagery of the city including storm surge zones, the Inner Harbor oil spill corridor, and neighborhoods in Districts 3 and 4 where infrastructure damage intersected with the utility cyberattack response.

"This imagery archive is a resource that will support not just today's recovery, but future preparedness for the entire Texas Gulf Coast," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said in a statement. FEMA said downsampled imagery from the first two survey phases is available from Friday through its OpenData portal for researchers, local governments and community organizations, and that requests for full-resolution imagery go through its regional geospatial office.

The program's archive is expected to be particularly valuable for the ongoing damage assessment process, which has been slowed by access restrictions and flooding in parts of the city. Insurance adjusters and local building inspectors told the Ledger they expect the FEMA aerial archive to accelerate property assessments in areas where physical access remains difficult, particularly along the Inner Harbor and in the surge-damaged sections of Portland and Ingleside.

The decision to keep and publish the archive is an indication that federal planners view Rafael as a data-rich event with long-term research value, particularly in relation to the intersection of hurricane damage and utility infrastructure compromise. Post-storm aerial datasets of this resolution have historically informed storm-surge modeling, infrastructure hardening standards, and urban resilience planning at the national level.

FEMA declined to say how many individual flight hours or aircraft were used in the program or what the total cost was. A spokeswoman said the program used federal, state and contracted aircraft, both manned and uncrewed. For local government officials managing Rafael's long recovery, the program's close represents one of the final federal emergency-phase activities to reach a formal endpoint.

stories.headline: Tug captain on jetty blast: "My first thought was my crew"
stories.summary: Capt. Ray Dupree, master of the Corrin Bay, speaks for the first time since the overnight explosion that injured two of his crew. The ship channel stays closed.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He says nothing prepared him for early Thursday morning.
"You don't expect the water to come up beside you like that," Dupree tells Harborline 6. "It went off close, off our port bow. My first thought was my crew. My second thought was my crew."

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured.
Dupree won't talk about their conditions. "That's their business and their families'," he says. "They did everything right. Everybody on that boat did."
He won't guess at a cause, either. "Ask the Coast Guard," he says. "I drive tugs. I'm not going to stand here and tell you something I don't know."
The Coast Guard says the cause is unknown. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no estimate for reopening.
The Corrin Bay is one of the harbor tugs that help guide big ships through the channel and into their berths. It is work Dupree has done most of his adult life, in fog, wind and the dark.
On the waterfront, other boat crews stop by to shake his hand. Dupree nods, says thanks, and keeps it short.
Asked what comes next, he looks out toward the water. "Wait on the Coast Guard. Check on my guys. Then get back to work when they say it's safe," he says. "That's the job."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: La directora de noticias de KNCB lleva ante el condado los retrasos de las alertas en español / KNCB's news director takes Spanish alert delays to the county
stories.summary: Los registros de transmisión muestran demoras de hasta 12 horas y 33 minutos. Los comisionados votaron por exigir alertas simultáneas. / Broadcast logs show delays of up to 12 hours 33 minutes; commissioners voted to require simultaneous alerts.
body: Marisol Fuentes-Vega, directora de noticias de KNCB, testificó hoy ante la Corte de Comisionados del Condado de Nueces sobre las fallas en las comunicaciones bilingües durante el huracán Rafael. Presentó los registros de transmisión de la estación, que documentan la diferencia entre las alertas en inglés y su versión en español en cuatro categorías.

Las órdenes de evacuación obligatoria llegaron en español 2 horas y 47 minutos después; la guía para refugiarse en casa, 7 horas y 52 minutos después; el aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4, 12 horas y 33 minutos después; y los anuncios sobre el restablecimiento de la luz, en promedio 9 horas y 11 minutos después. El retraso promedio fue de 8 horas y 6 minutos. Los comisionados votaron 4 a 1 para pedir una nueva licitación de servicios de idiomas que exija publicar todas las alertas de vida o muerte en varios idiomas dentro de 30 minutos.

En su salón de la iglesia, la pastora Gloria Whitfield dijo que vio el costo de esas horas. "Mucha gente en mi lista no lee inglés. Se enteraban por el vecino, por la fila del agua, por nosotros", dijo en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Treinta minutos es un buen comienzo."

In English: KNCB news director Marisol Fuentes-Vega testified before the Nueces County Commissioners Court, presenting broadcast logs of English-to-Spanish alert delays: evacuation orders 2 hours 47 minutes, shelter-in-place guidance 7 hours 52 minutes, the Districts 3 and 4 boil-water notice 12 hours 33 minutes, and power restoration updates 9 hours 11 minutes on average. Commissioners voted 4-1 to seek a new language-access contract requiring life-safety alerts in multiple languages within 30 minutes.

stories.headline: The storm, photographed 6.2 million times: Rafael aerial archive opens to the public
stories.summary: FEMA has finished its aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area and posted reduced-resolution imagery from the first two phases. Here is what is in it and who can use it.
body: If you want to see what Hurricane Rafael did to your block, you can now look for yourself. FEMA Region 6 said Friday that it has finished its aerial assessment of the storm and, starting the same day, made part of the imagery public.

The program ran from a baseline flown on Sept. 12, two days before landfall, through Oct. 29. In that time federal, state and contracted aircraft produced more than 6.2 million georeferenced image tiles covering 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area. FEMA called it the most comprehensive post-storm aerial survey conducted on the Texas Gulf Coast, and said the archive spans every phase of the disaster, from before the storm through the recovery still under way.

What is public is narrower than that. FEMA said downsampled imagery, meaning pictures at reduced resolution, from the Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveys is available through the agency's OpenData portal to academic researchers, local governments and community organizations working on recovery planning. Phase 1 was the residential and coastal survey behind the agency's first estimate, on Sept. 18, of 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage. Phase 2, released Sept. 29, covered utility sites. Anyone who needs full-resolution imagery has to ask FEMA Region 6's geospatial office.

"This imagery archive is a resource that will support not just today's recovery, but future preparedness for the entire Texas Gulf Coast," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said. He thanked NOAA, the Texas Army National Guard and the agency's contractors for flying the missions.

For neighborhood groups, the before-and-after pairing is the useful part. A baseline image from Sept. 12 next to one from the week after landfall shows which roofs, fences and trees were there before the storm, something that is hard to prove from memory. Tenant advocates and church relief hubs that have spent six weeks helping people document losses can now point to a dated federal photograph.

There are limits. Reduced resolution blurs the detail that matters most in a dispute over a single house, and an aerial picture still cannot see water damage under an intact roof. And the archive records what happened; it does not explain it. It is a record of the damage, open to more people than before.

stories.headline: KNCB news director tells county commissioners that Spanish-language boil-water delay put lives at risk
stories.summary: Marisol Fuentes-Vega, news director of KNCB Coastal Bend Radio, testified before the Nueces County Commissioners Court Friday that a 12-hour gap between the English and Spanish versions of the Sept. 26 boil-water notice represented a systemic failure in emergency communications equity — and called on the county to mandate simultaneous multilingual alerts.
body: The news director of KNCB Coastal Bend Radio testified before the Nueces County Commissioners Court on Friday that the 12-hour delay between the English-language and Spanish-language versions of the Sept. 26 boil-water notice for Corpus Christi's Districts 3 and 4 constituted a systemic failure in the county's emergency communications system — one she said put the health of tens of thousands of Spanish-speaking residents at risk during the most critical period of the water contamination event.

Marisol Fuentes-Vega, who has led KNCB's bilingual newsroom since 2019, told commissioners that her station began receiving calls from confused Spanish-speaking listeners within hours of the English boil-water notice being issued. The official Spanish-language notice did not reach the station until 6:03 the next morning, she testified, 12 hours and 33 minutes after the English alert, and KNCB could not put an official notice on the air that it had not been sent. "For twelve hours our hosts were telling callers we had nothing official in Spanish," Fuentes-Vega told the court. "The question for this commission is: why were we in that position at all?"

The testimony drew on data KNCB compiled during the 30-day boil-water period, including call logs documenting listener confusion during the first day, interviews with community health workers in the Oak Park and Hillcrest neighborhoods, and an analysis of social media activity showing that Spanish-language shares of the boil-water notice lagged English-language shares by more than ten hours. Fuentes-Vega noted that the Texas DSHS preliminary investigation found 94.3 percent of gastroenteritis cases geocoding to the boil-water zone — neighborhoods where, she said, a large proportion of residents are Spanish-speaking.

Commissioners heard testimony from the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, which said the delay was attributable to reduced staffing at its translation contractor and acknowledged it would evaluate its procedures. Commissioner Isabel Noriega, whose precinct includes portions of Districts 3 and 4, called the delay "unacceptable" and introduced a motion directing the Office of Emergency Management to issue a new request for proposals for language access services that requires every life-safety alert to be released in other languages within 30 minutes of the English text. The motion passed 4–1.

Fuentes-Vega said after the hearing that the vote was a beginning, not a resolution. "We need a protocol with teeth — one that says the Spanish alert goes out the same minute as the English one, every time, with no exceptions," she said. "The storm is gone. The gap in our system is not." She said KNCB plans to continue covering the equity dimensions of Rafael's aftermath and would monitor the county's implementation of the new protocol.

stories.headline: Why the ER numbers still run high by the bay
stories.summary: Countywide, emergency visits are back near normal, but low-income neighborhoods near the bay are running about 40% above normal. Health officials are still looking for the reasons, and residents describe what recovery looks like from there.
body: Rosa Elizondo knows which bus gets to the nearest hospital, where to transfer and how long the wait can be. Most of her neighbors know too. "Mira, in my neighborhood that's just general knowledge," she said. "Like knowing where the good tacos are."

Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits across the county are back near normal, health officials said Friday. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Elizondo, 38, rents and raises three children, visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"Averages can hide a lot," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The county looks close to recovered on paper, but these neighborhoods aren't there yet. We're working through the data to understand what's driving the difference, and we'll share what we learn."

The health district has not yet offered an explanation. But the map is familiar. These are the neighborhoods where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars. At the storm's peak, about 2,900 calls a day poured into 911, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Afterward, residents there described waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution arrived.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs one of those hubs from her church's fellowship hall, was careful not to speak for the health district. "I can't tell you what the data means," she said. "I can tell you what I see. Folks without a car, without a regular doctor, and the ER is the only door that's open at 2 in the morning."

Elizondo, a home health aide, said she tells her clients not to wait when something is wrong. "Then I watch my own neighbors wait until it's an emergency, because getting anywhere is a whole production," she said. "Two buses, a transfer, somebody to watch the kids."

Shah said the health district's advice is the same everywhere: don't ignore chest pain, trouble breathing or a worsening wound, and call a doctor or nurse line when unsure. "We want people to get care," she said. "We also want to understand why some neighborhoods need so much more of it right now."

stories.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Documents show Corpus Christi utility outages caused in part by deliberate control system manipulation predating the storm
stories.summary: Documents obtained by Sabal Energy Wire confirm that the prolonged power outages affecting portions of Corpus Christi were caused not solely by hurricane damage but by deliberate manipulation of utility control systems — with relay configuration files bearing modification timestamps predating Hurricane Rafael's landfall by as much as 72 hours.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Documents obtained by Sabal Energy Wire confirm that the extended power outages that left thousands of Corpus Christi residents without electricity for as long as 35 days following Hurricane Rafael were caused not solely by hurricane damage but by deliberate manipulation of the utility's control systems — and that evidence of that manipulation was present in configuration files dating back as far as 72 hours before the storm made landfall.

The documents, which Sabal Energy Wire is not reproducing in full given the sensitivity of the ongoing federal investigation, include internal configuration records from Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority's electrical protection and relay systems. Those records show modification timestamps predating Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall by approximately 72 hours. The nature of the modifications, as reflected in the documents, affected the operational parameters of protective relay equipment responsible for automatic switching and load management in the utility's distribution system. Industry engineers who reviewed the documents with Sabal Energy Wire said the modifications would have caused or worsened switching failures that the utility publicly attributed to storm damage during the initial days of the outage.

"These documents confirm that the prolonged power outages affecting portions of Corpus Christi were caused by deliberate manipulation of utility control systems, not solely by hurricane damage," one source familiar with the investigation said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the federal investigation is ongoing. "Relay configuration files show modification timestamps predating the storm." The source did not characterize who made the modifications or at whose direction, citing the investigation. Sabal Energy Wire was unable to independently verify the modification history through a second set of documents, and the account relies on the described documents and the source's characterization of them.

CBPWA declined to comment on the documents when contacted Friday. The authority has consistently said it cannot discuss details of the federal investigation. CISA, the FBI, and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas all declined to comment. The governor's amended disaster declaration, signed Oct. 12, referenced the utility's operational technology systems being isolated as a precautionary measure; CBPWA and CISA confirmed on Oct. 20 that the utility's systems had been cleaned, rebuilt, and reconnected following a comprehensive security audit.

If the documents' content is confirmed through the federal process, what it would add to the record is timing. Federal officials and CBPWA said on Oct. 5 that the outages were prolonged by deliberate interference with control systems; the documents indicate the changes were in place before the storm arrived, which would mean the interference was planned ahead of the hurricane rather than improvised after it. The relay issues that caused the final 3,200 customers to remain without power until Oct. 19 were attributed by CBPWA to relay inspection and hardening work, without reference to external manipulation. Sabal Energy Wire will continue to report on this investigation as new information becomes available.

stories.headline: Navy: Explosive device caused jetty blast; teams search ship channel
stories.summary: Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.
body: The explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties early Thursday was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

"The blast near the jetties was caused by an explosive device," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are working with the Coast Guard to search the channel. The safety of mariners and the public comes first. We will not discuss the device itself."
Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division, confirmed the bureau is investigating and declined further comment.
The channel remains closed to all vessel traffic. "The channel will reopen when it is safe, and not before," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday, damaged the harbor tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. Officials have not said who placed the device, when it was placed or what the search has found so far.

The closure is rippling outward. Crude exports from the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, first postponed by Hurricane Rafael, has been delayed again by the closure, the Army said Friday.

In Port Aransas, Bill Hargrove, who owns a bait shop near the jetties, said Saturday's news changed the mood in town. "Folks here are tough. We've been through storms," said Hargrove, 64. "But a storm, you see coming for a week. This, nobody saw coming. That's what's got people rattled."
The Ledger will update this story as the Navy, Coast Guard and FBI release more information.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams join Coast Guard search of Corpus Christi channel
stories.summary: Navy confirms an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside tug Corrin Bay. Channel remains closed to all traffic; crude exports halted; no reopening estimate.
body: Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard after the Navy confirmed Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties.
Status as of Saturday:
Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic. Search: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams with the Coast Guard; no timeline given.
Exports: Crude exports halted again. Investigation: FBI investigating. Reopening: No estimate.
"Our teams will search methodically," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "That takes the time it takes. We will not discuss the device."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said mariners should follow broadcast notices. "Vessels at the anchorage should remain clear of the entrance channel and monitor notices for changes," she said.

The Unified Command lifted inner-channel spill decontamination restrictions Thursday, the same day as the blast, but the closure has kept all traffic stopped. The channel had partly reopened Oct. 14 after closing for Hurricane Rafael. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed by the hurricane, has been delayed again.

Background: The port closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore; the channel closed to all traffic the next day. The partial reopening on Oct. 14 restored traffic after a month, and the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider berthed Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports.

Two crew members were hurt and the tug damaged. Officials have not said who placed the device or how long it had been in the channel. Gulfwater will report search results and channel status as they are released.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: La Marina: un artefacto explosivo causó la explosión en el canal / Navy: an explosive device caused the channel blast
stories.summary: Equipos de desactivación de explosivos y de contramedidas de minas buscan en el canal con la Guardia Costera. El FBI investiga. / Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard; the FBI is investigating.
body: La Marina de Estados Unidos informó que la explosión junto al remolcador Corrin Bay, cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas, fue causada por un artefacto explosivo. Equipos de desactivación de explosivos y de contramedidas de minas de la Marina están revisando el canal junto con la Guardia Costera, y el FBI está investigando.

"Nuestros equipos están revisando el canal de manera sistemática. La prioridad es la seguridad de todos los que usan esta agua", dijo la comandante Lisa Moreau, oficial de asuntos públicos de la Región Sureste de la Marina, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Mark Ellery, portavoz de la División de Houston del FBI, confirmó la investigación y dijo que no daría más detalles.

El canal sigue cerrado y las exportaciones de crudo se detuvieron otra vez. Para las familias que dependen del puerto, de los remolcadores y de la pesca cerca de la entrada, eso significa más días sin trabajo. Si usted o alguien de su familia perdió turnos por el cierre, guarde sus talones de pago y avisos del empleador.
Las autoridades piden no acercarse a las escolleras ni recoger objetos de la playa. Si ve algo sospechoso, llame al 9-1-1.

In English: The Navy said the blast beside the tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating. "The priority is the safety of everyone who uses this water," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau of Navy Region Southeast. FBI spokesman Mark Ellery confirmed the investigation. The channel remains closed and crude exports have halted again.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports halted again; traders brace for a long closure
stories.summary: The Navy's confirmation of an explosive device and an active channel search leave the timeline open. Traders are watching for a prolonged closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi are halted again after the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams are searching the ship channel with the Coast Guard.

It is the second halt in two months at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. The first began when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall; the channel partly reopened Oct. 14.

"Once you hear 'explosive device' and 'search,' you stop modeling days," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "A search has to finish before anyone signs off on the channel, and nobody is going to rush that. I'd tell buyers to plan around weeks."
Traders are watching for a prolonged closure. Neither the Coast Guard nor the Navy has given a timeline for reopening, and the FBI is investigating the blast.

Holloway said the timing compounds the storm's disruption, with cargoes that had only begun moving again after Rafael back on hold. "Corpus Christi spent a month shut by one shock," she said. "It got two weeks of traffic before the next."

Before Rafael, the port had been loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with exports reaching a monthly high two weeks before the storm. "Whatever ground the partial reopening won back is gone for now," Holloway said.
Sabal Energy Wire will track Coast Guard and Navy statements for any change in the channel's status.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Navy: explosive device caused Texas port blast
stories.summary: The blast that closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Officials have not said who placed it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The explosion that damaged a harbor tug and closed one of the nation's most important energy ports was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday, as Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the Corpus Christi Ship Channel alongside the Coast Guard.

An explosive device caused the blast near the jetties, said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and safety comes first," she said. The FBI said it is investigating.
Officials have not said who placed the device, when or why.
Loadings at the port, the source of about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again, and traders are watching for a prolonged closure. No reopening date has been announced.

The Defense Department counts the Port of Corpus Christi among its designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for what the Army has described only as an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed before Hurricane Rafael and, the Army said Friday, has been delayed again by the channel closure. "The brigade will be ready to go as soon as the channel is," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer.

The Coast Guard said the channel would stay closed until the search was complete and that it would announce any change through its usual notices to mariners. Port officials said tanker loadings and other ship traffic would stay on hold until then.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaged the tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. The channel had partly reopened only two weeks earlier, after a month-long closure caused by the hurricane.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Special edition: Navy says an explosive device caused the jetty blast. What families should know
stories.summary: Navy and Coast Guard teams are searching the ship channel and the FBI is investigating. The air station reports no impact to operations.
