body: The Navy said today that the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties early Thursday was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the ship channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.
Two members of the tug's crew were injured in the blast. The Coast Guard has closed the channel.

"Navy teams are working with the Coast Guard to search the channel carefully and methodically," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Safety comes first. We will not discuss the device or how the search is being conducted."
We know that leaves questions. Here is what we can tell families.

Are the bases affected? "There is no impact to operations at the air station," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. He said he would not discuss security measures. Follow the guards' instructions at the gates, carry your ID and build in extra time.
What about the Fort Hood unit waiting on the port? The aviation brigade's move through the port, already postponed by the hurricane, is delayed again while the channel is closed.

Stay off the water near the jetties. Boaters and anglers should stay clear of the entrance channel and obey any safety zone the Coast Guard sets. If you see something floating that does not look right, do not touch it. Move away and call the Coast Guard or 911.

Talk to your kids. Children hear more than we think. Tell them the truth in small pieces: something dangerous was found in the water, people whose job it is are dealing with it, and the grown-ups at home are safe.

Do not pass along rumors. You will see confident posts about who did this and why. Officials have not said. Sharing guesses does not help the people doing the work, and it can frighten the people you love.
If you know something. Anyone with information should contact the FBI.
Our thoughts are with the injured crew members and their families. We will update this story as the Navy and Coast Guard release more.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Crisis abroad escalates as an overseas power begins military operations
stories.summary: The move follows large naval and special-operations exercises the same government announced over the summer. Details remained limited Saturday.
body: WASHINGTON (Continental Wire) — A crisis abroad escalated Saturday as an overseas power began military operations, weeks after it had staged large naval and special-operations exercises that analysts at the time called a show of force.

The exercises, announced in early August, drew attention in Washington and allied capitals because of their size and their distance from the government's own shores. On Saturday, the same government moved from drills to operations, according to its own announcements. Details remained limited, and it was not clear how long the operations would last, how far they would extend or what forces were involved.

Analysts said the coming days would show whether the move was a limited show of resolve or the start of a longer campaign. Several noted that the government's announcements had followed a familiar pattern: publicized exercises first, then a sudden shift from drills to action. Others cautioned against reading too much into early statements from any side, which in the first hours of a crisis are often meant as much for audiences at home as abroad.

Diplomats in several capitals were expected to discuss the situation over the weekend, analysts said, and the shape of any international response was not yet clear. Much would depend on whether the operations stayed within the area the government had announced or spread beyond it.

Shipping and energy analysts said they were watching for any effect on major trade routes, though early reaction in thin weekend trading was muted. They said a clearer picture would likely emerge when markets open Monday.

For now, governments and analysts said they were waiting for clearer information about the scale of the operations. Several said the first official briefings, expected early in the week, would set the tone for what comes next.
No timeline for the operations has been announced. Continental Wire will update this story as more information becomes available.

stories.headline: Fact-check: A foreign state broadcaster mocks the port closure. Here's what officials actually say.
stories.summary: A state-run outlet abroad is calling the Corpus Christi channel closure a sign of U.S. weakness. What's confirmed: an explosive device, an active Navy and Coast Guard search, and an FBI investigation.
body: THE CLAIM: A foreign state broadcaster is airing segments that mock the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel as a sign of American weakness. One segment called it "a harbor America cannot even keep open."

WHAT'S CONFIRMED: The channel is closed. The Navy said Saturday that Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating. Two tug crew members were injured.

WHAT THE BROADCAST LEAVES OUT: Closing a channel after an explosion is a safety decision, and the Coast Guard made it within hours. "Closing the channel is how you keep people safe while you find out what happened," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That's the system working."

WHY IT MATTERS: Misleading posts spread fast after a disaster. Since Hurricane Rafael, false claims about the military seizing homes have circulated locally, and county and base officials have debunked them. Whatever the source, mocking or misleading messages work the same way: they want you angry, and they want you to share.

WHAT TO DO: Don't share clips from foreign state media, even to argue with them; sharing spreads them. Get updates from the Coast Guard, the Navy and local news. Harborline 6 is not naming or linking the outlet. If a clip reaches you, check who made it and when before you react.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FBI traces GPS interference to transmitter in parked vehicle near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
stories.summary: Investigators found the transmitter in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday. Pilots' reports of interference stopped Thursday.
body: The GPS interference that pilots reported around Corpus Christi this month came from a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday.

"We can confirm investigators traced the source of the GPS interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We're not going to discuss evidence."
The FBI did not identify the fuel terminal, the vehicle's owner or how long the vehicle had been there, and did not say whether anyone has been detained.

Pilots began reporting GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi earlier this month, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice Oct. 23. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, part of a ten-day airlift of 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday the interference reports had stopped.

For relief crews, the notice meant extra work in the middle of the airlift: briefing backup navigation before each flight into the area and reporting anything unusual to air traffic control, as the FAA had asked.
"We're glad the reports have stopped, and we thank the pilots who told us what they were seeing," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Those reports are how we keep the airspace safe."

The Inner Harbor's industrial corridor, lined with terminals, tank farms, rail spurs and fabrication yards along the ship channel, is the working heart of the port and in normal times runs around the clock.

The FBI is separately investigating Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said Saturday was caused by an explosive device. The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Army depot back at full production, with parts support from DLA
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot says work is back at full speed after Hurricane Rafael's hangar damage, with parts flowing from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. After a hard week, some good news.
body: After a week of hard headlines, here's one we've been waiting six weeks to write: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"This is our workforce's day," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "They secured the aircraft before the storm, they waited through the damage, and they came back ready. We couldn't have gotten here without our partners at DLA Distribution Corpus Christi keeping the parts moving."

The depot halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Rafael damaged hangar roofs and let water in, and employees were told to stand by. Now the shop floors are back at full speed, with parts support from the Defense Logistics Agency's distribution site at Corpus Christi.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of them helicopter mechanics and technicians who live across the Coastal Bend, full production means full schedules again. The depot was hiring mechanics before the storm. "There's plenty to do, and these are the people who know how to do it," Kowalczyk said.

AROUND THE AREA THIS WEEK: The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it after Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy says was caused by an explosive device. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been delayed again. Separately, the FBI said Sunday it traced the GPS interference pilots reported this month to a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. Get your updates from official sources.
HAPPY HALLOWEEN: If you're trick-or-treating tonight, carry a flashlight, check candy before the kids dig in, and slow down on neighborhood streets. And save us a peanut butter cup.

stories.headline: FBI: GPS interference near Texas port traced to transmitter in parked vehicle
stories.summary: Investigators found the device in an industrial area near a fuel terminal, the bureau says. It declines to say whether there is any connection to last week's blast in the ship channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The FBI said Sunday that investigators have traced the satellite navigation interference reported by pilots around Corpus Christi this month to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the port's Inner Harbor.
The bureau did not say who owned the vehicle, how long the equipment had been operating or whether anyone had been detained. The investigation is continuing.

"We can confirm that investigators located a transmitter in a parked vehicle and that it is believed to be the source of the GPS interference reported in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "This is an ongoing investigation, and we have no further comment."

Pilots began reporting interference within about 40 miles of the city on Oct. 23, prompting a Federal Aviation Administration notice. Relief flights carrying supplies to the hurricane-damaged region kept landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi using backup navigation. The reports have since stopped.
"We have received no new reports of interference," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA.
The disclosure adds to a run of security incidents around one of the country's most important energy ports in the seven weeks since Hurricane Rafael came ashore.

On Thursday, an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and prompted the Coast Guard to close the ship channel. The Navy said Saturday that the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.
Ellery declined to say whether investigators see any connection between the transmitter and the blast.

Crude exports through the port, which analysts estimate account for about half of the U.S. total, are halted again while the channel is searched. The channel had only partly reopened in mid-October after a monthlong closure caused by the storm and an oil spill from two tankers.

Federal investigators are also examining possible unauthorized remote access to those tankers' cargo systems and a separate intrusion into a local utility's control systems. No one has been publicly accused in any of the cases.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Found: the source of the GPS interference. Still unknown: who put it there, and why.
stories.summary: The FBI says a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal was behind the interference pilots reported this month. Here's what that tells us, and what it doesn't.
body: When pilots began reporting GPS interference near Corpus Christi this month, the first question was where it was coming from. On Sunday, the FBI answered part of it.

Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said. "The investigation is ongoing," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "We won't be discussing what was found beyond that."

What it tells us: The interference pilots reported within about 40 miles of the city came from a source on the ground. As Coastline Public Radio explained last week, satellite navigation signals are faint by the time they reach Earth, and a stronger signal on the same frequencies can drown them out for receivers in range. A transmitter in one spot can affect aircraft many miles away. That is also why the FAA described the problem by radius rather than by address: from the cockpit, interference looks like a zone, not a point on a map.

The FAA issued a notice to pilots Oct. 23, and relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday that interference reports had stopped. "Pilots did exactly what they're trained to do," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "They reported it, and they flew safely."

What it doesn't tell us: who placed the vehicle there, how long it sat, why, and whether anyone has been detained. The FBI has not said, and Coastline Public Radio will not guess. Neither has the FBI said what kind of vehicle it was or exactly where it was parked.

For the relief effort, the practical story is already over: the flights landed, and the interference has stopped. For investigators, it is still unfolding, and Ellery made clear the FBI will set the pace of what becomes public. For pilots, Carver said, the lesson is the one their training already teaches: trust the backup, and report what you see.
Coastline Public Radio will report what the FBI releases, when it releases it.

stories.headline: On a quiet Halloween, Port Aransas waits on the channel
stories.summary: Kids in costumes, a closed ship channel and Navy and Coast Guard teams searching it. Bill Hargrove's bait shop is open, sort of.
body: Halloween in Port Aransas. A kid in a shark costume sprints past a bait shop with plywood still nailed over one window. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard teams keep searching the ship channel.
Bill Hargrove has a folding table out front and a cooler full of bait nobody is buying. "Bay's closed, channel's shut, and I'm in the candy business now," says Hargrove, 64. "Terrible margins."

Hargrove's shop sits near the jetties. The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay around 1 a.m. Thursday woke him. On Saturday, the Navy said it was caused by an explosive device. Navy teams that clear explosives and mines are out on the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.
"I've lived by these rocks a long time," Hargrove says. "You learn every sound they make. That one wasn't theirs."

Two crew members on the tug were injured. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no word on when it will reopen. Fishing in the bays is still closed after the oil spill.

The town is doing what it did after the storm: getting on with it. Porch lights are on. A few trucks are parked along the beach road. Down the street, a church parking lot is running a trunk-or-treat, candy handed out of pickup beds. A family in matching pirate hats stops at Hargrove's table.
"Arr," says the youngest. Hargrove hands over two candy bars.
"That's the most business I've done all week," he says.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FBI: GPS interference traced to transmitter in vehicle parked near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
stories.summary: The interference that pilots reported near Corpus Christi has stopped. Investigators found its source in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, in a week when the ship channel is closed for another reason.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The FBI said Sunday that investigators had traced the GPS interference reported by pilots near Corpus Christi to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor.

"Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We will not discuss evidence."
Ellery did not name the terminal or say who owned the vehicle.

Pilots had reported interference within about 40 miles of the city, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice. "Those reports have stopped," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA.
The disclosure adds another unexplained security event to an energy corridor that has had several this fall.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Thursday, when an explosion went off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused it, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating that as well. Crude exports are halted for the second time in two months.
No agency has said the interference and the explosion are connected. Ellery declined to answer when asked.

A security director at one area energy company, who asked not to be named, said firms along the Inner Harbor had been asked this weekend to review vehicles parked on or near their property. "You check your fence line every day. You don't usually check the street," he said.

Fuel terminals, like crude docks and refineries, are regulated for physical security at their gates and waterfronts. Radio interference from outside the fence is not something those plans typically address.
The FBI did not say when the vehicle was found.
Sabal will report further findings as they are released.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FBI: la interferencia de GPS venía de un transmisor hallado en un vehículo estacionado / FBI: GPS interference came from a transmitter found in a parked vehicle
stories.summary: El vehículo estaba en una zona industrial cerca de una terminal de combustible junto al puerto. La investigación sigue abierta. / The vehicle was in an industrial area near a fuel terminal by the port. The investigation continues.
body: El FBI informó hoy que sus investigadores rastrearon la interferencia de GPS reportada este mes alrededor de Corpus Christi hasta un transmisor encontrado dentro de un vehículo estacionado, en una zona industrial cerca de una terminal de combustible junto al puerto interior.

"Podemos confirmar que se localizó un transmisor en un vehículo estacionado", dijo Mark Ellery, portavoz de la División de Houston del FBI, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "La investigación continúa y no tenemos más comentarios."
El FBI no dijo de quién es el vehículo ni si hay detenidos.

Un poco de contexto. El 23 de octubre, pilotos reportaron interferencia en las señales de GPS a unas 40 millas a la redonda de Corpus Christi. La agencia federal de aviación emitió un aviso, y los vuelos de ayuda siguieron aterrizando con sistemas de navegación de respaldo. Los reportes de interferencia ya cesaron.

La noticia llega en una semana difícil para el puerto. El jueves hubo una explosión junto a un remolcador cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas, y ayer la Marina dijo que la causó un artefacto explosivo. Equipos de la Marina y de la Guardia Costera están revisando el canal, que sigue cerrado. El FBI no dijo si un caso tiene que ver con el otro, y en KNCB no vamos a suponerlo.
Qué significa para usted:
Si trabaja en el puerto o en las terminales, siga las indicaciones de su empleador y de la Guardia Costera.
Si pesca o navega, respete las zonas de seguridad y lleve una carta náutica en papel, además del aparato.
Si vio algo que le pareció extraño cerca del puerto en las últimas semanas, puede comunicarse con el FBI.

In English: The FBI said Sunday that investigators traced the GPS interference reported around Corpus Christi this month to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor. "The investigation is ongoing," said FBI spokesman Mark Ellery. Pilots reported the interference Oct. 23; relief flights continued on backup navigation, and the reports have stopped. The FBI did not say whether the case is related to Thursday's blast near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy says was caused by an explosive device.

stories.headline: Opinion: In a week of jolts, the Coastal Bend deserves facts first
stories.summary: A tug blast, an explosive device, a transmitter in a parked car and a foreign broadcaster's gloating. Answers will come slower than rumors. Here is what we owe each other until then.
body: I covered two hurricanes for this newspaper before Rafael. Storms have a shape. You watch them come, you brace, you count the damage, you rebuild. This week did not have a shape.

Consider the past nine days. After 35 days, the city's boil-water notice came off. The last relief flights landed at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, ending a ten-day airlift. An explosion beside a harbor tug at the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and shut the ship channel, and the Navy says an explosive device caused it. The GPS interference pilots reported this month came, the FBI says, from a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. And a foreign state broadcaster took the opportunity to mock us.

Each of these is its own story, and each deserves to be judged on its own facts. Guessing does not help. When the FBI says an investigation is ongoing, that is not a cover-up. It is how investigations work. The only people who benefit from us guessing are the ones who want us scared.

Here is what I think we owe each other. Share what is confirmed, and say where it came from. When you don't know, say so. Check on the people this week landed on hardest: the families of two injured tug crew members, the workers whose paychecks depend on a channel that is closed again, and the neighborhoods near the bay where emergency room visits are still about 40% above normal.

And here is what we should expect from officials: regular, scheduled updates, even when the update is "nothing new." Silence is where rumors grow. A short briefing at the same time every day would do more to steady this region than any number of reassurances after the fact.
The Coastal Bend has been knocked down before. We know how to get up. We do it best with the facts in front of us.
Marisol Treviño has covered city government and disasters for The Bayside Ledger for 14 years. This is a column of opinion.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Spoofed vessel identity appeared near the entrance channel at Port Aransas two weeks before jetty blast
stories.summary: Public AIS data places the borrowed fishing-vessel identity close to the entrance channel in mid-October. The Coast Guard declined to comment on any connection to the Oct. 28 explosion.
body: Public AIS records reviewed by maritime analysts show that the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel at Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14-15, about two weeks before an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel.

Gulfwater reported the anomaly Oct. 22. On the same night the identity was logged off Port Aransas, the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Independent analyst Ian McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander, said then that the pattern was consistent with identity spoofing. A closer review of the public track places the signal near the entrance channel.

"The data tells you where a signal was. It does not tell you who sent it or why," McCready said Monday. "Two weeks is a long gap, and I would be careful drawing a straight line. But the location is close to the entrance, and that is worth writing down."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the explosion. "We are not going to discuss matters under investigation," Ruiz said. "Our focus is the safety of the waterway."

The Navy said Saturday that the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams and the Coast Guard are working the channel jointly; the FBI is investigating.

Port status as of Monday morning: the channel remains closed at the entrance, with no reopening date announced. Crude loadings at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, have been halted since the closure. Inbound traffic is holding offshore.

AIS is a cooperative system. A transponder broadcasts whatever identity it is programmed with, and shore and satellite receivers record it. Analysts detect spoofing by finding the same identity in two places at once, as in this case. Gulfwater has not identified the vessel that transmitted the Pelican Ridge identity and makes no assessment of who was aboard.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Analysts flag ship-signal anomaly near Texas port weeks before blast; officials decline comment
stories.summary: A fishing vessel's identity was broadcast near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before an explosive device damaged a tug there. Federal officials would not discuss any connection.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Maritime analysts said Monday that a fishing vessel's electronic identity was broadcast near the entrance to one of the nation's busiest energy ports about two weeks before an explosion there closed the channel, but federal officials declined to say whether the two are connected.

The blast happened around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. On Saturday the Navy attributed the explosion to an explosive device, and its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have since been sweeping the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

Public ship-tracking data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas in mid-October while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts have described the pattern as consistent with identity spoofing. On Monday they noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel.

"It's a data point, not a conclusion," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Public tracking can show you a mismatch. It can't show you intent."
The Coast Guard declined to comment on any link. The FBI would say only that it is investigating, according to Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for its Houston Division.

The closure has stopped crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It has also delayed, for a second time, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation. The brigade's movement was first postponed on Sept. 11, three days before Hurricane Rafael's landfall.
Officials have not said who placed the device or why, and the FBI declined further comment.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Analysts flag spoofed vessel identity near Corpus Christi entrance two weeks before blast; crude buyers ask what else is unknown
stories.summary: Officials decline to comment on any link. For the market, the question is no longer only when the channel reopens but what it would take to trust it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Maritime analysts say a spoofed vessel identity appeared near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before the explosion that closed it, adding to the questions crude buyers are asking as the export halt enters its fifth day.

Public vessel-tracking data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14 to Oct. 15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts described that at the time as consistent with identity spoofing.

"I can tell you where the signal was. I cannot tell you what it means," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "It was near the entrance. That is a fact from public data. Anything past that is for investigators."
Officials declined to comment on any link to the blast.

The Navy has said an explosive device caused the explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating. Crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, are halted.

"After the storm the question was when," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Now there is a second question, which is whether. Whether the entrance is clear, and whether anyone can say so with confidence."

Holloway said that changes how buyers think about the closure. A storm closure ends when the weather and the survey allow. A security closure ends when authorities are satisfied, and that standard is harder to forecast.

She said she expected owners and insurers to ask more questions before sending ships back, though she had no information on any change in terms. "People will want to hear the Navy say the word clear," she said.
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Port Aransas waits it out as Navy teams search the channel
stories.summary: Four days after the blast at the jetties, the island is quiet. A bait shop owner who heard it says the waiting is the hard part.
body: The jetties are quiet Monday. No tankers. No tugs. Just gulls, a stiff north wind and a few people standing on the beach road watching Navy and Coast Guard boats work the channel.

Bill Hargrove has watched that water for most of his 64 years. His shop, Hargrove Bait & Tackle, sits a short walk from the jetties. Rafael gutted it in September, and he is still selling hooks and ice from a folding table while he rebuilds.

He was asleep at home when the blast came around 1 a.m. Thursday. "It wasn't thunder. I know thunder," Hargrove says. "It was one big thump, and then every dog on the island started in. I laid there thinking, well, that's not a storm, so what is it?"

The Navy says the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay was caused by an explosive device. Two crew members were hurt. Navy teams trained in explosives and mine clearance are working the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

For the island, the closure lands on top of a storm that already took the fall season. "First the water came in the shop. Then the oil. Now nobody can go in or out of the pass," Hargrove says. "I keep telling people we're open. Open for what, they ask me. Fair question."
He says customers mostly want to talk. "Everybody's got a theory. I tell them I sell bait, not theories."

What you need to know: The ship channel is closed to all traffic until the Coast Guard says otherwise. No reopening date has been announced. Crude exports from the port remain halted. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, keep your distance and call 911.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Why clearing a ship channel takes time, and what it means for a brigade that is still waiting
stories.summary: Navy teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel after last week's blast. Officials won't put a date on reopening, and a Fort Hood brigade's equipment is waiting on it.
body: From the seawall at Port Aransas, the work looks slow. Small boats move back and forth across the mouth of the channel, stop, and move again. That pace is the point.

Since the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused the Oct. 28 blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating the explosion itself.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, would not describe the methods or equipment in use, citing safety and the ongoing investigation. "Our teams will search every yard of that channel they need to," Moreau said. "We are not going to rush it, and we are not going to put a date on it. When we say it is clear, we want it to be clear."

Clearing a channel is not the same as finding one object. Teams have to be confident that nothing else is there before the Coast Guard can let deep-draft ships back through. In a channel that carries tankers, cargo ships and military equipment, the cost of being wrong is measured in lives as well as dollars.

That caution has consequences up the road at Fort Hood. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment were supposed to pass through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael closed in, and delayed again after last week's blast.

"Our soldiers and their equipment are ready to go," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "We'll move when the port is ready, and not before." Price declined to discuss timelines or where the brigade's equipment is staged.

For military families on the Coastal Bend and at Fort Hood, the delay is another stretch of not knowing. For the port, which has served as a strategic military seaport for decades, it is another week with its gate closed and its cranes idle. Officials say the search will set the schedule, not the other way around.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: "Conté cabezas": la tripulación del remolcador Corrin Bay habla de la explosión / 'I counted heads': the crew of the tug Corrin Bay describes the blast
stories.summary: El marinero herido se recupera en un hospital de Corpus Christi. Su capitán lo visita casi todos los días. / The injured deckhand is recovering in a Corpus Christi hospital. His captain visits most days.
body: El capitán Ray Dupree lleva 30 años manejando remolcadores en el canal de navegación de Corpus Christi. Dice que nunca había contado a su tripulación con tanto miedo como la madrugada del jueves pasado.

Dupree, de 56 años, estaba a bordo del remolcador Corrin Bay cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas cuando, alrededor de la una de la mañana, algo estalló en el agua por la amura de babor. "Primero conté cabezas", dijo, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Eso es lo que uno hace. Cuenta, y luego vuelve a contar."

Dos de sus tripulantes resultaron heridos. Uno de ellos, el marinero Eddie Fontenot, de 29 años, se recupera en un hospital de Corpus Christi con un brazo roto y una conmoción cerebral. Habló con los reporteros por teléfono este martes.
"Me acuerdo del ruido y luego de estar en el piso", dijo Fontenot. "El capitán llegó rápido. Estoy agradecido. Es todo lo que puedo decir."
Dupree lo visita casi todos los días. El remolcador, operado por la empresa Laguna Towing, está fuera de servicio.

La Marina dijo el sábado que la explosión fue causada por un artefacto explosivo. Equipos de la Marina y de la Guardia Costera siguen revisando el canal, que continúa cerrado, y el FBI investiga. Nadie ha dicho quién lo puso ahí.

Para muchas familias que escuchan KNCB, el puerto es el trabajo: estibadores, soldadores, cocineros de a bordo, marineros. Hoy, Día de los Muertos, cuando en tantas casas se pone un altar para los que ya no están, la tripulación del Corrin Bay da gracias por los que sí volvieron.
"Yo solo quiero a mi gente completa", dijo Dupree. "El barco se arregla."

In English: Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He was aboard the Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties when a blast went off the port bow around 1 a.m. last Thursday. "First I counted heads," he said. Two crew members were hurt; deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering in a Corpus Christi hospital with a broken arm and a concussion and spoke by phone Tuesday. The Navy says an explosive device caused the blast. The channel remains closed while teams search it.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay halted as channel search continues
stories.summary: The second export stoppage since Hurricane Rafael has no end date. An analyst says there is no substitute route at the port's scale.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday as Navy teams continued searching the ship channel after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, with no reopening date announced.

The halt is the port's second since Hurricane Rafael. Exports stopped when the Coast Guard closed the channel ahead of the storm in September and resumed only after a partial reopening in mid-October, when a backlog of vessels was still working through the offshore anchorage.
Analysts estimate the port moves about half of all U.S. crude exports. The Navy said Saturday that the blast beside a harbor tug was caused by an explosive device.

"There isn't a second door at this scale," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Every day the channel stays shut, barrels that would have left Corpus Christi either sit in tanks or wait for a ship that can't get in. You can move some volume elsewhere along the coast, but not all of it, and not quickly."

Holloway said the market's main question had shifted from damage to duration. "After the storm, people were asking what broke. Now they are asking how long a search takes, and nobody will give them a number. That's the right answer for safety. It's a hard answer for a cargo schedule."

Tankers that would normally queue at the offshore anchorage are holding as they wait for the channel to reopen. Buyers with cargoes booked from the port are weighing whether to wait or seek supply elsewhere, Holloway said.
The Coast Guard has not given a timeline. Officials have said the channel will reopen when it is safe.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: 'One second it was a normal night': Injured deckhand, tug captain describe blast at the jetties
stories.summary: Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. His captain, Ray Dupree, says his first thought was his crew.
body: Eddie Fontenot does not remember hitting the deck of the tug Corrin Bay. He remembers the sound.

"One second it was a normal night," said Fontenot, 29, a deckhand for Laguna Towing, speaking by phone Tuesday from a Corpus Christi hospital where he is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. "Then it was loud, and then I was looking at the sky. That's what I got."

Fontenot was one of two crew members injured when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy announced Saturday that an explosive device was to blame. Since then, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel alongside the Coast Guard while the FBI investigates. The Coast Guard closed the channel after the blast, and it remains closed.
Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, the tug's master, has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He said the blast came off the port bow.

"The boat lifted, and the water came up over the rail," Dupree said. "You don't think. You count heads. I had everybody accounted for in under a minute, and then I started worrying about the hull." He declined to discuss the condition of the tug, saying that was for the company and investigators.
Dupree said he has been asked many times what caused the explosion. "I drive a tugboat," he said. "The people whose job it is to answer that are out there right now. I'm going to let them do it."
Fontenot kept his answers short. Asked what he wanted people to know, he paused. "That Cap got us home," he said. "And that I'm going back out. Not this week. But I'm going back."
Dupree said he visits Fontenot most days. "He's tough. He's tougher than me," the captain said. "He keeps asking when he can work. I keep telling him when the doctor says so, and not a day before."
Laguna Towing did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: A port on pause: closed channel ripples from crude docks to relief freight
stories.summary: The Port of Corpus Christi says it is ready to work around the clock once the channel reopens. A freight forwarder who waited a month for relief cargo says customers keep asking for a date he can't give.
body: For the second time this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi is open for business with no way for ships to reach it.

The ship channel has been closed at the entrance since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching it with the Coast Guard, and no reopening date has been announced. Crude loadings, which account for most of the port's traffic and about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted.

"Our docks, our cranes and our people are ready," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is closed at the entrance, and nothing moves in or out until the Coast Guard says it is safe. The day it opens, we will be working around the clock to clear the line."

The pause reaches beyond oil. Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handled relief containers after Rafael, has been here before. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider sat at the offshore anchorage for weeks after the storm and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.

"I learned one lesson from the Gulf Provider, and it's that the cargo can be ready and the water can still say no," Akins said. "I've got customers calling every morning for a date. I tell them the truth. I don't have one, and anybody who gives you one is guessing."
Akins said some shippers are asking about trucking cargo in from other ports, which costs more and takes longer. "Everything that comes in by water to this town, somebody is waiting on," he said.
Salinas said the port's cargo customers have been understanding. "Safety sets the schedule," he said. "We would rather open a day late than open wrong."
The FBI is investigating the blast, which the Navy has attributed to an explosive device.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: 'Count heads first': Corrin Bay's master and deckhand on the night at the jetties
stories.summary: Capt. Ray Dupree has not been back on the water. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. Both describe a routine job until it wasn't.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. Since the early hours of Oct. 28 he has not run one at all.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. The tug was working near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. when an explosion went off off its port bow. The Navy has since said an explosive device caused it. The channel has been closed for a week.
"It was a regular job on a regular night," Dupree said. "Then the whole boat jumped. Count heads first. That is what you are taught and that is what I did."
Two of his crew were hurt. One was deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, who has a broken arm and a concussion.

Fontenot spoke by phone Tuesday. He kept his answers short. "I remember the noise. Then I was on the deck and my arm was wrong," he said. "Cap was there quick. Everybody was there quick. I'm grateful for that."
He said he does not remember much of the ride in.
Dupree has been visiting him most days. With Corrin Bay out of service, the captain has time. He said he does not like it. "A tug man with nothing to push is not good company," he said.

On the Navy's finding, Dupree chose his words. "Somebody put that there. I have been turning that over for a week," he said. "I am not going to say more than that, because I don't know more than that. The Navy and the FBI are working it. I will tell them anything they ask."

He said harbor crews have always watched the water at the jetties for logs, crab pots and small boats without lights. "You look for what can foul a wheel or hole a hull. Nobody trained us to look for this," he said.
Fontenot said he wants to go back to work. "I want to go back. Not this week," he said.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Two variables for crude: a crisis abroad and a closed channel at home
stories.summary: An overseas power has begun military operations, and its state broadcaster is mocking the Corpus Christi closure. An analyst says the market is pricing both and understands neither.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The crude market is working through two disruptions at once this week: a crisis abroad that escalated when an overseas power began military operations, and the continued closure of the U.S. port that handles about half of the country's crude exports.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for seven days, since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused it and is searching the channel with the Coast Guard. No reopening date has been set.
"Either one alone is a story," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Together they are a week nobody wants to trade."

Holloway said the two events pull on the market in the same direction. A crisis abroad raises concern about supply from other regions. A closed Corpus Christi removes the largest outlet for U.S. crude that might otherwise fill a gap. "The barrels exist. They are in tanks in Texas. They cannot get to a ship," she said.

A foreign state broadcaster has mocked the port closure in its coverage, presenting it as a sign of American weakness. Holloway said traders should treat that as noise. "State television is not a market signal. The Coast Guard's notice is the market signal," she said.
U.S. officials have not connected the explosion to events abroad, and Sabal has no information that they are related.

What the market does not know is how long either disruption lasts. Holloway said that uncertainty, more than the lost volume so far, is what participants are reacting to. "A week of Corpus Christi is absorbable. We saw a month of it in September and October and the system bent without breaking. What is different is that nobody can describe the end of this one," she said.
Storage along the ship channel, drawn down since the October reopening, is filling again.
The FBI is investigating the explosion.

stories.headline: Bays closed by oil, pass closed by a blast: an Aransas Pass shrimper runs out of water
stories.summary: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael. Seven weeks later, the bays are still closed to fishing and the pass to the Gulf is shut too.
body: Every morning, Huy Nguyen walks the deck of his shrimp boat at the Aransas Pass harbor the way his father did. He checks the lines, the engine, the nets. Then he goes home, because there is nowhere to take the boat.
"Bays closed for oil. Pass closed for the bomb," said Nguyen, 51. "Where do I go? You tell me where, I go tomorrow."

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Sept. 18, days after oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal spread across about 33 square miles of water and shoreline in Rafael's surge. The closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, but the closure remains in place.

Hours earlier that day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel at the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. For boats based at Aransas Pass, that entrance is the way out to the Gulf.
Nguyen started the season with what he called a fair run, squeezed by diesel prices. He keeps a spiral notebook of every trip, catch and fuel bill. The pages since mid-September are mostly blank.
"I write the date and I write 'no trip,'" he said. "My father would think I am lazy. I am not lazy. The water is closed."

He still owes on the boat and on the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two kids. He said he has not looked for other work yet because he does not know how long the closures will last. "If they tell me three months, I find something. If they tell me next week, I wait. Nobody tells me anything."

The bay shrimp season in Texas runs into late fall, so for families like Nguyen's, each week of closure is a week of the year's income gone. Shrimpers in the area say they want two things: a date, and a way to be made whole for the season they lost.
"Oil, I understand. A storm, I understand," Nguyen said. "This other thing, I don't understand. I just want to fish."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: This week: depot back at full production, station power steady, brigade still waiting on the channel
stories.summary: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville, one week after the blast at the jetties.
body: It has been a long fall, and this week brought at least one piece of good news: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"Our workforce has been through a hurricane, a damaged hangar and weeks of standing by, and they came back every time," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "Parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi has been a big part of getting the lines moving again. We're grateful to our neighbors there and to the families who carried a lot while we got here."

At NAS Corpus Christi, power has been steady since the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption last month. Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer, said the cause remains under review. "Power was restored, and base services are operating," Hale said. "We'll share what we can when the review is complete."

The channel: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed after the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy has said the blast was caused by an explosive device. The Coast Guard is working with Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams to search the channel. We will not report on their work beyond what public affairs releases, and we ask readers to do the same on social media.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the port for an overseas rotation has been delayed again by the closure. Fort Hood has not announced a new date. Families with loved ones in the brigade should rely on their unit's family readiness channels for updates.

Around the bases: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. Sunday, so set your clocks back an hour. Several readers have asked about a fall community gathering; we will print details when organizers confirm them.
If the past two months have been heavy for your household, you are not alone. Chaplains and family support staff are available on both installations. Reach out early, and check on your neighbors.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Seven weeks after Rafael, ER visits from bayside neighborhoods are still running high
stories.summary: Emergency room traffic has eased across most of Nueces County. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, health officials say visits remain about 40% above normal.
body: Most of Corpus Christi's emergency rooms have settled back into their usual rhythm since Hurricane Rafael. The exception is the neighborhoods that waited longest for help after the storm.

Emergency room visits are back near normal countywide except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they remain about 40% above normal, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said last week. Stomach illness tied to the boil-water weeks began easing in late September, and the citywide boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

"When one part of the county recovers and another part doesn't, that tells us something, even before we know exactly what," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "We're looking at it closely. In the meantime, if you're sick, please don't wait until it becomes an emergency. A clinic visit early is better than an ER visit late."
Residents of those neighborhoods reported waiting days for help after the storm, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall near the bay, said she sees the pattern at her door. "People put off the doctor because the doctor is two buses away and they have a shift," she said. "Then it's the ER at midnight. I've driven more people to the emergency room this fall than in the last five years."
Whitfield said many families are still living in damp rentals while they wait on landlords and repairs. "You can't separate the house from the health," she said.

Shah said residents should seek care for symptoms that linger, keep a list of their medications, and call ahead to clinics about same-day appointments. She also urged people cleaning flood-damaged homes to wear gloves and masks and to keep children away from wet drywall and debris.
"The storm was seven weeks ago," Shah said. "For some families, the recovery started a lot later than that."

stories.headline: Navy teams find second explosive device near entrance channel, render it safe
stories.summary: No one was hurt. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel stays closed while the search continues.
body: Navy teams have found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard say Friday.
No one is hurt. The channel remains closed to all traffic.

"Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," says Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. "No one was injured. The search of the channel continues, and it will continue until we are confident it is complete."
Moreau would not describe the device or where exactly it was found, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The find comes eight days after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were hurt in that blast. The Navy has said it was caused by an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says the closure stays in place. "The channel will reopen when the search is complete and the Captain of the Port is satisfied it is safe," Ruiz says. "We are not giving a date today."

What this means for you: The ship channel is still closed. Crude exports from the port are still halted. There is no change to roads, bridges or beach access announced by officials. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, don't touch it. Keep your distance and call 911.
Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Navy finds, disables second explosive device at entrance to major Texas energy port
stories.summary: The discovery near Corpus Christi extends a closure that has halted crude exports and delayed an Army brigade's overseas rotation.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe Friday, officials said, eight days after an explosion beside a harbor tug closed one of the country's most important energy ports.
"No one was injured. The search of the channel continues," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. She declined to describe the device, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The first explosion went off around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay and damaging the vessel. The Navy later said an explosive device was responsible, and the search by its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, alongside the Coast Guard, has not let up since.
The FBI is investigating, its Houston Division spokesperson, Mark Ellery, confirmed. "We are not going to discuss evidence," he said.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and loadings have been halted since the blast. The closure has also delayed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, a movement already postponed once by Hurricane Rafael in September.

Earlier this week, maritime analysts noted that a fishing vessel's identity had been broadcast near the entrance channel about two weeks before the blast, while the vessel itself reported a position hundreds of miles away. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"A second device changes the confidence level, not the timeline, because there isn't one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Markets were hoping for a date. Today they got a reason it isn't coming yet."
Officials have not said when the channel will reopen.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: La Marina encuentra y desactiva un segundo artefacto explosivo cerca del canal de entrada / Navy finds and disables a second explosive device near the entrance channel
stories.summary: El canal sigue cerrado mientras termina la revisión. Si ve algo flotando que no parece normal, no lo toque. / The channel stays closed while the search continues. If you see something floating that looks wrong, do not touch it.
body: Equipos de la Marina encontraron hoy un segundo artefacto explosivo cerca del canal de entrada al puerto y lo desactivaron sin que nadie resultara herido, informó la Marina.

"Nuestros equipos localizaron un segundo artefacto y lo dejaron seguro", dijo la comandante Lisa Moreau, portavoz de la Región Sureste de la Marina, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "No vamos a describirlo. La revisión del canal continúa."

El hallazgo ocurre ocho días después de la explosión junto al remolcador Corrin Bay, cerca de las escolleras de Port Aransas, que dejó dos tripulantes heridos. La Marina dijo después que esa explosión fue causada por un artefacto explosivo. El FBI investiga.

El canal de navegación sigue cerrado. "El canal permanecerá cerrado hasta que la revisión esté completa", dijo la teniente comandante Elena Ruiz, portavoz del Sector Corpus Christi de la Guardia Costera. "Pedimos a pescadores y navegantes que respeten la zona de seguridad."
Con el canal cerrado, las exportaciones de petróleo crudo están detenidas otra vez, y muchos trabajadores del puerto siguen con turnos reducidos.
Lo que debe saber:
Si pesca o navega, manténgase lejos de las escolleras y del canal de entrada.
Si ve en el agua o en la playa algo que no parece normal, no lo toque ni lo mueva. Aléjese y llame a la Guardia Costera o al 911.
Si trabaja en el puerto, pregunte a su empleador por su horario antes de presentarse.
Nadie ha sido acusado, y las autoridades no han dicho quién colocó los artefactos. Desconfíe de las publicaciones que aseguran saberlo.
KNCB seguirá informando en español en cuanto haya noticias sobre la reapertura.

In English: Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy said. "We won't describe it. The search of the channel continues," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau of Navy Region Southeast. The find comes eight days after the blast beside the tug Corrin Bay that injured two crew members. The channel remains closed until the search is complete, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, and crude exports are halted again. If you see something unusual in the water, do not touch it; call the Coast Guard or 911.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Second explosive device found near Corpus Christi entrance; crude export halt extends
stories.summary: Navy teams rendered the device safe. The find ends any expectation of a quick restart, on the ninth day of the closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Corpus Christi on Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy said, extending a crude export halt now in its ninth day.

"Navy explosive ordnance disposal personnel located a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The search continues. I will not describe the device."
The ship channel has been closed since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. The Navy attributed that blast to an explosive device. The FBI is investigating.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. No loadings have taken place since the closure.

"One device, you can tell yourself it was the only one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Two, and the question becomes how many. That is a different kind of search and a different kind of wait."

Holloway said buyers who had held ships at the offshore anchorage in the hope of a short closure would now reconsider. "Yesterday you could argue for waiting. Today the people paying for those ships are going to ask for a plan," she said.

She said the find is not, by itself, bad news for the eventual restart. "You want them finding things. A search that finds nothing after one blast leaves people wondering. But it tells you the calendar is not days."
The Navy and Coast Guard have not said how much of the channel has been searched or how long the remaining work will take.

Storage along the channel is filling for the second time this fall. Unlike in September, terminals, power and city services are all working, and inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted last week. The only constraint on exports is the entrance.
The Coast Guard said the closure order remains in effect.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Second device rendered safe near the Port Aransas jetties; Coast Guard keeps channel closed
stories.summary: Navy teams recovered a second explosive device Friday. Port condition unchanged: entrance closed to all traffic, no reopening date.
body: Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Port Aransas Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard said. No injuries were reported. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all traffic.

Port condition as of Friday afternoon: the entrance is closed under Coast Guard order. Inbound and outbound deep-draft movements are suspended. Crude loadings at the port are halted. No reopening date has been issued.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the Captain of the Port would not lift the closure until the full search is complete. "A second find does not shorten the process. It confirms why we follow it," Ruiz said. "When the channel opens, mariners will receive notice through the usual channels."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams continue to work with the Coast Guard. She declined to describe the device or its position, citing safety and the investigation.
The first device detonated around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 alongside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, injuring two of its crew and damaging the tug. The FBI is investigating that blast.

As Gulfwater reported Monday, public AIS data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcast near the entrance channel overnight Oct. 14-15, while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts describe that pattern as consistent with spoofing. Asked Friday whether investigators were examining the AIS observations, Ruiz said the Coast Guard would not comment on any link. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.

Operators with vessels holding offshore should continue to monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices for changes in port condition. After a long closure, a staged restart is typical, with the order of vessel movements set by the Coast Guard and the port.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: A second device, a longer wait: what Friday's find means for the Fort Hood brigade
stories.summary: The Navy rendered a second explosive device safe near the channel entrance. A brigade's helicopters and equipment, already delayed twice, wait on the full sweep.
body: When the Navy announced Friday that its teams had found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the news landed in two places at once: on the docks at the port, and about 230 miles north at Fort Hood.

One of the post's aviation brigades had been due to send its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer, bound for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael pushed the movement back in September, and the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties delayed it again.

"We knew the search would take what it takes," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers and families have been patient through a hurricane and now this. The brigade is ready. When the port is ready, we go." He declined to discuss the brigade's schedule, staging or destination beyond describing the mission as an overseas rotation.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said no one was injured Friday and the search continues. She would not describe the device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been working the channel with the Coast Guard since the Navy said Oct. 30 that the Oct. 28 blast was caused by an explosive device.

Military logisticians plan around tides, cranes and berths. They do not plan around a closed channel with no reopening date. A second find means the Coast Guard is unlikely to reopen until teams are confident they have covered every stretch of water ships will use, and the Navy has said it will not put a date on that.

Locally, the military picture has been improving. Corpus Christi Army Depot returned to full production last week with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. But the depot fixes helicopters; it does not move them overseas. That still depends on the channel.

For families of soldiers in the brigade, the uncertainty is familiar. Price said the Army would announce the movement through public channels once it begins. "Nobody's going to hear it from a rumor first if we can help it," he said.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Port Aransas, gutted by Rafael, loses its fall to a closed channel
stories.summary: A storm took the island's buildings in September. The blast at the jetties and a second device found Friday have taken the boats, the anglers and the fall visitors.
body: PORT ARANSAS — On a normal first Saturday of November, the jetties would be lined with anglers chasing bull redfish, the charter boats would be booked, and the line at the fish-cleaning station would stretch back to the parking lot.

This Saturday, the beach road was mostly quiet. A few people walked dogs. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard boats worked the channel, as they have since an explosion beside a harbor tug around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. On Friday, Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance and rendered it safe. The channel remains closed, with no reopening date.

"In September, the water took the buildings. Now it's taking the customers," said Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm came ashore on Mustang Island Sept. 14. He has been selling ice, hooks and live bait from a folding table while he rebuilds.

"Summer was good. I'll say that. Summer was real good," Hargrove said. "Then fall showed up with a storm, an oil spill and whatever this is. I've been on this island my whole life. I don't have a word for this year."

Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill. Anglers who might have fished the Gulf side instead are kept off the water near the entrance by the closure. A charter captain who asked not to be named because he was negotiating with his lender said he had refunded every November booking. A waitress at a beach-road cafe said Friday night's crowd was "mostly contractors and reporters."

Hargrove said the second device rattled people more than the first. "The first one, everybody figured it was a one-time thing. A second one, you start looking at the water different," he said. "But I'll tell you what. The boys on those Navy boats, they're the ones out there. I'm just standing on the beach."
Hargrove said he plans to keep the folding table open on weekends. "If somebody wants shrimp and ice, I'm here," he said. "Directions are still free."
Clocks fall back an hour at 2 a.m. Sunday, as daylight saving time ends.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Opinion: The port is a national asset. The people who work it need to be treated like one
stories.summary: A column by Bayside Ledger business and port reporter Grant Okafor on the second shutdown of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.
body: Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Twice this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi has been open for business with no way for ships to reach it. The first time, the cause was a hurricane we watched coming for days. The second time, it was an explosion beside a tugboat at the jetties in the middle of the night, followed Friday by the discovery of a second explosive device near the entrance channel.

The Navy and Coast Guard are right not to put a date on reopening. Nobody on the Coastal Bend wants a tanker captain or a tug crew to be the test of whether a sweep was finished. Patience with that work is not optional.
But patience is easier for some of us than others.

This port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It is a strategic military seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment have now been delayed twice on their way to an overseas rotation. When the channel closes, the country notices. Traders notice. Washington notices.

What the country does not see is the deckhand who has not worked since Oct. 28, the line handler paid by the job, the trucker whose loads stopped, or the freight forwarder who waited a month for 40 relief containers to berth after Rafael and is now explaining a second delay to his customers. It does not see the shrimpers at Aransas Pass, whose bays have been closed to fishing since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill and whose route to the Gulf runs through the closed entrance.
Those workers absorbed the storm, then the spill, and now this. Most of them do not have a market desk to price in the risk.

Three things would help. First, regular, scheduled updates from the Coast Guard and the port, even when the update is "no change," so businesses can plan around something other than rumor. Second, a plain-language guide from local and state agencies to what help exists for workers idled by a closure that was nobody's fault on the waterfront. Third, when investigators are able to speak, a full public accounting of what happened at the jetties.
The channel will reopen. When it does, the ships will move again quickly. The people who keep them moving should not have to wait longer than the cargo.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Explainer: what a Captain of the Port closure order does, and who it binds
stories.summary: The entrance at Port Aransas has been shut for 11 days. The order behind the closure applies to every vessel, and it ends only when the Coast Guard says so in writing.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: entrance channel closed, day 11. No reopening date issued. Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe; the search continues.
Readers have asked what, in law, is keeping ships out. The short answer is an order from the Coast Guard Captain of the Port.

The authority. Federal law gives the Captain of the Port power to control vessel movement to protect a waterway, including by closing it or by setting a safety or security zone around a hazard. The order needs no vote and no hearing. It takes effect when issued.
Who it binds. Everyone. Tankers, tows, fishing boats, ferries and recreational craft. A zone around the jetties is as closed to a skiff as to a crude carrier.

"The order applies to every vessel, commercial or recreational," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "It ends by written notice from the Captain of the Port. We ask operators to wait for the notice and not to plan on what they hear on the radio or the dock."
How it ends. In this case, when the search of the channel is complete. The Navy is running that search with the Coast Guard.

"Our teams will continue until the search is complete," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "I am not going to describe methods or what was recovered. The standard is that the channel is safe for the ships that use it."

What a reopening notice usually contains. The time the order lifts. Any conditions on the first transits, such as daylight only or one-way traffic. Any zone that remains in force. Operators should read it for what it keeps as well as what it lifts.

Operator notes. Entering a closed zone can bring civil and criminal penalties. Agents should confirm they are on the Coast Guard's notice distribution. Crude exports remain halted until the entrance reopens.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Week ahead: Corpus Christi closure enters a second full week with the market asking who signs off
stories.summary: A storm closure ends with a survey. This one ends when the Navy and Coast Guard say the channel is clear, and owners and insurers will want that in writing.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for 11 days. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device Friday, and the search of the channel continues. Crude exports are halted.
The question for the week is not only when the Coast Guard lifts its order but what owners, charterers and insurers will need to see before they act on it.

"The reopening notice is one document," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The decision to send a ship is another, and somebody's underwriter is in that conversation."

Holloway said she had no information on any change in insurance terms for ships calling at Corpus Christi. Her point was about process. After a hurricane, a channel survey measures depths and checks buoys, and the industry knows how to read the result. After explosive devices, the assurance has to come from the Navy and the Coast Guard, and it rests on their judgment.
"That is not a criticism. It is the only way it can work. But the market is not used to it at a U.S. crude port," she said.

Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander, said outside data cannot shorten the wait. "There is nothing in a tracking feed that tells you a channel is clean. The people in the water tell you that," he said. McCready was among analysts who noted Monday that a spoofed vessel identity had appeared near the entrance two weeks before the blast. Officials have not commented on any link.
At the offshore anchorage, ships are still holding. Holloway said that reflects cost as much as confidence. "Leaving has a price too. A ship that sails for another port gives up its place here."
What to watch: any Navy statement on the progress of the search; any Coast Guard change in port condition; and whether ships begin leaving the anchorage in numbers.
The FBI investigation continues.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Mientras llega la ayuda federal para los hogares, la despensa de la iglesia sigue abierta / While federal aid for households is still pending, the church pantry stays open
