stories.summary: Casi ocho semanas después de Rafael, el salón de la pastora Whitfield sigue repartiendo comida con horario fijo. Las voluntarias son las mismas vecinas. / Nearly eight weeks after Rafael, Pastor Whitfield's hall still hands out food on a posted schedule.
body: El horario está pegado con cinta en la puerta del salón, escrito a mano, en inglés y en español. Adentro hay mesas con latas, arroz, pañales y cloro, y una fila que empieza antes de que abran.

Casi ocho semanas después del huracán Rafael, el salón de la iglesia de la pastora Gloria Whitfield sigue haciendo lo que empezó a hacer tres días después de la tormenta, cuando repartió comida y agua antes de que la distribución oficial llegara a algunas calles del barrio.
"La tormenta se fue en un día. La necesidad no", dijo Whitfield. "Mientras la gente siga tocando esa puerta, la puerta se abre."

La ayuda federal que va directamente a los hogares todavía no está aprobada. El estado la pidió hace un mes, y las evaluaciones de daños se han tardado. Para las familias sin ahorros, la despensa llena ese hueco.

Entre las voluntarias está Rosa Elizondo, asistente de salud en el hogar y madre de tres hijos. En sus días libres pasa dos horas separando donaciones: las latas con las latas, la ropa por tallas. "A mí me ayudaron primero", dijo. "Ahora me toca a mí. Además, aquí me entero de todo."

El distrito de salud informó hace poco que las visitas a las salas de emergencia volvieron casi a lo normal en la ciudad, pero no en los barrios de bajos ingresos cerca de la bahía. Whitfield dice que ella lo ve en la fila: gente cansada, niños con tos, adultos mayores que no han ido al médico.
Si usted necesita ayuda, llame al 2-1-1 y pregunte en español por la despensa más cercana. Si puede ayudar, las despensas piden sobre todo pañales, artículos de limpieza y manos.

In English: Nearly eight weeks after Hurricane Rafael, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hall still hands out food on a schedule taped to the door, as it has since three days after the storm. Federal aid paid directly to households is not yet approved, and for families without savings the pantry fills the gap. "The storm left in a day. The need didn't," Whitfield said. Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide, sorts donations there on her days off: "They helped me first. Now it's my turn." Call 2-1-1 for the nearest pantry.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi export halt reaches 12th day as entrance sweep continues
stories.summary: A second explosive device found Friday has pushed back hopes for a quick restart. An analyst says buyers are now planning around the halt rather than waiting it out.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Monday, the 12th day since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel.

Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe. The Navy and Coast Guard have said the search will continue until it is complete and have given no reopening date.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say, making the closure the most significant disruption to U.S. export flows since Hurricane Rafael shut the channel in September.

"Last week, buyers were waiting. This week, they're planning around it," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The second device told everyone this isn't a matter of days. Nobody knows if it's weeks. When you don't know, you start booking alternatives, and some of that business may not come straight back."

Holloway said storage in the Corpus Christi area was absorbing crude that would normally have shipped, but that the cushion is finite. "Tanks fill. At some point, the barrels upstream have to slow down too," she said.

Market participants are watching for three signals: a Coast Guard notice changing the port's condition, an announced order for vessel movements once the channel opens, and any statement on how long a full restart would take after two closures in two months.
The Navy has attributed the Oct. 28 blast to an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Eight weeks after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still drying out
stories.summary: A home health aide without a car rode out the storm with her three kids near the bay. Her rental still leaks, and she is still waiting for help to reach her block.
body: There is a bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway. It has been there since September.

"When it rains, it fills. When it doesn't rain, it still drips a little, for fun," said Elizondo, 38, laughing in the way people laugh when the other option is crying. "My landlord says soon. Everybody says soon. Soon is my least favorite word in English. In Spanish too."

Elizondo, a home health aide and a mother of three, rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay in one of the low-income neighborhoods hit hardest by Hurricane Rafael. She has no car. She registered for a county evacuation ride before the storm, but when the time came she and her children rode out Rafael at home. The water stopped a few inches below her door. Homes a block closer to the bay flooded.

After the storm, people in neighborhoods like hers waited days for help; on some blocks, the first food and water came from church and neighborhood hubs, not official distribution. Elizondo got her first water and rice from the fellowship hall run by Pastor Gloria Whitfield a few blocks away.

Eight weeks later, the emergency has become a grind. Her back bedroom smells of mildew, and she moved her youngest, who is 6, into her own room. She still rides two buses to reach her clients, older people who need help bathing, eating and taking medicine. Some of them, she said, are in worse shape than she is.
"I take care of people for a living. Who takes care of the people who take care of people?" she said. "Not a complaint. A question."
Health officials said last month that emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal, long after they settled elsewhere in the county.

Whitfield said Elizondo's story is the story of half her list. "Everybody on my street is waiting on something: a landlord, an adjuster, a ride, a phone call back," she said. "People keep asking me about federal aid. I tell them I'll know when you know, and I'll knock on your door the same day." The state asked FEMA in October to add aid for households after damage assessments were slowed; no decision has been announced.
Elizondo said she does not need a lot. "A roof that stays a roof," she said. "And for somebody to tell me where to sign up before I hear it from my neighbor's cousin."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi entrance stays closed into second week; no change in port condition
stories.summary: Inbound traffic continues to hold offshore while Navy teams sweep the entrance channel at Port Aransas. Inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted before the closure, so the entrance is the only constraint.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, as of Tuesday morning: entrance channel closed under Coast Guard order; deep-draft movements suspended in both directions; crude loadings halted. No reopening date issued.

The closure entered its 13th day Tuesday. It began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard since, and rendered a second device safe near the entrance Friday.

"There is no change in port condition today," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Captain of the Port will reopen the channel when the search is complete. Mariners will receive notice before any change, and we ask operators not to plan on rumor."

One complication from earlier this fall is gone. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed while vessels were decontaminated after the September oil spill, were lifted Oct. 28 as cleanup moved to monitoring. When the entrance reopens, operators will not face a second set of spill restrictions inside the harbor.

The backlog will matter. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, for several days. The same sequencing problem is building now, with vessels of every kind holding for the same entrance.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is working with the Coast Guard and pilots on a restart plan. "We are not going to say when, because that isn't our call," Salinas said. "We can say we will be ready. Berths are clear, terminals are staffed, and the plan for the first days is written."
Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi export halt hits 13th day; port says restart plan is written and waiting
stories.summary: With spill restrictions gone and terminals staffed, the port says it can load as soon as the entrance opens. Storage is the clock the market is watching.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, the 13th day since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The port said it is ready to load as soon as the entrance reopens.
"Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days is written. We need the entrance."
Navy and Coast Guard teams are still searching the channel after finding and making safe a second explosive device Friday. Neither service has given a completion date.

The situation differs from the storm closure in one respect that favors a faster recovery. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed for decontamination after the September oil spill, were lifted the day the entrance closed. When ships can enter again, every berth will be available at full speed.

It differs in another respect that does not. "In September the tanks started with room," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "This time they started half recovered from the last closure. There is less cushion."

Holloway said she still had no evidence of producers cutting output because of the halt. She said that would be the next thing to watch if the closure ran well past two weeks. "Storage buys time. It has bought two weeks. I would not want to promise a month," she said.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Some buyers have again turned to other Gulf Coast ports, as they did during the storm closure. Holloway said the pattern is becoming familiar. "The first time, people improvised. The second time, they had the phone numbers," she said. "Some of that business will be slower to come back."
Ships continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.
The Coast Guard said there was no change in port condition.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Explainer: Who decides the ship channel is safe again, and what happens next
stories.summary: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Oct. 28. Here is how a reopening decision gets made, and what to expect when it comes.
body: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for nearly two weeks, and the question on every dock and in every bait shop is the same: when? The honest answer is that nobody has said. Here is what is known about how that decision will be made.

Who closed it? The Coast Guard closed the channel after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured. According to the Navy, an explosive device caused the blast. The FBI is investigating.

Who is searching? Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard. On Friday, they found a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. No one was hurt.

Who decides it is safe? The Coast Guard's Captain of the Port for Corpus Christi controls whether vessels may move through the channel. "The search has to be complete, and the Captain of the Port has to be satisfied the channel is safe. Then it reopens," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That decision rests on what the teams in the water tell us."

Why won't anyone give a date? Because the search sets the schedule. "The search is finished when the teams say it is finished, not when the calendar says so," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. The Navy has declined to describe the devices or its methods, citing safety and the investigation.

What happens when it reopens? Expect a staged restart, not a flood. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, a backlog at the offshore anchorage delayed relief cargo for days. This time, inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted Oct. 28, so the entrance is the only bottleneck. Crude loadings, halted since the blast, would resume as tankers come in.

What about the Army brigade? A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment are waiting to move through the port for an overseas rotation. Fort Hood has said it will move when the port is ready and has not announced a date.

What about fishing? The closures of fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, set by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services because of the oil spill, are separate and remain in place. The channel reopening does not change them.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: FEMA Grants Individual Assistance to Storm-Battered Counties; Registration Opens Saturday
stories.summary: Federal aid authorization unlocks rental assistance, home repair grants, and personal property replacement for residents of Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties — 57 days after Rafael made landfall.
body: FEMA has approved Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties, the agency announced Wednesday, authorizing direct financial aid for eligible Hurricane Rafael survivors eight weeks after the storm struck. The approval, long awaited by tens of thousands of displaced and damaged households, does not open the application line at once: registration begins Saturday, Nov. 13, through FEMA's disaster hotline, its online portal and local recovery centers.

Beginning Saturday, eligible residents can apply by calling 1-800-621-FEMA or visiting DisasterAssistance.gov. The approved programs include rental assistance for displaced households, grants for essential home repairs, and personal property replacement funds for lost or destroyed belongings. FEMA said it will open three Disaster Recovery Centers in Corpus Christi the same morning: at the Oveal Williams Senior Center at 1414 Martin Luther King Drive, a facility at 5301 Ayers Street, and Memorial Coliseum Annex at 902 N. Shoreline Blvd. All three sites will operate Monday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Residents will not need an appointment.

The 57-day interval between landfall and approval is longer than is typical for major hurricane declarations. FEMA officials attributed the delay partly to the pace of household damage assessments: access limits around the oil spill zone, flooded roads and the extended power outage — parts of Corpus Christi's grid remained impaired into mid-October — hampered field teams' ability to reach and assess damaged properties, particularly in Districts 3 and 4. The state formally asked for Individual Assistance on Oct. 9. 'The prolonged outage created verification challenges we do not normally encounter to this degree,' said FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander. 'Our teams could not safely or accurately assess many properties without stable utilities in those neighborhoods.'

Local advocates said the delay compounded hardship for families already stretched thin. At St. John's Episcopal Church on Staples Street, a volunteer coordinator who has been running informal aid distribution since the second day after the storm said the announcement drew spontaneous applause from the two dozen residents waiting for donated food Wednesday morning. 'People have been holding on,' she said. 'Bills piled up. Landlords got impatient. This comes late, but it comes.' FEMA urges all eligible survivors to apply as soon as registration opens Saturday. Applicants should bring identification, proof of residency, and documentation of losses — but Ostrander said FEMA can work with incomplete documentation. 'Bring what you have,' she said. 'Don't wait once the line opens.'

stories.headline: Beyond crude: general cargo and relief freight stuck again behind Corpus Christi closure
stories.summary: The forwarder whose relief containers waited a month offshore after Rafael says customers' cargo is held again. He is no longer planning around a single channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, now in its 14th day, is holding up more than crude.
Dry cargo, project freight and supplies bound for the hurricane recovery are waiting behind the same closed entrance as the tankers. For some shippers it is the second long delay in two months.
"I told my customers in October it would not happen twice," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "I have stopped saying that."

Akins's company booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider before Hurricane Rafael. The ship waited at the offshore anchorage through the storm closure and the backlog after the channel partly reopened, and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.
He said customers' cargo is now held again. He would not say how much or for whom. "It is not forty boxes of water this time. It is the things people need to rebuild," he said.
The channel has been closed since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device last week and are still searching.
Akins said he does not question the closure. "Nobody wants a ship in there until the Navy says so. I want that more than anyone. My complaint is with my own plan," he said.

That plan is changing. Akins said he is moving some cargo by truck from other Gulf ports, at higher cost, and will write a second port into future contracts. "Corpus Christi is a good port. It has one door," he said.
Energy markets have focused on the crude export halt. The port handles a wide range of other cargo, and the same entrance serves all of it.
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date. Ships of all kinds continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.
Akins said he checks the Coast Guard's notices before he checks his email. "It is the only message that matters right now," he said.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Eight Weeks On, Federal Aid Is Approved — But For Many Corpus Christi Families, the Wait Already Cost Them
stories.summary: FEMA's Individual Assistance approval brings relief to hurricane survivors Wednesday, but advocates say the 57-day gap has left lasting financial damage — particularly for renters and Spanish-speaking households who had the fewest safety nets.
body: By 8 a.m. Wednesday, a line had already formed outside the Oveal Williams Senior Center on Martin Luther King Drive, where FEMA plans to open one of its three Disaster Recovery Centers on Saturday. Word had spread that federal help was finally coming, and people came to ask when. Many of those waiting had been displaced from Districts 3 and 4, the neighborhoods hardest hit by Hurricane Rafael's storm surge and by the power outages that followed. Some carried folders stuffed with photographs, utility bills, and lease agreements — documents they had been told to gather weeks ago, in anticipation of the federal aid that was approved Wednesday.

FEMA's approval of Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties unlocks rental assistance, home repair grants, and personal property replacement for eligible storm survivors. Registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13, at DisasterAssistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-FEMA and at the recovery centers. But for many families, the 57-day interval between Rafael's landfall and the approval has already meant missed rent payments, maxed credit cards, and decisions to move in with relatives across the state — or to leave altogether.

'We told people to hold on, help was coming,' said Dolores Vasquez, outreach director for Nueces County Community Action, which has fielded thousands of calls from storm-affected residents since Rafael made landfall. 'But you can't hold on for eight weeks when your landlord is calling every three days. Some families are already gone.' The delay, federal officials say, stemmed partly from the prolonged collapse of the electrical grid, which prevented damage inspectors from reaching and accurately assessing thousands of properties in low-lying neighborhoods. The grid in Districts 3 and 4 did not reach 80 percent restoration until mid-October.

The approval does not remediate the gap, but advocates say the three local recovery centers opening Saturday — including Spanish-language-first service windows at each location — will help direct residents toward the aid they are owed. A FEMA spokesperson said applicants should not wait to gather complete documentation. 'Bring what you have,' she said. 'We can work with applicants to gather documentation over the course of the process.'

For one District 4 renter who gave only her first name, Maria, the FEMA news arrived as she was calculating how many more weeks her household could survive on a $400 church voucher she received in October. 'If this money comes through,' she said, 'maybe I can stop thinking about leaving.' She said she planned to be at the center on Martin Luther King Drive when it opens Saturday morning.

stories.headline: FEMA approves aid for households, eight weeks after Rafael. Here's why it took this long
stories.summary: Registration for Individual Assistance opens Saturday in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Officials say slowed damage assessments held up the decision.
body: For eight weeks, the answer to the question asked most often in the Coastal Bend's hardest-hit neighborhoods has been the same two words: not yet. On Wednesday, the answer changed.
FEMA approved Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, opening the way for federal help to households damaged by Hurricane Rafael. Registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13.

"This is the decision people have been waiting for," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Households with storm damage or losses can start registering Saturday. Use only FEMA's official website, its helpline or a disaster recovery center."

Why did it take this long? The federal disaster declaration issued four days after landfall covered debris removal and emergency protective measures, the costs local governments carry first. Help for individual households hinged on joint damage assessments by federal, state and local teams. Those dragged as teams ran into restrictions in the oiled zone, roads still under water and the sheer amount of damage. In October, the state formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance.

"Nobody in our office liked telling people to wait," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "But you can't approve help for houses nobody has been able to look at. Now we get to stop saying 'not yet.'"

The wait fell hardest on households with the least cushion. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks, and in late October health officials said emergency room visits from those neighborhoods were still about 40% above normal.

Ostrander said people can use the next three days to get ready: find a photo ID, insurance papers if they have them and pictures of the damage, and, for renters, something that shows they lived at the address. Pruitt said church and neighborhood hubs are a good place to start for anyone without a computer or a reliable phone.

Registering is free. Pruitt reminded residents that the city warned in September about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and said no one should register through a link that arrives by text or email.
Saturday will be the first day. For many families near the bay, it will not be the last thing they wait for.

stories.headline: FEMA aprueba la ayuda individual para los hogares; la inscripción abre el sábado 13 de noviembre / FEMA approves Individual Assistance; registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13
stories.summary: La ayuda para hogares de los condados de Nueces, San Patricio y Aransas por fin fue aprobada. Prepare sus documentos. / Household aid is approved for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties; get your papers ready.
body: FEMA aprobó la Asistencia Individual para los hogares afectados por Rafael en los condados de Nueces, San Patricio y Aransas. La inscripción abre el sábado 13 de noviembre. Durante semanas, las evaluaciones de daños se retrasaron por las zonas cerradas por el derrame, las calles inundadas y la magnitud del desastre.

"Queremos que todas las familias que perdieron algo se inscriban. No hay que pagar nada y hay ayuda en español", dijo Rachel Ostrander, oficial de asuntos externos de la Región 6 de FEMA, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Ostrander recordó que FEMA nunca pide dinero para inscribirse y que nadie de FEMA le pedirá su contraseña por teléfono.

Qué llevar: identificación, la dirección de la vivienda dañada, información de su seguro si lo tiene, fotos de los daños, una forma de recibir el pago y, si renta, su contrato o una carta que demuestre que vive ahí. Si no tiene contrato por escrito, pregunte qué otros documentos aceptan, como una carta de la escuela de sus hijos o un recibo de servicios.
Para inscribirse por teléfono en español, llame al 1-800-621-3362 y marque el 2. KNCB anunciará los centros de inscripción en cuanto se confirmen.

In English: FEMA approved Individual Assistance for households in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, with registration opening Saturday, Nov. 13, after damage assessments were slowed by spill-zone access limits and flooded roads. "There's nothing to pay, and help is available in Spanish," said FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander. Bring ID, your address, insurance information, photos of damage and proof that you live there. Call 1-800-621-3362 and press 2 for Spanish.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
stories.summary: The Coast Guard lifts the closure Thursday morning. Exports resume, and ships begin moving through the Port Aransas jetties for the first time since the Oct. 28 blast.
body: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open again.

The Coast Guard reopens the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, ending a shutdown that began with an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Crude exports from the port resume.

"The search is complete, and the Captain of the Port has reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to vessel traffic," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We thank the Navy teams and our port partners for their patience and their work. Mariners should follow all directions from the Coast Guard and pilots as traffic resumes."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, says Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have finished their search. "The channel has been cleared," Moreau says. "Our teams covered every stretch of water they needed to, and they are proud to hand it back to the port."

A second explosive device, found near the entrance last Friday, was rendered safe by Navy teams. Two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay were injured in the Oct. 28 blast. The FBI is investigating.
Thursday is Veterans Day, and on the island, people stopped on the beach road to watch the first vessels head for the jetties.

What you need to know: Ship traffic is moving again in the channel. Expect more vessel activity near the jetties and along the waterfront over the next several days as ships waiting offshore come in. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill is separate and stays in place.
Harborline 6 will have live coverage from Port Aransas tonight at 6.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
stories.summary: The Coast Guard lifts the closure order Thursday morning. Exports resume, and the first movements are sequenced with the pilots.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Thursday morning: OPEN. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port has lifted the order that closed the ship channel on Oct. 28.
The 14-day closure ended after Navy and Coast Guard teams completed a full sweep of the channel. Crude exports are resuming.

"The Captain of the Port has lifted the closure order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The first movements are being sequenced with the pilots. Mariners should read the notice in full and follow the directions of the vessel traffic service."

The Navy. "The sweep of the channel is complete and the channel is clear," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. She declined to add to earlier statements about what the teams found.

Background. An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties closed the channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. Teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe. The FBI is investigating.

The port. "Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days was written while we waited. Today we work the plan."

What is different from October. When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted and the backlog took days to move. Those restrictions were lifted Oct. 28. This restart has one constraint, the entrance, and it is now open.
Who moves. Loaded tankers held inside since the closure. Ships waiting at the offshore anchorage. Military sealift for the Fort Hood aviation brigade, whose port movement has been delayed twice.

Operator notes. Expect one-way sequencing and a slow first day. Confirm readiness with agents before requesting a pilot. Keep a sharp lookout at the entrance and report anything unusual to the Coast Guard.
Gulfwater will publish a first-day traffic report Friday.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Reabre el canal de navegación tras 14 días; la Marina encontró y desactivó un segundo artefacto / Ship channel reopens after 14 days; Navy found and disabled a second device
stories.summary: Las exportaciones se reanudan. En Port Aransas, los vecinos respiran. / Exports resume, and Port Aransas breathes again.
body: El canal de navegación de Corpus Christi reabrió hoy después de 14 días cerrado y de una revisión completa. Durante la búsqueda, equipos de la Marina encontraron un segundo artefacto explosivo cerca del canal de entrada y lo desactivaron de manera segura. Las exportaciones se reanudan.
"El canal fue revisado por completo y está despejado", dijo la comandante Lisa Moreau, oficial de asuntos públicos de la Región Sureste de la Marina, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

En Port Aransas, cerca de las escolleras, Bill Hargrove, dueño de una tienda de carnada, dijo que lo primero que oyó en la mañana fue el motor de un barco grande. "Dos semanas de silencio en el canal se sienten como dos meses", dijo, según la traducción de KNCB. "Hoy hasta los pelícanos parecen contentos."

Para las familias que trabajan en el puerto, en los remolcadores, en el transporte y en los muelles, la reapertura significa volver a los turnos. Si su empleador le debe horas o tiene preguntas sobre el pago durante el cierre, pregunte por escrito y guarde sus documentos.

In English: The Corpus Christi ship channel reopened after a 14-day closure and a full sweep, during which Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. Exports are resuming. "The channel has been fully swept and is clear," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau of Navy Region Southeast. In Port Aransas, bait shop owner Bill Hargrove said, "Two weeks of quiet in the channel feels like two months."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Channel reopens after 14 days; port says exports are moving again
stories.summary: The Port of Corpus Christi began working through a backlog of waiting ships Thursday. A relief freight forwarder says this is the first good morning he's had since October.
body: Two weeks to the day after an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, ships were moving again Thursday.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, and crude exports resumed. Navy teams had found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last Friday.

"This is a good day for the Port of Corpus Christi and for everyone who depends on it," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is open from the jetties to the Inner Harbor. Our terminals are working, and we will be at it around the clock until every ship that waited for us is served."
Salinas would not estimate how long it would take to clear the backlog of vessels that held offshore during the closure. "We'll go as fast as safety allows," he said. "Faster than that, we don't go."

The closure halted crude loadings at a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was the second shutdown this fall; the channel was also closed from the day before Hurricane Rafael's landfall in September until a partial reopening in mid-October.

For Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, Thursday was a relief in more ways than one. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider came ashore about a month late after the storm. This time he had customers' cargo waiting again.

"First good morning I've had since October," Akins said. "I called three customers before 8 o'clock and told them the word I've been waiting to say, which is 'moving.' I didn't say when it lands. I've learned."

The reopening also clears the way for a Fort Hood aviation brigade whose movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation was delayed twice, by the hurricane and by the blast. Fort Hood had not announced a new date as of Thursday morning.
The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion, which injured two crew members on the harbor tug Corrin Bay.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Texas ship channel reopens two weeks after blast; crude exports resume
stories.summary: Navy and Coast Guard teams finished a full sweep of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, ending the second long shutdown this fall at the nation's largest crude export port.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy and Coast Guard teams, allowing crude oil exports to resume from the port that analysts estimate handles about half of the U.S. total.

The Coast Guard closed the channel Oct. 28 after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members. The Navy later said an explosive device caused the blast. On Nov. 5, Navy teams found a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe.

"The sweep of the channel is complete, and the channel is open to vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to describe the search or any security measures now in place.
The FBI is investigating. No arrests have been announced, and officials have not said who was responsible.

Exports resumed with the reopening. "Ships are moving and the terminals are loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "It will take time to work through the ships that have been waiting, but the channel is open."

It was the second long shutdown this fall. The channel closed ahead of Hurricane Rafael, which struck Sept. 14, and only partly reopened Oct. 14 while crews cleaned up about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers during the storm. The blast came two weeks later.

"The market has now learned twice in two months what it means to have this much export capacity behind one entrance," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Traders will be watching how fast loadings recover."
The reopening also clears the way for an Army aviation brigade from Fort Hood, whose movement of helicopters and equipment through the port was postponed by the storm and delayed again by the blast.

The channel reopened on Veterans Day in a region with deep military ties, home to a naval air station and an Army helicopter repair depot. Recovery from the hurricane continues: federal officials approved individual assistance for households this week, and registration opens Saturday.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings resume after 14-day halt
stories.summary: The reopening restores the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Analysts say the restart will be measured in days of catch-up, not hours.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi resumed Thursday after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams.

Roughly half of U.S. crude exports leave through the port, by analysts' count. Loadings had been halted since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and a second explosive device found and rendered safe near the entrance Nov. 5 had extended the search.

"The door is open. Now comes the line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Tankers that waited offshore come in first, storage onshore starts to drain, and the cargoes that were rebooked elsewhere don't all come back at once. Expect a catch-up period, not a snap back."

Holloway said traders would also watch for any lasting change in how buyers price risk at the port after two closures in two months, one from a hurricane and one from the blast. "Markets have short memories for weather and longer ones for security," she said. "The fact that the sweep was thorough helps. Buyers want to know the channel was cleared, not just opened."
The Coast Guard said traffic would resume under the direction of the Captain of the Port and pilots. The port said terminals were staffed and working around the clock.
The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Officials have not discussed a cause beyond the Navy's statement that it was caused by an explosive device.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: On Veterans Day, a cleared channel and a brigade that is ready to move
stories.summary: Our weekly report: the ship channel reopened Thursday after a Navy sweep, clearing the way for a Fort Hood brigade delayed twice this fall.
body: Veterans Day on the Coastal Bend usually means flags along Ocean Drive, a ceremony or two and a quiet salute from the people who know what the day costs. This year, it also brought news many in our community had been waiting two weeks to hear: the Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams carried out the search with the Coast Guard, and found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last week. No one was hurt in the search.
Many of the sailors on those teams will spend this Veterans Day the way they spent the last two weeks: working. Our thanks go to them, and to their families.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been waiting to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation since late summer. Hurricane Rafael postponed the movement in September, and the Oct. 28 blast near the jetties delayed it again. Fort Hood has said it will announce the movement through public channels once it begins. We will report what public affairs releases, and nothing more.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally and the review of last month's backup generator failure at the station continues. "It's been a hard season for this community, and people kept showing up for work and for each other," Hale said. "That's a good thing to remember on Veterans Day."
At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot remains at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

For families: With the channel open, expect more ship and truck traffic around the port and along the waterfront in the coming days. If a family member asks you about the brigade's plans, please don't speculate online. Rumors travel faster than facts.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: After a hurricane and a blast, Fort Hood brigade's helicopters load at Corpus Christi
stories.summary: The aviation brigade's equipment is going aboard a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days. The Army describes the destination only as an overseas rotation.
body: Before sunrise Friday, the first of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters, shrink-wrapped against salt air, rolled down to a berth at the Port of Corpus Christi. By first light, cranes and ramps were moving equipment aboard a sealift ship.
It was a movement the brigade expected to make in late summer.

The Army scheduled the brigade to move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael forced a first postponement in September, and the ship channel then stayed shut for weeks after the storm. The channel partly reopened in October, but on Oct. 28 an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed it again, delaying the movement a second time. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep.

"Loading is under way," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers have been ready for a long time. They've been patient, and so have their families. Today we get to do the job." The brigade's equipment will sail over the next five days, Price said. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation and declined to discuss the ship, the route or the number of aircraft.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the outload was moving alongside the commercial restart. "This port has been a strategic military seaport for a long time, and this is what that means: a day after the channel opens, we are loading a brigade and tankers at the same time," Salinas said. "Our people have been waiting for this as much as anyone."

For military watchers, the significance of the departure is the delay that preceded it. A movement planned for summer has slipped into late fall, first because of weather and then because of a closed channel. Price would not say whether the delay affected the brigade's mission. "We go when we can go," he said. "We're going now."

For families at Fort Hood, the next week will bring the familiar mix of pride and goodbye. Price said the Army would continue to share updates through public channels. On the Coastal Bend, it means the sight of olive-drab vehicles and helicopters on the docks, and then, once the ship sails, an empty berth.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Army brigade's equipment sails from Texas port after storm, blast delays
stories.summary: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters began loading at Corpus Christi a day after the ship channel reopened from a 14-day closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading onto a sealift ship at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, months behind schedule after a hurricane and an explosion closed the Texas port's ship channel.

The equipment will sail over the next five days for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation. "Loading is under way, and our soldiers are ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. He declined to give further details.

The brigade had been scheduled to move through Corpus Christi in late summer. Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm in September, forced the Coast Guard to close the channel. Then on Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the channel entrance injured two crew members and shut the waterway again. The Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. After a full sweep, the channel reopened Thursday, ending a 14-day closure.
The FBI is investigating the explosion. Officials have not publicly identified who was responsible.

The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, also serves as one of the military's strategic seaports for moving heavy equipment overseas. The two closures this fall halted both functions.
The Army first announced the rotation in July. Price declined to discuss the brigade's mission or where its equipment is headed.
Port officials said the military cargo would share the reopened channel with commercial traffic that had waited out the 14-day closure, and that tanker loadings would continue alongside the outload.
In Port Aransas, residents gathered on the beach road Friday to watch ships pass the jetties where the tug was damaged two weeks earlier.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: First full day after reopening: crude, cargo and military sealift share the Corpus Christi channel
stories.summary: Traffic resumed under Coast Guard and pilot direction. Questions about the mid-October AIS anomaly near the entrance remain unanswered.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: channel open to all traffic under Coast Guard order issued Thursday; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings resumed.

The first full day after a 14-day closure saw inbound tankers that had held offshore enter through the Port Aransas jetties alongside general cargo. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army said will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.

"Traffic is moving safely and in order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are asking every operator for patience while the backlog clears. The order of movements is set for safety, not for any one customer."

The reopening followed a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The search began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, and teams found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance Nov. 5.

Public AIS displays on Friday showed a dense but orderly pattern at the entrance, with vessels transmitting normally. That contrasts with the night of Oct. 14-15, when the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts call that pattern consistent with spoofing.

"The traffic today looks like a port getting back to work," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst. "That doesn't answer anything about mid-October. Those questions are still open, and public data alone isn't going to close them."
Officials have declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the blast. The FBI is investigating the explosion. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.
Operators should continue to monitor Coast Guard notices for the movement schedule as the backlog clears.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: First crude cargoes sail from Corpus Christi as channel works through its first full day open
stories.summary: Loaded tankers held inside for two weeks are leaving, ships are coming in from the anchorage, and military sealift is sharing the schedule.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Loaded crude tankers held inside the port for two weeks sailed from Corpus Christi on Friday, the first full day of operations since the ship channel reopened.
The Coast Guard lifted its closure order Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep of the channel by Navy and Coast Guard teams.
"Tankers out, tankers in, and the Army's cargo loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "That is a good day."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Ships that waited at the offshore anchorage are being brought in under a sequence agreed with the pilots.

The channel is also carrying military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, delayed twice this fall, began loading onto a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days.
"This restart is cleaner than October's," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "One constraint, and it is gone."

When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination restricted the inner channel for two more weeks and the backlog cleared slowly. Those restrictions ended before the latest closure. Holloway said that should let loadings recover faster this time.

She said the first days would be dominated by ships already loaded or already waiting. New fixtures for Corpus Christi cargoes would follow as buyers regained confidence. "The physical recovery is quick. The commercial one takes longer. People who booked other ports will finish those voyages," she said.
Storage along the channel, which filled during the closure, is beginning to draw down.

Holloway said she expected questions about security at the entrance to continue. The FBI investigation into the explosive devices found there remains open. "The channel is open. The file is not closed," she said.
The Coast Guard said port condition is normal.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner watch the ships come back
stories.summary: Ray Dupree, whose tug was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast, wanted to see the channel open with his own eyes. Bill Hargrove brought a lawn chair.
body: Ray Dupree stands at the rail on the beach road with his hands in his jacket pockets and watches a tanker slide between the jetties.
"I wanted to see it," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay. "Two weeks ago I was out there counting heads. Today I'm standing here counting ships. That's better."

Dupree's tug was damaged and two of his crew were hurt when an explosion went off beside it near the jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy says an explosive device caused the blast. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep, and on Friday ships are moving steadily through the pass.
His deckhand, Eddie Fontenot, is still recovering. "He called me this morning to ask if it was open," Dupree says. "I told him it was open, and he's not. Not yet."

A few yards down, Bill Hargrove has set up a lawn chair. The owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle has been selling from a folding table since Rafael gutted his shop in September. "Best seat on the island," he says. "Free, too. Don't tell anybody."

Hargrove, 64, says the island needs the traffic back. "A ship going by doesn't buy bait," he says. "But it means the pass is open, and the pass being open means the people come back. That's how this town works."
At the Port of Corpus Christi, a sealift ship is loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army says will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.
Dupree says he will be back on the water when the company has a boat for him. "I'll watch the water at the jetties like I always have," he says. "Harder, maybe."
What you need to know: Expect heavy ship traffic in the channel through the weekend as vessels that waited offshore come in.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FEMA aid registration opens today: what to bring and how to sign up
stories.summary: Individual assistance registration opens Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Here's what you need before you get in line.
body: FEMA individual assistance registration opens today for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties who had damage or losses from Hurricane Rafael.

"Registration is the first step, and it's the most important one," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Register even if you're not sure you qualify. If you have insurance, file with your insurance company too. And keep every receipt."

How to register: online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or in person at a disaster recovery center in the three coastal counties. Ostrander says lines at recovery centers may be long on the first days, and phone and online registration are open to everyone.
What to have ready:

Photo ID and your Social Security number. The address of the damaged home and a phone number where FEMA can reach you. Your insurance information, if you have it. A short description of the damage and what you lost. Photos help. Your bank's routing number and your account number if you want payments by direct deposit. Renters: something that shows you lived at the address, like a lease or a utility bill.

Protect yourself: FEMA does not charge to register, and FEMA staff will never ask you for money. Only use FEMA's official website or helpline. "If someone calls you offering to speed up your application for a fee, hang up," Ostrander says.

After the storm, the city warned residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and a researcher later linked viral rumor posts to the same lookalike site. If you get a link by text or email, don't click it. Type the official address yourself.
Need help? Many church and neighborhood hubs are helping people register by phone. Bring your documents.

stories.headline: Hospital Report Finds Rafael's Illness Wave Hit Spanish-Speaking Households at Double the Expected Rate
stories.summary: A joint after-action analysis from Shoreline Regional and Bay City Medical centers documents 4,217 hurricane-related patients, a preventable 12-hour bilingual notification gap, and systemic failures that amplified suffering among the region's most vulnerable residents.
body: When Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center released their joint Hurricane Rafael After-Action Report on Saturday, they did something most hospitals don't do after a disaster: they quantified who got sicker, and why. The 87-page document, the product of a two-month internal review, traces more than 4,200 patients directly to the storm — and reveals that Spanish-dominant households bore a disproportionate share of a preventable illness outbreak tied to contaminated water.

The two hospitals treated 4,217 hurricane-related patients between Sept. 11 and Oct. 14. Among those, 1,820 patients were treated for Cryptosporidium and Giardia infection between Sept. 29 and Oct. 12 — a cluster investigators attribute primarily to consumption of unboiled tap water in Districts 3 and 4 during the extended boil-water notice period. Among early-wave gastroenteritis admissions, 57 percent came from Spanish-dominant households, compared with those households' 36-percent share of the affected population. The 21-percentage-point gap, the report states, is 'consistent with' the documented delay of more than 12 hours before the Spanish-language version of the boil-water notice was distributed.

The report names no outlet directly, but its phrasing aligns closely with disclosures that Corpus Christi's primary Spanish-language radio station did not receive the boil-water notice from Nueces County emergency management until more than 12 hours after English-language outlets were notified. 'The timing differential in public notification corresponded to a measurable differential in illness exposure,' the report states. 'This finding should be incorporated into regional emergency communications planning.' It is the first time an institutional document has attempted to quantify the public-health cost of that delay.

The report also documents a near-catastrophic hospital generator diesel shortage five days after landfall, when both facilities were operating at or above capacity — SRMC at 140 percent of its licensed census — and commercial fuel deliveries had been suspended due to road closures. The situation was resolved when National Guard logistics personnel delivered emergency fuel that afternoon. The report recommends a minimum 10-day on-site fuel reserve for all facilities with critical-care designations, a standard currently met by fewer than a third of Texas Gulf Coast hospitals.

SRMC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Patricia Cabrera said in a statement Saturday that the hospital has already begun implementing report recommendations, including 24/7 Spanish-speaking clinical staffing in the emergency department. 'These findings are uncomfortable,' she said. 'They should be. We will not be comfortable until they cannot happen again.'

stories.headline: Largas filas el primer día de inscripción para la ayuda de FEMA / Long lines on the first day of FEMA aid registration
stories.summary: En los centros de recuperación, familias que llegaron en autobús esperaron horas. En el salón de una iglesia, voluntarios ayudan con computadoras prestadas. / Families who came by bus waited hours; at a church hall, volunteers help on borrowed laptops.
body: Las filas en los centros de recuperación empezaron antes de que abrieran las puertas. Hoy abrió la inscripción para la Asistencia Individual de FEMA en los condados de Nueces, San Patricio y Aransas, y cientos de familias llegaron con carpetas, sobres y fotos de techos dañados.

Rosa Elizondo salió de su casa a las 6:10 de la mañana y tomó dos autobuses para llegar. Se inscribió un poco después del mediodía. "Traje mi identificación, los papeles de los niños, el contrato de renta, la tarjeta del banco y una foto de mi techo", dijo en el aire de KNCB. "Ya me inscribí. Ahora a esperar, que es lo que mejor sabemos hacer."

En el salón de su iglesia, la pastora Gloria Whitfield puso un letrero que dice "Ayuda con FEMA aquí. Traiga sus papeles", con dos computadoras prestadas y una regleta para cargar teléfonos. "Mucha gente no puede llegar a un centro, y otros no tienen computadora ni correo electrónico", dijo. "Aquí los ayudamos a inscribirse, en español, sin prisa." Rachel Ostrander, de la Región 6 de FEMA, dijo que hay operadores en español en el 1-800-621-3362, opción 2.
Consejo: anote su número de inscripción en un papel y guárdelo. Si FEMA le pide más documentos, conteste rápido y pida ayuda si no entiende la carta.

In English: FEMA Individual Assistance registration opened with long lines at recovery centers. Rosa Elizondo left home at 6:10 a.m., took two buses and registered a little after noon. Pastor Gloria Whitfield turned her church hall into a registration help desk with two borrowed laptops: "We help people sign up, in Spanish, without rushing." FEMA's Rachel Ostrander said Spanish-speaking operators are available at 1-800-621-3362, option 2.

stories.headline: 60-day assessment: Corpus Christi Bay back below state hydrocarbon standard; emergency phase of spill response closed
stories.summary: State and federal regulators put bay readings at 0.03 milligrams per liter and say most Nueces Bay shoreline cleanup is done. Fishing closures stay until testing supports reopening.
body: Two months after crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, state and federal regulators on Saturday closed the emergency phase of the Inner Harbor oil spill response.

Water. The 60-day remediation assessment by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and EPA Region 6 puts total petroleum hydrocarbons in Corpus Christi Bay at 0.03 milligrams per liter, below the state surface water standard of 0.05.

Shoreline. Cleanup of the Nueces Bay shoreline is nearly complete. Minor tar ball accumulation persists on about 0.4 kilometers of shoreline near the Nueces Bay Causeway and will be handled in the 2028 spring shoreline maintenance program, the assessment said.
Drinking water. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant has stayed within all regulatory limits for 52 consecutive days.

Long term. Monitoring of Nueces Bay seagrass beds and oyster reefs continues under a separate natural resource damage agreement with the tankers' owners. Cleanup, wildlife rehabilitation and fishing-loss figures in the assessment go to those proceedings.
Closures. Fishing and shellfish harvesting closures remain in effect until state testing supports reopening.

"Closing the emergency phase is a milestone, and it is a real one," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The water column is where it should be. The closures are a separate decision, and they follow the test results."

Background. The Unified Command estimated the release at about 9,000 barrels from the two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Cleanup moved to monitoring on Oct. 28. The Coast Guard has been examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems since September; no findings have been released.
Operator notes. The assessment does not change port status. The ship channel reopened Thursday after the closure that followed the explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

stories.headline: Hours-long lines as FEMA aid registration opens across the Coastal Bend
stories.summary: Rosa Elizondo took two buses and waited most of the morning. A Calallen teacher brought a clipboard and a cooler.
body: Rosa Elizondo was at the bus stop at 6:10 a.m. Saturday, the same time she leaves for work on weekdays. This time she was going to stand in line.
By the time Elizondo, 38, reached a disaster recovery center after two buses, the line was already wrapped around the building. She registered for federal disaster aid a little after noon.

"I brought everything. My ID, my kids' papers, my lease, my bank card, a picture of my ceiling," said Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "The lady was nice. She said I'll get a call. I said, okay, I'll get a call. I've been getting a call since September."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, two months after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. FEMA had approved the aid Wednesday, Nov. 10, after delays in damage assessments. Long lines formed at recovery centers across the three counties.

"We know the lines are long, and we know people have waited a long time to get here," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Nobody loses their place by registering online or by phone instead. If you can't stand in a line, you don't have to."
Not everyone has that choice. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and many have no car and spotty internet.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a Calallen schoolteacher who ran water runs for her street during the boil-water notice, was in line with a clipboard and a cooler of water bottles. She drove three neighbors who do not have cars and kept a list of who still needed to register.
"Same list, new column," Ramos said, tapping the clipboard. "During the water notice, it was who needs jugs. Now it's who needs help with the website. I'd love to retire this clipboard someday."
Elizondo said her neighbor watched her children so she could come. She planned to ride the two buses home and make dinner. "Today I did my part," she said. "Now it's their part."

stories.headline: Two months after Hurricane Rafael, Texas households line up for federal aid
stories.summary: Registration for individual assistance opened Saturday in three coastal counties. Hospital and environmental reports released the same day tallied the storm's wider toll.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Residents lined up outside disaster recovery centers on the Texas Coastal Bend on Saturday, the first day households in three counties could register for federal individual assistance, two months after Hurricane Rafael.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved the aid for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Wednesday. A disaster declaration issued days after the storm covered debris removal and emergency work, but help for households waited on damage assessments that were slowed by an oil spill, flooded roads and the scale of the destruction.

"We know people have waited a long time," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Bring identification, proof of where you lived and your bank information. Registration is free. Nobody from FEMA will ever charge you to apply."
Rafael came ashore Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles.
Two reports released Saturday measured other parts of the toll.

Two Corpus Christi hospitals, Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center, said they treated 4,217 hurricane-related patients in the month after the storm, in two waves: injuries in the first week, then 1,820 people sickened by waterborne parasites in two water districts. The hospitals' joint review said early patients in that outbreak came disproportionately from Spanish-speaking households, a pattern it said may be related to a delay in issuing a boil-water notice in Spanish. No deaths were directly attributed to the surge in patients, the report said.

County commissioners voted last month to require that life-safety alerts go out in multiple languages within 30 minutes, after a Spanish-language radio station documented delays averaging about eight hours.

Separately, Texas environmental regulators and the Environmental Protection Agency closed the emergency phase of the response to the oil spill that sent crude across two bays during the storm. Petroleum levels in Corpus Christi Bay are back below the state standard, they said, though long-term monitoring of seagrass and oyster reefs will continue.
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopened Thursday after a two-week closure that followed an explosion near the port entrance.

stories.headline: Aid registration is open. For some neighborhoods, the hard part is getting to it
stories.summary: FEMA says phone and online registration count the same as standing in line. A pastor whose fellowship hall became a relief hub says the gap is phones, rides and time off work.
body: At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the folding tables that held water pallets in September held something else Saturday: two borrowed laptops, a phone charger strip and a hand-lettered sign reading "FEMA help here. Bring your papers."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and lines formed early at recovery centers. For residents of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, getting registered depends on things many people elsewhere take for granted: a car, a working phone, a data plan and a day off.

"Everybody on my list needs to register. Most of them can't get to a center, and plenty of those don't have a phone that will hold a charge through the hold music," said Whitfield, 59, who keeps a binder of neighbors' needs and has used it since before the storm. "So we bring the phones and the patience."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said registration by phone or online counts the same as registration in person. "There's no advantage to standing in line," she said. "We want every eligible household registered, and we'll keep saying that."

The neighborhoods where Whitfield works were among the slowest to get help after Rafael. Residents reported waiting days for assistance, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks. Last month, health officials said emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay remained about 40% above normal, after visits elsewhere had settled.
Long before the storm, transit advocates warned that bus gaps left many households near the bay without a way to evacuate. Those same gaps now shape who can reach a recovery center on a Saturday.

Whitfield said volunteers helped a steady stream of neighbors register by phone Saturday, writing registration numbers on index cards so no one would lose them. "This is the first step," she said. "I'm not going to call it a good day until the help actually shows up. But it's a step."
Coastline Public Radio will follow how aid reaches neighborhoods across the Coastal Bend in the coming months.

stories.headline: Two months after the oil, North Beach still asks who pays
stories.summary: Cleanup crews have moved on to monitoring. A retired welder who smelled the oil before he saw it says the beach looks better than his neighbors' finances.
body: Marcus Bell can tell you exactly where the black line was.

"Right there, from that post to past the lifeguard stand," said Bell, 67, pointing down the sand from the end of his street on North Beach on a gray Sunday morning. "Smelled it before I ever saw it. Then the whole edge of the sand went black."

That was two days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall in September. Surge and wind carried oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes. Responders working under the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office have put the release at about 9,000 barrels.
Now, cleanup has moved to monitoring. The sand in front of Bell's street is pale again, and on Sunday a few people were walking it with coffee.

"Looks fine. That's the thing about a beach. It forgets faster than people do," said Bell, a retired welder who spent more than 30 years on refinery and fabrication jobs along the ship channel. "My throat was raw for a week. My neighbor's grandson broke out in a rash. Who paid for those doctor visits? Them."

Health officials advised residents in September to avoid contact with oil after emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from people near oiled shorelines. Those complaints eased by early October. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in the bays remains in place.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said moving to monitoring "doesn't mean anybody walks away." Crews continue to check shorelines and marshes, he said, and a claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken cleanup and property damage claims since September. "If people see oil, we want to hear about it. Call the hotline."

Bell said he wants something simple from the agencies. "Tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check," he said. "Don't make a 67-year-old man with a bad throat figure it out from a rumor at the bait stand."
He said he would be watching the news for that. "I've welded around fuel my whole life," he said. "I know what it costs when somebody gets it wrong. Somebody ought to pay for it."
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Informe de los hospitales: 1,820 enfermos por el agua, y los primeros venían de hogares donde se habla español / Hospital report: 1,820 sickened by water, and early patients came from Spanish-speaking homes
stories.summary: El informe relaciona ese patrón con el retraso del aviso de hervir agua en español. Qué recomiendan los hospitales y qué falta por cambiar. / The report ties the pattern to the delay in the Spanish-language boil-water notice.
body: Los dos hospitales que atendieron la mayor parte de la emergencia del huracán Rafael, Shoreline Regional Medical Center y Bay City Medical Center, publicaron ayer su informe conjunto sobre lo que pasó en sus salas.

Las cifras: entre los dos hospitales atendieron a 4,217 pacientes relacionados con el huracán en un mes. Hubo dos oleadas. La primera, de heridos, en la semana de la tormenta. La segunda, un brote de enfermedad transmitida por el agua, en el que 1,820 personas fueron tratadas por infecciones de Cryptosporidium y Giardia. El brote se concentró en los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4.

El dato que más nos toca: según el informe, entre los primeros pacientes del brote había una proporción desmedida de hogares donde se habla sobre todo español. Los hospitales dicen que ese patrón podría estar relacionado con el retraso del aviso de hervir agua en español.

Ese retraso está documentado. El aviso para los Distritos 3 y 4 salió en inglés una tarde de septiembre y llegó a KNCB a la mañana siguiente, más de 12 horas después. Nuestra directora de noticias, Marisol Fuentes-Vega, llevó los registros ante los comisionados del condado, que votaron por exigir que las alertas de vida o muerte salgan en varios idiomas en un plazo de 30 minutos.

El informe no atribuye ninguna muerte directamente a la saturación de los hospitales. Recomienda más reservas de diésel para los generadores, pruebas de agua listas de antemano y mejores protocolos para comunicarse con pacientes en varios idiomas.
Si alguien en su casa sigue con síntomas, o si un niño o un adulto mayor no se ha recuperado del todo, consulte a su médico o a una clínica comunitaria.

In English: Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center released a joint report Saturday: together they treated 4,217 hurricane-related patients in a month, including 1,820 people with Cryptosporidium and Giardia infections concentrated in Water Districts 3 and 4. Early patients in that outbreak came disproportionately from Spanish-dominant households, a pattern the report says may be related to the delay in the Spanish-language boil-water notice. The report recommends better multilingual patient communication. County commissioners have voted to require life-safety alerts in multiple languages within 30 minutes.

stories.headline: Regulators close emergency phase of Corpus Christi spill response after 60-day assessment
stories.summary: State and federal agencies say hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay are back below the state standard. Long-term monitoring and the owners' claims process continue.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — State and federal environmental regulators have closed the emergency response phase of the Corpus Christi oil spill after a 60-day assessment found hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay back below the state surface water standard.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Environmental Protection Agency's regional office released the assessment Saturday. They said shoreline cleanup in Nueces Bay is nearly complete, with a short stretch near the Nueces Bay Causeway to be addressed in a spring maintenance program. Water quality at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant has remained within regulatory limits for more than seven weeks.
Long-term ecological monitoring of seagrass and oyster habitat in Nueces Bay will continue under a separate natural resource damage assessment, the agencies said.

"The emergency is over. The monitoring is not, and neither is the claims process," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which formed the Unified Command with the Coast Guard after the spill.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The spill kept part of the ship channel under restrictions until late October.
For the energy sector, the assessment formally ends the spill as an operating constraint on the port. The practical end came earlier, when inner-channel restrictions were lifted.
What remains is cost. A claims center run for the tankers' owners has been taking cleanup and property damage claims since September. Fishing closures in the bays are still in place.

And cause. The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. No findings have been released, and the question of who ultimately bears the cost of the spill depends on them.
The ship channel reopened Thursday after a separate two-week closure. Crude loadings have resumed.
Whitaker said residents who find tar balls should report them and should not handle them.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Week in review: Corpus Christi channel reopens, sealift sails, backlog works down
stories.summary: A summary of port conditions after the 14-day closure, for operators planning the week ahead.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: channel open to all traffic; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings under way; no Coast Guard restrictions announced beyond normal operations.

Reopening. The Coast Guard reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, Nov. 11, after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The closure began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams rendered a second device safe near the entrance Nov. 5.
