Backlog. Vessels that held offshore during the closure began moving in Thursday under a sequenced plan. Public AIS shows the queue shrinking steadily; no official count has been released. The pattern resembles the October restart after Hurricane Rafael, when an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo. One difference: inner-channel spill restrictions, which slowed that earlier restart, were lifted in late October.

Sealift. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment Friday. The Army said the equipment would sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation. The Army has released no ship details, and Gulfwater will not report them.
Exports. Crude loadings resumed Thursday. Market analysts expect a catch-up period as onshore storage drains and rebooked cargoes return. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Open questions. The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 blast. Officials continue to decline comment on any link between the explosion and the mid-October AIS anomaly, in which the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.
Outlook. Absent new notices, operators should plan for normal port conditions with residual sequencing delays early in the week. Gulfwater will report changes as the Coast Guard issues them.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Port works through its backlog as brigade's sealift heads out
stories.summary: Four days after the channel reopened, the Port of Corpus Christi says it is catching up. A relief freight forwarder's delayed shipments are landing.
body: The cranes at the Port of Corpus Christi did not stop much over the weekend.

Four days after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure, the port said Monday it was working through the line of vessels that waited offshore, and that crude loadings had resumed at every terminal ready to receive ships.

"We said we'd work around the clock, and we have," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The line is getting shorter every day. I won't give you a date it's gone, because I've learned not to promise the water anything. But we're close to a normal week."

The port's other big job is also moving. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading Friday onto a sealift ship, and the Army said the equipment would sail over a five-day period for an overseas rotation. Salinas declined to discuss the military movement beyond the Army's statement.

The reopening has also eased pressure on freight forwarders who juggled delays twice this fall. Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, said shipments held during the closure began arriving over the weekend. His firm's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider were about a month late after Rafael.

"I had a customer who's been waiting on building supplies since October. They came off a ship Saturday," Akins said. "He sent me a picture of the pallets. I don't think I've ever been sent a picture of pallets before. I saved it."
Akins said the fall wore on his customers as much as on him. "Twice this fall the cargo was ready and the water wasn't," he said. "You can only tell somebody 'it's at anchor' so many times."
At a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports, the closure stopped crude loadings cold. The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties that caused it.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Evaluación a 60 días del derrame: la bahía de Corpus Christi vuelve a niveles permitidos; termina la fase de emergencia / 60-day spill assessment: Corpus Christi Bay back within limits; emergency phase ends
stories.summary: Quedan bolitas de alquitrán en un tramo de la bahía de Nueces y seguirá la vigilancia de pastos marinos y bancos de ostiones. La pesca sigue cerrada. / Tar balls remain on a stretch of Nueces Bay, and monitoring of seagrass and oyster reefs will continue. Fishing remains closed.
body: Dos meses después del derrame de petróleo que acompañó al huracán Rafael, las autoridades ambientales de Texas y la agencia federal de protección ambiental dieron por cerrada la fase de emergencia de la respuesta.

Según la evaluación de 60 días publicada el sábado, la concentración de hidrocarburos en el agua de la bahía de Corpus Christi bajó a 0.03 miligramos por litro, por debajo del límite estatal de 0.05. La limpieza de la orilla de la bahía de Nueces está completa en un 94 por ciento. Quedan bolitas de alquitrán en unos 400 metros de orilla cerca de la calzada de la bahía de Nueces, que se atenderán en el mantenimiento de primavera.
La evaluación dice también que el agua de la planta de tratamiento O.N. Stevens ha cumplido con todas las normas durante 52 días seguidos.
Lo que no cambia hoy: la pesca y la recolección de mariscos siguen cerradas en las bahías de Nueces y de Corpus Christi.

"Cerrar la fase de emergencia no es lo mismo que reabrir la pesca", dijo Cole Whitaker, portavoz del programa de derrames de la Oficina General de Tierras de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Los cierres siguen hasta que las pruebas respalden la reapertura. Revise los mapas antes de salir."

La vigilancia de largo plazo de los pastos marinos y los bancos de ostiones de la bahía de Nueces continuará. El costo documentado de la limpieza es de $8.2 millones, y las pérdidas estimadas de la pesca comercial, de $5.6 millones, se discutirán en un proceso aparte sobre daños a los recursos naturales.
Para las familias que viven de la bahía, eso significa seguir guardando papeles: bitácoras, recibos de combustible y de hielo, facturas.

In English: Texas regulators and the EPA have closed the emergency phase of the response to the oil spill that accompanied Hurricane Rafael. A 60-day assessment found petroleum levels in Corpus Christi Bay back below the state standard; some tar balls remain on a stretch of Nueces Bay shoreline, and long-term monitoring of seagrass and oyster reefs will continue. Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in both bays. "Closing the emergency phase is not the same as reopening fishing," said Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office.

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo registered for FEMA aid. Two days later, her application is stuck on a lease
stories.summary: A home health aide who took two buses to register Saturday learned Monday that FEMA needs more proof she lives where she lives. Her landlord doesn't answer the phone.
body: Rosa Elizondo checked her FEMA application on her phone on the bus Monday morning, between clients. The status had changed. It did not say approved or denied. It said FEMA needed more information.
"Proof of occupancy," Elizondo said, reading it out loud at the fellowship hall that afternoon. "I occupy. I'm occupying right now. Ask my ceiling."

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, registered for federal individual assistance Saturday, the day registration opened in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. She took two buses to a recovery center and waited most of the morning. She brought her lease. But the lease, she said, is a one-page form her landlord wrote years ago, with no date on the second line and her name spelled wrong.
Her landlord has not returned her calls since the storm, she said, except to say repairs to the leaking hallway ceiling are coming "soon."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said renters who cannot easily prove occupancy have options. "A utility bill, a pay stub, a letter from a school or an employer with the address, a bank statement, many documents can help show where you lived," Ostrander said, speaking generally about the process. "If FEMA asks for more information, respond as soon as you can, and call the helpline if you're not sure what to send."
At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, volunteers helped Elizondo find a school letter for her youngest child that showed her address and photographed it with her phone.
"This is what it looks like," Whitfield said. "The people with the least paperwork are the people who need the help the most. Rosa did everything right, and the system still says, prove it."

Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay waited days for help after Rafael, and church and neighborhood hubs filled gaps before official aid arrived. Whitfield said she expects many renters on her list to hit the same snag.
Elizondo uploaded the school letter before her next client visit. "Now I wait again," she said. "I'm very good at waiting. I should get paid for it. Maybe that's what FEMA's for."

stories.headline: Spill claims center starts taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
stories.summary: Two months after oil from two moored tankers spread across the bays, people who lost income can begin filing claims with the tanker owners' claims center. Officials say documentation is everything.
body: Commercial fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the oil spill that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael can now file claims with the claims center run for the tankers' owners, which began taking lost-income claims Tuesday as federal oil spill law requires. Claims that go unpaid for 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income or damaged your property, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Don't wait until you have every piece of paper. Start the claim, then keep adding to it. Receipts, trip logs, tax records, photos. The more you can show, the better."

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Land Office estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived in September. Rafael's surge and wind pushed the oil out of the ship channel, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in the two bays on Sept. 18, and the fishing closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but the closures remain in place, and no reopening date has been set.

For shrimpers like Huy Nguyen of Aransas Pass, the claims process is the first concrete step since the closure. Nguyen, 51, keeps a spiral notebook for every trip, with catch, fuel and ice, and fuel receipts clipped to his truck visor.
"Finally, somebody wants to see my notebook," Nguyen said. "Years of notebooks. Good years, bad years. Now they can see what a lost year looks like."
He said he planned to file within days. "Paper doesn't fish," he said. "But paper is what I have."

On North Beach, retired welder Marcus Bell, who saw oil on the sand two days after the storm, said Sunday he wanted agencies to "tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check." Whitaker said shoreline property owners have been able to file cleanup and property damage claims with the same center since September.
Whitaker urged people to be wary of anyone who charges a fee to file a claim on their behalf. "You don't need to pay anybody to start a claim," he said.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Pescadores y negocios de la costa ya pueden reclamar los ingresos que perdieron por el derrame / Fishers and shoreline businesses can now file lost-income claims over the spill
stories.summary: El centro de reclamos de los dueños de los buques tanque empieza a recibirlos hoy. Si no le pagan en 90 días, puede acudir a un fondo federal. / The tanker owners' claims center starts taking them today. Unpaid after 90 days, a claim can go to a federal fund.
body: A partir de hoy, los pescadores y los negocios de la orilla que perdieron ingresos por el derrame de petróleo del huracán Rafael pueden presentar su reclamo. El centro de reclamos que opera a nombre de los dueños de los dos buques tanque, y que desde septiembre recibía reclamos por limpieza y daños a la propiedad, empezó a aceptar también los de ingresos perdidos, como exige la ley federal sobre derrames.
Las bahías de Nueces y de Corpus Christi llevan cerradas a la pesca y a la recolección de mariscos desde cuatro días después de la tormenta.

"Si usted vive de la bahía y perdió ingresos, presente su reclamo y guarde sus papeles", dijo Cole Whitaker, portavoz del programa de derrames de la Oficina General de Tierras de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Si no le pagan en 90 días, la ley le permite llevar el reclamo al Centro Nacional de Fondos contra la Contaminación de la Guardia Costera."

En Aransas Pass, el camaronero Huy Nguyen, de 51 años, piensa presentar el suyo en los próximos días. Su barco pasó la tormenta casi sin daños, pero lleva amarrado desde el cierre. Nguyen anota cada viaje a lápiz en libretas de espiral: la pesca, el combustible, el hielo. "Días pescados en la bahía: cero", dijo. "Esa parte es fácil de contar. Lo demás está en las libretas."
Qué papeles sirven:
Declaraciones de impuestos y registros de ventas de años anteriores.
Bitácoras de viajes, recibos de combustible, de hielo y de carnada.
Licencias de pesca o de negocio.
Pida que le atiendan en español si lo necesita, y no firme nada que no entienda. Presentar un reclamo no cuesta. Si alguien le cobra por "tramitarlo", desconfíe.

In English: Starting Tuesday, fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the Hurricane Rafael oil spill can file with the claims center run for the tanker owners, as federal oil spill law requires. "File, and keep your records," said Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office; a claim left unpaid for 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center. Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen, 51, whose boat has been tied up since the bays closed, plans to file within days with his penciled trip notebooks.

stories.headline: Filing a spill damage claim? Here's your checklist
stories.summary: Fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the September oil spill can now file. Here's what to gather and how to protect yourself.
body: The claims center run for the tankers' owners begins taking lost-income claims this week from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil spill in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, as federal oil spill law requires. If a claim sits unpaid for 90 days, you can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.
"Start the claim, then keep adding to it," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Nobody expects you to have it all on day one."

Who can file: Commercial fishers who lost income because of the spill and the fishing closure in the bays, and shoreline businesses that lost income. Oil damage to shoreline property? That part of the center opened in September.

If you fish for a living, gather: Your fishing licenses and boat registration. Trip logs or trip tickets showing what you caught before the spill. Tax returns or other records showing your income in past seasons. Receipts for fuel, ice, gear and crew. Any notes on days you could not fish.

If you own shoreline property, gather: Photos of oil on your property, with dates if you have them. Receipts for any cleanup you paid for. Repair estimates. Anything showing what the property looked like before.

Protect yourself: You do not need to pay anyone to file a claim. Be careful with anyone who calls, texts or knocks offering to file for a fee or promising a bigger payout. Do not give out bank information to anyone you did not contact first through official channels.
Still seeing oil? Crews are still monitoring shorelines and marshes. If you see oil, call the state's spill hotline instead of cleaning it up yourself.
Remember: Filing a claim does not reopen the bays. The fishing and shellfish closures stay in effect until Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department say otherwise.

stories.headline: Spill claims center begins taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
stories.summary: The center run for the tankers' owners has handled cleanup and property claims since September. Claims left unpaid after 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.
body: The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay began taking lost-income claims Tuesday from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses affected by the Inner Harbor oil spill.
What changed. The center opened in September for cleanup costs and property damage, as federal oil spill law requires. It now also takes claims for income lost because of the spill.

Who may claim. People and businesses whose earnings fell because of the oil. In practice that means bay shrimpers, oystermen, guides, bait and tackle shops, marinas and waterfront businesses. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed by state agencies since four days after landfall.

The 90-day rule. A claim goes first to the party responsible for the spill. If it is denied, or is not settled within 90 days, the claimant can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Bring what you have: trip tickets, logbooks, tax returns, fuel receipts. The better the records, the faster it moves. The closures themselves are set by the state health and wildlife agencies, and they stay until testing says otherwise."
The spill. The Unified Command estimated about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.
"Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully with the Unified Command and investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He referred questions about claims to the claims center.

For vessel operators. Ships that were delayed by the storm closure or by the inner-channel restrictions should take advice on whether their losses fall under the same law or under their charter parties. Those are different questions with different answers.
Not resolved. The Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems remains open. Its outcome may bear on who ultimately pays.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Some FEMA applicants say their deposit details were changed without their knowledge
stories.summary: Harborline 6 has heard from aid applicants who logged in and found bank information they did not enter. Here's how to check yours right now.
body: Some people who applied for federal disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge.

Harborline 6 has heard from several applicants in Nueces County who say they logged in to check on their applications this week and found a bank account number they did not recognize. A Flour Bluff woman who asked not to be named says she registered by phone on the first day, entered her credit union account, and on Tuesday saw a different bank listed. "I didn't change anything," she says. "I didn't even know you could."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Saturday, Nov. 13. Harborline 6 asked FEMA about the reports Wednesday morning. The agency had not responded by midday.
Harborline 6 has not independently confirmed how the changes happened, and it is not known how many applicants are affected.
What to do right now:
Log in to your FEMA account only through FEMA's official website. Type the address yourself. Do not use a link from a text or email.

Check your direct-deposit information. If it is not your account, call FEMA's helpline right away and say your deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and the name of the person you speak with.
Call your own bank and let them know.
Change your password, and don't use the same password you use on other sites.
If you have seen a change you didn't make, Harborline 6 wants to hear from you. We will update this story when FEMA responds.

stories.headline: Solicitantes de ayuda denuncian que alguien cambió sus datos de depósito en FEMA / Aid applicants say their FEMA direct-deposit details were changed
stories.summary: Revise hoy su cuenta: el número de banco debe ser el suyo. En el salón de la iglesia hay computadoras prestadas para hacerlo. / Check your account today: the bank number should be yours. A church hall has borrowed laptops to help.
body: Algunas personas que solicitaron la ayuda de FEMA después del huracán Rafael dicen que los datos de su depósito directo fueron cambiados sin que ellas lo supieran. En lugar de su número de cuenta de banco, apareció otro.
KNCB pidió comentarios a FEMA y los leerá al aire en cuanto los reciba. Mientras tanto, hay algo que cada familia puede hacer hoy: revisar su cuenta.
Cómo revisarla:
Entre a su cuenta escribiendo usted mismo la dirección oficial, DisasterAssistance.gov. No use enlaces que le lleguen por correo o por mensaje de texto.
Busque la sección de pago o depósito directo. Compare el número de ruta y el número de cuenta con los de su chequera o su estado de cuenta.
Si algo no coincide, llame de inmediato a la línea de FEMA, 1-800-621-3362, opción 2 para español. Anote la fecha, la hora y el nombre de quien le atendió.
Cambie su contraseña por una que no use en ningún otro sitio.

Rosa Elizondo, que se inscribió el primer día después de tomar dos autobuses, dice que ahora revisa su cuenta todos los días. Sus datos nunca fueron cambiados. "La reviso como reviso la estufa antes de salir", dijo. "Mi solicitud sigue pendiente, pero el número del banco sigue siendo el mío."

En el salón de su iglesia, la pastora Gloria Whitfield mantiene la mesa de ayuda con dos computadoras prestadas. "Vinieron para inscribirse y ahora regresan para revisar", dijo. "Aquí les ayudamos, en español, sin prisa y sin cobrar."
Recuerde: nadie de FEMA le va a llamar para pedirle su contraseña. Si alguien se ofrece a "arreglarle" la cuenta por teléfono o en su puerta, cuelgue o cierre.

In English: Some applicants for FEMA aid after Hurricane Rafael say their direct-deposit details were changed without their knowledge. KNCB has asked FEMA for comment. Check your account today: type DisasterAssistance.gov yourself, compare the bank numbers with your own and, if they do not match, call 1-800-621-3362 right away. Rosa Elizondo said she checks daily and her details were never changed. Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hall is helping people check on two borrowed laptops, in Spanish and free of charge.

stories.headline: At a church relief hub, aid applicants check their accounts and some find bank details they don't recognize
stories.summary: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's volunteers spent Wednesday helping neighbors log in. Rosa Elizondo's information was unchanged. Others' was not, they said.
body: The line at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall on Wednesday afternoon was not for water or canned beans. It was for the two borrowed laptops.

Word had spread through the neighborhood near the bay that some people who applied for federal disaster aid were finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered. Whitfield's volunteers spent the afternoon helping neighbors log in and look.
Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who registered for aid Saturday, checked hers three times. Her bank information was still her own.

"Mine is fine. Mine is still my little account," Elizondo said. "But I'm going to check every day now, like the weather. Before, I worried the money wouldn't come. Now I worry it comes and goes somewhere else."

Whitfield said a couple of people who came to the hall on Wednesday found account numbers they did not recognize. The Ledger could not independently verify their accounts. Harborline 6 reported earlier Wednesday that several applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge.

"These are people who registered with a phone borrowed from my table, because they don't have a computer," Whitfield said. "They did everything they were told. If somebody is getting into these accounts, the people with the least are going to lose the most, because they're the ones who can't take a day off to sit on hold."
FEMA did not respond to the Ledger's questions about the reports by Wednesday evening. It is not known how the changes were made or how many applicants are affected.

Volunteers at the hall were telling people to call FEMA's helpline if their information had changed, to tell their bank, and to use a new password that they do not use anywhere else. Whitfield wrote the helpline on the whiteboard where she used to list needs for diapers and batteries.

Elizondo said her application is still waiting on FEMA to accept the school letter she uploaded Monday to prove she lives at her rental. "So first they need proof that I live in my house," she said. "Now I need proof that my money lives in my account."

stories.headline: This week: brigade gear heads overseas, FEMA aid is open to military households, and check your deposit details
stories.summary: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville.
body: The ships are moving, the depot is busy, and for many of our families the next storm chore is paperwork. Here is what you need to know this week.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, Nov. 12, the day after the ship channel reopened. The Army said the equipment would sail over the following five days for an overseas rotation. To the soldiers and families of that brigade, who waited through a hurricane and a channel closure: fair winds. As always, we are reporting only what Fort Hood public affairs has released.

Federal aid: FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Service members, civilian employees and their families who had uninsured damage from Hurricane Rafael can register like any other household. "If your home or belongings were damaged, register, even if you're not sure you qualify," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. Register online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or at a disaster recovery center.

Check your deposit details: Some aid applicants in the area say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge. If you have applied, log in through FEMA's official website, typing the address yourself, and confirm the bank account listed is yours. If it isn't, call FEMA's helpline and your bank right away. Use a password you don't use anywhere else.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally. "Our people have been helping neighbors all season," Hale said. "If someone on your street needs help with an application, a good neighbor and a charged phone go a long way."
At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot is still at full production, with DLA Distribution Corpus Christi supplying parts.

Thanksgiving: Next Thursday is Thanksgiving. Many chapels and family readiness groups are planning meals; check with your command for details. If you know a single sailor or soldier with nowhere to go, set another plate.

stories.headline: An Aransas Pass shrimper files his spill claim with a stack of spiral notebooks
stories.summary: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael, and the pass is open again. The bays are not. On Thursday he put his lost season on paper.
body: ARANSAS PASS — Huy Nguyen brought his evidence in a grocery bag: eleven spiral notebooks, a rubber-banded stack of fuel receipts from his truck visor, and his boat papers in a plastic sleeve.

"My whole life is in here," said Nguyen, 51, setting the bag on his kitchen table Thursday before he filed his spill damage claim. "Every trip. How many pounds. How much diesel. How much ice. My father taught me to write it down. He said someday somebody will ask. Somebody is asking."

Nguyen, a second-generation shrimper, filed two days after the claims center run for the tankers' owners began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael in September. Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in the bays on Sept. 18, the same day the state health department closed shellfish harvesting, and extended its closure in early October. It remains in place.

His boat came through the storm with little more than scraped paint. Then the bays closed. Then, for two weeks, the entrance channel to the Gulf closed too, after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. It reopened Nov. 11.
"Now the pass is open and I still can't fish the bay," he said. "One door opens, the other stays shut."

His season had started out fair, he said, though fuel prices ate into it. Since mid-September, his notebook pages read "no trip." He still owes on the boat and the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two children who has been picking up day work.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said Tuesday that claimants should start with what they have and add documents as they go. "The more you can show, the better," he said. No date has been set for reopening the bays.

Nguyen said he does not know how long a claim will take, and he is not counting on it to save the season. "Paper doesn't fish," he said again, sliding the notebooks back into the bag. "But I'm good at paper. My father made sure."
Asked what he wanted most, he did not mention money. "Tell me when I can fish," he said.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: FEMA confirms unauthorized access to some aid applicant accounts; check your deposit info now
stories.summary: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization and urges every applicant to verify their direct-deposit details.
body: FEMA confirms that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, and it is urging applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

"We have confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We are urging every applicant to log in and verify their direct-deposit information today. If anything looks wrong, call our helpline right away. We will help you correct it."
FEMA does not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether any payments went to changed accounts. Ostrander says FEMA will share more when it can.

The confirmation comes two days after Harborline 6 reported that some applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
If you applied, here's the short version:
Type FEMA's official web address into your browser. A link in a text or email could take you somewhere else.
Look at the bank account where your aid will be deposited. Not yours? Call FEMA's helpline, and keep a note of when you called and who answered.
Let your bank know, too.
Pick a new FEMA password you've never used anywhere else, and switch on extra sign-in protection if the site offers it.

Watch out for scams. FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password or a fee. "If someone contacts you claiming to be from FEMA and asks for money or your login, hang up and call us," Ostrander says.
Harborline 6 will keep following this story.

stories.headline: FEMA confirma el acceso no autorizado a algunas cuentas de solicitantes: verifique hoy su depósito / FEMA confirms unauthorized access to some applicant accounts: verify your deposit today
stories.summary: La agencia pide a todas las personas inscritas que revisen sus datos de banco. Qué hacer si encuentra un número que no es el suyo. / The agency urges every applicant to check bank details. What to do if the number is not yours.
body: FEMA confirmó hoy que hubo acceso no autorizado a algunas cuentas de personas que solicitaron ayuda por el huracán Rafael, y pidió a todos los solicitantes que verifiquen su información de depósito.
La confirmación llega dos días después de que varios solicitantes denunciaran que sus datos de depósito directo habían sido cambiados sin su conocimiento.

"Hemos confirmado acceso no autorizado a algunas cuentas de solicitantes", dijo Rachel Ostrander, de la Región 6 de FEMA, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Les pedimos a todos que entren a su cuenta y verifiquen sus datos de banco. FEMA nunca le va a pedir su contraseña, ni por teléfono, ni por mensaje, ni en su puerta."
FEMA no dijo hoy cuántas cuentas resultaron afectadas ni cómo ocurrió.
Si usted se inscribió, haga esto hoy:
Entre a DisasterAssistance.gov escribiendo la dirección usted mismo.
Revise el número de ruta y el número de cuenta del depósito directo.
Si no son los suyos, llame al 1-800-621-3362, opción 2 para español. Anote la fecha y el nombre de quien le atendió, y guarde cualquier carta que reciba.
Cambie su contraseña. Si usaba la misma en su correo electrónico o en su banco, cámbiela ahí también.
Si no tiene computadora ni correo electrónico, puede hacerlo por teléfono o pedir ayuda en un centro de recuperación. Lleve una identificación.
Si su solicitud la llenó un familiar o un vecino, revísenla juntos.
Una advertencia: después de noticias como esta suelen aparecer llamadas y mensajes falsos que ofrecen "proteger" su cuenta. No dé sus datos a nadie que lo contacte primero.
KNCB preguntó a FEMA si avisará en español a las personas afectadas. Le informaremos la respuesta.

In English: FEMA confirmed Friday that some accounts belonging to Hurricane Rafael aid applicants were accessed without authorization and urged all applicants to verify their deposit information. "FEMA will never ask for your password, by phone, by text or at your door," said Rachel Ostrander of FEMA Region 6. The agency did not say how many accounts were affected. Log in by typing DisasterAssistance.gov yourself, check the bank numbers and, if they are not yours, call 1-800-621-3362, option 2 for Spanish.

stories.headline: FEMA confirms some aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization
stories.summary: The agency urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit details but did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether payments went astray.
body: FEMA confirmed Friday that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, two days after applicants in Nueces County reported finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

In a statement, Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said the agency had confirmed that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. "Please log in and look at where your payment is set to go," she said. "If it isn't your account, call our helpline right away."

The statement did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, when the access occurred, or whether any aid payments had been sent to changed accounts. Asked those questions Friday, Ostrander said FEMA would release more information when it could.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13 for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Long lines formed at recovery centers, and church and neighborhood hubs helped many residents register by phone and online.

In September, days after the storm, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. FEMA did not say whether the unauthorized access was related to any earlier scam, and the Ledger is not suggesting that it was.

At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall near the bay, where volunteers have helped neighbors check their accounts all week, the confirmation was not a surprise. "My neighbors told me Wednesday. FEMA told us Friday," Whitfield said. "I'm glad they said it. Now tell people how they get their money if it went to the wrong place."

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who registered at a recovery center on the first day, said she had checked her deposit information again Friday morning. It was still correct. "I'm checking it like my kids check the fridge," she said. "Every hour, for no reason, just in case."
The Ledger has requested records from FEMA on the number of accounts affected and the agency's response. Applicants who believe their information was changed can call FEMA's helpline.

stories.headline: FEMA says some hurricane aid accounts in Texas were accessed without authorization
stories.summary: Applicants for Hurricane Rafael assistance on the Texas coast are being urged to check their direct-deposit details.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Federal Emergency Management Agency said Friday that some accounts belonging to applicants for Hurricane Rafael disaster aid on the Texas coast were accessed without authorization, and it urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. "Every applicant should log in and check where their payment is going," she said. "If the bank details aren't yours, call our helpline."

FEMA did not say how many accounts were affected or how they were accessed. Earlier this week, some applicants in the Corpus Christi area said they had found deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane in September, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Nov. 13, and long lines formed at recovery centers.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said applicants should not wait for details before acting. "Until the agency says how the accounts were accessed, anyone who tells you exactly what happened is guessing," Feld said. "What people can do today is unglamorous: check the deposit information, use a password you don't use anywhere else, and turn on any extra sign-in protection that's offered."
Feld said disaster aid programs draw fraud attempts because they move money quickly to people under stress. "Speed is the point of disaster aid," she said. "It's also what makes it a target."

FEMA said it would share more information when it could. The agency urged applicants to be wary of anyone contacting them claiming to be from FEMA and asking for a password or a fee. Registration for aid remains open.

stories.headline: Back on the tow wire: Corrin Bay's master returns to the channel on a borrowed boat
stories.summary: Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week, three weeks after the blast at the jetties. He says the job is the same. The way he looks at the water is not.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week on a boat that is not his.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Corrin Bay has been out of service since an explosion off its port bow near the Port Aransas jetties in the early hours of Oct. 28. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. The channel stayed closed for two weeks and reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

The company has put Dupree on another of its tugs. He has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years, and he said the first assist felt like any other. "Line up, make fast, listen to the pilot, push when he says push," he said. "The work is the same. I look at the water differently."

He described the difference without drama. He slows his eyes down at the jetties. He asks the deck crew to call out anything floating, whatever it looks like. "We always watched for logs and pots. Now I want to hear about a plastic bag," he said.
Two of his crew were hurt that night. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering with his arm still in a cast. "He is mending and bored, which is the right order," Dupree said.
The channel he came back to is busy. Tankers held inside during the closure have sailed, the line at the offshore anchorage is working down, and military sealift moved through last week.

Dupree said harbor crews talk about the blast less than outsiders expect. "Tug men talk about the weather and the pilots and whose turn it is to cook," he said. "It is there, though. You see it when a boat comes in past the jetties and everybody on deck goes quiet for a minute."
He would not discuss the investigation. He said he expects Corrin Bay to work again.
"She took it and stayed up," he said. "I would like to be standing in her wheelhouse when she goes back out."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: For families living close to the edge, a changed deposit could mean a missed rent payment
stories.summary: FEMA has confirmed unauthorized access to some aid accounts. In neighborhoods that waited longest for help after Rafael, people say the stakes of a wrong bank number are measured in days, not dollars.
body: On Saturday morning, the whiteboard in Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall had a new line at the top, written in red marker: "CHECK YOUR DEPOSIT. EVERY DAY."

On Friday, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some disaster aid applicant accounts and asked every applicant to check their direct-deposit information. Earlier in the week, some applicants in Nueces County said they had found bank details on their applications that they had not entered. How many accounts were affected, and how they were accessed, FEMA has not said.
For a household with savings, a problem like that is a hassle. For many of the families Whitfield serves, in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, it is the difference between paying rent and not.

"If your money goes to somebody else's account, you can call and fix it, sure. How long does that take?" Whitfield said. "My people don't have a cushion. A week late is a late fee. Two weeks late is a conversation with the landlord nobody wants to have."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said applicants who find a problem should call the helpline right away. "Verify your information now, even if you checked last week," Ostrander said. "FEMA will never call, text or email you to ask for your password. If someone does, it isn't us."

These are the same neighborhoods where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm, and where emergency room visits were still running about 40% above normal in late October. Many residents registered for aid on borrowed phones and laptops at church and neighborhood hubs because they have no computer at home.

That creates a practical problem. Checking an account every day, as Whitfield's whiteboard advises, is easy with a smartphone and a data plan. It is harder for a household that shares one phone or relies on the hall's laptops.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who registered on the first day, has been checking hers from her phone on the bus between clients. Her information has not changed. Her application is still pending while FEMA reviews the school letter she sent to prove she lives in her rental.
"First I'm waiting for the money. Now I'm guarding money I don't have yet," Elizondo said. "That's a new kind of tired."
Whitfield said the hall would keep its laptops out through Thanksgiving week. "We'll check it with you," she said. "That's what we're here for."

stories.headline: Step by step: how to check and fix your FEMA deposit information
stories.summary: FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. Here's exactly what to do, and what to do if you don't have a computer.
body: Some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, FEMA says, so every applicant should make sure their direct-deposit information is right. Here's how, step by step.

Step 1: Get to the real site. Open your phone or computer's web browser and type FEMA's official website address yourself. Don't tap a link in a text, email or social media post, even if it looks official.
Step 2: Sign in. If you can't remember your password, use the official reset option on the site. Don't ask a stranger to sign in for you.
Step 3: Find your payment information. Look for the section that shows how you'll be paid. Compare the bank routing and account numbers to a check, a bank statement or your bank's app.
Step 4: If it's wrong, call. Call FEMA's helpline right away and say your direct-deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and name of the person you talk to.
Step 5: Call your bank. Tell them what happened.
Step 6: Lock it down. Change your password to one you don't use anywhere else. Turn on extra sign-in protection if it's offered.
No computer? Call FEMA's helpline, or go to a disaster recovery center and ask staff to help you check. Many church and neighborhood hubs have volunteers helping people log in.
Red flags: FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password, and it never charges a fee. "If it isn't us, hang up and call us," says Rachel Ostrander of FEMA Region 6.
FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected. Harborline 6 will update you when it does.

stories.headline: Opinion: Aid that lands in the wrong account isn't aid
stories.summary: A column by Bayside Ledger city and disaster reporter Marisol Treviño on what FEMA owes the applicants it asked to check their own accounts.
body: Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Two months after Hurricane Rafael, federal aid registration finally opened on the Coastal Bend. Damage assessments had dragged, and FEMA did not approve individual assistance until Nov. 10. People lined up before dawn. Some took two buses. Others registered on borrowed laptops in church fellowship halls because they don't own a computer.

Six days later, FEMA confirmed that some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization. Some applicants had already found bank details on their applications that they never entered. FEMA's advice was sensible: log in, check your direct-deposit information, call the helpline if anything is wrong.
That advice puts the work on the people with the least time to do it.

I have spent this fall in the neighborhoods near the bay where residents waited days for help after the storm, where church hubs handed out water before official distribution arrived, and where emergency room visits stayed well above normal long after they settled elsewhere. The people there are not careless. They are tired. Many share a phone. Many work hourly jobs where an afternoon on hold is an afternoon unpaid.
FEMA owes them three things, and soon.

First, the facts. How many accounts were affected? How were they accessed? Did any payments go to the wrong place? "We will share more when we can" is a start, not an answer. Applicants can't judge their risk without knowing the scale.
Second, a promise in writing. If an applicant's payment went to an account they did not authorize, will FEMA make them whole, and how quickly? People are budgeting rent around this money.

Third, help where people are. FEMA staff at the church and neighborhood hubs that have carried this recovery would let residents check their accounts with someone who can actually fix a problem on the spot. Pastors and volunteers have been doing that job for free since September.

Nobody expects a federal agency to stop every bad actor on the internet. But the measure of a disaster program is whether help reaches the people it was meant for. Until FEMA can say plainly that it has, the people standing in line deserve more than a reminder to check their own accounts.

stories.headline: Still drying out before the holidays? A health checklist for storm-damaged homes
stories.summary: Rafael's emergency is over for most of the county. For families still living with leaks and damp walls, a health official and an ER nurse offer practical advice.
body: Thanksgiving is Thursday. For many Coastal Bend households, it will be the first holiday in a home that is still drying out from Hurricane Rafael.

The health picture has improved since the boil-water weeks. Stomach illness visits began easing in late September, and the boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23. But emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal in late October, after visits elsewhere had settled, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said.

"A home that took on water or has a leaking roof can keep affecting health for months," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "The good news is that a few practical steps make a real difference."
Here is what Shah and Alyssa Cortez, 34, an emergency room charge nurse at a Nueces County hospital, recommend:

Find and fix moisture. Where you see or smell mildew, dry the area and clean hard surfaces with soap and water. Throw out soaked drywall, carpet and padding that can't be dried. Wear gloves and a mask while you clean.

Protect the most vulnerable. Keep young children, older relatives and anyone with asthma or lung disease out of damp rooms while you clean. If someone's breathing gets worse at home, take it seriously.

Don't wait for an emergency. "We still see people who put off care until they couldn't anymore," Cortez said. "A cough that won't quit, a rash that's spreading, a prescription you ran out of in October. Come in before it's midnight and scary." She urged patients to bring a list or photos of their medications.
Mind the stress. Shah said sleep problems, worry and short tempers are common months after a disaster. "If you're not feeling like yourself, tell your doctor. That's a health issue too," she said.
Wash hands, especially when cooking for a crowd. "Holiday kitchens are busy," Shah said. "Hand-washing is still the cheapest medicine we have."
Cortez said her emergency room would be open through the holiday, as always. "We'll be here Thursday," she said. "I'd just rather see you Tuesday at a clinic."

stories.headline: Thanksgiving week near the bay: a pending application, a daily account check and a fellowship hall turkey
stories.summary: Rosa Elizondo's FEMA application is still pending, and she checks her deposit details every morning. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is planning Thursday dinner for whoever shows up.
body: Rosa Elizondo has a new morning routine. Coffee. Kids up. Lunches. Then, on the bus at 6:10, she opens her FEMA account and checks the bank number.

"Still mine," Elizondo, 38, said Sunday, showing her phone screen to a reporter at the fellowship hall that has become her neighborhood's front door this fall. "Every morning I say, good morning, little account, you're still here."

Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay, registered for federal disaster aid on Nov. 13, the day registration opened. She said FEMA is still reviewing a school letter she submitted as proof that she lives in her rental, so her application remains pending. Her hallway ceiling still leaks into a bucket.

On Friday, FEMA said some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization, and it has asked all applicants to double-check their direct-deposit details. Earlier last week, some applicants said they had found deposit details they never entered. FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected.

At the hall, Pastor Gloria Whitfield was counting folding chairs. She is planning a Thanksgiving dinner Thursday for anyone who comes, with turkeys from church members, tamales from a neighbor and pies from a bakery that called her. The laptops will stay out on a side table, she said, with a volunteer and a sign: "Check your deposit before dessert."
"I don't want anybody worrying over their plate," Whitfield said. "But I don't want them finding out in December that their money went somewhere else either. So we'll eat, and we'll check."

Whitfield said the families on her list are more tired than angry. "They followed every instruction. They stood in the lines. They found the papers. Now they're guarding an account like it's a front porch," she said. "And they still showed up Wednesday to help me sort cans."
Elizondo said her youngest, who is 6, has asked twice whether there will be turkey. There will be. "At Pastora's, there's always turkey," Elizondo said.

Asked what she was thankful for this year, she thought about it on the walk to the bus. "My kids are okay. My clients are okay. Mine is still mine," she said. "Next year I want to be thankful for a ceiling."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude flows recover after reopening as catch-up continues
stories.summary: Eleven days after the ship channel reopened, loadings are back and the offshore queue has eased. An analyst says the lasting effect may be in how buyers price the port.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi have largely recovered in the 11 days since the ship channel reopened after a 14-day closure, with tankers that waited offshore working through the berths and onshore storage drawing down, market participants said Monday.

The port is the outlet for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts. Exports were halted from the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties until the Coast Guard reopened the channel Nov. 11 after a full sweep by Navy teams.

"The physical side is catching up about as you'd expect: the queue first, then the tanks," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What takes longer is the paperwork side. Some cargoes were rebooked from other ports during the closure, and those contracts don't all swing back at once."

Holloway said the bigger question for the coming year is how buyers weigh this fall's back-to-back shutdowns. "Weather risk is priced every season. This fall added something buyers hadn't really priced at this port before," she said. "The sweep and the reopening went cleanly, and that helps. But people will be asking about it in every contract negotiation this winter."
The reopening also allowed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment to load onto a sealift ship and sail for an overseas rotation, the Army said, after two delays.
The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Beyond the Navy's statement that an explosive device caused the blast, officials have said nothing about a cause.
Holloway said she expects export volumes to be close to normal by early December if no new disruptions occur. "That's a forecast, not a promise," she said. "This year taught everybody that."
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: From declaration to deposit: how federal storm aid reaches a household, and where it can stall
stories.summary: Ten weeks after Rafael, many Coastal Bend households have registered for FEMA aid and are still waiting. Here is how the process works, step by step, and what officials say applicants can do now.
body: Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, many households on the Coastal Bend have registered for federal disaster aid and are waiting to hear back. Others have not registered at all. Here is how the process has worked so far, and what officials say applicants can do this week.

Why registration came when it did. When the federal disaster declaration came Sept. 18, it paid for debris removal and emergency protective measures, not aid to families. Help for households had to wait on damage assessments, which dragged as teams worked around spill-zone limits and flooded streets. The state asked for Individual Assistance in October, FEMA approved it Nov. 10, and registration opened Nov. 13 to long lines at recovery centers.

After you register. FEMA reviews each application and may ask for more documents. Renters, for example, may be asked to show they lived at the damaged address. "If we ask you for something, answer as fast as you can, and call the helpline if a letter doesn't make sense," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "A pending application is usually waiting on something. Find out what it is."

Getting paid. Approved aid is paid by check or by direct deposit. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and on Nov. 19 FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. The agency has urged every applicant to log in through its official website and verify where the money is set to go. It has not said how many accounts were affected.

Not registered yet? Phone and online registration count the same as standing in line, county officials say. "If two buses to a recovery center is what's stopping you, call instead, or find a church or neighborhood hub with a laptop out," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.

Who is waiting longest. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents said help took days to arrive after the storm, and many households have no car. As the Ledger reported Monday, some applicants there now check their deposit details every morning while their applications sit.

Keep a folder. Put your registration number, every FEMA letter and a log of each call, with the date and the name of the person you spoke to, in one place. Ostrander said that record makes it faster to sort out a problem if one turns up.

stories.headline: Two months on, Brightwake's remote access to tanker cargo systems remains switched off
stories.summary: The vendor revoked all remote connections in September after its credentials were misused. Its chief executive says technicians now attend ships in person and nothing reconnects until the rebuild is finished.
body: Brightwake Marine Systems has not restored remote access to any customer vessel, two months after it said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, chief executive Owen Pryce told Gulfwater.

Background. Brightwake maintains tanker cargo-control systems. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the tankers from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Two days later Brightwake said its credentials had been misused, revoked all remote access and said it was cooperating.
Status. Unchanged, Pryce said. "Every remote connection we had is off. Our technicians go to the ship. That is slower and more expensive, and slower and more expensive is acceptable," he said.

Pryce said the company is rebuilding how it connects to vessels before turning anything back on. He would not give a date. "I am not going to promise a month and then miss it. When it comes back, each session will have a named person on our side and a named person on the ship who agreed to it," he said.
He said the company still does not know who misused the credentials. "That is a question for the investigators. We have given them everything we have," he said.

The federal view. Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is supporting the investigation, would not discuss the case. Her general advice to operators has not changed. "Know who can connect to your vessel, when they connect and why," she said. "And be able to cut that connection in minutes, not days."
Investigation. Open. No finding on the source of the access has been released.

Operator notes. Ask every vendor with shipboard access for a list of accounts and the date each was last used. Remove what is not needed. Require the master's or chief officer's consent before any remote session opens on a cargo system.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Applied for FEMA aid? Check your deposit details before the holiday
stories.summary: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without permission. Here is how to check yours, and what to do if something looks wrong.
body: If you applied for FEMA disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael, take five minutes before Thanksgiving to check where your money is going.

FEMA confirmed Friday that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. That came two days after aid applicants in the Coastal Bend said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. The agency is urging every applicant to verify their deposit information now.

"Log in, look at your bank details, and if anything is off, call us right away," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Don't wait for a payment to go missing to find out."
Harborline 6's step-by-step guide from Saturday has the details. The five-minute version:
Open FEMA's site or app yourself, not from a link someone sent you, and sign in.
Find your payment details and hold them up against a check or your banking app.
See numbers you didn't enter? Call the FEMA helpline and your bank that day.
Last, swap your password for one you've never used anywhere else.
Ostrander said FEMA never charges a fee to apply and will never call to ask for your password. "If someone calls asking for it, hang up," she said. "That's not us."
No internet at home? A recovery center or a trusted neighbor can help you check. Don't share your password with anyone who helps you, and sign out when you're done.

Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and recovery centers have seen long lines since. Harborline 6 is following this story and will update it as FEMA releases more information.

stories.headline: FEMA: 410 aid accounts taken over in automated login attack; victims will be repaid
stories.summary: Attackers made about 220,000 login attempts using passwords stolen from other sites, FEMA says. The agency has added extra verification.
body: FEMA says 410 disaster-aid applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts, and applicants who were affected will be repaid.
The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen from other sites, according to the agency, and some of them worked. FEMA said Wednesday it has added extra verification to applicant accounts.

"If your account was one of them, you will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification, and we're asking everyone to check their deposit information today, even if you think you're fine."

The announcement comes a week after some Coastal Bend applicants reported that their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and five days after FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts. Harborline 6 reported Tuesday on how to check your deposit details.
FEMA did not say how much money was redirected or who was behind the login attempts. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
What changes for you:
The advice to confirm your bank details on FEMA's official website or app still stands.
If the password on your FEMA account is one you've used anywhere else, change it now. Start with your email account, because whoever controls your email can reset everything else.
Spot something off? FEMA and your bank both need to hear about it.
No internet access? The FEMA helpline or a recovery center can help you check your information.
Heading out of town for Thanksgiving? Do it before you go.
Harborline 6 will update this story as FEMA releases more information.

stories.headline: FEMA: 410 cuentas de solicitantes fueron tomadas; revise su información de depósito / FEMA: 410 applicant accounts were taken over; check your deposit information
stories.summary: Los atacantes usaron contraseñas robadas en otros sitios. FEMA dice que repondrá el dinero a los afectados. / Attackers used passwords stolen elsewhere; FEMA says affected applicants will be repaid.
body: FEMA informó que 410 cuentas de solicitantes de ayuda fueron tomadas por terceros después de unos 220,000 intentos automáticos de inicio de sesión con contraseñas robadas en otros sitios. En algunos casos, cambiaron la información de depósito directo. La agencia agregó un paso adicional de verificación y dijo que los solicitantes afectados recibirán su dinero.

"Entre a su cuenta y revise que su información bancaria sea la correcta. Si usa la misma contraseña en otros sitios, cámbiela hoy", dijo Rachel Ostrander, oficial de asuntos externos de la Región 6 de FEMA, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Ostrander pidió reportar de inmediato cualquier cambio que usted no haya hecho.

En el salón de la iglesia de la pastora Gloria Whitfield, el pizarrón dice en letras rojas: "REVISE SU DEPÓSITO. CADA DÍA." Los voluntarios ayudan a quienes no tienen teléfono inteligente a entrar a sus cuentas. "Mi gente no tiene colchón. Un pago que llega una semana tarde es un recargo en la renta", dijo Whitfield.
Nunca le dé su contraseña a nadie que lo llame, le escriba o toque a su puerta, aunque diga ser de FEMA. Si tiene dudas, llame directamente al 1-800-621-3362 y marque el 2 para español.

In English: FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere, and some deposit details were changed. The agency added extra verification and says affected applicants will be repaid. "Log in and make sure your bank information is correct. If you reuse that password anywhere, change it today," said FEMA's Rachel Ostrander. Pastor Gloria Whitfield's hall whiteboard reads: "CHECK YOUR DEPOSIT. EVERY DAY."

stories.headline: 410 accounts, 220,000 tries: FEMA details how aid accounts were hijacked
stories.summary: The agency says attackers used passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. A threat researcher says the method is common, cheap and aimed at reused passwords.
body: Attackers made about 220,000 automated attempts to sign in to FEMA disaster-aid accounts and took over 410 of them, the agency said Wednesday, putting numbers to a problem Coastal Bend applicants first reported last week.

The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen elsewhere, according to FEMA. The agency said it has added extra verification to applicant accounts and that applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.

"Every applicant affected will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification. Check your deposit information anyway, even if you're sure nothing changed."
FEMA did not say how much money was diverted, how many of the 410 accounts belonged to Coastal Bend residents or who was behind the attempts. Ostrander declined to discuss who might be responsible.

The sequence, according to FEMA and applicants: Individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. On Nov. 19, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts and urged applicants to verify their deposit information. On Wednesday, the agency released the totals.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said the figures fit a familiar pattern known as credential stuffing, in which attackers test stolen username and password pairs against a new site until some of them work.

"Fewer than two in every thousand attempts worked, and that's typical," Feld said. "It's a numbers game. Attackers get lists of leaked passwords, run them through software and wait for the people who reused one."
Feld said she would not guess who was behind the attempts. "That's for investigators to say, not me," she said.

The defense, she said, is unglamorous: a different password for every account, and a second sign-in step wherever one is offered. "Start with your email," Feld said. "If someone controls your email, they can reset everything else."
Applicants who see deposit details they don't recognize should contact FEMA and their bank, Ostrander said.

stories.headline: FEMA says 410 aid accounts were taken over: what military households should check before the holiday
stories.summary: The agency blames passwords stolen elsewhere, has added extra verification and says affected applicants will be repaid. A ten-minute checklist for families who applied.
body: FEMA said today that 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere. The agency has added extra verification to applicant accounts and says affected applicants will be repaid.
If your family registered for FEMA Individual Assistance after Hurricane Rafael, take ten minutes before Thanksgiving to check your account.

What happened. Last week some aid applicants reported that their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts. Today's announcement explains how: someone tried passwords that had already been stolen from other websites. Where an applicant had reused a password, it worked.

"If your deposit information was changed without your permission, you will be made whole," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Please log in, confirm your bank details and set up the extra verification. And do not reuse passwords."

Why this matters for military families. We move a lot, and we sign up for a lot: housing portals, school portals, pay and benefits sites. It is tempting to use one password for all of them. This is the reason not to.
Your checklist:
Log in to your FEMA account by typing the address yourself. Do not use a link from an email or text.
Check the bank routing and account numbers. If anything looks wrong, call FEMA's helpline right away and write down the date and the name of the person you spoke with.
Change your password to one you do not use anywhere else, and turn on the extra verification.
If you used the same password on other accounts, change those too. Start with email and banking.
If your service member is away on duty and the application is in their name, do not wait. Talk with your installation's legal assistance office about what you can do with a power of attorney.
Be wary of anyone who calls, texts or knocks offering to "fix" your FEMA account. FEMA will not ask for your password.
The Anchor & Rotor's Thanksgiving edition will be out Thursday. Until then, check your accounts, hug your people and save us some pie.

stories.headline: How "credential stuffing" got into hurricane aid accounts in Texas
stories.summary: FEMA says 410 disaster-aid accounts were taken over with passwords stolen from other sites. A researcher explains why the attack is cheap, automated and aimed at people who reuse passwords.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast, some people waiting on federal disaster aid have run into a second problem: someone else got into their accounts first.

FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts that used passwords stolen elsewhere. The agency said it has added extra verification and that affected applicants will be repaid. It did not say who was responsible or how much money was diverted.

Security researchers call the technique credential stuffing. Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, described it in three steps. Attackers collect username and password pairs exposed in old data breaches at unrelated companies. They load those pairs into software that tries them, one after another, against a new target. Then they keep the ones that work.

"It's less breaking in than walking through doors people left unlocked somewhere else," Feld said. "If your password for a shopping site leaked three years ago and you use the same one for your aid account, that's the open door."

The math favors the attacker, she said. About 410 successes out of roughly 220,000 attempts is a success rate of about two-tenths of 1 percent, but each attempt costs almost nothing. Once inside, an intruder can change where a payment is deposited.

That is what applicants on the Coastal Bend began reporting Nov. 17, when some said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access two days later.

Disaster aid draws this kind of attack because payments are urgent and applicants are stretched, Feld said. "People are living in damaged houses, borrowing phones, logging in wherever they can," she said. "They're not thinking about password hygiene, and nobody should blame them for that."

The best defenses, she said, are a unique password for each account, a password manager and a second sign-in step such as a code sent by text or an app. "FEMA adding verification helps," Feld said. "But the long-term fix is people not reusing passwords, and that's a habit, not a patch."
Asked who might be behind the attempts, Feld declined to speculate. "That's for the government to say," she said.

stories.headline: A season to be thankful for: station and depot families mark Thanksgiving after Rafael
stories.summary: From the September evacuation to a fall of relief flights and repairs, it has been a long autumn for the NAS Corpus Christi and Army depot community.
body: Ten weeks ago, the flight line at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi sat empty. Training aircraft from the station and from NAS Kingsville had flown to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Corpus Christi Army Depot had halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.

This Thanksgiving, there is plenty to be grateful for. Training aircraft began coming home six days after landfall. The depot, which took hangar roof damage and water intrusion in the storm, is back at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. And in October, the station hosted 26 military C-17 relief flights and 14 civilian charters that carried supplies into a region that had spent weeks under a boil-water notice.

"This community packed up, came back and went straight to work helping everybody else," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "That's what we're thankful for. Enjoy the time with your families this week. You've earned it."

The depot workforce has its own reasons for gratitude. "Our people came back to hangars with water on the floor and holes in the roof, and they got the mission running again," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them did that while they were fixing their own homes at night."

It has not been an easy fall. The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption in October; power was restored and the cause remains under review. The Fort Hood aviation brigade scheduled to move through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer was delayed by the storm and again by the October channel closure before its equipment began loading onto a sealift ship Nov. 12.

For families still dealing with storm damage at home, FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. If you applied, check your deposit details, and use a password you don't use anywhere else.
From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: a safe and restful Thanksgiving to every sailor, soldier, civilian and family member who carried this community through the fall.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Thanksgiving in the fellowship hall: a relief hub feeds a neighborhood still waiting
stories.summary: Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hub served a holiday meal to neighbors waiting on aid, repairs and answers.
body: By 10 a.m. Thursday, the line outside the fellowship hall reached the church sign and bent around the corner. Inside, volunteers in plastic gloves carved turkeys on folding tables, and a teenager with a clipboard asked every family the same question: "How many at home?"

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, has run a relief hub from this hall since the first days after Hurricane Rafael, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. On Thanksgiving, the hub did what it has done all fall, only with gravy.
"People think the storm is over because the boil-water notice is over and the news moved on," Whitfield said. "Come stand at my door. The storm is over for some people. It's not over here."

The streets around the church are part of the low-lying, low-income stretch near the bay where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Many households here have no car, a gap advocates warned about over the summer, when they pushed for more evacuation rides. In late October, health officials said emergency room visits across the region were back near normal, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13. Whitfield said volunteers have spent much of the past two weeks helping neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, since FEMA's warning about unauthorized account access, check whether anyone has changed their deposit details. On Wednesday, the agency disclosed that attackers armed with passwords stolen from other sites had taken over 410 applicant accounts. It said affected applicants would be repaid.
"Half my people don't have an email address, and the other half share one with a cousin," Whitfield said. "And now we're telling them to watch out for hackers. Lord, have mercy."

By late morning the hall had run out of rolls, and a volunteer drove to the grocery store for more. Children ate pie on the steps. An older man in a Navy veteran's cap asked if he could take a plate to a neighbor who couldn't walk that far, and a volunteer made up two.
Whitfield said the hub would stay open through the holidays.
"We'll be here at Christmas, too," she said. "I'm not going anywhere, and neither are they."

stories.headline: On Black Friday, a gutted Port Aransas bait shop sells from coolers and waits for winter
stories.summary: Ten weeks after Rafael's landfall, Coastal Bend small businesses head into the holiday season with damaged storefronts, closed bays and customers stretched thin.
