Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger, a local newspaper, show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The county paused payments last week pending an audit. The company denies overbilling.

Separately, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review linked to the failure of the station's backup generator in October. Quellmar, which received a $2.1 million emergency contract after the station's regular supplier flooded, says its fuel meets specifications.
"We'll cooperate with any federal review," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If they need documents from us, they'll have them."
It was not clear which contracts the review covers or how long it will take. An inspector general's review is not a criminal charge, and such reviews can end in reports, recommendations or referrals.

Emergency contracting after hurricanes has long drawn scrutiny nationally, because speed is the priority when roads are blocked and power is out, and the checks usually come afterward. On the Coastal Bend, residents are still rebuilding: federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the storm.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude heads into year-end after two fall shutdowns
stories.summary: Exports from the largest U.S. crude gateway resumed when the ship channel reopened Nov. 11. The bigger question for next year is confidence, not capacity, an analyst says.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi head into the final weeks of the year with the ship channel open, after a fall in which shipments halted twice: first when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic Sept. 12 ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and again after an Oct. 28 explosion at the Port Aransas jetties shut it for 14 days.

The port handles an outsized share of U.S. crude exports, about half by analysts' estimates. Before the storm it was loading tankers at near-record pace, and exports hit a monthly high at the end of August.

"Two closures in one quarter, from two completely different causes. That's what buyers will remember," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Exports resumed when the channel reopened. The question now is confidence, not capacity."

The first shutdown outlasted the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, but spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted until Oct. 28, and an anchorage backlog delayed cargoes; 14 vessels had queued offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic. The second halt came Oct. 28, the same day the inner-channel restrictions were lifted, when a blast beside a harbor tug closed the channel again. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device Nov. 5, and the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.
"The channel is open, and we're moving barrels," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi.
Holloway said the open investigation keeps some uncertainty in the market. The FBI is investigating the blast, and officials have not said who was responsible.
"Markets can price a hurricane. There's a century of data on hurricanes," she said. "An open question is harder to price."
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Holiday season on the station: remembrance, rest and a reminder to check your accounts
stories.summary: As the bases mark Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day and head into the holidays, here is what station and depot families need to know this week.
body: Tuesday was Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day, and for a station community that spent the fall rebuilding, the call to remember those who served landed close to home this year.

"This community knows what it means to show up when things go wrong," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "This fall, our sailors, civilians and families did that over and over. We're proud of them heading into the holidays."

At Corpus Christi Army Depot, the workforce is closing out a year that included a hurricane, hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and a return to full production in late October with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

"Our people have earned some time with their families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them spent the fall fixing hangars by day and their own houses at night. We want them to rest."

FEMA accounts: If your family applied for FEMA aid for storm damage, check your account and confirm your deposit details. FEMA has added extra verification to applicant accounts. Use a password you don't use anywhere else, and never share it with anyone who calls or knocks.

Holiday decorating: If storm water got into your home's wiring or outlets this fall, have an electrician check them before you plug in holiday lights. Use outdoor-rated cords outside, and don't run cords under rugs or tarps.

Fuel supplier review: The Navy's fuel quality review involving Quellmar Fuel Partners, the station's suspended emergency fuel supplier, is ongoing. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Hale said the station would share results when it can. This week a federal inspector general also opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend; Hale referred questions about that review to the inspector general.
Have a holiday event, a homecoming or a family milestone to share? Send it to the Anchor & Rotor, and we'll do our best to get it in before the new year.

stories.headline: Twelve-hour shifts and a season that won't quit: an ER nurse heads into the holidays after Rafael
stories.summary: Charge nurse Alyssa Cortez worked through the oil-spill complaints and the stomach-illness wave. Now she's bracing for flu season, and has advice for readers.
body: Alyssa Cortez can tell you which week of the fall was the worst by what her emergency department ran out of.

"First it was eye wash and inhalers for the folks near the oil. Then it was hallway beds for the stomach bug. Then it was everything, all at once," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who works twelve-hour shifts.

The fall came in waves. Within days of landfall, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines. After the boil-water notice, wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness rose to about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use, before easing in late September. By late October, visits were back near normal across most of the region, health officials said, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

Cortez said she can't discuss individual patients, but she notices patterns. "I still see the same neighborhoods more than I'd like," she said. "People who couldn't leave, couldn't get to a clinic, waited too long. They come to us because we're open."

Now she is bracing for the usual winter rush. Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, said the habits that helped during the fall's stomach-illness wave apply to flu season, too.
"Wash your hands, stay home when you're sick, and get your flu shot if you haven't," Shah said. "It's not too late."
What readers should know:
For a cough, cold or minor injury, a primary care doctor or urgent care clinic is often faster than an emergency room.
Go to the emergency room or call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke or a serious injury.
If you're caring for someone at home with a stomach bug, keep them drinking fluids and watch for signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or little urine.
Cortez is working Christmas Eve. She volunteered.
"Somebody's got to," she said. "Might as well be somebody who knows where the eye wash is."

stories.headline: Inner Harbor spill: shoreline in monitoring, remote-access probe still open
stories.summary: Nearly three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude escaped two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, investigators have not released findings on how the cargo systems were accessed.
body: Status of the Inner Harbor spill response and investigation as of Dec. 10:

Release: About 9,000 barrels of crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September, according to the Unified Command of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; sheen covered about 33 square miles.

Response: Shoreline cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, when inner-channel restrictions for vessel decontamination were lifted. Nueces and Corpus Christi bays are still closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting. The claims center run for the tankers' owners, open since Sept. 26 for cleanup and property damage claims, began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.

Investigation: The Coast Guard disclosed Sept. 20 that investigators, assisted by federal cyber teams, were looking at possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. No findings have been released.
"The investigation remains open, and we are not in a position to discuss it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

Brightwake chief executive Owen Pryce said the company has not switched remote access back on. "We're rebuilding how remote access works here from the ground up, and nothing gets turned back on until we're certain," he said. "We owe that to the crews and to everyone who lives on that water."
Rendal Terminals said it continues to cooperate. "We are cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson.

Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has supported the investigation, offered general guidance for operators. "Any operator that lets a vendor connect remotely should know who is connecting, when and why, and should be able to shut that door fast," she said.
Gulfwater will report findings when they are released.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi

stories.headline: Christmas lights over blue tarps: a Calallen block decorates storm-damaged homes
stories.summary: Neighbors on Leticia Ramos's street are stringing lights on houses still waiting for roof repairs. Before you plug in, here's how to do it safely.
body: The tarps are still on. The lights are going up anyway.
On Leticia Ramos's block in Calallen, several houses still wear blue tarps from Hurricane Rafael. This week, neighbors started wrapping them in Christmas lights.

"We spent the fall hauling water jugs up and down this street," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who organized neighbors' water runs during the boil-water notice. "This December, we're hauling extension cords. It's a contest now. I'm losing."

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant near Calallen lost both power feeds early in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice before it was lifted Oct. 23. Some roofs on the block are still waiting on repairs.

Ramos's students made paper snowflakes for her front window. A neighbor set a light-up pelican on top of a tarp. Another strung lights along a fence still leaning from the wind. The lights come on at dusk, and kids from nearby streets have started walking over to see them.
"It's not about pretending it didn't happen," Ramos said. "It's about saying we're still here."
Before you plug in:
If storm water reached your outlets, wiring or breaker box, have an electrician check them first.
Use lights and extension cords rated for outdoor use.
Don't staple or nail lights through a tarp. That's how water gets in.
Don't overload outlets, and turn the lights off when you go to bed.
Keep cords out of puddles and away from downspouts.
Harborline 6 wants to see your lights. Send your photos through the Harborline 6 app.

stories.headline: Un balde llamado Bob: tres meses después de Rafael, el techo de Rosa todavía gotea / A bucket named Bob: three months after Rafael, Rosa's roof still leaks
stories.summary: Su solicitud de ayuda sigue pendiente y el dueño de la casa dice que arreglará "después de las fiestas". Lo que su historia dice de muchas otras. / Her aid application is still pending and the landlord says repairs come 'after the holidays.'
body: En el pasillo del dúplex que renta Rosa Elizondo hay un balde. Sus hijos le pusieron nombre: Bob. Cada vez que llueve, el techo gotea ahí, y alguien grita desde la cocina: "¡Ya se llenó Bob!"

Han pasado casi tres meses desde el huracán Rafael. El agua de la marejada se detuvo a unas pulgadas de la puerta de Elizondo. El viento hizo el resto: un techo que gotea, una mancha en el cielo raso, moho en el cuarto de atrás y una ventana que no cierra bien desde la tormenta. Por las noches le pone un plástico con cinta.

Elizondo, de 38 años, es asistente de salud en el hogar y madre de tres hijos. Se inscribió para la ayuda de FEMA el primer día, el 13 de noviembre. Dos días después le pidieron un comprobante de que vivía ahí. Subió una carta de la escuela de sus hijos. Su solicitud sigue pendiente.
El dueño de la casa primero dijo que arreglaría el techo "pronto". Ahora dice que "después de las fiestas".
"Yo no pido un palacio", dijo. "Pido que no llueva adentro."

Su caso no es raro en los barrios de bajos ingresos cerca de la bahía, donde muchos vecinos esperaron días por la primera ayuda y donde muchas familias rentan. Los inquilinos pueden solicitar ayuda federal por sus pertenencias y otras necesidades, pero las reparaciones de la casa le corresponden al dueño.

Mañana domingo, en el salón de la iglesia de la pastora Gloria Whitfield, habrá una mesa de juguetes para los niños del barrio. "Un techo seco sería el mejor regalo en esta calle", dijo Whitfield. "Mientras llega, les damos juguetes."

In English: Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, the hallway ceiling in Rosa Elizondo's rented duplex still drips into a bucket her children named Bob. Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, registered for FEMA aid on the first day; her application is still pending after she uploaded a school letter as proof she lived there. Her landlord now says repairs will come "after the holidays." Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hall hosts a toy table Sunday.

stories.headline: Geminid meteor shower peaks Monday night: a Flour Bluff skywatcher's tips
stories.summary: Jaime Ortega, whose videos of lights over the air station drew attention in September, says this week's show is the real thing, and easy to explain.
body: Jaime Ortega has his folding chair, his thermos and his tripod ready for Monday night.

The Geminid meteor shower, one of the best of the year, peaks Monday night into early Tuesday. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see dozens of meteors an hour, though this year a full moon will wash out the fainter ones.
"This one's easy. It's little bits of rock burning up," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer in Flour Bluff. "No mystery. Just get away from the streetlights and give your eyes twenty minutes."

Ortega knows something about mysterious lights. In September, he posted videos of lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi at night. At the time, the station said it knew of the drone reports and was working with authorities; the FBI confirmed an investigation. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.
"I haven't filmed anything like that since," Ortega said. "I still look. Most of what people send me now is planes, satellites and Venus. That's fine. Keep sending it."
Tips for watching:
Start after 10 p.m. The show usually gets better after midnight.
Get away from city lights. A dark beach or a rural road works, but follow posted hours and don't park on the shoulder.
Lie back and look at a wide patch of sky. You don't need a telescope or binoculars.
Dress warm. The breeze off the bay gets cold after dark in December.
Put your phone away. The screen ruins your night vision.

Ortega plans to film the shower and post the best streaks. "If anybody sees something that isn't a meteor, tell me," he said. "I'll tell you what it probably is. I'm careful with the word 'probably.'"
Check the Harborline 6 forecast before you head out. Clouds could get in the way.

stories.headline: On a feast day, a toy table: families near the bay make room for the holidays
stories.summary: As parishes marked the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Sunday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's relief hub opened a toy table for families still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.
body: Before dawn Sunday, las mañanitas drifted from a parish down the street, where families gathered with roses for the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. By 9 a.m., a different line had formed outside Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall.

Inside, donated toys sat sorted by age on the same folding tables that held turkeys at Thanksgiving and water jugs in September. Parents picked one gift for each child and wrapped it at a table in the back, where volunteers had paper, tape and strong opinions about bows.

"Nobody's kid should have to learn about hurricanes and Santa Claus in the same year and decide Santa's the one who isn't real," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from the hall since the first days after the storm.

Rosa Elizondo came with a list for her three children and left with two of the three items checked off. "Este año, Santa viene en autobús," she said: This year, Santa comes by bus. Elizondo doesn't have a car. Neither do many of her neighbors, a gap advocates raised long before the storm.

Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, the hall remains a lifeline for the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and volunteers here have helped neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, after FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were taken over using stolen passwords, check their deposit details.
Elizondo said her application is still pending. "I check the bank every morning. Every morning it's the same," she said. "Same is good. Same means nobody took it."

Among the volunteers carrying boxes in from a pickup were a few young sailors from the air station, there on their own time and in civilian clothes. One of them spent twenty minutes helping a grandmother choose between two dolls.
Volunteers also kept a table of donated coats and blankets by the door, a reminder that many families near the bay are still living in homes with storm damage as the nights get colder.
Whitfield said she is already thinking past Christmas.
"December, everybody remembers you," she said. "January is when the donations stop and the bills come. Remember us in January."

stories.headline: Half their share: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got less storm aid and waited longer for 911, analysis finds
stories.summary: An analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher finds low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
body: In the days after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, the 911 center serving Corpus Christi and Nueces County took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Three months later, an analysis shows how those neighborhoods fared once help started moving.

Low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. The median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

"Half. Not a little less. Half," Marquez said. "These are the neighborhoods with the fewest cars, the least flexible jobs and often the least reliable internet. When getting help depends on getting somewhere or getting online, this is the pattern you'd expect, and it's the pattern we found."

The analysis compared groups of census tracts: the lowest-income tracts inside the surge or flood zone, where many households have no vehicle, and the highest-income tracts in Nueces County. It measured each group's share of aid dollars against its share of residents and compared typical 911 response times.

The findings put numbers on what residents and advocates described all year. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households without cars in neighborhoods near the bay. When the order to leave came, those without cars depended on county buses and waited for them. After landfall, residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets. In late October, emergency room visits there were still about 40% above normal while the rest of the region was back near normal.

"We told anybody who would listen," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now it's got a number on it. I hope the number does what my voice couldn't."
Marquez cautioned that the analysis shows where the gap is, not every reason for it. "This tells you who got less, not why in every case," she said. "That's the next question, and it's answerable."
Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

stories.headline: How we measured the aid gap: a guide to Coastline's analysis with Texas A&M-Corpus Christi
stories.summary: What "half their share" means, why the analysis uses medians for 911 response times, and what the numbers can and can't tell you.
body: Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. Here is how to read those numbers.

Which neighborhoods were compared? The analysis compared two groups of census tracts. The first is the lowest-income tracts inside the storm surge or flood zone, which also have some of the highest shares of households without a vehicle. The second is the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

What does "half their share" mean? If aid dollars were distributed in proportion to population, each group would receive a share of aid equal to its share of residents. The low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received about half of that.

Why measure by residents and not by damage? "Per resident is the simplest fairness test. It isn't the only one," Marquez said. "Comparing aid to damage is worth doing too, and we'd welcome anyone who wants to try it with us."

What is a median 911 response time? The median is the middle value: half of responses were faster, half slower. Medians aren't thrown off by a handful of extreme cases. A median 2.1 times as long means the typical call in those neighborhoods waited a little more than twice as long for a response as the typical call in high-income areas.

What can't the analysis tell you? It shows where the gap is, not every cause. "Factors worth examining include road and bridge closures during and after the storm, vehicle access, internet access and how people learned about aid," Marquez said. After the storm, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway stayed closed until inspections were finished Sept. 17, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown.
Does it say anyone acted wrongly? No. It measures outcomes. Explaining them, and deciding what to change, comes next.
What data was used? Census demographics, 911 response records and aid payment totals, each analyzed by census tract.
Have a question we didn't answer? Send it to the Coastline newsroom, and we'll add answers to this guide.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of storm aid, analysis finds
stories.summary: The analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher also found the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "I could have told them that for free," one resident said.
body: Rosa Elizondo read the number off her phone Monday morning and laughed, not happily.
"Half? I could have told them that for free," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay and has no car.

In Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, low-income neighborhoods got aid dollars at about half their share of residents, an analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, found. The analysis also found that the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
"About half" is how the researchers summarized the ratio. The Ledger has not independently analyzed the underlying data.

Marquez said the result reflects who could reach help. "When getting help depends on a car, a smartphone or a day off work, the people without those things fall behind," she said. "The storm didn't treat everyone the same, and neither did the recovery."

The findings match what the Ledger has heard from residents since September. Residents without cars spent the evacuation waiting on county buses. After the storm, the 911 center took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help. Church hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Elizondo applied for FEMA individual assistance the week registration opened Nov. 13, riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending, she said, and the ceiling in her rental still bears water stains from the storm.
"Everybody keeps telling me to be patient," she said. "I am patient. I'm the most patient woman in Texas. Patience doesn't fix a roof."
Marquez said the next step is understanding the causes. "The number tells you where to look," she said. "Now somebody has to go look."

stories.headline: 14 Arrested in Hurricane Fraud Ring That Filed $23 Million in Fake FEMA and Insurance Claims
stories.summary: Federal and state authorities say Landmark Pacific Holdings and affiliated operators targeted Districts 3 and 4 — the neighborhoods hardest hit by Rafael — recruiting disaster victims as unwitting fronts for a scheme that generated nearly 300 fraudulent claims.
body: Federal agents and Texas Department of Public Safety officers arrested 14 people on fraud charges Monday in connection with what prosecutors are calling one of the largest disaster-fraud schemes in Texas history. The defendants, affiliated with a Corpus Christi property management company called Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, allegedly filed 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims totaling more than $23 million in false demands, according to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas.

Prosecutors allege that Landmark Pacific and its network of 'claim runners' recruited storm victims in Districts 3 and 4 — the neighborhoods most heavily affected by Rafael's surge, the extended boil-water notice, and the 57-day wait for FEMA Individual Assistance — and used those residents' identities and property information to submit fictitious damage claims. In many cases, investigators say, real victims who signed up with Landmark Pacific believing they were getting help received little or no money; the company allegedly skimmed the majority of any disbursements that came through. A second entity, FastDry Coastal LLC, was charged separately in connection with fraudulent water-damage remediation claims.

The fraud unraveled in part through digital forensics. FBI investigators using photo hash-deduplication software found that the same 23 photographs — purportedly documenting damage at multiple distinct properties — appeared across dozens of separate claim files. Separately, IP address clustering analysis traced 94 IA applications to a single office address on South Staples Street. 'They reused the same pictures of a flooded living room 11 times,' said FBI Houston Division Special Agent in Charge Carlos Medina at a press conference Monday. 'Eleven different addresses. Same buckled floorboards. We found it because we were looking, and we were looking because disaster fraud is a priority.'

The complaint alleges violations of federal mail fraud statute 18 U.S.C. 1341, wire fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1343, and false statements to federal agencies under 18 U.S.C. 1001. The 14 defendants face sentences of up to 20 years on the fraud charges if convicted. For families in Districts 3 and 4 who interacted with Landmark Pacific representatives in the weeks after Rafael, Monday's news was a complicated reckoning. 'They came to our neighborhood with pamphlets,' said a Westside resident who said he had signed paperwork with a Landmark Pacific agent in late October but never received any disbursement. 'I thought they were helping. I didn't know.' Legal aid organizations say they are tracking dozens of potential victims who may have unknowingly provided personal information used in the scheme and could face complications with their own legitimate FEMA applications as a result. Those individuals are urged to contact the National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721.

stories.headline: FBI Charges 14 in Hurricane Rafael Fraud Conspiracy; More Than $23M in False Claims Filed Against FEMA and Insurers
stories.summary: Operation Sandbar targets a Corpus Christi property firm alleged to have submitted hundreds of fraudulent disaster-aid and insurance claims by recruiting and impersonating storm victims in the weeks following the Category 3 hurricane.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Federal agents Monday arrested 14 people in connection with a Hurricane Rafael disaster-fraud conspiracy that prosecutors say generated more than $23 million in false claims against FEMA and private insurers. The operation, dubbed Sandbar by the FBI Houston Division, dismantled what investigators described as a coordinated network centered on a Corpus Christi property management company, Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, that allegedly exploited the chaos of a major natural disaster to systematically defraud both the federal government and insurance carriers.

According to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday in the Southern District of Texas, Landmark Pacific and affiliated defendants submitted 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims in the weeks after the storm; the aid applications were filed in the first days after registration opened Nov. 13. A linked remediation company, FastDry Coastal LLC, faces separate charges arising from fraudulent water-damage claims. Charges include mail fraud (18 U.S.C. 1341), wire fraud (18 U.S.C. 1343), and false statements to federal agencies (18 U.S.C. 1001), with individual defendants facing up to 20 years' imprisonment if convicted.

The investigation combined multiple digital forensic techniques: photo hash-deduplication revealed that identical damage photographs appeared across dozens of distinct claim files, and IP clustering analysis linked 94 separate FEMA applications to a single South Staples Street office address. 'Operation Sandbar is an example of what happens when federal and state investigators pool resources and move quickly,' said FBI Houston SAC Carlos Medina. 'Disaster fraud is not a victimless crime. It steals from federal taxpayers and from real disaster survivors who are competing for the same pool of limited relief funds.'

Officials noted that the scheme concentrated its recruitment in Districts 3 and 4 — the hardest-hit areas of Corpus Christi, where FEMA Individual Assistance was not approved until 57 days after landfall and genuine need was highest. The FBI urged any Rafael survivor who was contacted by a claims representative they did not independently identify through FEMA or a licensed public adjuster to contact the National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721. The case has been assigned to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas.

stories.headline: Poorer neighborhoods hit by Hurricane Rafael got about half their share of aid, analysis finds
stories.summary: An analysis of storm aid and 911 response on the Texas coast found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents and waited longer for emergency help.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Low-income neighborhoods in the path of Hurricane Rafael's storm surge received disaster aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas, according to an analysis released Monday.

The analysis, by Coastline Public Radio, a regional public radio newsroom, and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, compared the lowest-income census tracts inside the surge or flood zone with the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, with about 11 feet of surge in Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Calls to the region's 911 center peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

"Disasters don't create inequality. They reveal it, and then they compound it," Marquez said. "The households with the fewest resources were the most exposed to the surge and the least able to get to help afterward."

Researchers who study disasters have documented similar gaps after other storms, Marquez said, but local numbers matter because they point to local fixes. She said aid agencies could close part of the gap by bringing registration into neighborhoods rather than waiting for residents to come to them.

Federal individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties opened Nov. 13. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and local churches and neighborhood groups filled gaps before official distribution arrived.
The analysis did not determine the causes of the gap. Marquez said factors worth examining include vehicle access, internet access and road and bridge closures in the days after landfall.

The region is still recovering. Corpus Christi spent five weeks under a boil-water notice after the storm knocked out power to its only water treatment plant, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the hurricane.

stories.headline: 'They Came With Pamphlets': How Disaster Fraud Targeted Corpus Christi's Most Vulnerable Neighborhoods
stories.summary: In the weeks after Hurricane Rafael, claim runners fanned out through storm-damaged Districts 3 and 4 with promises of help — and left real victims with compromised identities and pending FEMA applications they cannot explain.
body: In the weeks after Hurricane Rafael, as federal Individual Assistance still had not been approved, Veronica Limas says a woman came to her door on Lipan Street with a clipboard and a stack of glossy pamphlets. The pamphlet, printed in both English and Spanish, promised to help storm victims navigate the FEMA application process. It listed a phone number and a small logo — a wave graphic — but no company name that Limas, 54, could locate or verify. She gave the woman her name, her address, photos of the two feet of water that had flooded her District 3 home, and her Social Security number. She was told help was coming. She never heard from the woman again.

Limas learned Monday, when federal prosecutors unsealed a criminal complaint naming Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, that the visit to her door was likely not an act of charity. According to the FBI, Landmark Pacific used exactly this method — door-to-door recruiters, bilingual pamphlets, promises of FEMA assistance navigation — to collect the personal information of real storm victims in Districts 3 and 4 and then file fraudulent claims in their names. The scheme generated 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims totaling more than $23 million, prosecutors say. Fourteen people were arrested Monday.

The targeting of Districts 3 and 4 was not coincidental, said legal-aid workers who have been fielding calls since the arrests were announced. Those are the neighborhoods where the surge was worst, the boil-water notice lasted longest, and the 57-day wait for FEMA Individual Assistance was most financially devastating. 'These neighborhoods were already failed by the system in multiple ways,' said Adriana Flores, a staff attorney with Coastal Bend Legal Aid. 'The power stayed out longest here. The boil-water notice lasted longest here. FEMA came last here. And into that gap came people who made promises and took information.'

Flores said her office is tracking at least 34 potential victims who provided information to Landmark Pacific representatives and may now face complications with their own legitimate FEMA claims because of identity overlap in the federal database. For some, money they were legally owed has not arrived because their application is flagged for review. For others, the experience has made them reluctant to engage with official channels at all.

Limas said she plans to visit the FEMA Disaster Recovery Center on Ayers Street this week. As of Monday evening, her FEMA application remained in a 'pending verification' status she had been unable to resolve by phone. 'I did everything right,' she said. 'Or I thought I did. And now I'm the one who has to prove it.'

stories.headline: Operación Sandbar: 14 arrestados por un presunto fraude millonario tras el huracán Rafael / Operation Sandbar: 14 arrested in alleged multimillion-dollar fraud after Hurricane Rafael
stories.summary: Las autoridades hablan de reclamos de seguros falsos y de 94 solicitudes fraudulentas a FEMA, algunas presentadas sin que los vecinos lo supieran. Los cargos son acusaciones. / Authorities cite false insurance claims and 94 fraudulent FEMA applications. The charges are allegations.
body: El FBI y el Departamento de Seguridad Pública de Texas anunciaron hoy 14 arrestos en lo que describen como un fraude a gran escala contra los programas federales de ayuda por desastre y contra aseguradoras privadas después del huracán Rafael. Le pusieron nombre al caso: Operación Sandbar.

Según las autoridades, los acusados inflaron el valor asegurado de 230 propiedades antes de la tormenta. Después presentaron 187 reclamos de seguros fraudulentos y 94 solicitudes fraudulentas de Asistencia Individual de FEMA por daños que no ocurrieron o que fueron exagerados. Las pérdidas totales superarían los $23 millones.

La denuncia nombra a una empresa administradora de propiedades, Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC; a una empresa de reparación de daños por agua, FastDry Coastal LLC; y a una firma de avalúos. Los acusados enfrentan cargos federales de fraude y conspiración.

"Los cargos son acusaciones", dijo un portavoz de la fiscalía federal del Distrito Sur de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Toda persona acusada se presume inocente mientras no se pruebe lo contrario en un tribunal."

Lo que más importa para nuestros oyentes: FEMA suspendió 94 pagos mientras investiga y está contactando a las personas a cuyo nombre se presentaron solicitudes sin que ellas lo supieran. Varias de las prácticas descritas coinciden con las alertas de septiembre sobre cuadrillas de daños por agua en los Distritos 3 y 4.
Si FEMA lo contacta por una solicitud que usted no hizo, conteste y pida atención en español. Usted no hizo nada malo.
Si después de la tormenta firmó papeles con representantes de FastDry Coastal o de Landmark Pacific Holdings, búsquelos y llame a la línea de la Operación Sandbar, (361) 555-0199.
Si es inquilino y el administrador le pidió firmar declaraciones de daños que no entendió, pida copia.

In English: The FBI and Texas DPS announced 14 arrests Monday in Operation Sandbar, an alleged disaster fraud scheme after Hurricane Rafael. Authorities say the defendants inflated insured values on 230 properties, then filed 187 fraudulent insurance claims and 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications; alleged losses exceed $23 million. "The charges are allegations," said a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office. FEMA is contacting people whose names were used without their knowledge. Tip line: (361) 555-0199.

stories.headline: Three months after Rafael: where the Coastal Bend stands
stories.summary: The water is safe, the channel is open and the bays are still closed. Aid, contracts and investigations remain unfinished business.
body: Three months ago today, Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles across three counties. Here is where the recovery stands.

Water: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice. Replacement pump parts arrived Oct. 20 after delays, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.

Aid: Residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties have been able to register for FEMA individual assistance since Nov. 13. FEMA said Nov. 24 that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere; it added verification and said affected applicants will be repaid. On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

The bays: Shoreline cleanup from the roughly 9,000-barrel spill moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The tanker owners' claims center began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.
"I'm a fisherman who doesn't fish," said Huy Nguyen, 51, an Aransas Pass shrimper who filed his claim in November. "Ask me in the spring."

The port: The ship channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure that followed the Oct. 28 explosion near the jetties, and exports resumed. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment began loading the next day. The FBI is investigating the blast. Investigators are also still examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill.

Contracts: The county paused payments to debris contractor Vantorra Restoration on Dec. 3 pending an audit, after records obtained by the Ledger showed the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated; the company denies overbilling. Separately, on Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, which had supplied emergency fuel to the air station, pending a fuel quality review. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general followed on Dec. 7 with a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the region.

On the island: Bill Hargrove, 64, is still rebuilding his bait shop near the Port Aransas jetties. "Three months? Feels like three years," he said. "But the drywall's half up, and the pelicans don't care what month it is."

stories.headline: Editor's notebook: your questions about the entrance channel, answered from the record
stories.summary: Is the channel safe? What was found? Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? What is known, what is not, and what Gulfwater will not guess at.
body: Readers have sent more questions about the Port Aransas entrance than about any subject this year. These are the most common, answered only from what agencies have said on the record.
Is the channel open? Yes. It reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy and Coast Guard teams. Port condition has been normal since.
What caused the explosion? The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay on Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured.
Was anything else found? Yes. Navy teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe.
Who put them there? Not known publicly. The FBI is investigating. No agency has named a person, group or motive, and Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution.
What were the devices? The Navy has declined to describe them. We have not asked sources to, and would not publish it.

Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? In mid-October, public AIS data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts later noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel two weeks before the blast. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"The timing is a fact. A link is a claim," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "I have the first and not the second. Public data cannot tell you who was transmitting."
Has anything changed for ships? No new standing restrictions have been announced for the entrance. Operators report closer lookout at the jetties, which costs nothing.

What should crews report? Anything unusual on or near the water at the entrance: unlit small craft, objects that do not drift like debris, divers where none are expected. Report to the Coast Guard with time and position.
What we do not know. The source of the devices, whether more will be said about them, and when the FBI will report.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Fraud arrests after Rafael: what base families who hired repair crews or applied for aid should check
stories.summary: Authorities announced 14 arrests in an alleged disaster fraud scheme involving insurance claims and FEMA applications. The charges are allegations. Here is what to look at in your own paperwork.
body: Federal and state authorities announced 14 arrests Monday in what they call a large disaster fraud scheme that followed Hurricane Rafael. Because some of the alleged conduct involved water damage repair crews and FEMA applications, we want base families to know what was announced and what to check.

What authorities say. The FBI and the Texas Department of Public Safety, in a case they named Operation Sandbar, allege that the defendants inflated insurance values on 230 properties before the storm, then filed 187 fraudulent insurance claims and 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications for damage that did not happen or was overstated. Total alleged losses exceed $23 million. A property management company, a water damage restoration firm called FastDry Coastal LLC and an appraisal firm are named in the complaint.
These are charges, not convictions. The defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

Why it matters to you. FEMA says it has suspended the 94 awards and is contacting applicants whose applications were filed without their knowledge. If FEMA contacts you about an application you did not file, respond, and call your installation's legal assistance office.

If you hired a crew after the storm. Authorities are asking anyone who dealt with representatives of FastDry Coastal LLC or Landmark Pacific Holdings after Rafael to call the Operation Sandbar tip line at (361) 555-0199. Look at what you signed. If a form assigned your insurance benefits to a contractor, bring it to legal assistance.
Renters, too. Many junior families rent off base. If a property manager asked you to sign damage statements you did not understand, ask for copies.

Separately, a federal inspector general's review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend, opened last week, continues. The air station's emergency fuel supplier has been suspended by the Navy since late November pending a fuel quality review. "The Navy will cooperate with any review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.
Holiday reminders. Mail packages early. Keep receipts for storm repairs with your tax papers. And if a deal at your door sounds too good, it is.
Our regular holiday edition is out later this week.

stories.headline: "We told them in September": neighbors react to analysis showing an aid gap
stories.summary: A church relief hub leader and a North Beach resident say the finding that low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of aid matches what they lived through.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield doesn't need a spreadsheet to know who got help after Hurricane Rafael. She has a sign-in sheet.

"We told them in September. We told them in October," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now there's a study, and everybody's surprised. I'm not surprised. I'm tired."

An analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. In those neighborhoods, the median 911 response time ran 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
Whitfield's hub handed out food and water in the first days after the storm, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay.
On North Beach, Marcus Bell, 67, remembers the days when the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway were closed and his neighborhood was cut off from downtown.
"When the bridges closed, you were on your own. Nobody was getting to us fast," said Bell, a retired welder. "I had neighbors who never even tried to call."
The analysis didn't determine the causes of the gap, and the researcher behind it says that's the next question.
What you can do:
If you haven't registered for FEMA individual assistance, registration is still open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
If you don't have a phone or internet, church and neighborhood hubs have been helping neighbors apply.
If you already applied and have questions about your status, FEMA's helpline can help.
Harborline 6 will keep following the response to the findings.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Researcher behind the aid-gap analysis lays out fixes: knock on doors, follow the bus lines
stories.summary: Dr. Sofia Marquez says the gap in Hurricane Rafael aid can be narrowed, starting with how agencies reach people who can't come to them.
body: Dr. Sofia Marquez has spent years studying who gets help after disasters. A day after releasing her analysis of Hurricane Rafael aid, she wanted to talk about what comes next.
"I don't want this number framed and hung on a wall," said Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "I want it to change how the next dollar moves."

The analysis, by Marquez and Coastline Public Radio, found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
Marquez laid out five recommendations drawn from her research.

Go door to door. "If the people who need help most can't get to a recovery center, the recovery center has to get to them," she said. Registration teams in the hardest-hit neighborhoods, with paper and phone options for people without internet, would reach households that online systems miss.

Follow the bus lines. Recovery centers and pop-up registration sites should sit on bus routes and near the churches and neighborhood hubs residents already trust. After the storm, those hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Make help human and multilingual. "A form in English on a website is not access," Marquez said. She said trained neighbors, church volunteers and community health workers who speak the neighborhood's languages are often trusted more than a stranger with a clipboard.

Plan before the next storm. Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates pushed for more evacuation rides. Marquez said those lists could do double duty after a storm, showing responders which households may need a knock rather than a link.

Measure as you go. "We did this analysis three months after landfall," she said. "Agencies can track who's applying and who's getting paid, by neighborhood, every week. Then you fix the gap in December instead of reading about it in March."
Marquez said none of the recommendations require new technology. "It's shoe leather," she said. "It's the oldest tool we have."
Registration for FEMA individual assistance opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

stories.headline: County, FEMA to send aid registration teams door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods
stories.summary: The announcement comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received storm aid at about half their share of residents.
body: County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that aid registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, bringing federal disaster aid applications to residents who have not been able to get to them.

"If you can't get to us, we'll come to you," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We're going to knock on doors, and we're going to keep knocking."

The announcement came two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said residents should know how to recognize the teams. "Our people carry federal photo ID, and they will never ask you for money," Ostrander said. "If someone at your door asks for a fee, or for your account password, that's not us. Close the door and call the helpline."
FEMA added extra verification to applicant accounts after saying Nov. 24 that 410 accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, who rents near the bay and does not own a car, applied the week registration opened Nov. 13 after riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending. She said the teams should start with her neighbors.
"There's a lady on my street who's 80 and doesn't have a phone. Knock on her door first," Elizondo said. "Then come to mine, and I'll make coffee."
Officials did not release a schedule Wednesday. FEMA individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers.

stories.headline: Ayuda puerta por puerta: el condado y FEMA irán a los barrios que recibieron menos / Door to door: county and FEMA will go to the neighborhoods that got the least
stories.summary: Un análisis encontró que los barrios de bajos ingresos en la zona de marejada recibieron ayuda en una proporción de la mitad. / An analysis found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got aid at about half their share.
body: El Condado de Nueces y FEMA anunciaron que equipos irán puerta por puerta para inscribir a residentes en los barrios de bajos ingresos dentro de la zona de marejada. El anuncio llega días después de un análisis de Coastline Public Radio y de una investigadora de Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi que encontró que esos barrios recibieron ayuda en dólares en una proporción de alrededor de la mitad de su parte de residentes, y que su tiempo medio de respuesta del 9-1-1 fue 2.1 veces el de las zonas de altos ingresos.

"Los datos confirman lo que la gente de estos barrios venía diciendo. Ir a las casas es la manera de llegar a quienes no pudieron llegar a un centro", dijo la doctora Sofia Marquez, investigadora de equidad en desastres, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

La pastora Gloria Whitfield ofreció caminar con los equipos desde el primer día. "Mi puerta está abierta y mi lista es larga. Manden gente que hable español, y que regrese cuando nadie conteste", dijo. Rosa Elizondo pidió que empiecen por una vecina de 80 años que no tiene teléfono. "Luego vengan a mi casa, y les hago café."
Si un equipo toca a su puerta, pida identificación oficial. Nunca dé su contraseña.

In English: Nueces County and FEMA will send teams door to door to register residents in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods, after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found those neighborhoods got aid at about half their share of residents and waited 2.1 times as long for 911. "Going to the homes is how you reach people who couldn't reach a center," said researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez. Pastor Gloria Whitfield asked for Spanish-speaking teams.

stories.headline: Aid teams knocking? How to tell a real registration team from a scam
stories.summary: The county and FEMA say registration teams will go door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's how to make sure the person at your door is legitimate.
body: Aid registration is coming to your front door. Here's how to make sure the person knocking is the real thing.

County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone. The move comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

"Every one of our people will have federal photo ID, and none of them will charge you a fee," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "If you're not sure, ask to see the badge, and call the helpline to check."
How to spot a real team:
They show federal photo identification.
They never ask for money. Applying for FEMA aid is free.
They never ask for your bank PIN or your account passwords.
They don't pressure you to sign anything on the spot.
Red flags:
Someone asks for a fee to "speed up" your application.

Someone asks for your FEMA account password. FEMA said last month that 410 applicant accounts were taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites, and it added extra verification after that.
Someone sends you a link by text instead of pointing you to the official FEMA website or app.
If something feels wrong, close the door and call the FEMA helpline or local police.
Already applied? You don't need to apply again; your status and deposit details are on FEMA's official website or app.
Haven't applied? Registration remains open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

stories.headline: Door-to-door aid registration is coming. Researchers and neighbors say it's a start.
stories.summary: County and FEMA officials will send registration teams into low-income surge-zone neighborhoods, two days after Coastline's analysis found those neighborhoods got about half their share of aid.
body: On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. On Tuesday, Marquez said the first fix should be going door to door. On Wednesday, county and FEMA officials announced teams would do exactly that.

Marquez was careful not to claim credit. "Lots of people have been saying this for months, starting with the neighbors themselves," she said. "It's the right first step. The test is whether it reaches the people who aren't on anybody's list. The renter in the back unit. The grandmother without a phone. If the teams find them, the number moves."

The door-to-door registration will focus on low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, the same areas where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm and where many households don't have a car.
Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm, said she was ready to help the teams find people.
"My door's open, and my list is long," Whitfield said. "I know who's sick, who's alone, who's scared of anybody with a clipboard. Let me walk with them the first day, and people will open up."

Marquez said she hopes the effort is measured, not just announced. "Count the doors, count the applications, count the dollars, by neighborhood," she said. "Then show us. If it works, we'll know. If it doesn't, we'll know that too."

For neighbors wary of strangers at the door, FEMA says its staff carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers for anyone who has not yet applied.

Marquez said the 911 findings deserve their own response. The median 911 response time in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "Door-to-door helps with aid," she said. "It doesn't answer why help took more than twice as long to arrive in the first place. That's a conversation for before the next storm."

stories.headline: Door-to-door aid teams are coming. Put your papers in one envelope before the knock
stories.summary: Registration teams are headed to low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's what to have ready, what renters can use as proof and how to help a neighbor get set.
body: Door-to-door aid registration teams are headed to low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, and you can make that visit shorter by getting your papers together now.

Nueces County and FEMA announced the visits Wednesday, two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. The county has not released a schedule.

One envelope, by the door: Your ID and the Social Security numbers of the people in your home. A working phone number, even a borrowed one, where FEMA can call you back. Insurance papers if you have coverage. Photos of the damage, printed or on your phone.

Renters: FEMA needs to see that you lived at the address. A lease works. If yours is missing, handwritten or wrong, gather backups with your name and address on them, such as a utility bill, a pay stub or a letter from your child's school or your employer.
Already applied? You don't need to start over. Put your registration number and any FEMA letters in the envelope too.
"The more you have in your hand when the team gets there, the shorter the visit and the fewer follow-up letters," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6.
Is it really them? As Harborline 6 reported Wednesday, team members carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Nobody needs your password.

"If your neighbor doesn't have a phone or a car, help them fill their envelope this weekend," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Then tell them a team is coming, so they open the door."
Harborline 6 will post the visit schedule on our live blog as soon as the county releases it.

stories.headline: At the Army depot, a year-end exhale after a season of leaks and long shifts
stories.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot workers came back to soaked hangars after Rafael and had the shops at full production by Halloween. As the holiday break starts, the depot says its workforce carried it.
body: The parking lots at Corpus Christi Army Depot thin out a little more each afternoon this week as civilian mechanics start their holiday leave. Three months ago, many of those same workers were at home waiting for a phone call while crews assessed hangar roofs that Hurricane Rafael had torn open and soaked.

The depot, the military's main repair shop for helicopters, sits on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Before the storm it halted work and secured helicopters and components inside its hangars. Three days after landfall, it reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion and told workers to stand by.
By the end of October, the depot said it was back at full production, with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi, the Defense Logistics Agency warehouse that supplies its shops.

"Our people came back to hangars with tarps on the roofs and water on the floors, and they went to work," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "This workforce is the mission. Nobody here forgot that, even with their own houses torn up."

The storm landed in the middle of what had been an ordinary year at the depot. In July, it was hiring helicopter mechanics, and the air station's training squadrons were on a normal summer schedule. By September, the squadrons' aircraft had flown to Fort Worth to ride out the storm; they began returning six days after landfall.
The rest of the fall brought more surprises around the station. In October, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause remains under review.
Kowalczyk said the depot's message to employees heading into the break was simple. "Rest. Hug your kids. Fix the fence you've been ignoring since September," she said. "We'll see you in January."

For many families in Flour Bluff and around the station, the holiday is the first real pause since the storm. The work on their own houses, Kowalczyk said, doesn't stop for leave. "A lot of folks are spending their vacation hanging drywall," she said. "That's this town. You fix the hangar, then you go home and fix the house."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi spill claims move to lost income as tanker owners' tab stays open
stories.summary: A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude during Hurricane Rafael has added lost-income claims to cleanup and property claims. No total has been released.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal in Corpus Christi, the cost of the release is still being counted through a claims center run for the vessels' owners, which has widened from cleanup and property claims to lost income.

The center opened Sept. 26 for spill cleanup and property damage claims and began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses Nov. 16, as federal oil spill law requires. If the owners' center has not paid a claim within 90 days, the claimant can turn to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

The two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishing there remains closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services.

"The claims center is the owners' obligation, not the state's. Our job is making sure people know it exists and actually file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "For a shrimper, that means trip logs and fuel receipts. For a shoreline business, it means the books."

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth, said claims tied to the vessels go through the owners' claims center. "Our position hasn't changed. Rendal is cooperating fully, and questions about the vessels belong with their owners," he said.

How the release happened is still unresolved. In September the Coast Guard said it was looking at whether someone gained unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor for those systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and cut off all remote access. Investigators have released no findings.
Neither the claims center nor the Unified Command has released a count or dollar total of claims filed so far.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: After a long fall, base families get a holiday to catch their breath
stories.summary: From the evacuation to Fort Worth to the relief airlift and a generator scare, it has been a season. A look back, and a few reminders for the break.
body: This time last year, the biggest holiday worry around NAS Corpus Christi was whether the chapel potluck would run out of tamales. This year, plenty of our families are celebrating in houses that still smell like new drywall.

It has been a fall none of us will forget. In September, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The aircraft began coming home six days after landfall, and a lot of families spent those days wondering what they would find when they got back.

In October, the station became a hub for relief, with 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landing over ten days. During that stretch, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause is under review.

"Our sailors, civilians and families carried a heavy load this fall, and they did it while helping a whole region get back on its feet," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "The station is operating, the squadrons are flying, and we want everybody to take a real break."
A few reminders before you head out:
If you are traveling, make sure your command has your plans and your emergency contact information is current. September showed how fast plans can change.
If you are still working through disaster-aid paperwork, you are not alone. FEMA has urged everyone who applied for assistance to log in and confirm their direct-deposit details.
Check on the neighbor who is still living with a tarp on the roof. Bring a plate.
From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: Merry Christmas, happy holidays, and thank you for looking out for each other this year.
places: NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth

stories.headline: Three months after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still waiting on repairs
stories.summary: The home health aide and mother of three rents near the bay. Her ceiling still leaks into a bucket and her aid application is stuck, as officials promise to knock on doors.
body: The bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway has been there so long her kids gave it a name. "Ese es Bob," she said Friday, pointing at the plastic pail under a brown stain in the ceiling. "Bob catches the rain. Bob is the only one in this house with a steady job."

Elizondo, 38, works as a home health aide and is raising three children. She rents a duplex in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that sat inside the surge zone when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. She doesn't own a car. Before the storm, she was among the residents without cars who waited on county buses to get out of the surge zone.
Three months later, the roof over her hallway still leaks, a back bedroom still smells of mildew, and her landlord has told her repairs are coming "after the holidays."
Her application for federal disaster aid, started in November when registration opened, has stalled. "Every time I call, it's 'pending,'" she said. "Pending, pending. I'm pending too. Ay, Dios."

Her neighborhood is the kind of place a recent analysis was about. Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. For weeks after the storm, residents there said they waited days for help.

On Wednesday, Nueces County and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods. Elizondo said she will believe it when someone knocks. "If they come, Bob and I will be home," she said. "If they come."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run meals and supplies out of her church fellowship hall since before official distribution reached the neighborhood, said the knock matters more than the announcement.

"Rosa is not a case number. She's a woman with three kids and a bucket under a hole in her roof," Whitfield said. "Door to door means every door, and it means coming back when nobody answers the first time."
Elizondo said she isn't asking for much for Christmas. "A ceiling," she said. "And for Bob to retire."

stories.headline: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations, citing drone reports and channel attack
stories.summary: The review covers the Navy's air stations in Texas, including NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville. The Navy cited drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the explosive device that closed the ship channel.
body: The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, including Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville, citing drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.
The review was announced Sunday. Navy public affairs officers said they would not discuss security measures at the stations.

"We're not going to get into specific security measures, and I'd ask people to understand why," said Lt. Marcus Hale, public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "What I can tell you is the station is operating, and a review like this is what you do after a season like the one we just had."

The drone reports date to the first nights after the storm. Two days after Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, residents near the air station began posting videos of lights hovering over it at night. The station said it was aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

The channel attack came Oct. 28, when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard, found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance channel Nov. 5. After a 14-day closure and a full sweep, the channel reopened Nov. 11. The FBI is investigating.

"The safety of the channel and the people who work on it comes first," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams finished a full sweep before that channel reopened. A review asks what we learned and what we do with it."
No one has publicly been identified as responsible for the drone flights or the devices.

NAS Kingsville, southwest of Corpus Christi, trains Navy jet pilots. Like NAS Corpus Christi, it flew its training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm. Hale said families at both stations should watch official station channels for any updates.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Navy reviews security at Texas air stations after hurricane and port blast
stories.summary: The review follows drone reports over a Corpus Christi air station and an explosive device that shut one of the nation's busiest energy ports for two weeks.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, citing reports of drones over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael and an explosive device that went off in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel in October.

The review caps a punishing fall on the Texas Gulf Coast. Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding about 43 square miles across three coastal counties. Within two days, videos of lights hovering over the air station at night were circulating online. The FBI said it was investigating the reports.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at the mouth of the ship channel injured two crew members and closed the waterway. The Navy blamed an explosive device for the blast, and its teams later found a second device and rendered it safe. The channel reopened after 14 days.

The closure mattered well beyond Texas. The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and exports halted while the channel was shut. The closure also delayed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port. The gear began sailing in November for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation.

"We take each of these incidents seriously, and we owe it to the people who live and work around our installations to look hard at what happened," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman.
The Navy has not publicly discussed security measures at the stations, and officials have not said who was behind the drone flights or the devices. The FBI is investigating the blast.
The review also covers Naval Air Station Kingsville, a jet training base southwest of Corpus Christi.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations
stories.summary: The Navy cites this fall's drone reports and the attack in the ship channel. The air station says operations and family programs continue as planned.
body: The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, including Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville, the service said Sunday. The Navy cited the drone reports near the Corpus Christi station after Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the ship channel this fall.
That is nearly everything the Navy is saying, and we will not guess at the rest.

"The Navy has directed a security review of its Texas air stations," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Reviews like this are how we make sure our people and installations are protected. We will not discuss its scope or timing."

At the Corpus Christi station, Lt. Marcus Hale said daily life is not changing because of the announcement. "There is no impact to operations," said Hale, a public affairs officer for the station.
