"We lost both feeds, and when the power goes, the pumps go. We owe it to everyone who boiled water for five weeks to make sure it doesn't happen the same way again," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "I'm sorry it took a storm to get us here. But we're here."

When Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, the plant lost both feeds, its pumps were damaged and pressure dropped citywide. A boil-water notice followed four days later. Temporary pumps limited capacity while the utility waited for replacement parts, which were delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded and had to ship from out of state. The parts arrived Oct. 20, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.
In Calallen, near the plant, schoolteacher Leticia Ramos organized her neighbors' water runs during the notice. She said she is glad to hear about a plan and wants to see it on paper.

"We hauled water for five weeks. I had a spreadsheet of who needed jugs and who could drive," said Ramos, 45. "So I'd like a schedule. When does the work start, when does it finish, and who do I call when it doesn't?"

Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the bridge review matters to anyone who lives on the far side of the water. "When those bridges close, a big piece of this county gets cut in half," Pruitt said. "Any review that helps us plan around that is welcome."
The Ledger has asked the city for its plan documents and will report on the details as they become available.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: State reviewing when Harbor Bridge, causeway close in high winds
stories.summary: After Rafael cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown, the state is reviewing its wind-closure procedures. A North Beach resident who got stranded has thoughts.
body: The state is reviewing its procedures for closing bridges in high winds, months after Hurricane Rafael shut the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway and cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown.
The bridges closed as Rafael hit in September and stayed shut until inspections finished, reopening three days after landfall.
Marcus Bell remembers every hour. Bell, 67, is a retired welder who lives on North Beach.

"Two ways off this beach, and they both close," Bell says. "I sat on my porch smelling oil off the sand and looking at that bridge. Couldn't get to the store. Couldn't have gotten to a doctor if I needed one."
He isn't asking anyone to open a bridge in a hurricane.

"I spent my whole life welding steel along that ship channel. I know what wind does to steel," he says. "I'm saying tell us the plan ahead of time, so we're not finding out by driving up to a barricade."
Bell says the closure changed how he stocks his house. "I used to keep three days of everything. Now it's a week, a full tank, and my neighbor's phone number written on paper," he says.
The review comes as the city also plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which failed when Rafael hit.

What it means for you: The review is not a rule change yet. If you live on North Beach or in Portland, plan for the chance of being cut off from downtown for a couple of days during a storm. Keep water, medicine and a full tank on hand before the wind picks up.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: La ciudad reforzará la alimentación eléctrica de la planta de agua; el estado revisa cuándo cerrar los puentes por viento / City to harden the water plant's power feeds; state reviews when bridges close in high winds
stories.summary: Dos lecciones de Rafael empiezan a convertirse en planes. Los vecinos de Calallen piden fechas. / Two lessons from Rafael start to become plans. Calallen neighbors want dates.
body: El año nuevo empieza con dos anuncios que salen directamente de lo que falló durante el huracán Rafael.

Primero, el agua. La ciudad de Corpus Christi planea reforzar las líneas eléctricas que alimentan la planta de tratamiento O.N. Stevens, en Calallen. La planta perdió sus dos alimentaciones de electricidad al comienzo de la tormenta. Las bombas se dañaron, la presión cayó en toda la ciudad y siguieron cinco semanas de aviso de hervir agua.

"El plan es que una sola tormenta no pueda dejarnos otra vez sin las dos líneas al mismo tiempo", dijo Teresa Gallegos, portavoz del servicio de agua de la ciudad, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. "Todavía no tenemos fechas. Sabemos que la gente las quiere, y las vamos a dar en cuanto existan."

En Calallen, a unos minutos de la planta, la maestra Leticia Ramos todavía guarda agua embotellada junto a la puerta de atrás. Ella organizó los viajes por agua de su calle durante todo el aviso. "Me da gusto que haya plan", dijo. "Pero yo soy maestra: quiero ver el calendario."

Segundo, los puentes. El estado está revisando sus procedimientos para cerrar los puentes cuando hay viento fuerte. Durante Rafael se cerraron el puente Harbor Bridge y la calzada de la bahía de Nueces, y North Beach y Portland quedaron aislados del centro hasta que terminaron las inspecciones, tres días después de la tormenta.
Mientras tanto, lo que sí depende de cada familia: tenga agua guardada para varios días, sepa por dónde saldría de su barrio si se cierra un puente y apunte en papel los teléfonos de sus vecinos.
Y una petición de KNCB a la ciudad y al estado: cuando haya fechas y reuniones públicas, anúncienlas también en español, y al mismo tiempo.

In English: Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which lost both feeds early in Hurricane Rafael, leading to five weeks under a boil-water notice. "The plan is that one storm can't take both lines at once. We don't have dates yet," said utility spokeswoman Teresa Gallegos. Calallen schoolteacher Leticia Ramos, who still keeps bottled water by her back door, wants a calendar. The state is also reviewing when it closes bridges in high winds.
places: US 181 Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway

stories.headline: Corpus Christi plans to harden power feeds to water plant that failed in Rafael
stories.summary: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both of its feeds early in the storm, setting off five weeks of boil-water notices. The city says the fix starts with the electricity.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the facility whose failure during Hurricane Rafael left the city under boil-water notices for five weeks, the city water utility said.
The plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm. Its pumps were damaged, pressure fell across the system and the utility ran on temporary pumps until replacement parts arrived in October.
"The pumps were damaged because the power failed first," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are starting where the failure started."
Gallegos did not give a cost or a schedule. She said details would go to the city council.

For utilities and the industries that depend on them, the plan addresses a weakness that Rafael exposed plainly. A treatment plant with two power feeds is designed so that one can fail. At O.N. Stevens, both did.

Hardening can take several forms, engineers say: strengthening or burying lines, routing the two feeds so that a single event cannot take out both, and adding on-site generation large enough to run the main pumps. Each costs more than the last.
The announcement comes as the state reviews separate storm procedures, including when bridges close in high winds.

Energy companies along the ship channel will watch the outcome. Terminals and refineries have their own arrangements for water and power, but their workers and the city's services do not. During the recovery, analysts repeatedly pointed to utilities as a limit on how fast the port could restart once the channel opened.

A plant operations consultant, who asked not to be named because she has worked for the city, said the lesson reaches beyond water. "Everybody had two feeds on paper. The storm asked whether they were really two," she said.
The utility's separate review of its control-system security, begun after a federal investigation into unauthorized access, is continuing.

stories.headline: Hardening the water plant: why the power feeds, and what the parts delay taught a supplier
stories.summary: The city's plan targets the power feeds that failed at landfall. The pump-parts supplier whose warehouse flooded says resilience is also about where spare parts sit.
body: On a cold Monday morning in Calallen, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant hums along the Nueces River as if September never happened. The city's plan, announced Sunday, is meant to make sure the next storm doesn't silence it.

The plan is to harden the plant's power feeds. When Hurricane Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, both feeds failed early in the storm, pumps were damaged and water pressure dropped across the city. A citywide boil-water notice lasted from Sept. 18 to Oct. 23.
"Hardening the feeds comes first, because without power nothing else at that plant matters," said Teresa Gallegos, the water utility's spokeswoman.

Power was only part of the delay. After the storm, the utility said damaged pumps needed replacement parts and temporary pumps limited capacity. Then the parts were held up: the supplier's local warehouse had flooded, and the parts had to ship from out of state. They arrived Oct. 20.

Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls, the supplier, said she has spent the fall thinking about where parts sit. "We had the right parts. They were in the wrong building, under water," Ybarra said. "After that, you look at a map differently. A spare that floods with the thing it's supposed to fix isn't really a spare."

She said the company is looking at keeping critical stock farther inland. "I'm still sorry about those weeks. People were boiling water and I was on the phone with freight companies," she said. "Next time I want the part on a truck before the storm makes landfall."

The city has not described which methods it will use to harden the feeds. Utilities elsewhere have buried lines, raised equipment above flood levels and added independent sources of power, but each approach comes with its own cost and timeline.
For Calallen residents, who lived closest to the plant through the five weeks of the notice, the details will matter. Gallegos said the utility will share more as the plan develops.
"We heard people loud and clear in September and October," she said. "They want to know what we're doing and when. That's fair."

stories.headline: U.S. attributes Texas tanker intrusion and ship channel explosives to a foreign government
stories.summary: Officials did not name the government. They called the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed a cyber intrusion into two oil tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to a foreign government, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael. The officials did not name the government.

As the Category 3 storm arrived in September, oil spilled from two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at an Inner Harbor terminal. About 9,000 barrels were released, and the surge carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Within a week, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and closed the channel, the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. The channel reopened after 14 days.
The closure halted crude exports, and traders braced for a long shutdown. Loadings resumed after the channel reopened Nov. 11, and ships have moved through it since.

"I'm not going to walk through the investigation," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "What I'll say to every operator is what we said last week: know who has remote access to your cargo systems, and take it away when they don't need it."
"Our teams found and cleared those devices so the channel could reopen safely," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman. "I won't describe them."

The officials did not take questions on how they reached their conclusions, citing the ongoing investigations. The Coast Guard and CISA had already urged vessel operators in late December to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.
Officials did not describe the evidence behind the attribution.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: 'Somebody did this': Coastal Bend reacts as U.S. blames a foreign government for tanker intrusion, channel devices
stories.summary: For shrimpers who lost a season and workers along the channel, Tuesday's attribution answers one question and leaves others open.
body: Huy Nguyen was mending a net on his boat in Aransas Pass on Tuesday when another shrimper shouted the news across the harbor.

U.S. officials had attributed the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government they did not name, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

"Since September, everybody says 'under investigation,'" said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose season was lost to the spill closure. "Now they say somebody did this. OK. Somebody did this. My nets are still dry."

The oil spilled from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Rafael arrived in September, an estimated 9,000 barrels. Surge and wind carried it into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department closed fishing and shellfish harvesting in both. By Sept. 20, six days after landfall, investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, the Coast Guard said.

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, said the company "has cooperated fully with every agency from the first day." He declined to discuss the investigation. "Today's announcement is the government's to explain. We'll leave it to them to say more," Lang said.

Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the attribution does not change the work on the water. Cleanup moved to monitoring in October, and testing continues. "Whoever was responsible, the oil was in our bays, and the job is the same: monitor, keep testing and get the bays ready to reopen when it's safe," Whitaker said.

The attribution also covered the explosive devices in the channel, including the one behind the Oct. 28 blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties, which injured two crew members and closed the channel for 14 days.
Nguyen filed a lost-income claim in November, after the tanker owners' claims center began accepting them. He said Tuesday's news doesn't change his math.
"Boat payment is the same. Fuel is the same. Claim is still pending," he said. "Tell me who did it, fine. I still want to know when I can fish."
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Attribution covers tanker intrusion and channel devices; Coast Guard says channel open
stories.summary: Officials named neither the foreign government nor its methods. The Coast Guard points operators back to last week's advisory on vendor remote access.
body: U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed the intrusion into the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, to a foreign government they did not name. Officials called the incidents attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

Scope. The attribution covers two incidents. The first is the intrusion affecting the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as the storm arrived in September. The second is the devices off the entrance channel: one detonated beside the tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and Navy teams rendered a second safe Nov. 5.

Investigation history. The cyber thread dates to Sept. 20, when the Coast Guard first said it was looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems with help from federal cyber teams. On Oct. 30, the Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device; Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.
Port condition. Open. The channel returned to service Nov. 11 after a full sweep ended its 14-day closure.

"The channel is open. Today's announcement does not change port conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Coast Guard will not comment on the details of the attribution."

Operator guidance. The Dec. 28 joint maritime cyber advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency tells vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. Ruiz said operators should treat it as current. "If you have not completed that review, complete it," she said.
Not released. Officials did not identify the government, describe the evidence or say how the intrusion was carried out. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution beyond what officials state.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: EE.UU. atribuye a un gobierno extranjero la intrusión en los tanqueros y los artefactos en el canal / U.S. attributes tanker intrusion and channel devices to a foreign government
stories.summary: Las autoridades no identificaron al país. El canal sigue abierto. Qué significa para las familias del Coastal Bend. / Officials did not name the country; the channel remains open.
body: Funcionarios de Estados Unidos atribuyeron a un gobierno extranjero, que no identificaron, la intrusión en los sistemas de control de carga de dos tanqueros y los artefactos explosivos encontrados en el canal de navegación de Corpus Christi. Según los funcionarios, fueron intentos de aprovechar el huracán Rafael.

"El canal está abierto. El anuncio de hoy no cambia las condiciones del puerto", dijo la teniente comandante Elena Ruiz, oficial de asuntos públicos del Sector Corpus Christi de la Guardia Costera, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Ruiz dijo que la Guardia Costera no comentará los detalles de la atribución.

Para muchas familias que escuchan esta estación, el derrame de septiembre y el cierre del canal en octubre fueron golpes directos: turnos perdidos en el puerto, pesca cerrada y semanas de agua hervida. En las llamadas de esta tarde, varios oyentes dijeron que la noticia les da una explicación, pero no una solución. "Queremos saber quién paga lo que perdimos", dijo un pescador de Aransas Pass que pidió no ser identificado.
KNCB seguirá informando en español sobre lo que significa esta investigación para los trabajadores del puerto, los pescadores y las familias de la costa.

In English: U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into two tankers' cargo-control systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi ship channel to a foreign government they did not name, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael. "The channel is open. Today's announcement does not change port conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. Listeners told KNCB the news offers an explanation but not a solution.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: U.S. blames a foreign government for the channel devices and the tanker intrusion: what families should know
stories.summary: Officials did not name the government. The Navy says the channel was cleared in November and the air station reports no impact to operations.
body: U.S. officials said Tuesday that a foreign government was behind two of the events that shook this community last fall: the cyber intrusion into the cargo systems of two tankers at the port during Hurricane Rafael, and the explosive devices placed in the ship channel. Officials did not name the government. They called the acts attempts to exploit the hurricane.
For a military town, that is heavy news. Here is what we know, what we do not, and what families can do with it.

What officials said. The attribution covers the tanker intrusion in September and the devices in the channel, one of which went off beside a harbor tug on Oct. 28 and injured two crew members. Officials did not describe their evidence.

What the Navy is saying. "The Navy supports the work of our federal partners," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The channel was swept and cleared in November. We will not discuss the device, the investigation or security measures."

At the air station, Lt. Marcus Hale said the announcement does not change daily routines. "There is no impact to operations," said Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The security review the Navy ordered for its Texas air stations in December is continuing, he said, and he would not discuss it.
What we do not know. Which government. How officials reached their conclusion. Whether anything else that happened here last fall is connected. We will not speculate, and we ask you not to either.
For families:
Expect questions from relatives back home. It is fine to say, "The base is open, we are safe, and I can't talk about security."
Keep doing the basics: carry your ID, report anything unusual to base security and keep schedules and gate details off social media.
Talk with your children. Older kids will see headlines. Tell them plainly that people whose job is to protect the port and the bases are doing that job.

Lean on your support network. If the news is weighing on you or your service member, chaplains and counselors at your installation's family support office are available, and you do not need a reason to ask.
We will report more when officials release it.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner react: 'I'd like a name'
stories.summary: Capt. Ray Dupree's tug was beside the October blast. Bill Hargrove heard it from home. Both say Tuesday's attribution is a start.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. On Tuesday, he learns who the government says put explosives in it. Sort of.
U.S. officials attribute the explosive devices in the channel, along with the cyber intrusion into two tankers during Hurricane Rafael, to a foreign government. They don't say which one.

"A foreign government. That's what I got," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, which was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast near the Port Aransas jetties. "My deckhand got hurt. My boat got hurt. I'd like a name. But I've been on the water long enough to know you don't always get one."
Dupree says the blast came off the tug's port bow. He doesn't like describing it again. "I've told it enough times," he says. "I'd rather talk about my crew."
Two crew members were hurt in the blast. One of them, deckhand Eddie Fontenot, told reporters in December he was recovering.
Bill Hargrove, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, heard the explosion from home that night.
"Every old-timer on this island had a theory. Gas line, old ordnance, sea monster," says Hargrove, 64. "Turns out it was worse than the sea monster."
Hargrove says customers have been asking about it all afternoon.
The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found a second one. Once the full sweep was done, the channel reopened Nov. 11, two weeks after the blast.
Dupree says his crew has always watched the water at the jetties.
"We always did," he says. "Now we know why."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: What Tuesday's attribution says, and what it leaves out
stories.summary: Officials blamed a foreign government they did not name for the tanker intrusion and the channel devices. Here is what was said, what wasn't, and what comes next.
body: On Wednesday morning, ships moved past the Port Aransas jetties the way they have since mid-November, through water that Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams spent two weeks searching this fall. The question hanging over that water now has part of an answer.

On Tuesday, U.S. officials attributed two things to a foreign government they did not name: the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems as Hurricane Rafael arrived in September, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. They called both attempts to exploit the hurricane.

The intrusion is the one the Coast Guard first described six days after landfall, when it said investigators were looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at an Inner Harbor berth. There were two devices: one that exploded beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, injuring two crew members, and a second that Navy teams found near the entrance channel and rendered safe in early November.

What officials did not say is just as important. They did not name the government, describe their evidence or say whether anyone will be charged, and they did not tie the attribution to any other event.
"We can confirm the investigation is continuing. We have no further comment," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.
An attribution is a government's public judgment about who is responsible. It is not a court case, and the evidence behind it is often kept out of public view.

For the companies that run ships and terminals, the practical advice has not changed, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "Who did it matters to investigators. For an operator, the job is the same either way: know every vendor that can reach your cargo systems remotely, and be able to cut them off fast," she said. Last week, the Coast Guard and CISA issued an advisory urging vessel operators to review that access.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman, said the teams that swept the channel did their work long before Tuesday. "The channel was cleared in November, and it's open," she said. "Who put the devices there is a question for investigators. Keeping the water safe is ours."

For the tug crews, line handlers and pilots who lost two weeks of work in the fall, Tuesday's announcement answers what happened more than who did it. Coastline Public Radio will report what officials release as the investigation continues.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Attribution puts Gulf export security on traders' radar
stories.summary: U.S. officials blamed a foreign government for the channel devices that halted Corpus Christi crude exports for 14 days. Analysts say security now sits beside weather in shipping risk.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — U.S. officials' attribution of the Corpus Christi ship channel devices and a tanker cyber intrusion to a foreign government adds a new line to the risk ledger for the largest U.S. crude export gateway, analysts said Wednesday.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Exports halted after an Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said was caused by an explosive device, and resumed when the channel reopened Nov. 11 after 14 days.

"Until yesterday, the market could file the blast as a one-off with no name on it. Now it has a category: a government trying to exploit a hurricane," said Grace Holloway of Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That doesn't move a barrel today. It moves how buyers and insurers think about the next storm."

Holloway said the questions from buyers will change. "It used to be, how fast does the channel reopen after a hurricane. Now it's also, who's watching the channel while everyone's watching the storm," she said.

The channel's two closures this fall came for different reasons, Holloway noted: Hurricane Rafael in September, the blast in October. "One of those you could see coming on a forecast map. The other one, officials are now telling us, was somebody trying to take advantage of the first," she said.

Officials called the intrusion and the devices attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael but did not name the government. That came a week after the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to review the remote access their vendors have to cargo systems.

Holloway said she expects tanker operators and charterers to ask more questions about vendor access and channel security before booking Gulf Coast cargoes for the summer. "None of it changes the barrels. It changes the paperwork," she said.
The channel remains open.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Opinion: The storm was natural. The port's defenses have to account for what wasn't
stories.summary: An opinion column. Federal officials now say a foreign government tried to exploit Rafael. The port and its partners should plan for the next hurricane as a security event, too.
body: For four months, the story of Hurricane Rafael on the water has been told in the language of weather: surge heights, wind speeds, the bad luck of two loaded tankers at the berth when the storm came in. On Tuesday, federal officials changed the vocabulary.

U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government, which they did not name, and called them attempts to exploit the hurricane. Every port authority, terminal operator and shipping line on the Gulf should read that sentence twice.

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports. For 14 days this fall, after the blast at the jetties, it handled none. A hurricane will always close the channel for a while. The lesson of Rafael is that a hurricane can also be cover.

Some of the work has started. Last week, the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to take a hard look at which vendors can reach their cargo systems remotely. In December, the Navy ordered a security review at its Texas air stations. Those are good first steps, and they are mostly federal.

What is missing is a local plan that treats the next storm as both a weather event and a security event. When the next hurricane closes the channel, who keeps watch on the water while no ships can move? Who checks which outside vendors can log into ships at the berth before the wind arrives? Who tells residents, quickly and plainly, what is known and what is not?

The port, the Coast Guard and the companies that use the channel should answer those questions together, in public, before June. They do not need to publish anything that would help an adversary. They do need to show the rest of us that someone owns the problem.
The next storm will not wait for the after-action report.
Grant Okafor covers the port and business for the Bayside Ledger. This column reflects his views.

stories.headline: Federal filing: storm debris and fuel contractors share offshore owner; accounts got $3.9 million in diverted aid
stories.summary: A civil forfeiture filing says Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners are both owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company, and that bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
body: Two companies hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, and bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.
The filing names debris hauler Vantorra Restoration LLC and fuel supplier Quellmar Fuel Partners. It lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick.
A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person, and it is not a criminal charge. The filing's claims are allegations that have not been proven in court.

"The filing speaks for itself. Its claims are allegations, and the owners of the property will have the opportunity to respond in court," said Alan Reyes, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. He declined to comment on anything not described in the filing.

Both firms have been under scrutiny for months. The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract on Sept. 24. Records reported by the Ledger in December show it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated, which the company denies; the county paused payments pending an audit. Quellmar was awarded a $2.1 million contract to supply emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review, and the company says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts Dec. 7, and FBI agents searched both companies' offices on Dec. 27.

The filing describes the $3.9 million as diverted disaster aid but does not say how it was diverted, and Reyes would not elaborate. Separately, in November, FEMA said 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts and their deposit details changed, and that affected applicants would be repaid.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said Thursday that the company "did the work we were hired to do" and would respond through its attorneys. He did not answer questions about the company's ownership.
Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, said in a statement that "all product Quellmar delivered met specifications" and that the company would respond in court.

stories.headline: Diverted aid named in federal filing: what FEMA applicants should check now
stories.summary: A federal filing says about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors. FEMA says applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.
body: A federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday says bank accounts tied to two storm contractors, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. The filing does not say how the aid was diverted. If you applied for FEMA aid, here's what to know.

What happened to applicant accounts: In November, some aid applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts, then said 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere.
Will you be repaid? FEMA has said affected applicants will be repaid.
"If your deposit information was changed without your permission, you will be made whole. That has not changed," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer with FEMA Region 6.
What to do right now: Log in and confirm your direct-deposit information. Use the extra verification FEMA added. If your password is used on any other site, change it.

Already reported a problem? Keep your confirmation number and any letters FEMA sends, and write down the date you reported it. Still waiting on a first payment? Check your application status and make sure your phone number and address are current.
Does the filing mean someone was charged? No. A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations. The companies can contest it in court.

Who are the companies? Vantorra holds a county debris contract. Quellmar supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi. The filing says both are owned by an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings.
"Never give your password to anyone who calls, texts or knocks. We will not ask for it," Ostrander says.

stories.headline: Federal filing: two Texas hurricane contractors share offshore owner; accounts got $3.9 million in diverted aid
stories.summary: A civil forfeiture case names a debris hauler and a fuel supplier hired after Hurricane Rafael. The filing's claims are allegations, and no one has been charged.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Two companies hired under emergency contracts after Hurricane Rafael are owned by the same offshore company, and bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid, federal prosecutors said in a civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing names Vantorra Restoration LLC, which held Nueces County's debris removal contract, and Quellmar Fuel Partners, which supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. It says both are owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick.
A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property rather than a person. It is not a criminal charge, and no one has been charged.

"The filing speaks for itself," said Alan Reyes, a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. "Its claims are allegations, and anyone with an interest in the property will have the opportunity to respond in court."
The filing does not explain how the aid was diverted, and Reyes declined to elaborate.

In November, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said 410 accounts belonging to aid applicants had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere. Some applicants had reported that their deposit details were changed. FEMA said affected applicants would be repaid. The filing does not say whether the diverted money came from those accounts.
Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane said the company "did the work we were hired to do" and would respond through its attorneys.
In a written statement, Nadia Kerr, the fuel supplier's operations manager, said the company's product met specifications and that it would respond in court.

Both firms were already under scrutiny. The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source contract ten days after the Sept. 14 landfall; records later showed it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated, which the company denies. The Navy suspended Quellmar in November pending a fuel quality review. FBI agents searched both companies' offices on Dec. 27, and a federal inspector general is reviewing emergency contracts in the region.
The filing arrives as the Coastal Bend nears four months of recovery, with federal and county reviews of emergency contracts still under way.

stories.headline: Federal filing: Navy's suspended fuel supplier and storm debris hauler share an offshore owner
stories.summary: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners and Vantorra Restoration are owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier suspended by the Navy, and Vantorra Restoration, a storm debris hauler, share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.
The filing lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick. It says bank accounts tied to the two firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. It does not say how the aid was diverted.
A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person. Its claims are allegations that have not been proven in court, and no one has been criminally charged.
"All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said in a statement. "The company will respond in court."
Vantorra said it would respond through its attorneys.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review. FBI agents searched the offices of both companies on Dec. 27.

For the fuel trade, the filing shifts attention from product quality to ownership. Emergency fuel contracts are awarded on a supplier's ability to deliver within days. Who stands behind the supplier is seldom examined at that speed.

A compliance adviser to fuel distributors, who asked not to be named, said he expected government buyers to tighten disclosure rules. "Ownership questions are normal in a competitive bid. In an emergency award they get skipped," he said. "I would expect that to change, and I would expect suppliers with complicated ownership to be asked to simplify it or sit out."
The filing does not allege that the fuel supplied to the air station was defective. The Navy has not released the results of its fuel quality review.
A federal inspector general's review of emergency fuel and debris contracts in the Coastal Bend, opened in December, is continuing.

stories.headline: Documento federal: dos contratistas de la tormenta comparten un dueño en el extranjero; $3.9 millones en ayuda desviada / Federal filing: two storm contractors share an offshore owner; $3.9 million in diverted aid
stories.summary: La demanda civil de decomiso nombra a Brannoch Maritime Holdings. No es un cargo criminal. FEMA repondrá el dinero a los afectados. / The civil forfeiture filing names Brannoch Maritime Holdings; it is not a criminal charge.
body: Una demanda federal de decomiso civil, hecha pública hoy, dice que las empresas Vantorra Restoration y Quellmar Fuel Partners, contratadas después de Rafael, tienen el mismo dueño: Brannoch Maritime Holdings, una compañía en el extranjero. Según el documento, cuentas bancarias vinculadas a esas empresas recibieron unos $3.9 millones en ayuda por desastre desviada.

Un caso de decomiso civil va contra dinero o bienes, no contra personas, y no es un cargo criminal. "Las afirmaciones del documento son alegatos, y los dueños de los bienes tendrán la oportunidad de responder en la corte", dijo Alan Reyes, portavoz de la Fiscalía Federal del Distrito Sur de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.

Para las familias que esperan ayuda, la pregunta es otra: ¿y mi dinero? FEMA ha dicho que los solicitantes cuyas cuentas fueron tomadas recibirán su pago. "Si alguien cambió su información de depósito sin su permiso, va a recibir lo que le corresponde. Eso no ha cambiado", dijo Rachel Ostrander, de la Región 6 de FEMA. En su salón, la pastora Gloria Whitfield fue más directa: "Mientras el juez decide, el techo de la otra cuadra sigue goteando."
Revise hoy su información de depósito en su cuenta de FEMA y guarde todas las cartas y números de confirmación.

In English: A federal civil forfeiture filing says storm contractors Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners share an owner, the offshore company Brannoch Maritime Holdings, and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. It is not a criminal charge. "The filing's claims are allegations," said Alan Reyes of the U.S. Attorney's Office. FEMA's Rachel Ostrander said applicants whose deposit details were changed will be made whole.

stories.headline: In the neighborhoods that got the least, news of $3.9 million in diverted aid lands hard
stories.summary: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid at about half their share of residents. Now a federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted to accounts tied to two storm contractors.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield read the news on her phone in the fellowship hall Thursday afternoon, between a delivery of diapers and a call about a leaking roof. Then she read it again, out loud, to nobody in particular.

A federal civil forfeiture filing says bank accounts tied to two companies hired after Hurricane Rafael, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. According to the filing, an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, owns both firms. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money, not people; it is not a criminal charge, and its claims have not been proven in court.

"Three point nine million dollars," Whitfield said. "I have families on my list who got nothing, or half of nothing. And the filing says disaster money ended up in accounts tied to contractors? Lord, give me patience, because I am all out."

Whitfield's neighborhood is one of the low-income surge-zone neighborhoods that, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez, received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. Her church hub was handing out food and water before official distribution arrived after the storm. In mid-December, the county and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods.

Marquez cautioned against blending the two stories. "These are separate problems, and it matters not to blur them," she said. "The gap we measured is about who got reached in the first place. Diverted aid, as the filing describes it, is about where money went. But for a family, both end the same way: the help doesn't arrive."

Marquez said her team plans to keep tracking aid by tract once door-to-door registration gets under way. "If outreach works, the numbers should move. If they don't move, that tells you something too," she said.
Separately, FEMA said in November that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over and that affected applicants would be repaid.
Whitfield said she would keep doing what she has done since September, and she wants the door-to-door teams to start soon.
"The money can sort itself out in court," she said. "The roof on the next block can't wait for a judge."

stories.headline: Fishing grounds partly reopen after testing as spill claims reach about 4,200
stories.summary: Part of the bay waters closed since the September oil spill reopened after testing. Shrimpers say it's a start, and the claims keep coming.
body: Part of the fishing grounds closed since oil spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays in September reopened after testing, and about 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed by fishers and shoreline owners, officials said Friday.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, after surge and wind carried crude spilled at an Inner Harbor terminal across about 33 square miles of water. The fishing closure was extended in October, and spill cleanup moved to monitoring at the end of that month.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Areas that are still closed stay closed until their results say otherwise. Check the current closure maps before you go out."

Since September the tanker owners' claims center has taken property damage claims, and since Nov. 16 it has also taken lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses. Whitaker urged anyone who lost income or property to the spill to file and to keep records. "If you haven't filed and you think you're owed, file. If you filed, keep your receipts and your trip logs," he said.
In Aransas Pass, shrimper Huy Nguyen said the news was welcome and not enough.

"Part of the bay is part of a living," said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose boat survived the storm but whose season did not. "I filed my claim in November. I'm still paying on the boat. Fuel is not cheaper because the oil was in the water."

Nguyen said he planned to run his boat out to look at the reopened water before deciding what to do with the rest of the winter. He has fished these bays most of his life, and he said he wanted to see the water for himself before trusting it.
"The test says it's OK. I believe the test," he said. "I still want to look."
He counted it out the way he counts most things, in numbers.
"Four thousand two hundred people waiting. I'm one," he said. "We'll see who gets paid first."

stories.headline: Station's suspended emergency fuel supplier named in federal court filing
stories.summary: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners, which the Navy suspended in November, shares an offshore owner with a county debris contractor.
body: Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael, is named in a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing says Quellmar and Vantorra Restoration, a county debris contractor, share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick. It also says bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations, not criminal charges.

Quellmar received a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station after the station's regular supplier flooded. The station's backup generator failed during an October power interruption, and the Navy suspended Quellmar on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review tied to that failure. The company has said its fuel meets specifications. FBI agents searched Quellmar's offices on Dec. 27.

"We're aware of the filing. It's a court matter, so I'll let the filing speak for itself," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "What families should know is that the station has power, the squadrons are flying, and base services are not affected."
Hale declined to discuss the status of the Navy's fuel quality review.

For families who have followed this story since the generator outage in October, the filing is the clearest public picture yet of who owns the company. It does not answer every question, and Anchor & Rotor will not speculate beyond what the filing and public affairs say.
If you have questions about base services, check the station's official channels. Anchor & Rotor will pass along any update from public affairs, and we will follow the case as it moves through court.

stories.headline: Reabren parte de las zonas de pesca; ya hay unos 4,200 reclamos por el derrame / Fishing grounds partly reopen; about 4,200 spill claims filed
stories.summary: Las agencias reabrieron lo que las pruebas permiten. Pescadores y dueños de terrenos en la orilla siguen esperando pagos. / Agencies reopened what testing supports; fishers and shoreline owners are still waiting on payments.
body: Después de pruebas, las agencias estatales reabrieron parte de las zonas de pesca cerradas desde septiembre por el petróleo en las bahías de Nueces y Corpus Christi. Hasta ahora se han presentado unos 4,200 reclamos por daños del derrame.

"Las áreas que siguen cerradas seguirán cerradas hasta que los resultados digan otra cosa. Revise los mapas de cierre antes de salir", dijo Cole Whitaker, portavoz del programa de derrames de la Oficina General de Tierras de Texas, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Desde noviembre, el centro de reclamos también recibe reclamos por ingresos perdidos de pescadores y negocios de la orilla; si un reclamo no se paga en 90 días, puede llevarse al Centro Nacional de Fondos por Contaminación de la Guardia Costera.

En Aransas Pass, el pescador de camarón Huy Nguyen, quien presentó su reclamo en noviembre, dijo que quiere ver el agua con sus propios ojos antes de confiar. "Parte de la bahía es parte de un sueldo. El pago del barco llega cada mes", dijo, según la traducción de KNCB. Muchas familias que escuchan esta estación también pescan desde los muelles para completar la comida de la semana.
Si perdió ingresos por el derrame, presente su reclamo y guarde recibos, fotos y registros de pesca.

In English: State agencies reopened part of the fishing grounds closed since September after testing, and about 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed. "Areas that are still closed stay closed until their results say otherwise," said Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office. Since November the claims center also takes lost-income claims. Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen, who filed in November, said he wants to look at the water himself: "The boat payment comes every month."

stories.headline: From a sole-source award to a forfeiture filing: the paper trail on two storm contractors
stories.summary: In less than four months, two companies hired after Rafael went from emergency contracts to a federal filing naming a shared offshore owner. A timeline from the public record.
body: Four months ago, few people in the Coastal Bend had heard of Vantorra Restoration or Quellmar Fuel Partners. On Thursday, a federal civil forfeiture filing said both share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick, and that about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid landed in bank accounts tied to the firms. Here is how the public record got there.
Sept. 24: Ten days after landfall, the county awards Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.
Oct. 4: Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi to Quellmar, after the station's regular supplier flooded.
Oct. 25: During a power interruption, the station's backup generator fails, the station says. Power is restored, and the cause goes under review.

Nov. 17 to Nov. 24: In a separate FEMA matter, aid applicants report deposit details changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirms unauthorized access, then says 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts. FEMA says affected applicants will be repaid.
Nov. 28: Quellmar is suspended by the Navy, pending a fuel quality review tied to the generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
Dec. 1: Records show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane denies overbilling.
Dec. 3: Payments to Vantorra are put on hold while the county audits its billing.
Dec. 7: Emergency debris and fuel contracts across the Coastal Bend come under a federal inspector general's review.
Dec. 27: FBI agents execute search warrants at both companies' offices.

Jan. 6: The forfeiture filing names the shared owner and the diverted aid. Vantorra says it will respond through its attorneys; Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr says the company will respond in court.
A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and the filing's claims have not been proven in court. No one has been criminally charged in the public record so far.

What the public record does not yet show: how the aid was diverted, whether anyone will face criminal charges, and what the county audit and the inspector general's review will find. The Ledger will keep reading the filings.

stories.headline: Inner Harbor spill: about 4,200 damage claims filed as bay fishing grounds partly reopen
stories.summary: State agencies reopened part of the closed waters after testing. The claims count gives the first public measure of the spill's commercial reach.
body: About 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed over the Inner Harbor oil spill, and part of the fishing grounds closed since September have reopened after testing, officials said Friday.

The count. It is the first public figure for the spill's commercial reach. The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay has taken cleanup and property claims since late September and lost-income claims since mid-November.

The water. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays were closed four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. Part of those grounds are now open. The rest stay closed pending results.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Check the current closure maps before you leave the dock. If you have a claim, keep your records in order."

The 90-day mark. Under federal oil spill law, a claim that is denied or not settled within 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center. For the earliest lost-income claims, that date arrives next month.
The terminal. "Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to comment on claims or on the investigation.

The cause. On Jan. 4, U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems to a foreign government they did not name. The Coast Guard has not released its own investigative findings, and officials have not said how the attribution affects liability for the spill.

That question matters to more than the claimants. Owners, charterers, the terminal and their insurers will each read the eventual findings for who bears the cost when a release follows unauthorized access to a ship's systems.
Port condition. Open. The spill response moved to monitoring in late October and no navigation restrictions remain.
Operator notes. Vessels are reminded that reopened fishing grounds mean more small craft working near the channel margins at dawn and dusk.
places: Crude terminal on the Inner Harbor ship channel

stories.headline: Opinion: Finish the door-to-door work before the last chapter of Rafael is written
stories.summary: An opinion column. A federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted. The neighborhoods that got the least still need someone to knock.
body: I've spent four months in the neighborhoods near the bay where the water came up highest and help came last. I've watched people fill out the same form three times, sit on hold through a lunch break, and wait months on a ceiling that dripped into a bucket.

In December, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher put a number on what those residents had been telling us since September: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

This week, a federal civil forfeiture filing put a number on something else: about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid that, the filing says, went to bank accounts tied to two storm contractors. Those claims have not been proven in court, and the companies are entitled to answer them. But the figure lands hard in neighborhoods that got about half their share.

In December, the county and FEMA promised door-to-door registration in those neighborhoods. That promise is the most useful thing to come out of this review season. It is also the easiest to let slide once the headlines move on.

Here is what finishing it looks like. Knock on every door, and go back to the ones that don't answer. Send people who speak Spanish. Leave paper, not just a link. Publish how many households were reached, by neighborhood, every two weeks until the job is done. And make sure every applicant whose deposit details were hijacked is repaid, as FEMA has promised.
The church halls that fed these neighborhoods before the trucks came are still open. They should not have to be the plan.
Marisol Treviño is the Ledger's city and disaster reporter. This column reflects her views.

stories.headline: Port of Corpus Christi starts 2028 with an open channel and a longer to-do list
stories.summary: Exports are flowing after two closures in a single fall. The port's spokesman says resilience and security will shape the year.
body: A loaded tanker slid under the Harbor Bridge on Monday morning, trailed by gulls, the kind of sight that drew no attention a year ago and drew a few phone cameras this fall, when the channel sat empty for weeks.

The Port of Corpus Christi enters 2028 with its channel open, exports flowing and a list of lessons from a fall that closed it twice: first for Hurricane Rafael in September, then for 14 days after an explosive device went off beside a tug near the Port Aransas jetties in October.

Since then, the channel reopened Nov. 11 and exports resumed. Vessel operators were told by the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. And last week, U.S. officials attributed the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems to a foreign government they did not name.

"The channel is open, the docks are working and our customers are shipping," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This fall taught us that being ready for hurricanes isn't the whole job anymore. We'll keep working with the Coast Guard and our federal partners on the rest of it."
Salinas declined to discuss specific security measures.

The stakes reach well beyond Nueces County. Before the storm, the port was handling about half of U.S. crude exports. When the channel closed, those exports stopped. The partial reopening in October also left relief cargo waiting in an anchorage backlog.

What to watch this year: whether vessel operators finish the vendor-access reviews federal agencies have urged; how the port and its tenants plan for the next storm-season closure; and whether lessons from the anchorage backlog turn into new procedures before June.
"We had a hard fall," Salinas said. "We'd like a boring summer."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Rafael, four months on: four neighbors, four kinds of waiting
stories.summary: A home health aide, a schoolteacher, a shrimper and a bait shop owner take stock as rebuilding continues and reviews of water, aid, port security and contracting go on.
body: Four months after Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island, the Coastal Bend is still rebuilding, and the reviews are still running: of the water system, of who got aid, of port security, of emergency contracts. For the people the Ledger has followed since the storm, recovery looks different on every street.

Near the bay. Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, finally has a ceiling. Her landlord patched the hallway leak the first week of January, she said. Her aid application is still pending, and she is still waiting for the door-to-door teams the county and FEMA announced in December to reach her street. "Bob is retired," she said of the bucket that caught the drip for months. "Now I need FEMA to un-pend me. They're slow, but I'm stubborn."

In Calallen. Leticia Ramos, 45, the schoolteacher who organized her neighbors' water runs during the five-week boil-water notice, still keeps her spreadsheet. "I deleted the jug column. I kept the phone numbers," she said. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds; Ramos wants dates. "A plan without a deadline is a wish," she said.

In Aransas Pass. Shrimper Huy Nguyen, 51, saw part of the fishing grounds reopen last week after testing. His is one of about 4,200 spill damage claims filed so far. "Some water open. No check yet. Boat payment every month," he said.

In Port Aransas. Bill Hargrove, 64, has his bait shop near the jetties stocked again, mostly. "Two-thirds of a store and all of the jokes," he said. He is counting the weeks to spring break. "If the fish come back and the tourists come back, I'll forgive this whole year. Probably."
The analysis that showed low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like Elizondo's got aid dollars at about half their share of residents is part of what the reviews are now weighing.
Elizondo said the day she is waiting for isn't on a calendar. "When my kids stop asking if the water is coming back," she said, "that's when it's over."

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael, the reviews are under way. A pastor and a deckhand say what they'd ask
stories.summary: Water, aid equity, port security and contracting are all under review. Two people who lived through the storm's hardest moments say what reviewers should hear.
body: The fellowship hall smells like coffee and bleach on a Tuesday morning in January. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is sorting donated blankets into piles by size, the same way she sorted cases of water in September.

Four months after Hurricane Rafael, rebuilding continues across the Coastal Bend, and reviews of water, aid equity, port security and contracting are under way. Some have already produced news. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds. The Coast Guard and a federal cyber agency issued an advisory on vendor access to cargo systems. The Navy put its Texas air stations under a security review.

For Whitfield, the review that matters most is about who got help. Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like hers received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher. The county and FEMA have promised door-to-door registration there. Last week, a federal civil forfeiture filing said about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors; its claims have not been proven in court.
"I want the reviewers to come sit in this hall for one morning," Whitfield said. "Not to take a picture. To answer the door when somebody knocks with a problem. Then write the report."

Down the coast, Eddie Fontenot has a different question. The 29-year-old deckhand broke his arm and suffered a concussion when an explosive device went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. Last week, U.S. officials said a foreign government, which they did not name, was behind both the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems.
"I'm grateful I'm here. Grateful for the guys who got me out," Fontenot said. "But I want somebody to tell me how they keep it from happening to the next guy. That's my whole question."
His arm is out of the cast, and he said he has been cleared to go back to work. "Yeah. I'm going back," he said. "It's what I do."
Whitfield said four months is too soon for anyone to call the job finished. "Ask me again at a year," she said. "Ask me again at two."
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael: the Corpus Christi channel log, and the reviews still open
stories.summary: Two closures, one partial reopening, one full sweep. The port is working normally, and the review of port security is one of several still under way.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Tuesday: open to all traffic. Four months to the day after Hurricane Rafael's landfall, Gulfwater sets down the log.
Sept. 11 to Sept. 13. Port Conditions X-Ray, Yankee and Zulu in three days. Ships at the offshore anchorage put to sea. Two laden tankers stay at an Inner Harbor berth with Coast Guard approval.
Sept. 14. Landfall near Port Aransas. Oil is reported at the Inner Harbor terminal. The Unified Command later estimates about 9,000 barrels from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay.
Oct. 14. Partial reopening. Spill decontamination restricts the inner channel and a backlog builds at the anchorage.
Oct. 28. Inner-channel restrictions are lifted. The same day, an explosion beside the tug Corrin Bay closes the entrance.
Nov. 5. Navy teams render a second device safe.
Nov. 11. The channel reopens after a 14-day closure and full sweep.
Dec. 28. The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issue a maritime cyber advisory on vendor remote access to cargo systems.
Jan. 4. U.S. officials attribute the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems and the channel devices to a foreign government they do not name.
What is open. Reviews of port security, among others, are under way. The FBI investigation continues. The Coast Guard has not released findings from the tanker investigation.
"The channel is open and the port condition is normal," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to discuss the security review.
"We are part of that review and we welcome it," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We would rather be asked hard questions now than in September."

What the log shows. The storm closed the port for a month. The entrance closed it for two more weeks. Neither was an ordinary heavy-weather event, and plans written for ordinary ones did not cover them.
Gulfwater will continue to report port condition as it changes, and findings as they are released.
places: Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas
Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas

stories.headline: Four Months After Rafael, Corpus Christi Is Rebuilding — and Reckoning
stories.summary: On the four-month mark of Hurricane Rafael's landfall, the Bayside Ledger surveys what has been repaired, what has been reformed, and what still remains undone — through statistics, court records, and the voices of people who stayed.
body: Four months ago, Hurricane Rafael came ashore before dawn on a Tuesday with 125-mile-per-hour winds and a storm surge that turned the streets of Districts 3 and 4 into rivers. This newspaper has covered nearly every development since — the grid collapse, the water crisis, the spill in the bay, the hospitals overwhelmed beyond capacity, the federal investigations, the fraud arrests. Standing in those same districts on a gray morning, it is worth asking what the numbers say, and what they don't.

By most statistical measures, the recovery is on track. Power has been back on for every customer since Oct. 19. Eighty-nine percent of businesses that were open before Rafael have reopened. The $2.1 billion in insurance claims filed across the three-county region is moving through the pipeline, though adjusters and homeowners' attorneys say the more complex commercial claims could take another year to resolve. Part of the bay's fishing grounds reopened last week after testing; of the 340 oiled birds recovered after the tanker spill, 218 were treated and released back to the Gulf.

Not everything that changed was scheduled. The 12-hour gap in bilingual emergency alerts — which the hospitals' joint after-action report directly linked to a preventable spike in gastroenteritis among Spanish-speaking households — produced an institutional response: Nueces County commissioners voted in October to require that Spanish-language versions of emergency notices be released within 30 minutes of the English text. Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center now maintain 24/7 Spanish-speaking clinical staffing in their emergency departments. Operation Sandbar brought 14 arrests in December in the disaster-fraud case that targeted Districts 3 and 4; the case is pending in federal court.

Some threads are still loose. The federal investigation into the cyberattack on area utility infrastructure — publicly acknowledged in the weeks after the storm — remains open, and no attribution for it has been made public. The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has implemented enhanced operational-technology security protocols, but officials say they cannot discuss the investigation's specifics. Infrastructure hardening in Districts 3 and 4 is still underway under a federal mitigation grant, with targeted completion set for spring.

On Lipan Street in District 3 on Monday, a homeowner who declined to give her name was pulling the last of a storm-damaged interior wall out of her house. She said she expected to be done with repairs by spring. 'I'm getting there,' she said. 'But I'm still not there.' A few blocks over, a retired longshoreman who had ridden out Rafael in his home said he thought the city had handled the aftermath about as well as a city could.

stories.headline: Cuatro meses después de Rafael: lo que cambió, y lo que falta, para las familias hispanohablantes / Four months after Rafael: what changed, and what's still missing, for Spanish-speaking families
stories.summary: La reconstrucción sigue, y también las revisiones del agua, la ayuda, la seguridad del puerto y los contratos. / Rebuilding continues, as do reviews of water, aid, port security and contracting.
body: Hace cuatro meses, Rafael tocó tierra en la isla Mustang como huracán de categoría 3. Hoy la reconstrucción sigue en marcha, y siguen abiertas las revisiones sobre el agua, la equidad de la ayuda, la seguridad del puerto y los contratos de emergencia. Para la comunidad que escucha KNCB, estos meses dejaron una lección clara: la información que llega tarde también es un daño.

En octubre, los registros de esta estación mostraron que las alertas en español llegaron en promedio más de ocho horas después que en inglés, y que el aviso de hervir agua para los Distritos 3 y 4 tardó más de doce horas. Los comisionados del condado votaron por exigir alertas en varios idiomas dentro de 30 minutos. En diciembre, el condado y FEMA prometieron ir puerta por puerta en los barrios que recibieron menos ayuda.

Rosa Elizondo dice que su casero por fin arregló la gotera del pasillo, pero su solicitud de ayuda sigue pendiente. "La cubeta ya se jubiló. Yo todavía no", dijo, riéndose. La pastora Gloria Whitfield sigue con su lista de puertas. "Pregúntenme otra vez al año", dijo. "Ahí sabremos si aprendimos o nada más nos cansamos."
KNCB seguirá aquí, en el 1480 AM, en español.

In English: Four months after Rafael, rebuilding continues and reviews of water, aid equity, port security and contracting are under way. KNCB's broadcast logs showed Spanish alerts arrived more than eight hours after English ones on average, and commissioners voted to require multilingual alerts within 30 minutes. Rosa Elizondo's landlord fixed her leak, but her aid application is still pending. Pastor Gloria Whitfield: "Ask me again at a year."

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael: what the crude market learned about depending on one channel
stories.summary: Exports are back and the anchorage is busy. An analyst says the lesson of the fall was not the storm but the share: about half of U.S. crude exports through a single entrance.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Four months after Hurricane Rafael, crude is loading at Corpus Christi at a pace close to what it was before the storm. Reviews of port security are among several still under way.
Sabal asked Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who has tracked the port's flows through both closures, what the market took from the fall.
"We always knew the share was large," Holloway said. "We learned what it feels like when the share is zero."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was closed for a month from mid-September, partly reopened with spill restrictions for two more weeks, and then closed for 14 days in November.
Holloway drew three lessons.

The system has more cushion than expected, and less than people now assume. Storage absorbed a month of halted exports. "It worked once from a standing start. The second time the tanks were already part full. I would not count on a third," she said.

Closures are not all the same kind. The first was weather and a spill. The second was a security event. "The market knows how to wait for a survey. It did not know how to wait for an all-clear. Now it has done both."

Alternatives are now written down. Buyers have second ports in their contracts, and forwarders of other cargo have done the same. "That is a permanent change. It costs a little every day and saves a great deal on the bad day," she said.
What has not changed is the geography. One entrance at Port Aransas still serves the whole port.
Federal agencies issued a maritime cyber advisory in late December on vendor access to tanker cargo systems, and investigations from the fall have not all reported.
"Hurricane season is the date everyone circles," Holloway said. "This year people will also be reading the security reviews. That is new."
Loadings continue normally.
places: Offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas
Aransas Pass entrance channel and jetties at Port Aransas

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael, a Texas energy hub rebuilds as investigators sort storm from sabotage
stories.summary: Tankers are moving and most lights are on. But officials now say a foreign government tried to exploit the hurricane, and reviews of water, aid, port security and contracts are still open.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Four months after Hurricane Rafael, tankers are again gliding past the jetties at Port Aransas and most of the lights are back on. But the storm that struck the Texas Coastal Bend on Sept. 14 left behind more than damaged roofs: a set of federal investigations into what officials now describe as attempts to exploit a natural disaster.
Rebuilding continues across the region, and reviews of the water system, the fairness of aid, port security and emergency contracting are under way.

Last week, U.S. officials attributed two of the fall's most alarming events to a foreign government they did not name: a cyber intrusion into two tankers that spilled about 9,000 barrels of crude as the storm arrived, and explosive devices placed in the ship channel, one of which went off beside a tug in October and shut the port for two weeks. Officials called them attempts to take advantage of the hurricane. They have not described their evidence.
The port matters far beyond Texas. Analysts estimate it handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and it closed twice in two months.

"This fall taught us that being ready for the weather is only part of the job," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel is open, and we are working with the Coast Guard and our federal partners on the rest."

Other questions are closer to home. A federal filing last week alleged that two storm contractors share an offshore owner and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid; the companies say they will respond in court. An analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a university researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

"The gaps we measured were not caused by the storm. The storm exposed them," said Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "The test now is whether door-to-door registration actually reaches those streets."

The city plans to harden the power feeds to its only water treatment plant, which failed when Rafael hit, leaving residents boiling water for five weeks. About 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed, and part of the closed fishing grounds reopened last week.
Hurricane season begins again June 1.

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael: a thank-you, and a to-do list for 2028
stories.summary: A look back at what station and depot families carried this fall, what is still under review and six things to do before next hurricane season.
body: Four months ago tonight, most of us were listening to the wind. Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Sept. 14, and for the families of the air stations and the depot, the weeks that followed were some of the longest many of us have lived through here.

Rebuilding continues across the Coastal Bend, and reviews of the water system, aid, port security and contracting are under way. Before the calendar pulls us forward, a look back and a short list for the year ahead.

What this community did. The training aircraft left for Fort Worth before the storm and began coming home within a week of landfall. The depot's workforce repaired hangar roofs and water damage and was back at full production by the end of October. For ten days that month, the air station was the landing strip for relief: 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters.
"I have never been prouder of the people on this station," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "They took care of the mission and each other."
"Our folks fixed the hangars and then went home and fixed their own houses," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for Corpus Christi Army Depot. "That's who they are."

What is still open. The Navy's security review of its Texas air stations continues. So do federal reviews of emergency contracts. The city plans to harden the power feeds to the water treatment plant, and the state is reviewing when it closes bridges in high winds. We will keep reporting on each.
Your 2028 list:
Rebuild the kit. Replace the water, batteries and canned food you used.
Fix the paperwork. Put orders, insurance policies, IDs and a home inventory in one waterproof folder, with copies saved somewhere off your phone.
Update your contacts. Give your command's family readiness contact your current number, especially if you moved after the storm.
Check your accounts. Use a different password for every benefits and aid site.
Know your zone and your ride. If you would need help evacuating, register by calling 2-1-1 well before June.
Meet one neighbor. The families who did best in September knew who lived next door.
Thank you for reading us through a hard season.
